Private Notes on the Meaning of the Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra, Volume One.
Composed by the monk Mingkong of Fayun Temple in Weiyang.
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-yi-shu*.
[Commentary] This is a private collection by the King of Jōgū in the Great Wa (Japan) and is not the original text from across the sea.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding this sutra, there have been two translations; one is called the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and it is also called the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-upāya-sūtra*.
This was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty. The annotation states:
The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-vaipulya-sūtra* was translated at the capital of Yangdu by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty;

it is recorded in the *Kanding lu*. The commentary explained herein is that of Wang of the Shanggong Palace, which is the later translation of the sūtra consisting of twenty-one sheets. This commentary dates to the seventh year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty.

The Japanese monk-envoys Gaimyō, Tokkai, and seven others—eight persons in total—brought four fascicles of a commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to Yangzhou to present to the Great Vinaya Ācārya Lingyou of Longxing Temple.
His Royal Highness, the Prince of Shanggong, is the maternal uncle of Zhao Hong, the Commander-in-Chief of Annan.
It is traditionally said that [Lingyou] was a dharma-descendant of the eminent monk Sita (Bodhidharma’s successor) of Mount Nanyue during the Liang dynasty.

The Master’s successor, Zen Master Xian, first fashioned a precious casket for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras inscribed with golden characters and placed them within the Grotto of Prajñā.

No one knew of this. When King Shangong, acting as the king, dispatched five envoys to retrieve the golden sūtra caskets from Mount Yue, they arrived at the specific time and place to collect the golden sūtras and install them upon the stone.

The *Kū* (Cave) [Commentary] currently exists. Regarding the note stating "not the *Hai* (Sea) version," this may refer either to the sub-commentary by the author of the *Shu* (Exegesis) himself or to the notes of another person;
both interpretations are acceptable. This refers to this country [China] and the kingdom of Silla, while Japan is referred to as one of these two lands, both being designated as "the other" (*pi*).
This is because the kingdom of Silla possesses the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* commentary by Dharma Master Xiao.
In this land as well, there was once a commentary on this sutra consisting of one fascicle and over ten sheets of paper;
since its author’s name was not recorded in order to distinguish it from the commentaries of those two lands, it was said to be "not the version by Huihai."
The Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra on the Great Expedient Means of the One Vehicle, translated by Guṇabhadra.

[Commentary] The commentary is divided into two main sections: first, a brief explanation of the title of the sūtra; second, an entry into the body of the text. Regarding the first section, it is further divided...
Third, first explaining the specific name, which is *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda*; next, explaining the general name, which refers to the word "sūtra";
third, concluding with the different ways the names are derived. The initial section is divided into five parts: first, distinguishing the original and manifested aspects of Śrīmālā;

second, clarifying what she has taught; third, explaining the meaning of the name Śrīmālā; fourth, explaining the term "lion’s roar"; and fifth, a general summary. First, the explanation of the original aspect.

Regarding the "traces" (*ji*), there are again two aspects: first, the fundamental (*ben*) and the trace (*ji*). Generally speaking, "fundamental" refers to the *dharmakāya*, while "trace" refers to the manifested traces (*yìngjì*).
Because the principle of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas serves as the basis for being able to give rise to ten kinds of manifested traces, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"One should preach the Dharma using a Buddha-body," and so forth, including the passage concerning Śakra and others.
Although there are thirty-three bodies—namely, those of the six realms and the four classes of noble beings—the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* also says: "According to their respective kinds of sounds, his great voice universally proclaims [the teaching].

Since this is so for the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*), it is likewise the case for the wheel of mind (*cittacakra*) in discerning capacities and the wheel of body (*kāyacakra*) in manifesting responses.
Thus, regarding the original source within this [text]:

[The Commentary] states that since Queen Śrīmālā herself was originally inconceivable, how could one know whether she was a transformation-body of the Tathāgata or a Great Being of the Dharma-cloud stage?
[Commentary] "Inconceivable" means that its levels—high or low—are difficult to fathom; it cannot be reached by the mind or expressed through speech and deliberation.
As for the "Dharma-Cloud Great Being," this refers to a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fascicle 39, in its explanation of the ten stages, says:
"O Son of the Buddha, at this stage, the Bodhisattva, by the power of his own vows, gives rise to great compassion."
The great Dharma-thunder resounds from the clouds, with penetrating wisdom and fearlessness as its lightning,
and merit and wisdom as its dense rain-clouds. Manifesting various bodies, they travel back and forth within a single thought-moment,
pervading hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds as numerous as the atoms of dust, expounding the Great Dharma in accordance with all sentient beings.
That which the mind delights in pours down the rain of nectar, extinguishing all the dust and flames of delusion; for this reason, this stage is named "Dharma-Cloud" (*dharmameghā*).
The scriptural text is extremely extensive, yet its essential meaning regarding the "trace" and "origin" is sufficient.

As for the term "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*), Master An states that it is called "Opening Being" (*kaishi*) because the mind first opens; he also says it is called "Initial Being" (*shishi*) because it is the very beginning of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
This name was first given to him; its full form in the Western language (Sanskrit) should be *bodhisattva*.
Master Shi [Kumārajīva], fearing prolixity, omitted the two characters *ti* and *duo*, calling him simply "Bodhisattva. Translations vary, so here I provide one interpretation:
*bodhi* means "unsurpassed path," and *sattva* means "great mind. Thus, it refers to a person who possesses the unsurpassed path and the great mind.

One is called a Bodhisattva because they resolve their mind to seek the Unsurpassed Way for the sake of sentient beings; there are various interpretations of this, and for now, one explanation shall be retained.
Next, the Trace [of the Buddha]. [Commentary]:
It was simply to illuminate afar the capacities and needs of the people of Yuga that he used the substance of a woman as a means of transformation; therefore, at the beginning, he manifested birth.
In Śrāvastī, she perfected the way of filial devotion toward her king; among the people of Ayodhyā, she was known as Lady Youcheng and manifested the propriety of the three obediences;
in the end, like a shadow following a form, she accompanied Śākyamuni to jointly propagate the Mahāyāna path.

[Commentary] "Only [the Buddha] illuminates from afar the capacities of those in Odra," etc., clarifies that the Trace Dharmakāya (jishin) perceives from a distance; thus it is said he "illuminates from afar.

This means that while the Bodhisattva was on the stage of the Dharmakāya, he perceived from afar that the people of the single country of Odra possessed the capacity for the Mahāyāna, and that they should be converted by means of a female form as a skillful means. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Those who should be saved by means of a female body..."
He immediately manifested in the form of a woman and preached the Dharma for her. Thus, at the beginning he was born in a lower state to demonstrate the aspect of manifesting traces;

this briefly shows the characteristics across three stages: the beginning, the middle, and the end. The character "Wang" (王) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), meaning "to arise" or "the beginning.
It signifies that, at the outset, he first gave rise to the way of filial support. "Mahāyāna" refers to the One Vehicle. Below...
The scriptural text explains this itself. II. Clarifying what is taught:
[Commentary] As for the essence of what is expounded, it takes fourteen items as its substance; regarding its general meaning, its principle is that what is not proximate is far-reaching.
Therefore, whenever the Tathāgata speaks, he praises and accords with all Buddhas, and his every utterance serves to complete the teaching.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the fourteen [chapters] constitute the essence": the fourteen chapters form the body of the main exposition.
Within each chapter, the immediate perspectives of the former followers of the Two Vehicles are contrasted with the ultimate principles of the present sutra;
this intent is consistently employed as the core tenet. For example, take the first chapter, which praises the Tathāgata’s true merits.
Furthermore, in the Chapter on Śrīmālā, it is stated that because she received a letter sent by her parents, she first heard of the eternal and profound principle as her refuge.
Is this not different from her former refuge in the impermanent and proximate? Is it not incorrect?

In the twentieth chapter, the "Chapter on the Great Receptions," since the refuge is already different from before, the precepts should also be modified from what was formerly held; therefore, one now receives the ten [precepts].

The precepts received differ from those of the five precepts of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) of former times. Third, in the Chapter on the Three Great Vows, since taking refuge and receiving the precepts differs from the past, the vows are likewise further developed as superior vows, looking far toward the eternally abiding Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is distinct from the former aspiration for the extinction of the body and the cessation of wisdom.
Fourth, in the Chapter on Upholding the True Dharma, [the stages] up to the seventh ground have already been discussed.
Returning to the two vehicles and their practices involving effort—this is considered "near.

From the eighth stage upward, the single thought-moment establishing the three modes of activity, the construction of the true and response bodies, and the production of the five fruits—this is considered "far.
Chapter Five: The One Vehicle. All previous distinctions regarding the three jewels of specific characteristics and the five vehicles were merely expedient means.
Approaching today’s assembly, [the teaching] takes the convergence of the five vehicles into the one vehicle as the cause and the single essence of the Triple Gem as the fruit;
this is the "distant" [teaching]. Chapter Six, on the Boundless Noble Truths: both types of noble truth are conditions for cultivating goodness.
Yet the followers of the two vehicles contemplate only one type of noble truth, whereas the Tathāgata has fully realized them both; this is the "near" [teaching].
The seventh chapter, "The Tathāgatagarbha," is for the purpose of praising the profound depth of the Eight Truths;
it states that because the Tathāgata preaches the Eight Noble Truths based upon the profoundness of the Tathāgatagarbha, how could the Eight Truths not be profound?
Thus, two kinds of Noble Truths are established, which exist only in the Tathāgata and not among the Two Vehicles. The eighth chapter, "The Dharmakāya," merely clarifies [the state of] concealment.
The Tathāgatagarbha is manifest as the Dharmakāya; though their manifestations differ, they are one and the same essence, with no separate entity.
Ninth, the meaning of emptiness: the chapter on "Concealment" clarifies the empty Tathāgatagarbha and the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.

Illuminating these two garbhas constitutes the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness. This wisdom is originally and eternally present, yet in the past it was obscured by impermanence and other such conditions.

The meaning of emptiness is that which conceals and covers. In the eleventh chapter on the Truths, it is about to be clarified that, among the seven truths, one must rely upon the ultimate by eliminating all else and selecting only the single truth of cessation through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-nirodha-satya*) as the ultimate.

Therefore, this truth is not an object of perception for the mental consciousness of ordinary beings, nor is it the domain of the wisdom of the two vehicles; it is like a seven-day-old infant who cannot see.
Chapter Eleven: The Sole Reliance on the Solar Orb. This clarifies that this single Truth of Cessation is the ultimate reliance for all beings;
therefore, it is not the domain of the Two Vehicles. Chapter Twelve: The Reality Beyond Inversion. This clarifies that non-constructive cessation is itself the Tathāgatagarbha.
Life and death are the spiritual luminosity that relies upon the Tathāgatagarbha; as it continues in succession, it is never extinguished.

Chapter Thirteen, "The Innate Purity of Self-Nature," clarifies that although the *tathāgatagarbha* is innately pure, even while within the midst of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is not defiled by birth and death; it is merely obscured.
Chapter Fourteen, "The True Sons of the Tathāgata," clarifies the bodhisattvas of the three levels of patience (*kṣānti*).
"Traversing by means of this vehicle" refers to that which the practitioners of the two vehicles and ordinary beings are unable to traverse.

Therefore, whenever the Tathāgata speaks—as in the case of the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*—the Tathāgata immediately expresses his approval and concurrence with all Buddhas. Thus, the subsequent passage states:
"That which is spoken regarding the upholding of the true Dharma has already been [spoken] by all Buddhas of the past, present, and future."
Regarding what has been said, what is being said, and what shall be said, I have now attained unsurpassed bodhi and likewise constantly proclaim this upholding of the true Dharma;
to speak these words is to provide exposition and confirmation. As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha praised Vaśitā, saying, 'Excellent, excellent!
Your wisdom and skillful means are profoundly deep and subtle. You have long planted various roots of goodness, and for the sake of sentient beings in the world, you have come forth.'"
Only those who have long cultivated roots of goodness can understand what you have said. ○ Third, the explanation of the meaning of the name Śrīmālā.
[Commentary]: As for Śrīmālā, the world adorns her physical body with the seven treasures, whereas she now adorns her Dharma-body with the myriad practices;
therefore, she is called Śrīmālā.
[Commentary] Regarding "Śrīmālā" (勝鬘), the explanation of its name and meaning below is clear to see. As for the "seven treasures": first, gold; second, silver;
third, lapis lazuli; fourth, musāragalva; fifth, agate; sixth, coral; seventh, pearl garlands (*mālā*).

"Flower-bush ornamentation" (*huá róng shì*): *róng* means like a cluster of grass growing thickly. This signifies that the myriad practices adorn the Dharma-body, surpassing those of the mundane world.
It is because of adornment. In the first five chapters, the distinction between self and other does not transcend the One Vehicle;
this means that the myriad practices adorn the realms of the eight chapters, such as the Tathāgatagarbha, causing them to manifest.
Thus, the general title summarizes the essential meaning of the entire work almost exhaustively. ○ Fourth, the explanation of the Lion’s Roar.

[Commentary] "Lion’s Roar" (siṃhanāda) means to proclaim the great principle oneself without any fear; its meaning is identical to that of a lion who does not fear other beasts, hence it is called the "Lion’s Roar.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the "Lion’s Roar" below, there are four explanations of the meaning of the Lion’s Roar. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 25, states: "The lion..."
The "Roar" refers to the definitive teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and immutable.
Therefore, the fourteen chapters expounded by Śrīmālā are none other than the proclamation of the eternally abiding, self-nature pure [Buddha-nature] before the Buddha;
they elucidate the meaning of fearlessness and are identical in principle to the definitive teachings of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. ○
The fifth section is the summary title.
[Commentary]: The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* receives its name from its essential substance; "Lion’s Roar" is used as a metaphor for its title.
"The Great Skillful Means of the One Vehicle and the Vaipulya" refers to the Dharma it expounds.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Great Expedient Means of the One Vehicle" and so forth: these three names do not transcend the provisional and real teachings of the One Vehicle;
the *Śāstra* text merely lists them in general. Here, I shall briefly explain these three names so that their essential purport may be roughly understood.
As for the term "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*): the designation "vehicle" (*yāna*) arises from the sense of conveying or transporting; in this present sutra, it refers to the myriad virtues and so forth.

The "flow" (stream) is that which is capable of conveying, while the "Three Jewels of the One Body" is that which is conveyed. Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "The three vehicles are the one vehicle;

those who attain the one vehicle attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The following text provides an extensive explanation, but for now, I shall briefly clarify the principle of the non-duality of cause and effect, and of the provisional and the real. Thus, each and every one is designated as a "vehicle" (yāna) because it is without duality.

This "carrying forth" (yun-chu) constitutes the meaning of the cause; although the categories of wholesome factors (*kuśala-pakṣa*) differ within this context, they are said to be "one" because their underlying principle is identical.
"Great skillful means" (*mahopāya*) refers to expedient skill, methodology, and practical application. It is the skillful employment of all dharmas to bring sentient beings into accord.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "The Tathāgata preaches through skillful means according to what each being desires."

Furthermore, "Vaipulya" (fangguǎng) refers to the true principle. It is called "fang" (square/correct) because it is truly without falsehood; it is called "guǎng" (vast) because its endowed virtues are boundless.

Just as worldly objects that are square are neither crooked nor biased, so too is this sublime purport empty and harmonious, its meaning being without partiality or fixed limitation. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The self-nature pure Tathāgatagarbha is the Dharmakāya-garbha, the four pāramitās of permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
Although conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) are not false dharmas, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is therefore the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
One should know that these three dharmas are of one essence; the three names are established based on their respective meanings.

Furthermore, when divided according to the principles of persons and dharmas, in reality, the person is itself the dharma. Why? Because Śrīmālā is named after her myriad virtues, while Siṃhanāda is named after a metaphor.

Because it is taught that the manifestation of all virtues is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and that fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), one should know that persons and dharmas are not different. Therefore, the subsequent scriptural text states: "The Tathāgata is no different;
the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is no different; the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body. 2. Explanation of the General Name.

[Commentary: "Sūtra" is glossed as "dharma" (teaching) and "nitya" (constant). Although the teachings of the Sage may shift with the times and adapt to changing customs, they cannot alter what is right and wrong; therefore, it is called "constant. Furthermore, because it serves as a standard for all beings, it is termed "dharma. This is the terminology used in China; in foreign lands [India], it is called *sūtra*. The five meanings of *sūtra* are also explained as before. *Sū* means "to sew," and *tra* means "to protect. Just as one sews together a garment, so too does this teaching sew together the various dharmas. It is also like a rope (*sūtra*) that protects one from falling into a pit. Thus, it is called *sūtra*. Regarding the term "scripture" (*jing*), "jing" means "to purify"; it refers to the purification of the mind and the removal of afflictions. It also means "to refine," as in refining gold to remove its dross. It also means "to reach," as in reaching the ultimate destination. It also means "to command," as in commanding the people to follow the Way. It also means "to manifest," as in manifesting the Buddha's intent. It also means "to receive," as in receiving the Buddha's transmission. It also means "to verify," as in verifying the truth through the three proofs. It also means "to complete," as in completing the path to Buddhahood. It also means "to uphold," as in upholding the Dharma against decline. It also means "to transmit," as in transmitting the teachings to future generations. It also means "to contain," as in containing all dharmas within. It also means "to encompass," as in encompassing the entirety of the universe. It also means "to be supreme," as in being the most honored among all teachings. It also means "to be vast," as in being more expansive than the great ocean. It also means "to be profound," as in being deeper than the great earth. It also means "to be subtle," as in being finer than fine silk. It also means "to be clear," as in being clearer than a bright mirror. It also means "to be pure," as in being purer than flowing water. It also means "to be tranquil," as in being more tranquil than a still lake. It also means "to be eternal," as in being more eternal than Mount Sumeru. It also means "to be firm," as in being firmer than diamond. It also means "to be unchanging," as in being more unchanging than empty space. It also means "to be inexhaustible," as in being more inexhaustible than the flow of a river. It also means "to be boundless," as in being more boundless than the four oceans. It also means "to be infinite," as in being more infinite than the realm of sentient beings. It also means "to be peerless," as in having no equal in the three worlds. It also means "to be unsurpassed," as in being beyond all other vehicles. It also means "to be ultimate," as in reaching the final fruit of Arhatship, Pratyekabuddhahood, and Buddhahood. It also means "to be perfect," as in the perfection of the six pāramitās. It also means "to be complete," as in the completion of the three bodies and four wisdoms. It also means "to be universal," as in universally benefiting all beings. It also means "to be impartial," as in bestowing benefits equally upon all. It also means "to be spontaneous," as in acting without effort or deliberation. It also means "to be effortless," as in attaining liberation without striving. It also means "to be natural," as in following the nature of reality. It also means "to be true," as in corresponding to the ultimate truth. It also means "to be real," as in being free from falsehood. It also means "to be authentic," as in not being fabricated by humans. It also means "to be correct," as in being free from error. It also means "to be appropriate," as in being suited to the capacities of beings. It also means "to be timely," as in responding to the needs of the moment. It also means "to be expedient," as in employing skillful means. It also means "to be transformative," as in converting and guiding sentient beings. It also means "to be liberating," as in freeing beings from suffering. It also means "to be saving," as in rescuing those who have fallen into the three evil paths. It also means "to be compassionate," as in feeling pity for the ignorant. It also means "to be merciful," as in bestowing kindness upon the wicked. It also means "to be benevolent," as in providing for the destitute. It also means "to be gracious," as in bestowing favors upon the lowly. It also means "to be magnanimous," as in being broad-minded toward the small. It also means "to be generous," as in giving without attachment. It also means "to be open," as in being free from obstruction. It also means "to be accessible," as in being easy to approach. It also means "to be welcoming," as in receiving all with joy. It also means "to be inclusive," as in gathering all without exclusion. It also means "to be harmonious," as in reconciling contradictions. It also means "to be consistent," as in being without internal conflict. It also means "to be coherent," as in the logical sequence of cause and effect. It also means "to be continuous," as in the uninterrupted succession of the lineage. It also means "to be pervasive," as in permeating all places. It also means "to be omnipresent," as in appearing everywhere. It also means "to be all-encompassing," as in leaving nothing out. It also means "to be all-pervading," as in filling the ten directions. It also means "to be all-knowing," as in the wisdom of omniscience. It also means "to be all-seeing," as in the eye of the Tathāgata. It also means "to be all-hearing," as in the divine ear. It also means "to be all-smelling," as in the divine nose. It also means "to be all-tasting," as in the divine tongue. It also means "to be all-touching," as in the divine body. It also means "to be all-knowing of the thoughts of others," as in the divine mind. It also means "to be all-enlightened," as in awakening to the nature of reality. It also means "to be all-liberated," as in attaining nirvana. It also means "to be all-blissful," as in the bliss of the Dharma-realm. It also means "to be all-pure," as in the purity of the three wheels. It also means "to be all-vast," as in the expanse of the great vehicle. It also means "to be all-profound," as in the depth of the secret treasury. It also means "to be all-subtle," as in the fineness of the ultimate meaning. It also means "to be all-clear," as in the clarity of the Dharma-light. It also means "to be all-pure," as in the purity of the Dharma-nature. It also means "to be all-tranquil," as in the tranquility of the Dharma-body. It also means "to be all-eternal," as in the eternity of the Dharma-realm. It also means "to be all-firm," as in the firmness of the Dharma-seal. It also means "to be all-unchanging," as in the unchanging nature of the Dharma. It also means "to be all-inexhaustible," as in the inexhaustibility of the Dharma-treasury. It also means "to be all-boundless," as in the boundlessness of the Dharma-sphere. It also means "to be all-infinite," as in the infinity of the Dharma-expanse. It also means "to be all-pareless," as in the peerlessness of the Buddha-way. It also means "to be all-unsurpassed," as in the supremacy of the Mahāyāna. It also means "to be all-ultimate," as in the finality of the fruit of Buddhahood. It also means "to be all-perfect," as in the perfection of the ten powers. It also means "to be all-complete," as in the completeness of the eighteen unique qualities. It also means "to be all-universal," as in the universality of the four fearlessnesses. It also means "to be all-impartial," as in the impartiality of the three kinds of mindfulness. It also means "to be all-spontaneous," as in the spontaneity of the eight liberations. It also means "to be all-effortless," as in the effortlessness of the nine successive absorptions. It also means "to be all-natural," as in the naturalness of the ten totalities. It also means "to be all-true," as in the truth of the ten powers. It also means "to be all-real," as in the reality of the four analytical knowledges. It also means "to be all-authentic," as in the authenticity of the great compassion. It also means "to be all-correct," as in the correctness of the great loving-kind

Although *tara* has five meanings, its essential points lie in the two meanings of "surging spring" and "plumb line"; these correspond respectively to the two meanings of "Dharma" and "constancy" (*nitya*) in this sutra.
Therefore, this sutra is used as a substitute for that *sūtra*.
[Commentary] The passage beginning with "Next, as for the Sūtra" explains the general name [of the term]. Regarding the phrase "cannot alter its equality," Master Zhaolun says:

"Though ancient and modern times differ, the Way of Awakening does not change; because the various evils cannot displace it and sentient beings cannot differentiate it, it is called 'Constant' (nitya).
As for the five meanings of *sūtra*: first, the "Root of Dharma," also called "Birth"; second, the "Subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
"Arising" (*udbhava*) is also termed "manifestation. It refers to the three springs, the four measuring lines, and the five flower-garlands, as stated in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
Regarding the "one fundamental dharma," that which was spoken from the golden mouth of the Buddha takes a single word as its basis and flows forth as immeasurable teachings.

Because these reach sentient beings at the time they are encountered, those who hear them immediately attain the Way. Thus, a sutra says: "Each and every sūtra, moreover, possesses immeasurable sūtras."
Tārā serves as her retinue. Regarding the two subtle arisings: the Dharma taught by the Buddha is characterized by skillful phrasing and sequential analysis;
it is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, perfect and complete like the waters of the great ocean, which gradually deepen.
Those who hear the teaching receive it sequentially and discern the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); as a slight understanding arises, it gradually increases.

"Long-illuminating and thoroughly proficient," it is also said, "one who has extensively read and recited heterodox treatises, possesses broad knowledge of the intentions of the wise, and is learned with a powerful memory.
This leads to the attainment of Buddhahood. Regarding the "three surging springs," they are named after a metaphor:

the words and meanings of the Dharma taught by the Buddha are inexhaustible, and the flow of the Dharma never ceases; those who hear these teachings derive immeasurable understanding from even a single phrase of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that even hearing a single verse leads to the thorough understanding of immeasurable meanings.
One gradually comes to know the Dharma teachings—from the month, the four months, to the year—just as the wind moves freely and without obstruction through the sky.

As for the "four lines of measurement," these are the teachings of the Buddha that trim away the afflictions of craving; by not being overturned or deluded by the winds of heterodoxy, one enters the correct path, which is identical [to this].

The meaning of "cord and ink-line" (*shengmo*) is as follows: the five types of flower-garland knots refer to binding the Buddha’s teachings so that they do not fall away, just as one binds flowers into a garland to prevent them from scattering.
Regarding the essential point that the two meanings of "fountainhead" and "cord and ink-line" are equal:

the fountainhead flows constantly and without interruption, which can be equated with the eternal; the cord and ink-line eliminate the heterodox and manifest the orthodox, which can be equated with the Dharma.
Because it serves as a rule, the character "jing" (經) is used here as a substitute for the term "sūtra" (修多羅). ○ Third, the differences in the names by which [the scriptures] are designated.
[Commentary]: The various scriptures are designated by different names; now, this scripture is referred to above as the "Śrīmālā Lion’s Roar," which is an instance of citing [a title].

The title "Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-vaipulya Sūtra" is so named because it mentions both the Dharma and the person; specifically, it cites the Dharma as "the Great Expedient Means of the One Vehicle Vaipulya," thereby presenting both the teaching and the person together as the title.
Thus, it is called the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-vaipulya Sūtra*.
[Commentary] Regarding the third point, the differences in how titles are derived: as seen in the titles of various sūtras, these are derived from different sources.

Some are derived from the Dharma, such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* or the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; some are derived from phenomena (*vastu*), such as the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa-sūtra*; some are derived from persons, such as the *Sudāna-sūtra*;
some are derived from metaphors (*upamā*), such as the *Mahāmegha-sūtra* or the *Ratnakośa-sūtra*; and some possess both Dharma and metaphor, such as...
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other sutras may possess both the person and the dharma, such as this present sutra and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*;

or they may possess the person, the dharma, and the metaphor, such as the *Avataṃsaka* and others. From "As for the Great Sage" down to "preaching the Dharma" constitutes the second section: entering the commentary on the sutra text.
Within this, first the sutra text is divided into sections, and then the sutra text is explained.

[Commentary]: Now, when the Great Sage appears in the world to preach the Dharma for sentient beings, he does not select scriptures based on their length, nor does he distinguish between the profundity or shallowness of their principles;
in all cases, he employs a three-part structure for his teaching. First is the Introductory Section (*nidāna*), where "introductory" (*xu*) signifies gradual progression.

Second is the Main Exposition (*samyaksaṃbuddha-vyākaraṇa*), where "main" (*zheng*) refers to the essential body of the sutra. Third is the Dissemination Section (*parīndanā*), which means transmission.
In future ages, these three [teachings] will be required; this is because sentient beings have long been deluded by sensory dust and their faculties are further dulled.

If they were to suddenly hear the profound principle, they would not only be unable to accept and practice it, but would instead give rise to slanderous thoughts and fall back into the three miserable realms.
Therefore, the Sage first manifests extraordinary signs to cause beings to feel joy, and thus the multitude...

Because sentient beings, by virtue of this introductory sequence, immediately give rise to a mind that delights in hearing the profound principle, he therefore expounds the sequence of the true essence (*tattva*).
Once the sequence of the true essence is concluded, all sentient beings of that time will inevitably receive benefit.

Since the Great Sage bestows compassion through the teaching of the Dharma not only for the benefit of those present at that time, but so that it may reach far into future generations and cause all to share in this merit, [the sequence] of the conclusion follows.
The discourse on circulation is intended to exhort [the audience]. Regarding the structure of the three sections of the text:
from the beginning up to "all with a pure mind praise the Buddha’s true merits" is called the introductory section (*nidāna*).

From "The Tathāgata’s wondrous form and body, which the world has no equal" down to "You have already personally attended hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas and are able to expound this meaning" is the second section.

The "Exposition" (*Vyākhyāna*) constitutes the correct teaching; from that time when the World-Honored One emitted the supreme radiance illuminating the entire assembly until the end of the sutra, it is for the purpose of its circulation.
[Commentary]: Regarding the first section, although the Buddha’s teachings arise from diverse sources, they are virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.
Since the textual structure must necessarily be complete, Master Seng'an divided all the various sutras into the three sections of introduction, main body, and dissemination.
Later, seeing that the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* by Maitreya Bodhisattva contained this same text, it was seen to accord perfectly with the Sage’s intention.
As for those who give rise to further slanderous thoughts, they are not only unable to receive and practice [the teaching], but moreover...
Because [people] would give rise to slander, the Tathāgata ceased and did not speak; thus the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak.
If this matter were spoken, all devas and humans would be struck with alarm and doubt, and bhikṣus of overweening pride would fall into a great pit.
This "great pit" refers to the three miserable realms (*trāya*). The names for these three miserable realms appear in the *Sūtra on the Four Liberations*.

The hell named *Agnimāndala* (Fire-Coated) is a minor hell that extends throughout the great hells of cold and heat; it is specifically designated as "Fire-Coated" from the perspective of its location at the edge of the hot hells.

The realm of animals is called *Rudhiramāndala* (Blood-Coated), which is spoken of from the perspective of their mutual devouring. The realm of hungry ghosts is called *Śastramāndala* (Sword-Coated), which is spoken of from the perspective of being driven and coerced by them.
The term *māndala* (coated/path) is pronounced with the initial *ma* reversed [as *man*], meaning a road or a path for traveling through mud. It is distinct [from other meanings].

Regarding the characteristic of permanence (*nitya-lakṣaṇa*): as in the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is manifested by the rain of four kinds of flowers, the earth shaking in six ways, and the light from between the eyebrows illuminating eighteen thousand lands;

within each land, Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma, the three vehicles are practiced and realized, and they enter *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the emission of light from the face-gate (*mukha-dvāra*) signifies the teaching of permanence.
In the "Chapter on Abiding in the Buddha-nature" and the "Chapter on the Emission of Light from the Major and Minor Limbs," each is manifested differently;
this sutra takes internal and external conditions as its point of departure.
[Commentary]: Regarding the first section, the Prologue, it is initially divided into two: first, the general, and second, the specific. These constitute the five matters [of the prologue].
Because it universally penetrates all sūtras, it is called the "General Preface" (tōjū).
[Commentary] Regarding the two types of prefaces—the general and the specific—within the explanation of the preface:

as for the statement that the five matters constitute the general preface, because all sūtras establish these five matters, such as "Thus have I heard," it is also called the "Preface of the Final Bequest. It is the Tathāgata’s final instruction that these be set forth.
Because it stands at the beginning of the sutra, it is also called the "Preface" (nidāna). This has been the case for all Buddhas of the three periods of time prior to their sutras;

thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda had not yet eliminated the fetters of affection for his kinsmen, and his mind was submerged in an ocean of grief.
Then Aniruddha said to Ānanda: 'If you have any doubts regarding future matters, you should consult and resolve them now.'"
Sunk as he was in the ocean of sorrow like an ordinary worldly person, Ānanda regained his composure through the power of mindfulness of the Path;
his heart having been awakened from its distress, he immediately asked four questions: first, how one should practice the Path after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
second, who should serve as the teacher; third, how one should dwell together with the harsh-spoken Cāṇakya; and fourth, what should be placed at the beginning of the Buddha’s sūtras.

Regarding what [the Buddha] said, the Buddha told Ānanda: "Whether in the present or after my passing, the path to liberation based on the four foundations of mindfulness and the Sūtra on the Precepts is your true teacher.

As for the wicked-mouthed Cāṇakya, who would govern me according to the Brahma-punishment, he would first speak thus regarding the Dharma-treasury accumulated over three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas: "Thus have I heard: at one time, the Buddha..."
In a certain direction, in a certain land, and among a certain assembly, it is not only my teaching that is thus;

the sūtras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time were likewise at their beginning. Therefore, these five elements are called the "General Preface" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*). As for the specific explanation:
these five elements are all words intended to encourage faith. Regarding the doctrine and principle transmitted [herein], "I have heard" means that I personally received the sound [of the teaching].
The profound meaning is that those who can transmit it and those who receive the transmission are contemporaries;

at the time when the principle is realized, the Buddha—the dwelling one, the emanation master, and the recipient of the mandate—also acts as the preserver. Places such as Śrāvastī are the locations where the sutras were heard;
thus, they mutually corroborate one another to encourage faith that [the teaching] is not false, desiring that future generations may follow it without opposition. Within this:
"Sometimes five, sometimes six, due to the combination or separation of the primary location.

[Commentary]: The dispatching of a letter to invite the Buddha was specifically for the sake of this sutra and not for other sutras; therefore, it is called the "Separate Introduction" (Pratyeka-nidāna).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the "separate introduction" (bèixù) refers to the dispatching of a letter: because each sūtra relies on different circumstances, it is called a "separate teaching" (biéjiào).
Since the capacities of those to be taught (jī) differ, this is also called the "present introduction" (xiànzài xù), as such events occurred while the Buddha was in the world.
This separate introduction to the present sūtra concerns King Prasenajit, who, not long after he and Queen Mallikā had gained faith in the Dharma, dispatched a letter to Śrīmālā in brief.
The praise of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits and so forth concludes the explanation above regarding the purpose of the general and specific prefaces.
[Commentary] Regarding the first, the General Preface, there are two parts: first, clarifying that what Ānanda transmitted is not erroneous, thereby verifying the person who received it.

These two trustworthy points of reliance—the fundamental evidentiary dharmas of the clearly expounded sūtras heard in common—and the person who can propagate the Dharma are such that the former is established as the dharma, because the dharma is propagated by means of the person; thus, the latter is established subsequently.
*Thus have I heard at one time.* [Commentary]:
"Thus" (*evam*) generally summarizes the beginning and end of a single teaching. When two things resemble each other, they are called "thus-like" (*tathā*);

when there is nothing that is not so, it is called "is" (*iti*). The voices and mouths with which the Tathāgata and Ānanda conversed must necessarily be identical; yet, since the eight [vocal organs] are distinct...
Because gold and meat are not the same, the text says, "As with one [thing] and eight. Although gold and meat differ, that which they clarify is one and the same thing;
therefore, according to principle, it is said, "This is [the same].
[Commentary]: Regarding "necessarily one, eight, distinct, etc.": "One" refers to the single voice; the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, and the assembly...

Beings of various types each obtain understanding according to their kind; a single utterance of the perfect voice is understood differently by different classes. This resides in the Buddha’s eight qualities of voice:
first, most excellent; second, easy to understand; third, soft; fourth, harmonious; fifth, noble and wise; sixth, unerring; seventh, profound and subtle; eighth, not feminine. These reside in Ānanda.
As for the "single sound," it exists only in the Great One (the Buddha), who possesses these eight qualities of voice.

Because it encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the eight tones are used here as a provisional designation. "Gold" refers to the golden-colored body and the vocal karma spoken by the Tathāgata;

"flesh" refers to the physical body and the vocal karma spoken by Ānanda. Although the "gold" and "flesh" differ—one being the eightfold [teachings] and the other being the single [transmission]—Ānanda transmits what the Buddha spoke exactly as the Buddha spoke it. Thus, although there are two modes of exposition, the "gold" and the "flesh," they are called "as-it-is" (tathatā).
However, because that which is expressed is but a single principle, it is said to be "thus" (evam). [Section 18] Regarding the analogy of the Dharma and its teaching as a single object:
it is because the teaching accords with the principle. Many of the ancients have stated that the phrase "thus" (evam) refers to the text;

the text accords with the principle because it skillfully expresses it, and because there is nothing that does not accord with it. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma takes faith as its entry."
"To enter into such [a state]" is the expression of one with virtuous faith; those who do not believe say that this matter is not so, whereas those who believe say that this matter is indeed so.
This is the beginning of encouraging faith; "beginning" (duan) is synonymous with "head" (shou).

[Commentary: The phrase "Thus have I heard" indicates that Ānanda personally heard it from the Buddha, ensuring that what was transmitted is unerring; furthermore, it serves to distinguish [the teaching] from the claim of non-Buddhists that they know it spontaneously by themselves.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "I have heard": if one were to transmit what was heard from another, there would often be much falsehood and error; hearing it directly now makes it credible.

Thus, the multitude accepts it and has no grounds for doubt. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In accordance with worldly convention, I speak of 'self' and 'combination' when referring to 'hearing.

As for speaking of 'self' in accordance with worldly convention, this refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who, in propagating the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings, speak of 'self' in conformity with worldly custom."
It does not contradict what is proclaimed within, nor does it contradict reality. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that there are three types of self-view and pride:
ordinary worldlings possess all three; those in training (*śaikṣa*) possess two; and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possess one. Ānanda is one who is still in training;

he has eliminated false views regarding the self and subdued pride regarding the self. When he uses the name "I" in accordance with worldly convention, there is no fault. This is because when speaking of a combination [of conditions], the listener’s faculty of hearing is unimpaired.

When a sound is within the range of hearing, through the conjunction of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) to hear, the sense-object, and the ear-faculty (*śrotra-vijñāna*), consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) arises;
because it discriminates the various things heard through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, it is called "hearing.

Internally, Ānanda and others possessed keen and sharp auditory faculties, and externally, they received the Buddha’s single voice without omission; therefore, it is called "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*).

Furthermore, in order to distinguish [the Buddhist view] from that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others, it is said that what Ānanda hears must necessarily involve internal and external causes and conditions;
this is because the non-Buddhists fall into the error of asserting existence without causes and conditions or clinging to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

Thus, the Sarvāstivāda school clarifies that the self (*ātman*) exists merely as a name, while according to the Dharmaguptaka school, there is a provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*), and as for the self postulated by the Vātsīputrīya school—

In the fifth *anabhilāpya-nidhi*, although these [teachings] differ, they all refute the externalist conception of a self-nature (*ātman*) by explaining that the "self" is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Therefore, it is said that this serves to distinguish [the Buddha's teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Question: The *Mahā-śāstra* states, "Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained the Way;

he entered *nirvāṇa* twenty years after the Buddha’s enlightenment. This implies that Ānanda served as the attendant only after twenty years had passed since the Buddha’s attainment of *bodhi*. How is this so?
Question: Since the time before this, when the attendant Ānanda was not present while the Sūtras were being preached, how can it be said that he "heard from me" (evam mayā śrutam)?

Answer: The *Baoen jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states that Ānanda requested four vows from the Buddha, the fourth of which was: "I vow that the Buddha will repeat those Sūtras I have not yet heard.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts contain various passages that must be cited at length; the remaining three vows concern the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
[The *Shi'er yinyuan jing*] states: "He did not accept worn-out clothes, nor did he accept separate invitations; his comings and goings were without fixed regularity.

[The *Shu* (Commentary) says: "As for 'at one time,' this clarifies that although the number of sūtras and teachings spoken by the Tathāgata is immeasurable, Ānanda attained the Buddha-awakening samādhi and received them all at once; therefore, it is called 'at one time.'"
[Commentary] Regarding "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*): Master Zhaolun states that it refers to the time when the Dharma King inaugurated his auspicious reign;

it also refers to the time when the fourfold assembly, moved by the teaching, attained the Way. This further serves to establish the credibility of "I have heard. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The time of the discourse causes people's hearts to give rise to faith."
[Commentary: Second, the fact that the place of residence and the assembly of listeners are the same serves as proof that the Dharma is trustworthy.
The Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
[Commentary: Śrāvastī is the name of a city; the Liang dynasty translation says "Hearing Things" (聞物). This city was prosperous and wealthy, abounding in famous treasures from afar.

Because it is heard of in all four directions, it is called the "Land of the Heard" (*Śrāvastī*); its kingdom name is Kośala, but because the city is used here to designate the kingdom, it is called Śrāvastī.
It is one of the sixteen great kingdoms.
[Commentary] Second, citing the place where he resided as proof that the Dharma is trustworthy: "The Buddha’s dwelling" means that the Buddha is the teacher who reveals it;

this shows that the Master of Transformation is also a supporting factor for establishing the credibility of the tradition. Why? Because among the ninety-six types of heterodox paths, there is nothing worthy of taking refuge in.
Even the sages of the Three Vehicles reside in what is not ultimate and teach what is not final. Now, it is clarified that [the Buddha's teaching] is not so.

The Master, with great awakening, attained sudden enlightenment; what he spoke was truly authentic. From this time forth, as he heard the sutras and accorded with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, the hearts of the multitude were filled with joy and satisfaction.
What was formerly called "Buddha" refers to one who is awakened; because he awakens himself and awakens others, he is named "Buddha. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"Buddha" in the language of Qin means "the Knower. Of what dharma does he know? It means he knows all things throughout the three periods of time.

Because one clearly awakens to and knows all phenomena—such as those categorized as sentient beings and non-sentient beings, and the permanent and the impermanent—under the Bodhi tree, one is called a Buddha.
Regarding "abiding," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that one is called "abiding" because of abiding in the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
There are four kinds of abiding: first, celestial abiding, which refers to the three matters of generosity, ethical discipline, and a virtuous mind.
The two Brahma-abodes consist of abiding in the Four Truths, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless absorptions.
The three Noble Abodes consist of abiding in the principle of the three emptinesses, the Four Truths, and the twelve links of dependent origination.

The four Buddha-abodes consist of abiding in the power of immeasurable samādhis such as Śūraṅgama, the fearlessnesses, and all other Buddha-dharmas—the dharmas attained by a Buddha—within which [he dwells].
Dwelling in compassion for sentient beings, he manifested his residence at the Jetavana Grove.
As for the mention of the kingdom of Śrāvastī and so forth, this refers to the capital city of the Kosalā kingdom in Central India;
because it was distinct from the Southern Kosala, the name of the capital city was used as the designation for the kingdom. (Consulting the *Xiyu ji*, there were both Northern and Southern Kosalas.)
In the *Rājāvavādaka-sūtra*, sixteen great kingdoms are enumerated; first is Kośala in the south, and second is Śrāvastī in the north.
Although the distance from the south to the north is extremely vast and they do not interact with one another, commentators of both ancient and modern times have disagreed on this point.
This [present account] is the definitive explanation.
[Commentary]: Regarding "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park": Prince Jeta offered the grove and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada offered the land;
the two together established a vihāra. Because it is designated by the names of both patrons, it is called "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park."
[Commentary]: Regarding "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park": five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana (translated as "Victorious Grove"), which is the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Why? Because King Śreṇika had a minister named Sudatta, translated as "Good Giver" (Śrīdatta). This elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent;
he accumulated wealth but was able to disperse it, relieving the destitute, giving to the poor, and showing compassion and pity for the orphaned.
When he was old, the people praised his virtue, calling him Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver of Alms to the Destitute). He held the Tathāgata in high esteem and wished to construct a vihāra.
The Buddha commanded Śāriputra to go and survey various locations. Only the garden of Prince Jeta was fresh, open, and elevated; its ground was bright and radiant.
Upon hearing this, the Prince jokingly said, "I shall sell it only if one covers the entire site with gold. Sudatta (the Good Giver) was suddenly filled with joy and immediately...

Gold was brought forth from the treasury and spread upon the ground according to his words; where there was a small portion not yet filled, the Prince requested that it be left as is, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field;
one should plant the seeds of goodness therein. He then established a vihāra on that empty space. The World-Honored One then addressed Ānanda, saying:
"This garden site was well-donated by Sudatta, and the grove of trees was donated by Jeta. These two have joined their hearts in a single purpose to honor the Dharma."
From this point forward, this site should be called the Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park;
"Jeta" refers to Jeta. (The above is from the *Qinglong shu*.)
[Commentary]: The assembly of those who heard [the teaching] together is omitted briefly. Some say that when this sutra was preached, [the Buddha] was in the inner palace;

above were only the various devas, and below were only the court ladies. Lacking the great bodhisattvas (*mahāsattva*), it was insufficient to serve as proof for the sutra, and thus they were omitted.
However, at the beginning of the subsequent circulation of this sutra, it states: "He emitted a supreme radiance, universally illuminating the great assembly."

How could it be said that there were no assembly? Furthermore, if one says that what is heard at a common residence can serve as proof for the Dharma and is thus credible, how could this refer to the women of the palace within the Yūṣa Palace? This refers precisely to the assembly present at the time and place of the entrustment.
Therefore, it is clear that the brief account is sufficient.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the assembly of those who heard it together is briefly omitted," this refers to the witnesses of the Dharma.
It serves to certify that the Dharma is trustworthy and that it is not a mistaken transmission; however, the compiler of the sutra has merely omitted them here.

The intention of the Sub-commentary (*Shu*) is that, according to the text of the sutra, there should follow a passage stating that the Tathāgata returned to the Jeta Grove for the sake of Ānanda, Śakra, and others, [to provide] a further...
Regarding the teaching of this sutra and the place where it was entrusted for circulation, there were those who heard it together who did not take [the Buddha] into the Yuṣa palace;
thus, it is verified that the interpretations of the ancients are incorrect, and the summarized meaning is now clear.
[Commentary]: Regarding the second, the specific introduction (*prastāvanā*), it is also divided into two parts. First, from "At that time, King Prasenajit...
down to "...respectfully bestowed [this] upon Śrīmālā," is titled the "External Conditions Introduction. Second, from "When Śrīmālā received the letter and rejoiced...
down to "...praising the Buddha’s true merits," is titled the "Internal Causes Introduction. It says: "The Venerable One dispatched this letter to speak for her sake."

The external conditions for this sutra are called the "External Conditions Preface. Because Śrīmālā’s silent contemplation moved the Buddha to preach this sutra, it is called the "Internal Causes Preface.
[Commentary] Regarding "external conditions" and "internal causes," etc.: although the parents sent a letter, it was only able to trigger her internal mind; therefore, it is so described.

He gave rise to the aspiration for the Way and silently invoked the Buddha; through the resonance of this spiritual mechanism, the Way and the response met in union, and he heard the Dharma. Thus it is said that he was "moved" (*gan*);
because his mind was pure, he heard the Dharma. [Commentary:
Regarding the first section on external conditions, there are also three parts. First, the King and the Queen converse together regarding the excellence [of the teaching].
The second section, from "Māndhātṛ’s mental clarity and sharp faculties" down to "it is fitting that he hear the profound Dharma," describes his virtuous conduct.

The third section, from "the messenger received the letter" down to "he delivered it upon arriving at the kingdom of Ayodhyā," clarifies how the messenger presented the letter once he had reached the country of Ayodhyā.
At that time, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā, who had not long since placed their faith in the Dharma, said to one another:

"Queen Śrīmālā is our daughter; she is wise, of sharp faculties, compassionate, and easy to awaken. If she were to see the Buddha, she would surely and swiftly understand the Dharma, her mind free from doubt.
It would be fitting to send a messenger at once to inspire her toward the aspiration for the Way."

[Commentary] "At that time" refers to the time when Śrīmālā was to hear [the teaching on] eternal abiding. "Not long in believing the Dharma" means that her faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma had not yet been long established.
It is said that the King and his consort had only believed in the Hīnayāna for a long time and had not yet believed in the Mahāyāna.
At the time when the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma beneath a tree, King Prasenajit struck [the gong].
A drum was brought to present to the Buddha; knowing the reason for it, the Buddha asked, "What sound is this? Ānanda answered truthfully.
Then the Buddha said, "The worldly king beats the drum of birth and death, but I, as the Dharma King, ought to beat the Dharma drum. He then preached the *Dharmabherī-sūtra*.
Thereupon, the king and his consort first placed their faith in the Mahāyāna. Not long after, he dispatched a messenger to inform [the other kings]:
The woman is Śrīmālā.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says that King Prasenajit—here translated as "Harsh-and-Gracious"—and Queen Māllikā;
however, the *Adbhutadharma-sūtra* states that she was originally a maidservant named Yellow-Head (Pīṅgalā) belonging to the Brahmin Yaśoda of Rājagṛha. She constantly...
Knowing that she had offered dry rice to the Buddha as a result of her duty as a garden-keeper, King Prasenajit went hunting and entered the garden where he saw her.

The maidservant then provided the king with various services, including massage, which greatly pleased him. The king asked the Brahmin, "Will you sell her? He replied, "How could a lowly slave-girl be worth it? The king questioned him again, and she answered: [She said: "I am not for sale; I am a servant of the Buddha. The king then asked, "What is the price? She replied, "The price is the merit gained by offering food to the Buddha. The king then offered her a hundred thousand pieces of gold, saying, "Take this and go offer it to the Buddha. She accepted the gold and went to offer it to the Buddha. The Buddha then accepted the offering and bestowed a prophecy upon her. At that time, the king was filled with great joy and immediately returned to his palace. (Note: This passage describes the narrative of the *Sūtra on the Maidservant Who Offered Food to the Buddha*, corresponding to the *Buddha-bhāṣita-dāsī-puṇya-sūtra*.)
King [Prasenajit] then purchased her from him for one hundred thousand taels of gold, making her the foremost among his sixty thousand wives.

Regarding the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* and other such texts: this sūtra was later translated in two fascicles by Guṇabhadra at Dong’an Temple during the Song dynasty, titled the *Mahādharmabherī-sūtra*. It records that the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, Queen Mallikā, and immeasurable bodhisattvas from the ten directions, the Tathāgata then preached this Dharma to those four assemblies:
"Where there is existence, there is suffering and pleasure; where there is no existence, there is no suffering and no pleasure."
Therefore, being free from suffering and pleasure is Nirvana, the supreme bliss. At that time, King Prasenajit beat drums and blew conch shells as he went to the place where the Buddha was.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda, "For what reason are there the sounds of drums and conch shells?
Ānanda answered the Buddha in detail. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Now you, too, should beat the Great Dharma drum."

"I shall now proclaim the Mahādharmabherī-sūtra. The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "Although all those in this assembly are pure and of one mind, they do not correctly understand the teachings spoken with intentional concealment (*saṃdhābhāṣya*).

Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is meant by 'teachings spoken with intentional concealment'? The Buddha replied, "'Teachings spoken with intentional concealment' refers to speaking of the Tathāgata..."
Ultimately, although the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unextinguished, he manifests parinirvāṇa; this parinirvāṇa is not a phenomenon of destruction.

When this sūtra was being expounded—revealed through hundreds of thousands of causes and conditions with a voice that is free from obscuration, pure, and clearly manifest—among the assembly were sentient beings of inferior faith, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas at the beginning [of their practice].

The Bodhisattva Karmaprasiddhi was incapable of hearing and receiving the teaching that although the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa, he is nevertheless eternally present and indestructible;

thus, he rose from his seat and departed. Why was this? Because for a long night he had extensively cultivated the view of emptiness regarding parinirvāṇa, and upon hearing this Sūtra—which is free from concealment and pure—he rose from his seat and departed.
The full scriptural passage is very extensive.
[Commentary: One interpretation states that "time" refers to the time of the *Dharmabherī-sūtra*. Although not long after understanding this faith in the Dharma, various differing views arose;
however, when tracing back to the origin and end, only this [interpretation] is appropriate. Therefore, it was not recorded by me.
The phrase "my daughter" is a term of praise and esteem. It means that one does not surpass one's parents in knowing their child, and no king surpasses himself in knowing his own subjects.
This designation of "my child" makes no distinction between self and other; it depends solely upon virtue.
Now, since Śrīmālā is already my own child and possesses illustrious merit, she ought to hear the supreme path; therefore, she also refers to herself as "my child."

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "my son" and so forth: because Śrīmālā is named for her ability to adorn [herself] with the ten thousand practices, she constantly manifests only that which is excellent;
having thoroughly understood this, there is nothing further that is evil, and thus it is said that she does not distinguish between self and other.

[Commentary: Those who are intelligent and possess sharp faculties are called "acute" (*cóng*) when their ears are skilled at listening, and "wise" (*huì*) when their minds are clear in discernment. This clarity and brilliance of acute discernment is termed "sharp faculty" (*lìgēn*).
To be penetrating, agile, and quick to awaken—such that upon hearing an expression, one grasps both its surface and its inner meaning—is termed "penetrating" (*tōng*).

This results from being skilled at listening. To have deep illumination and clear understanding—such that upon encountering a principle, one immediately comprehends it—is termed "agile" (*mǐn*). This results from being skilled at discernment. Thus, one encounters a principle and understands it instantly.

This is called "easy awakening," which results from possessing sharp faculties; the preceding phrase discusses their inherent nature, while the subsequent phrase speaks of their functional capacity, together forming a complete whole.
Since receiving the teaching must depend on listening well, listening is praised as primary; this clarifies that the necessary equipment is already complete.
[Commentary] "Shuang" (pronounced *shu liǎng* in the second tone) means good, noble, and clear. "Min" (pronounced *pín yǔn* in the fourth tone) means sharp and swift.
"Zhi" (pronounced *zhī lì* in the fourth tone) means to reach, to attain, and to bestow. Having sharp faculties (*li-gen*) is one's innate nature; being easily awakened is the function.

Being easily awakened must be accomplished by means of sharp faculties, and sharp faculties must be manifested through being easily awakened; therefore, it is said that they mutually accomplish one another.
This is because these individuals already possess the faculties capable of hearing the doctrine of eternal abiding.
[Commentary: Those who will certainly and swiftly understand the Dharma are those who awaken upon hearing it once, without requiring further instruction; whose minds attain freedom from doubt;

whose spirits and countenances become clear and bright, free from the delusions and obstructions of the Hīnayāna; and who are fit to be sent a messenger at this time to inspire in them the aspiration for the Path.

At that time, there were two [opportunities]: the first being the timely moment (*kāla*) and the second being the opportune moment (*samaya*); neither should be lost. This clarifies that the reality may be received.
From the passage beginning with "The lady addressed [the Buddha]" onwards is the second section, the brief praise sent via messenger.

The lady said, "Now is precisely the right time. The King and the lady then composed a letter to Vaidehī briefly extolling the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata, and dispatched an attendant named Cāṇḍālī to deliver it.
[Commentary] Regarding the "immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata": because his noble virtues are immeasurable and cannot be fully recounted, three virtues are briefly indicated.
[Sub-commentary] "Briefly indicating three virtues" refers to the brief eulogy found in the subsequent scripture.
[Commentary] Third, it is shown that the messenger was sent to deliver the letter, which can be seen as follows:
The messenger, bearing the letter, arrived at the kingdom of Ayodhyā, entered its palace, and respectfully presented it to Śrīmālā.
[Commentary] This clarifies that the true inner reality can be perceived.
[Sub-commentary] "True inner reality" means that the parents send a letter to rectify their inner minds, causing them to give rise to the realization of true,
permanent, and abiding reality.

[Commentary] From "Śrīmālā received the letter" onwards, the second section, the "Internal Introduction on Causes," is divided into five parts. First, it clarifies the joy upon receiving the letter, which may also be seen [in the following]:
Śrīmālā, having received the letter with joy, received it upon her head, read and recited it, and upheld it, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder as she turned toward Caṇḍīla.
And he spoke in verse. [Commentary (Sū):
"Giving rise to a rare and marvelous mind" refers to hearing that [the Buddha] is eternally abiding. [Sub-commentary (Chāo):
"Hearing that [he is] eternally abiding" means hearing the aforementioned brief exposition of the three virtues (triguṇa).
[Commentary]: First, regarding the opening verse, the intention is to practice worship.
Having heard the Buddha’s voice, which has never before been heard in the world, one should practice worship toward that which is spoken with truth.
[Commentary]: However, the Śrīmālā-sūtra only perceives the penetration [of the Dharma] and treats it as eternally abiding and primordial;
because hearing this is rare, it is called "rare. How can the scripture say, "I heard the Buddha’s voice"? Sound is used to transmit meaning, while writing is used to transmit sound;
thus, the meaning of the scriptural text says one "hears the Buddha’s voice. Furthermore, regarding seeing, hearing, and awakening: understanding obtained from the scriptural text is also [included].
It is called "hearing what has never before existed in the world" because, although my principle is fundamentally thus, it is based on the former self that I say it has never been clearly understood.
Throughout one's life, one has never heard of the eternally abiding reality; the holy body is perfectly complete and not false, hence it is called "real" (*zhen*);
the supreme virtue is concentrated and unchanging, hence it is called "actual" (*shi*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "I have heard the Buddha’s voice," the *Wuming shu* (Commentary on the Nameless) states: "Because the sound of the Way is transmitted through writing, it is said 'I have heard.
'Perfect and complete' means being endowed with the three virtues (*triguṇa*). 'Cong' (pronounced *yūyīng*) means firm."
[Commentary: There is one verse that clarifies how silent recitation moves the Buddha to appear.

One should look up with reverence and think: "The World-Honored Buddha has appeared for the sake of the entire world; he should likewise bestow his compassionate pity and surely cause me to behold him."

[Commentary]: It is said that the Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of sentient beings without partiality; although I am ignorant, I am but a woman who also belongs to the ranks of the world, so I pray that you will bestow your compassionate heart upon me so that I may behold him.
[Commentary] As for silent recitation, it should correspond to the Buddha as prescribed in the sutra text.
[Sub-commentary] The first verse clarifies that the Buddha responds to such an invocation.
At the very moment this thought arises, the Buddha manifests in the sky, universally emitting pure light to reveal his incomparable body.

[Commentary: As for "he should appear in mid-air," this means that whether he is within the palace or traversing difficult terrain, it is intended to manifest that the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* is signless (*animitta*), just like empty space.

Although the constant radiance (*nityaprabhā*) behind the Tathāgata’s crown is only seven feet in height, it is now because he intends to manifest that Queen Śrīmālā is about to expound the principle of the eternal fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Thus, [he appears in the sky].
Light radiated from every part of their bodies. A single verse clarifies that they made offerings through the three karmas, as can be seen.
Śrīmālā and her retinue bowed their heads to his feet in salutation, and with pure minds, they extolled the Buddha’s true merits.

[Commentary] Regarding "prostrating by touching the feet": this refers solely to showing reverence by touching the feet while suspended in mid-air; it does not mean actually reaching out to touch them.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding "offering through the three karmas": since the sutra omits the first phrase, the remaining three phrases can be understood as corresponding to the three karmas (body, speech, and mind).
"Only being in mid-air" means only contemplating and recollecting. "Adapting" (shì; rhyme with chì) means joy or proceeding.
This means that one merely contemplates and remains in mid-air to express reverence; it does not mean actually staying in mid-air to touch the feet [of the Buddha].
[Commentary] From the passage "The wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata" onwards, this is the second section of the sutra, the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*).
Within this, there are fourteen chapters, which are broadly divided into three parts. First, the initial five chapters clarify the essence of the vehicle (*yāna-svabhāva*);

it is stated that all myriad virtues constitute the essence of the vehicle. Second, the middle eight chapters clarify the realm of the vehicle (*yāna-gocara*); it is stated that there are both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [realms].
The Eight Noble Truths all serve as the objective realm for the vehicle (*yāna*). To clarify the person who practices this vehicle, the final chapter is presented;

it speaks of the Bodhisattvas of the Three Patiences (*kṣānti*) who ride this vehicle and proceed. Regarding the first section, which clarifies the essence of the vehicle, its five chapters are further divided into two parts.
The first three chapters clarify the practice of self-benefit (*svārtha-pratipatti*), stating that although Śrīmālā is fundamentally inconceivable, yet...
The traces [of the teaching] reside in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). Now, the first three chapters clarify the practice of the seventh stage;

therefore, they are called "the practice of one's own portion" (*sva-bhāga-pratipatti*). The latter two chapters clarify the practice of others' portions (*para-bhāga-pratipatti*), as they elucidate the practices from the eighth stage upward, which are not the specific portion of the seventh stage.
Within the practice of one's own portion, there are three chapters; the first praises the Buddha’s true merit.
Chapter Twenty: On Virtue; Chapter Three: On the Three Great Vows. Now, the first is the Chapter Praising the Tathāgata’s Reality.
[Commentary] Regarding the initial five chapters that clarify the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*) and so forth, beginning from the very start...

Faith culminates in the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Among the myriad virtues of this vehicle, those from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onward that involve effortful practice are termed "self-directed practice" (*svabhāva-pratipatti*);
those from the eighth stage upward that are effortless are termed "other-directed practice" (*parabhāva-pratipatti*).

To enter from existence into non-existence and rely on earnest goodness as the means of transport to reach wondrous enlightenment is precisely what is called the "unconditioned truth of cessation" (*anabhisaṃskāra-nirodha-satya*) upon emerging from the entanglements.
Because it is the Dharma-body, from the very beginning it takes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as its object of focus (*ālambana*).
The subsequent seven chapters are likewise synonyms for the Truth of Cessation; they are merely established with different names according to the principles of concealment and manifestation.

Thus it is said that both the conditioned and unconditioned Eight Noble Truths serve as the objects of the vehicle (*yāna*). The true child is precisely the one who skillfully illuminates this vehicle.

When those in the realms reach the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), they partially realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and establish the two bodies—the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

They bring forth the causes and effects of the five vehicles to transform and deliver beings of the five vehicles; once this process is complete, they ultimately converge into the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and even at the stage of Buddhahood it is likewise so.
This is exactly as in Śākyamuni’s single transformation: first three [vehicles], then one, with no difference whatsoever. This is the intended meaning.
Profound indeed! Please explain this in detail.

[Commentary: As for the purpose of this chapter’s introduction: previously, when Śrīmālā had not yet heard of the eternal nature, she now, upon receiving a letter sent by her parents, was able to hear it;
therefore, she exclaims that the present eternal nature is truly real and vows to take it as her refuge, distinguishing it from other views.
In the past, the meaning of taking refuge in impermanence and practicing virtue was fundamentally based on taking refuge;
now, because I wish to extensively clarify the path of the myriad practices (*sādhana*), I place taking refuge at the beginning. Thus, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
