"If one does not rely upon the Three Jewels to receive the precepts, the precepts will not be firm and strong, just as colors without glue [will not adhere]. Regarding this:
Within this chapter, the text is further divided into two parts: first, five verses that directly praise the eternally abiding reality as the refuge;
second, from "Out of compassion, protect me" onwards to the end of the chapter, which requests rescue.
Within the first part, the direct praise, the five verses are divided into four sections; first, the initial two verses praise the *dharmakāya*.
The next line of verse praises liberation; the next line of verse praises *prajñā*; and the next line of verse generally praises the three virtues.
Yet, since it is commonly said that at the stage of Buddhahood all ten thousand virtues are perfectly complete, for what reason are the praises based solely on these three virtues?
It is because the *dharmakāya* is the primary essence of the ten thousand virtues, liberation is [the perfection of] severance, and *prajñā* is wisdom.
Nevertheless, among all the myriad virtues, these three are the essentials; if one brings forth these three virtues, all other virtues manifest of themselves.

This is why we rely solely on these three virtues for our praise. Furthermore, as it was previously stated that the parents’ mutual renown consists of immeasurable saintly virtues that cannot be fully detailed, we have merely offered a brief praise of these three virtues. This is why they are superior.
The *Mālā* [Sūtra] also merely extols these three virtues. Although various masters differ in their interpretations of this meaning, the essential point lies herein;
therefore, I have not recorded them. [Commentary]:
When these three virtues are mentioned, the remaining virtues are naturally revealed; thus, the Dharma-body subsumes both the Reward-body and the Transformation-body.

Wisdom encompasses all provisional and ultimate knowledge and insight; liberation severs the bonds of the five stages of dwelling and can give rise to all supernatural powers and transformative functions.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The place where the Buddhas discipline and subdue sentient beings is called liberation.
Thus, these three are essential among the thirty thousand virtues.
[Commentary]: Within the first section praising the Dharma-body, the two lines are divided into two parts:
the first one and a half verses praise the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and the second two phrases praise the true body (*dharmakāya*).

This is because there can be no manifestation of the trace without the fundamental source being present, and there can be no revelation of the fundamental source without the trace. Therefore, throughout all instances of praise, they are always praised as a pair.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "It is not without the fundamental that the provisional traces are manifested," etc.: the principle of the fundamental and the trace originated with Master Daosheng, who said, "It is not without the fundamental that the traces are manifested;
it is not without the traces that the fundamental is revealed. Although the fundamental and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one.
The present text is likewise so: the True Body is the fundamental and the Responsive Body is the trace; it is not the fundamental of the True Body [that is being discussed here].

Without manifesting the traces of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the traces of the response-body could not be revealed; without the traces of the response-body, the essence of the true-body (*dharmakāya*) could not be manifested.
Since the traces possess the capacity to manifest the essence, they must both be praised; this is also the identity of essence and function, as well as their non-duality.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form is peerless and incomparable in the world, inconceivable;
therefore, I now pay homage to the Tathāgata, whose form is inexhaustible and whose wisdom is likewise so.
[Commentary: "The Tathāgata’s wondrous form and body have no equal in the world" praises his peerlessness;

"Brahmā above cannot see the Buddha’s crown" describes his incomparable inconceivability. "The various consciousnesses cannot conceive of it" means that it is beyond the deliberations of the manifold cognitions.
"The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible" means that for those who respond with faith and behold him, one should say that there is arising and ceasing [of manifestations].
Therefore it is said: "If there is a response to a stimulus, it is without end. These four lines all praise the body;
that "wisdom is likewise" praises the mind in the same manner as the body was praised above—namely, as being incomparable and inexhaustible.

For this reason, the present homage concludes the praise of the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya*. Master Jiā says: "This line should instead be placed at the beginning of the second verse, before its first two lines."
Next, as for those who brought forth the sūtra, it was because they intended to conclude [the section] at the end of each verse; thus it is so. [The *Chao* states:
Regarding "Brahmā being above," etc., Brahmā resides in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); even when he came from that heaven, he had never seen the mark of the World-Honored One’s crown.
Regarding "Incomparable," the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "For example, when the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni with one..."
In verse, he praised Puṣya Buddha, saying: "In the heavens above and the world below, there is none like the Buddha;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer. Having seen all that exists within these worlds, I find that nothing at all is equal to the Buddha.

Regarding that which transcends the deliberations of the various consciousnesses, speaking in general terms and according to the actual reality, even Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) do not [attain it].
To contemplate the wondrous awakening: it is said that there must be arising and ceasing; when there is a response, [the manifestation] arises, and when the stimulus (*neng*) fades, it ceases.
Since stimuli and responses are inexhaustible, the Tathāgata’s manifestations throughout the Dharma-realm have never been exhausted.
Therefore, it is said that they are "without end" (as verified in the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, which states that Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage [perceive] all that is unspeakable).

Within the kingdom, he manifests his body according to the differences in the faith and inclinations of sentient beings; if this is so even at the eighth stage, it can be known that it is likewise at the stage of Buddhahood.
This is also like Avalokiteśvara’s universal manifestation of thirty-three bodies and his preaching of the Dharma in nineteen ways.
Furthermore, a sutra says: "His wondrous form is serene, responding to all. (All these should be verified. These are examples of this principle. Moreover, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
The Buddha-nature is both form and non-form. Why is it called form? Because it is the vajra-body. Why is it non-form?

Because the ten powers and fearlessnesses are non-form dharmas. Since the vajra-body possesses the thirty-two marks, and these are the form-aspect of the Buddha-nature, we know by verification that it is inexhaustible and eternal. Although the commentators offer two interpretations, both follow the doctrine of the two bodies.

To explain the meaning contained within the scriptural text: if one separates what was previously treated as two into three, then the first [of these]—the wisdom of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body)—is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), which is eternally abiding, and this is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). One should know that the union and separation of these two constitute their difference;
yet, though they differ, they are not different, and they too are eternally abiding.
"All dharmas are eternally abiding; therefore, I take refuge. [Commentary:

Regarding "all dharmas are eternally abiding," this is the second praise of the True Body (*dharmakāya*). It clarifies that while the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests according to the conditions of those who respond, the True Body itself remains eternally abiding and unchanging.
Furthermore, as other virtues are generally present even in the stage of the causal ground (*hetubhūmi*), [the True Body alone is emphasized here].

Regarding the praise of the eternally abiding [nature], my own interpretation differs slightly from the first line, which praises the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), while the subsequent line entirely praises the *dharmakāya* (true body).
As for "the form of the Tathāgata being inexhaustible," "inexhaustible" refers to its eternal abiding; this praises the true body as being without form yet eternally abiding.
How could that which is form, by its very nature, not be inexhaustible? Since it is said to be inexhaustible, it is therefore not [mere] form.
Because the form (*rūpa*) of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and self-luminous, it is said that his form is inexhaustible.

Furthermore, wisdom can also be regarded as form, as it is the very basis of the manifested form (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*); thus, it is said that "form and wisdom are likewise so," which is a praise of the true body (*dharmakāya*), stating that it too is eternally abiding and inexhaustible.
The phrase "all dharmas are eternally abiding" refers generally to all the dharmas of the true body.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the remaining virtues generally pertain to the causal stages (*hetubhūmi*) and so forth," this means that while the four virtues of the Buddha-stage—namely, self, bliss, purity, and permanence—as well as all other [virtues], generally apply to the lower stages, the single virtue of permanence resides only in the Tathāgata.
Therefore, this present sutra specifically praises him in terms of permanence. Thus, the *Śrīgarbha-vyūha-sūtra* says: "In ancient times, the Way of the two bodies of all Buddhas was identical."

"These two bodies of all Bodhisattvas are eternally abiding, yet both are impermanent. *Commentary:* Because from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) downward, there remains the subtle ignorance that causes the fruit of the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), the Sūtra says: "The three stages of Worthiness and the ten stages of Sagehood abide in the retributive fruit;
only the One Buddha-dweller resides in the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*). My private interpretation differs slightly [from the *Yingluo Sūtra*]: the *Yingluo*...
The *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma) states that there are two kinds of Dharma-body: first, the Dharma-body of ultimate fruition; second, the Dharma-body of responsive transformation.
This Dharma-body of responsive transformation follows the form like a shadow, for since the body of fruition is eternal, the responsive body is likewise eternal.
The *Fagu jing* (Dharma Drum Sutra) states: "Eternal liberation is not a name; it is wondrous form abiding in profound stillness, beyond the reach of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas."
...the realm. [Commentary: The next line praises liberation.
Having subdued the faults of the mind as well as the four types of faults of the body, one has reached the stage that is difficult to subdue; therefore, one pays homage to the Dharma King.
[Commentary]: "Mental transgressions" refers to the three poisons and the four inversions; "bodily [transgressions]" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

These two phrases praise his liberation from the evils of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) within the triple world. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows: the three bodily evils and the four types of verbal evils constitute the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśala-karmapatha*).
This clarifies that all evils within the triple world are fully encompassed. Having reached this stage, he has attained the ground that is difficult to subdue.
That which is difficult to subdue is called the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*). There are four kinds of Māras: first, the celestial Māra; second, the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*);
third, the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*); and fourth, the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*). The adamantine mind cannot be subdued by celestial Māras or non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Furthermore, when fetters and delusions are completely purified, one subdues the Māra of afflictions; yet, one has not yet escaped the Māra of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and the Māras of birth, cessation, and death.
Therefore, it is called the "Ground Difficult to Subdue" (*durjayā-bhūmi*). One interpretation states that the "Ground Difficult to Subdue" is precisely the Buddha-ground (*buddha-bhūmi*);

because the Buddha-ground cannot be subdued by the four Māras, it is called the "Ground Difficult to Subdue. This phrase praises liberation from the evil of the *avidyā-vāsabhūmi* (ground of the dwelling of ignorance) outside the three realms.
Furthermore, the first two phrases praise liberation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-vimukti*), while the final phrase praises liberation without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-vimukti*).
The exhaustion of causes refers to the cessation of remaining fruits, which is termed "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*);

the former praise regarding the departure from the four stages of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) is based on the exhaustion of causes to certify the cessation of fruits, while the subsequent praise regarding the departure from ignorance (*avidyā*) cites the cessation of fruits to certify the extinction of causes—thus it is clear that, in reality, both are simultaneously extinguished.
Master Fǎyún said: "There are two kinds of birth and death: first, birth and death by segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*); second, transformation [birth and death] (*nirmāṇa-jarāmaraṇa*)."
"Transforming birth and death" refers to the fruit of the *pariṇāmi-cyuti* (transformative birth and death); "faults and evils" refers to the cause of the *pariṇāmi-cyuti*;
and "the body" refers to the fruit of the *bheda-cyuti* (segmented birth and death). The "four kinds" refer to the cause of the *bheda-cyuti*.

The former clarifies that by severing the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), the fruit of the *pariṇāmi-cyuti* perishes; the latter clarifies that by eliminating the four grounds of abiding (*catur-āśraya-bhūmi*), the retribution of the *bheda-cyuti* is removed.
Regarding the statement that "because they are extinguished, one has subdued them and reached the stage difficult to subdue" (*durjayā-bhūmi*):
there are two ways in which afflictions (*kleśa*) subdue wisdom—first, by creating obstacles so that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are not seen; second, by inducing impermanence.

When the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) arises, these delusions are severed and exhausted, and one clearly perceives the characteristics of phenomena, thereby escaping the burden of delusion. Thus it is called the "stage difficult to subdue. However, because there are still afflictions that induce [impermanence], it is so named.
Since that arising mind cannot escape the burden of the fruit of impermanence, which still remains, it is not said to be "unsubduable. One's own words are merely errors;
when one reaches the stage of Buddhahood through the Vajra-mind, one escapes the burden of the fruits of birth and death of impermanence, and both cause and effect vanish.
Thus, liberation is attained. There is a slight difference from the private views regarding the Vajra-mind: that which is truly difficult to subdue is only the *skandhas* (aggregates).
Because the Tathāgata Mṛtyumara has transcended these two realms, it is said that he has already reached the "Ground Difficult to Subdue" (Durjayā-bhūmi).
Therefore, [the text] pays homage to the Dharma King and offers a concluding eulogy.

[Commentary]: Within the virtue of liberation, there are the three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the four inversions, namely, regarding the impermanent as permanent, and regarding what is non-self as self, and so forth. Regarding suffering as happiness... [and so on].
Purity and the others are likewise; "abandoning the ten non-virtues" means abandoning the mental faults of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Regarding the phrase "ground of the Subduer of Difficulties": first, the term "Difficult to Subdue" is explained, and subsequently, within the context of private intention, that which has already fallen is also explained.
The "Vajra-mind" refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); this Bodhisattva possesses a portion of the inconceivable.

The fruit of transformation (vaiparītya-phala) does not yet escape the demon of birth-and-death, because it involves the subtle arising and ceasing of shifting flux; thus, it does not yet escape the demon of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha-māra), as "formation" is defined by this shifting flux.
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) transcend the three demons but do not yet escape the demon of birth-and-death;
those of Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue) transcend all four demons, and their two bodies abide eternally. This is indeed the teaching of the sūtras and śāstras.
The various recensions differ.
[Commentary]: The next line praises Prajñā.
Because it is the wisdom-body that knows all *dharmas* and freely maintains all phenomena, it is now paid homage.

[Commentary]: "Knowing all *eryā* (realities) with mastery over the body of wisdom" means that *eryā*—in the Liang translation, "mother of wisdom"—refers to the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the basis for the arising of wisdom, it is called the "mother. Since emptiness is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not something produced; therefore, wisdom itself is sovereign.
These two phrases praise the wisdom of emptiness as that which encompasses and sustains all phenomena. "That which encompasses and sustains all phenomena" means...
"Illuminating existence with its variations and encompassing all objects"—this single phrase praises the wisdom of existence (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for even conventional truth can give rise to wisdom;

however, because the wisdom it generates is inferior, it is not given the name "mother. One interpretation states that the first two phrases praise ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) and the final phrase praises skillful means wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
*Er-yan* (the two flames) refers precisely to these two truths, which are capable of generating wisdom.
Therefore, the general designation "Mother of Wisdom" and "Mastery of the Body of Wisdom" refers to clearly illuminating the two truths;
the subsequent phrase "exerting mastery" indicates that she is able to sustain all phenomena through skillful means, transforming sentient beings so that they may give rise to goodness.
Thus, this current prostration both concludes and extols [the preceding].
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the virtue of *prajñā*, the Sūtra states: "Knowing is itself wisdom; all things are the various objects (*ālambana*).
These flames are the original nature of emptiness and quiescence of all objects; this is the emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Since this objective realm of emptiness is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), when one illumines this unconditioned state, the wisdom of emptiness arises spontaneously. The myriad diverse objects are the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

When the objects of the truths are illuminated such that this conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called "possessing wisdom"—because it gives rise to a slight understanding of emptiness—it does not receive the name "Mother.

In the second interpretation, because both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and conventional truths are simultaneously illuminated, they are said to be "distinct"; because the ultimate and conventional are unimpeded, they are said to be "sovereign" (*svatantra*).
One should know that the meaning of "sovereignty" is explained as being unrestrained. In the text, the ultimate truth is first taken as the "Mother."

Next, the two truths, which are able to produce true wisdom, serve as the mother; however, in the "Buddha-Mother Chapter" of the *Āvaśyaka-sūtra* (or *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*), the three truths are taken as the mother.
Thus, in that sūtra, the Bodhisattva Saṃcodana addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, from what do the two initial illuminating wisdoms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arise?
The Buddha replied: "Disciple, they are what are called the truth of existence (*satya*), the truth of non-existence (*asatya*), and the middle [truth]."
The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
even all phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Why is this? Because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are born from the Dharma.

Therefore, this commentary mentions only the two truths, whereby the middle truth (*madhyamasatya*) is subsumed within the ultimate truth. It is appropriate to separate them when the occasion demands.
All the sūtras are thus. [Commentary:
The next line of verse may be seen as a general eulogy:
"I pay homage beyond measure; I pay homage to that which is without analogy; I pay homage to the boundless Dharma; I pay homage to that which is inconceivable."

[Commentary] Regarding the fault of "exceeding measure" within the general refutation in the Sūtra: the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that there is no measure, having already transcended all measure.
The subsequent passage says that "ultimate" means being boundless (*ananta*), uninterrupted, and nameless;
because it has no end, it is called "boundless. How could the principle of the boundless ever be interrupted? It is simply another name for "eternal abiding" (*nitya*).
[Commentary]: From the verse beginning "Out of compassion, protect me" onwards, the second section of this chapter concerns the request for protection.
This is divided into four parts. First, one verse directly requests protection.
"Out of compassion, protect me so that the seeds of the Dharma may increase in this life and in future births; I pray that the Buddha will always sustain me.
[Commentary: Although I have praised the Buddha as the true refuge and the eternally abiding one, if the Buddha does not accord with and rescue me, then my refuge would not be honored.
Therefore, I petition the Buddha to protect the Dharma; for the myriad virtues of the Dharmakāya constitute the seeds.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the respect for the refuge and so forth": if the Buddha constantly follows and protects one, then one's mind of taking refuge becomes respectful.
Regarding "the seeds of the Sūtras and Dharma": the myriad virtues serve as the adornments of the Dharmakāya;
since the body has nothing by which it could be adorned, when the myriad virtues increase, the Dharmakāya is thereby manifested.
[Commentary: The next line of verse concerns the Tathāgata’s granting of protection:
"I have long established you; you were already awakened in former lives, and now I further embrace you; it shall be so likewise in future births."

[Commentary]: "I request that you permit only the two [lifetimes] of the present and future, while allowing for the inclusion of past lives as well, to clarify the profound and far-reaching nature of this protection.
[Sub-commentary]: "I request that you permit only the present and future, while allowing for the inclusion of past lives as well, to clarify the long-lasting duration of this protection."
[Commentary: The next one and a half lines concern her respectful salutation following the Buddha’s permission for her repeated request for protection.
She says, "I have performed meritorious deeds in the present life and in other worlds; may these roots of all such goodness be graciously accepted by you.
At that time, Śrīmālā and her retinue prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha's feet.
[Commentary]: To say that the Tathāgata has long since rescued me means that I must have already performed wholesome deeds; "other worlds" refers to the future.

If he were to constantly protect me throughout the three periods of time, then my performance of wholesome deeds would be uninterrupted; therefore, I further request that he grant me a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
[Commentary]: "I further request that you grant me instruction" refers to the passage "I pray only that you will take me into your care," which concludes the petition for salvation.
As for the nameless commentary stating, "The praise and eulogy of Śrīmālā is complete," by using the present to verify the past, we know that the realization of awakening was not remote.
Is it not fitting, then, that one should obtain a noble title based on these roots of goodness?
[Commentary] Fourth, from "The Buddha [spoke] among the assembly" onwards, the section clarifying the Buddha’s bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is also divided into six parts.
First, the granting of the causal basis:
while among the assembly, the Buddha immediately bestowed a prediction upon him, saying, "Because you have praised the Tathāgata’s true merits, by this root of goodness..."
Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, among gods and humans, as sovereign kings in all places of birth,
you shall always behold me appearing before you and praising me, no different from how it is now.
[Commentary]: The second section, from "Furthermore, he shall again make offerings" onwards, grants the fruit [of his practice].

He shall again make offerings to immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddhas; after twenty thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Samantaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
[Commentary] Third, from the passage "from that Buddha-land... onwards, it is affirmed that his land is free from defilement.

In that Buddha-land, there are no evil destinies, nor the sufferings of old age, sickness, decline, affliction, or anything disagreeable; furthermore, even the names of unwholesome and evil courses of action do not exist.
[Commentary: Fourth, from the passage "the sentient beings of that land" onwards, it records its utter purity.

The physical strength, lifespan, and the various requisites for the five desires of the sentient beings in that land are all joyful and superior to those of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Those sentient beings are exclusively of the One Great Vehicle (*ekamahāyāna*), being beings who have cultivated roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
All gathered there.
[Commentary] Fifth, from Lady Śrīmālā onwards, it clarifies the making of vows by humans and devas.
When Lady Śrīmālā received her prediction of enlightenment, immeasurable sentient beings, including devas and humans, vowed to be born in that land.
[Commentary] Sixth, it clarifies that the Buddha bestows predictions upon them such that both humans and devas may all behold them;
the World-Honored One records that they shall all attain rebirth there.
[Commentary] From the passage "At that time, after Queen Śrīmālā heard her prediction" onwards, it clarifies the practice of one's own level.
The twentieth chapter, "On the Great Receptions," praises the Buddha’s truthfulness and seeks reliance upon the eternally abiding [Dharma]. Its primary purpose is for the cultivation of goodness;
furthermore, taking refuge now differs from the past, and the precepts likewise ought to be modified from the former.

Thus, the great receptions received today differ from the five precepts of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) of yore. Within this, three sections are established, the first of which clarifies the reception of the precepts.
The second section, beginning from "World-Honored One, from this day forward," clearly explains the formal reception of the precepts.
The third section, beginning from "World-Honored One, Lord of the Dharma" and continuing to the end of the chapter, establishes a vow to sever doubts;

because one is about to receive the precepts, one first cultivates proper deportment to still the will. This cultivation of deportment and stilling of the will is essential for receiving the precepts. Thus, the second [section] follows immediately.
Having received the precepts, as soon as the ceremony was concluded, the great assembly harbored doubts: "Since Śrīmālā is a woman, her resolve ought to be weak;
yet the precepts she has received are exceedingly grave and far-reaching. We fear that her words may not correspond to reality.
Therefore, on the third occasion, she established a vow to sever these doubts and thereby perfect her reception of the precepts.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "to still one's will" in the twentieth chapter on Receiving [the Precepts]: "still" (jìng) means pure and secluded; "pure" (jìng) means clean and bright.
This refers to the profound importance of the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), which extend far back even unto *bodhi*.
At that time, having heard her prediction of enlightenment, Śrīmālā stood with reverence and received the ten great vows.

[Commentary] Regarding "standing with reverence": normally, when receiving the precepts, one must kneel upon the ground; however, since the Buddha was now in mid-air, if she had knelt on the ground, it would have been as if she were reaching out to grasp at something distant.
Therefore, she received them while standing. As for "receiving the ten great vows," this refers to the aforementioned vows.

This is the mind capable of receiving; it receives these ten precepts as the object to be received. Although one previously observed the five precepts, that which was sought was the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna);
now, because one takes the eternally abiding Bodhi as the goal, it is called the "Great Receiving."
[Commentary]: Within the second section, the formal reception of the precepts, there are ten precepts which are further divided into three categories.
First, the initial five precepts are called the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts for restraining conduct). "Śīla" (律) means category; "saṃvara" (儀) means deportment.

These five precepts restrain evil within the mind, ensuring that one’s deportment and its various aspects do not lose their integrity. Second, from "not acting for oneself" [the remaining five precepts follow].
The four types of restraint mentioned below are called the precept of gathering in sentient beings;
the third, from "gathering in the true Dharma" down to "never losing," consists of one type of restraint called the precept of gathering in wholesome dharmas.

[Commentary]: Regarding the bundling of the ten types of precepts into three, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (瓔珞經) also contains this text. Its "Chapter on the Great Assembly Receiving and Studying" states:
"O Son of the Buddha, I now bind together the root of all precepts for the sake of the bodhisattvas; these are what are subsumed within the three gates of receiving [precepts].
The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgraha*) consists of the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates; the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha*) consists of..."

The precepts of restraint encompassed by loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are what are known as the ten *pārājika* rules; the scriptural text is extensive, O Son of the Buddha.

These three [immeasurables] receive and sustain the three types of receiving the precepts—those already taught, those yet to be taught, and those currently being taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
and they are that which has been studied, will be studied, and is currently being studied by all Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present.

Regarding the precepts of the true Dharma of all Buddhas: it is impossible for any Buddha or any Bodhisattva to enter the gateway of these precepts of the true Dharma and yet attain the fruit of the unsurpassed path—the stage of emptiness and equality.

These three types of precepts do not apply to the Lesser Vehicle; they constitute the discipline of the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) and pervade the three superior karmas. Here, they are manifested through the aspects of body and speech.

It is called "Restraint" (*saṃvara*). Based upon this restraint, one gives rise to the bodhicitta; it can cease all unwholesome actions that do not lead to completion, and through diligent cultivation of all virtues, it fulfills the vow for enlightenment.
This is termed the Bodhisattva’s practice of "Gathering Wholesome Dharmas. Regarding the practice of "Benefiting Sentient Beings," one employs the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*):

with great loving-kindness, one bestows happiness; with great compassion, one extracts suffering; thus one gathers and rescues sentient beings, ceasing [selfishness] to benefit both oneself and others.
Because benefiting others is called "gathering sentient beings," these three are collectively termed "precepts" (śīla).

This refers precisely to the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (tri-vidha-śīla-saṃvara), for which there are extensive texts in such works as the Vaipulya, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, and the *Bhūmivibhāga-śāstra* (or *Dharaṇīśvararāja-paripṛcchā*).
[Commentary]: One who intends to transform others must first rectify their own person; therefore, one first receives the precepts for personal cultivation.
Because a Great Being (mahāsattva) rectifies themselves primarily in order to transform sentient beings, there follows next the precept for gathering in sentient beings (*sattvasaṃgraha-śīla*).

Since the path of transforming others does not consist merely of ceasing evil, but requires the cultivation of merit and goodness, the third is the precept for gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*). Thus, the first [precept] is for oneself...

The first section primarily clarifies manifesting for oneself while concurrently manifesting for others; the second takes manifesting for others as its primary tenet while still elucidating one's own practice;
the third explains both self-practice and manifesting for others together, thereby fully enumerating the conduct of a Mahāsattva. This is clear.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "One who wishes to transform others must first rectify one's own person," the Sūtra says:
"It is impossible for one who is themselves bound to be able to untie the bonds of others. Thus, it is said that this also reveals the second aspect of the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others:
namely, that the transformation of others still relies upon one's own practice. Therefore, within each and every precept, it is stated: "up until the attainment of Bodhi."
[Commentary]: Within the first category, the restraint of moral discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), the five precepts are divided into three parts.

First, regarding the initial [precept], it clarifies that one who has received the five precepts of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) from the past does not yet give rise to the thought of transgression.
“World-Honored One, from this day forth until I attain Bodhi, I shall not give rise to a thought of transgression regarding the precepts I have received.
[Commentary: The disciplinary laws of the Hīnayāna restrain only body and speech, but do not restrain the mind.

Now, furthermore, he refines that which was previously practiced to the utmost degree of clarity and purity. Since these precepts guard against what occurred in the past, they are placed at the beginning.
[Commentary]: "Refining what one previously practiced" means that while the five precepts were observed in the past, one now adds the restraint of a mind that does not transgress them.
[Sub-commentary]:
The second section has two types of vows, clarifying the commitment not to give rise to evil toward the two objects of honor and the lowly.
"Blessed One, from this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of pride toward my elders and superiors.
Blessed One, from this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of malice toward any sentient being."
[Commentary: Regarding those who do not give rise to arrogance toward elders and superiors, there are three categories for "elders" and "superiors": elder brothers and seniors.
Regarding those who do not give rise to anger toward sentient beings, this refers generally to all classes of conscious beings.

As for the reason why one restrains arrogance toward those above and forbids anger toward those below, there are three interpretations. The first states: In the nature of ordinary people, toward those above...
Because they delight in [superiority] and so forth, they give rise to pride; because they seek universality over those below, they give rise to anger.

Since both are not the Path, one honors the superior to cease pride and humbles the superior to prevent anger. Second, it is said that among the superior, anger arises frequently while pride is rare. Why is this?

It is because those who are honored rely upon their own nobility and take pleasure in overbearing the masses below; thus, those below frequently give rise to anger, yet their virtue remains [unmatched].
Because they are venerable, pride arises little; because they are superior, overweening pride (*adhimāna*) arises much, yet anger arises little. Why is this?
It is because it is naturally possible to treat them with contempt as being inferior to oneself, so pride arises much; furthermore, since they act according to their own will, anger arises little.

It is said that if even a slight pride does not arise toward those who are honorable and superior, how much less would overweening pride arise toward those who are inferior and superior? Moreover, regarding those who are inferior and superior...
If even minor anger cannot be ceased, how much less so for the great anger of those who are superior? These examples all use the light to illustrate the heavy.
Third, regarding superiors and elders as objects worthy of respect, one fears that pride (*māna*) may contradict respect; thus, toward superiors, one ceases pride.
Regarding inferiors as objects worthy of compassion, one fears that hatred (*dveṣa*) may contradict compassion; thus, toward inferiors, one ceases hatred.

[Commentary] Regarding "the three positions are honorable," etc.: "Honorable" (*zun*) refers to sovereign, father, and teacher. "Emolument" (*zhi*, pronounced *zhì*) refers to salary; it refers to the rank and position of an elder brother.
Because one seeks to oppress those who are inferior to oneself, anger arises; that is, because one delights in harassing those lower than oneself, anger arises toward them.
The terms "delight" (*hao*) and "seek" (*qiu*) are used interchangeably in the ornate prose, whether stated as such or implied.
Those who follow me crosswise say they dare not fail to comply with me; since we thus accord with one another, there arises little anger toward those below.
[Commentary] The third section has two types of feeling, clarifying that one vows not to give rise to evil toward the two objects of self and others.
"Bhagavān, from this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall not give rise to envy toward the physical forms of others or external requisites.
Bhagavān, from this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall not give rise to avarice regarding internal or external phenomena."
[Commentary] It can be seen that one does not give rise to envy toward others and does not give rise to stinginess toward oneself.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "toward the physical form and so forth of others" in the Sūtra: "physical form" refers to the primary retribution (*vipāka*), while "and so forth" refers to the various requisites, which are the secondary retribution (*upabhoga*).
Seeing another who is superior to oneself, one does not give rise to envy; internally, this refers to the primary retribution such as the head, eyes, hands, and feet; externally, it refers to...
The kingdom, city, wife, children, and so forth are the *paribhoga* (enjoyment) retribution; one should joyfully give these away to seek the wisdom of a Buddha. [Commentary:
Regarding the second [category], the precept of gathering sentient beings, the four types of vows are further divided into two parts.
First, there are two vows that together clarify the compassionate mind that bestows happiness; second, there are two vows that likewise clarify the mind of pity that uproots suffering. Regarding...
First, there are two types of receiving, which are further divided into two. First is the vow to receive and provide the fruit of happiness.
"World-Honored One, from this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not for my own sake receive or store up wealth and goods;
whatever I may receive shall be entirely for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of suffering beings."

[Commentary] The passage "not for one's own sake receiving or accumulating wealth and goods" clarifies the goodness of restraint (*śīla*). From "whatever one receives" onwards, it clarifies the goodness of action (*karman*).

[Sub-commentary] Within the granting of pleasant fruits, one restrains the hoarding for oneself; whatever wealth and goods one receives are intended solely to relieve the poverty and suffering of others.
Ultimately, they bring about accomplishment and cause them to obtain the fruit of happiness.
[Commentary] The subsequent section clarifies the bestowal of the causes of happiness.
"World-Honored One, from this day forth until I attain Bodhi, I shall not act for my own sake, but shall practice the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as one."
For the sake of all sentient beings, one gathers and sustains them with a mind free from attachment, a mind that knows no weariness, and an unobstructed mind.

[Commentary] Practicing the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) not for one's own sake clarifies the excellence of cessation (*śīla*); from "for the sake of all sentient beings" onwards, it clarifies the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding "with a mind free from attachment," this refers to a mind devoid of greed. "A mind that knows no weariness" refers to a mind that never tires of its efforts.

This refers to one who has no mind of anger, no mind of obstruction, and no mind of delusion. Furthermore, it says "by means of a mind free from attachment" (an-āsaṅga-citta), which means not acting out of affectionate views (*sneha-dṛṣṭi*).
If there were affectionate views, then the path of transformation would become a leakage (*āsrava*), and one would feel weary of or satisfied with saṃsāra;
moreover, there would be obstructions in transforming sentient beings. Furthermore, it says "do not use a mind stained by attachment," which explains that [one should not act] with such a mind.

He shares with ordinary beings their lack of a heart of insatiability, yet he does not share with those of the Two Vehicles their lack of an unimpeded mind; thus he is one with the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas).

[Commentary] Within the cause of bestowing happiness, he practices the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) himself; within the practice of goodness, he transforms sentient beings, yet he possesses a sense of weariness.
That which is "sufficient" (paryāpta) is precisely the absence of a mind of non-delight; that which possesses a mind of delusion is precisely that which has obstructions.

The mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) is threefold: first, the object-conditioned (*dharmālambana*); second, the sentient-being-conditioned (*sattvālambana*); and third, the objectless (*anālambana*). These are set forth in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Regarding the object-conditioned:

it is because the phenomena such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are empty. Regarding the sentient-being-conditioned: it is because one takes sentient beings as the object and perceives the aspect of their attaining happiness.

Those who have no object of focus take the Tathāgata as their object; because they realize that the principle of all sentient beings and all Buddhas is of one essence and non-dual, it is said that "all sentient beings are also suchness," and even Maitreya is suchness.
Now, since suchness is neither dual nor different, the compassion born of attachment and views is merely the object-condition of sentient beings, taking only sentient beings as its object.
Because they perceive the signs of attaining pleasure, they harbor a mind of attachment toward sentient beings;

once there is a mind of attachment, their transformative teaching becomes a leakage (*āsrava*), as it encounters obstacles regarding material things. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"A bodhisattva adorns the Buddha-lands and brings sentient beings to maturity with a mind free from attachment and views; within the sphere of non-action and emptiness, they discipline themselves without weariness."

This "disgust" is called the liberation through skillful means and wisdom. Regarding the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), these are called the "four integrations" because they integrate sentient beings.
That which is beloved by the hearts of sentient beings is precisely these four dharmas.

If a Great Being employs these sympathies to guide and lead them, they will become the refuge for all beings. Once sentient beings have taken refuge in him, he then leads them by means of the Mahāyāna.
Because he delivers them by means of the True Path, it is said: "First, one uses the hook of desire to draw them in; afterwards, one causes them to enter the Buddha-way.

Regarding the first, gathering [beings] through giving (*dāna*): the Bodhisattva, with a mind that has nothing to relinquish, practices two kinds of giving that can gather sentient beings—first, the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), and second, the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
If there are sentient beings who delight in material wealth, one then provides them with material wealth.
Regarding "gathering through giving": if one gathers beings who delight in the Dharma by means of the gift of the Dharma, these two types of giving can benefit all sentient beings.
Having received this grace and benefit, they consequently give rise to affectionate hearts and follow the Path to abide in the True Principle;
therefore, this is called "gathering through giving. Second is "gathering through kind speech."

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva uses words that are skillful and gentle to accord with the faculties and inclinations of all beings, comforting and instructing them, then all sentient beings will delight in hearing it;
because of this, they will give rise to affectionate hearts and rely upon the bodhisattva, subsequently receiving the Path and abiding in the True Principle.
For this reason, it is called "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*). Regarding the inclusion of the three beneficial practices (*arthacaryā*): the bodhisattva... [is so called].
The practice of body, speech, and mind is able to cause all beings to receive individual benefits. Once sentient beings have received these benefits, they rejoice in what they have gained;
because of this, they give rise to affection and attachment, relying upon [the teacher] to receive the Path and abide in the True Principle.

Therefore, it is called the "beneficial conduct" (*arthacaryā*) that encompasses the four *saṃgrahavastu*. Regarding the "encompassing through the four means of attraction" (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*): the Bodhisattva uses the Dharma-eye to clearly perceive sentient beings.

Because of this fundamental condition, all those who share a similar inclination follow along; they divide their forms and disperse their shadows, universally harmonizing their light and aligning with the activities of others so that each may receive benefit.

Since they skillfully participate in these same activities, affection and love arise, leading them to rely [on the teacher] and receive the Way, thereby attaining abiding in Nirvana. Thus, benefiting others through "common purpose" (samānārthatā) is called "attraction" (saṃgraha).
"Those with insatiable minds" means they are weary of or satiated by [salt] (yàn; alternatively read yàn). [Commentary:
The second section contains two precepts clarifying the compassionate mind that uproots suffering, which is also divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the uprooting of the fruits of suffering.
“World-Honored One, from this day forth until I attain enlightenment, if I see sentient beings who are solitary, imprisoned, diseased,

or beset by various calamities and hardships, I shall never abandon them for even a moment. I will surely seek their peace and security, benefiting them with righteousness and leading them to escape all suffering before finally departing.”

[Commentary] From "If one sees the orphaned and the solitary" onwards, it clarifies the goodness of *śamatha* (calm abiding). From "One must desire peace and security" onwards, it clarifies the goodness of *vipaśyanā* (insight cultivation).
One who lacks a father is called "orphaned" (*gu*); one who lacks a son is called "solitary" (*du*). To be in a prison is to be "dark" (*you*);

to have shackles and fetters is to be "bound" (*xi*). Affliction by punishment is called "sickness" (*ji*); when sickness is extreme, it is called "illness" (*bing*). When it concerns oneself, it is termed "calamity" (*e*); when speaking of others, it is termed "hardship" (*nan*).

That which arises from internal faults is called "distress" (*kūn*); that which is externally imposed is called "suffering" (*kǔ*). To benefit others through righteousness—where "righteousness" (*yì*) refers to principle (*lǐ*)—is to employ principle to alleviate the ten types of suffering.
Only after this may one say that causing them to reach *bodhi* constitutes "renunciation" (*shě*).
[Commentary]: "If one sees those below" clarifies that the goodness of cessation resides in the *lingyu* (囹圄)—*ling* (上力郎反, 下魚舉反, 又魚據反) means prison;
*wei* (危, 魚為反) means high or precarious; *an* (安) means not at peace; *nan* (難, 奴旦反) means calamity;
and *xi* (舋, 許覲反) means transgression—all of which follow the principle of simultaneously uprooting the ten sufferings.
[Commentary: The subsequent section clarifies the cause for uprooting suffering.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth until I attain Bodhi, if I should see those who follow the various evil disciplines of hunters and keepers of livestock, or those who violate the precepts, I shall never abandon them.
When I have attained power, wherever I may see these sentient beings, I shall subdue them as is appropriate."
Those who are to be subdued, he subdues; those who are to be gathered, he gathers. Why? Because through subduing and gathering, the Dharma is made to endure for a long time.
When the Dharma endures for a long time, devas and humans flourish and the evil realms diminish.
Seeing this benefit in being able to follow and turn the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata, he rescues and gathers them, never abandoning them.

[Commentary]: Regarding the extraction of the causes of suffering, there are also the practices of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). From the passage "if one sees [beings] being caught or raised" and below, it clarifies the goodness of *śamatha*.
From the passage "when I obtain power" and below, it clarifies the goodness of *vipaśyanā*. To seek externally is called "catching"; to keep within is called "raising.

The various evil vows (*duḥśīla*) refer to the sixteen types of evil vows; this is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and concerning those who violate the precepts, which refers to their transgressions.
Regarding those who possess fundamental vows, there are those who initiate evil through improper discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*) and commit transgressions that are good at first but evil in the end.
As for "when I have attained power," there are two kinds of power: first, the power of influence (*prabhāva-bala*); second, the power of the Path (*mārga-bala*).
Regarding "in various places": if one does not practice goodness, then all paths are closed, and one wanders through birth and death, migrating among the six destinies.
Therefore, in various places, the Great Being sees those with heavy evil and subdues them through his sovereign power; he sees those with light evil and gathers them in through the power of the Path;
he causes the cessation of evil and the cultivation of goodness, whereby the holy transformation endures for a long time.

When the holy transformation abides in the world, good beings come forth and evil ones depart; thus, devas and humans flourish while the evil realms diminish, and the vessels for the Path become abundant.
Once [the merit] has increased, the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma can be perpetually turned. [Commentary:
Within the section on uprooting the causes of suffering, "stopping" refers to stopping the act of abandoning [beings], while "gathering" refers to stopping [their] transgressions.

To practice gathering means to practice goodness. Regarding "catching and raising": "catching" (upper character *bǔ*, read as *gù*; lower character *tí*, read as *yǎng*) means to secure; "raising" (*chù*, read as *xǔ*) means to nurture.
It is a reversal of nourishment. Regarding the sixteen evil observances, the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra (Dà jīng) volume twenty-seven states:

"Good son, what further is meant by 'cultivating the precepts'? If one can destroy the sixteen evil observances of all sentient beings and cause them to be severed forever, this is called cultivating the precepts. What are the sixteen? First, for the sake of gain and food..."
1. Having fattened a black sheep, he sells it for profit; having bought it, he slaughters it for profit. 2. Having fattened a ram, he sells it for profit;

having bought it, he slaughters it for profit. 3. Having fattened a pig, he sells it for profit; having bought it, he slaughters it for profit. 4. Having fattened an ox-calf, he sells it for profit; having bought it, he slaughters it for profit. 5. Having fattened a steer, he sells it for profit;

having bought it, he slaughters it for profit. 6. Having fattened a bull, he sells it for profit; having bought it, he slaughters it for profit. 7. [Having fattened] a cow, he sells it for profit; having bought it, he slaughters it for profit.
1. Raising chickens to fatten them and then selling them; 2. Buying them for profit and slaughtering them;
3. Fishing with hooks; 4. Being a hunter; 5. Robbery; 6. Being an executioner; 7. Trapping birds in nets; 8. Divisive speech; 9. Being a jailer; 10.
Chanting spells to subdue dragons—may [the Buddha] enable sentient beings to forever sever these [ten evils].
These sixteen evil karmas are called "violating the original vow while practicing the precepts. This is because, prior to receiving the precepts, one's evil pervaded the entire *dharmadhātu*;

when one was about to advance to receive them, the mind of goodness arose in contrast to those previously evil objects, and thus the cause for the arising of the precepts likewise pervaded the *dharmadhātu*.
Now that one has violated the precepts, one contravenes the initial commitment; therefore, it is said that they are "violated."

The original vow constitutes the initial goodness at the time of first receiving [the precepts]; subsequent transgressions constitute the later evil. The non-restraint (*akuśala-saṃvara*) exists prior to the formal reception.
As for "power," it refers to the power of kings as well as the power of devas and nāgas; by these, all paths of untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala-mārga*) are shut off.

Regarding the "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*), the term "wheel" possesses two meanings: the sense of turning and the sense of crushing and grinding. Why is this? Because the Buddha has realized the Four [Noble Truths]...
Because the Truths (satya-dharma) possess the quality of being turned, they are called a wheel (*cakra*); because they can destroy afflictions (*kleśa*), they are also called a wheel.
Just as the precious wheel of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) can defeat enemies, so too the precious wheel of the Buddha’s Dharma can destroy afflictions.
Therefore, immediately after attaining enlightenment, the Buddha proceeded to Vārāṇasī and taught the Four Truths to the five bhikṣus and eighty thousand devas.
It is called "turning the wheel of Dharma" because it transforms that mind and destroys those afflictions.
Furthermore, as long as there are vessels for the path of the three vehicles up until the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, the wheel of Dharma constantly turns. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, I turned the wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, explaining in detail the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates; now, once again, I turn the supreme [wheel of Dharma]."
Because it is the wondrous, supreme, and great Dharma-wheel, it is said that it can be turned perpetually.
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-vyākhyā-ṭīkā-śi-yao*, Fascicle One;
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-vyākhyā-ṭīkā-śi-yao*, Fascicle Two.
[Commentary]: Regarding the third [category], there is one name for the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), which is also divided into two parts.
The first directly clarifies the non-forgetting of the gathering and upholding of the true Dharma:
"World-Honored One, from this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall gather and uphold the true Dharma, never forgetting or losing it."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "never forgetting the upholding of the True Dharma," since the upholding of the True Dharma is the practice of those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, it is called the "practice of others.
Now, although Śrīmālā’s manifest state is at the seventh stage, she says she does not forget;
this is simply because she aspires to attain the eighth stage and above, and thus she dares not for even a moment forget her resolve to uphold the True Dharma.
It is not that one attains it spontaneously and does not forget; rather, this is the second explanation of "not forgetting.
Why is this? One who forgets the Dharma forgets the Mahāyāna; one who forgets the Mahāyāna forgets the pāramitās;
one who forgets the pāramitās has no desire for the Mahāyāna; and if a bodhisattva is not resolute in the Mahāyāna, then [they will fall away].
Unable to grasp the true Dharma, they are utterly incapable of transcending the stage of ordinary beings according to their inclinations.
[Commentary] Within the second explanation, there are three types of practice and three types of desire. The three practices refer to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward;
the three desires refer to those from the seventh stage downward.
[Commentary]: Regarding the third point, the determination that [the practitioner] resides at or below the seventh stage, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths now further cultivates immeasurable merit, namely the ten *pāramitās*, up to the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās* of all gathered wholesome dharmas;
all these dharma-gates are subsumed within my mind, moment after moment."

The passage "departing from the mind" refers to the three types of aspiration in this present sutra; since two types of aspiration are already mentioned in that [other] sutra text, the aspiration for the Mahāyāna can be understood [as the third].
[Commentary]: Regarding the three practices: first, the practice of receiving and upholding the True Dharma; second, the Mahāyāna practice; and third, the practice of the pāramitās.
From the seventh stage downward, it is not that they do not possess the Mahāyāna, but rather that its great meaning has not yet been manifested. Why is this?
Because from the seventh stage downward, their severing of fetters is identical to that of the two vehicles, and they likewise emerge from the triple world.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that from the seventh stage downward, the severing of fetters is equal to that of the Two Vehicles:

the *Yíngluò jīng* (Ābhūṣaṇa-sūtra), in its explanation of the dharmas contemplated by the mind of a Bodhisattva at the seventh stage, states that this refers to the "knowledge that exhausts karmic retribution, which is unobstructed and unhindered.

This means that by means of the wisdom of the three emptinesses, one contemplates the cessation of the habitual tendencies of the three realms—the fruits of form and mind—without remainder, such that all merit and functional effort [are transcended].
The composition is completed.

[Commentary: However, because one has not yet reached the eighth stage and above, where one merges with the various streams so that there are no further divergent paths, the Great Meaning remains unclarified.
[Commentary] "Mysteriously merging with all streams" refers to the inconceivable, effortless contemplation (*anābhoga-bhāvanā*) explained in that sūtra regarding the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*).

It is called the great wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-mahāprajñā*) and the great function of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-mahāprayoga*). Therein, the habituation to form (*rūpa-vāsanā*) is absent and ignorance (*avidyā*) is also exhausted.
Matters spanning a million kalpas and matters of immeasurable Buddha-lands are realized and manifested simultaneously in a single moment of mind, appearing in the form of a Buddha.
It manifests the forms of all sentient beings by performing [deeds] simultaneously within a single thought-moment, because it is characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*).

As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fascicle 38, states: "When a Bodhisattva dwells in the eighth stage, the Immovable (*Acalā*), they immediately relinquish all practices involving effort and attain the dharma of effortlessness;
the activities of body, speech, and mind cease, and they abide in the practice of fruition."

Furthermore, it is said that, O Son of the Buddha, by the power of the original vows of the Bodhisattvas on this stage, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, personally appear before them and bestow the wisdom of the Tathāgata, enabling them to enter the gateway of the stream of Dharma. This is like one who wishes to board a ship to enter the great ocean:
before reaching the sea, much effort and labor are required; once they have reached the sea, they simply follow the wind.
Relying on human power to reach the great ocean, what one travels in a single day cannot be matched even after a hundred years before reaching it;
likewise, O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva likewise accumulates the vast provisions of roots of goodness and,
boarding the ship of the Mahāyāna, reaches the ocean of Bodhisattva conduct in a single thought-moment through effortlessness.

By employing wisdom, one enters the sphere of the knowledge of all-knowledge; this is something that cannot be attained even by those who practice with effort throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.

[Commentary]: "Pāramitā" means "reaching the other shore. From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downward, although it is also the signless (*animitta*) other shore, because one cannot yet illuminate all things simultaneously, the meaning of *pāramitā* is not yet fully manifest.

From the seventh stage downward, one also cultivates the myriad practices (*sādhana*), but because one cannot do so in equal measure within a single thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), one does not yet receive the name of "gathering and sustaining" (*saṃgraha*).
[Commentary]: "Illuminating all simultaneously" means that the ten *pāramitās* are practiced and illuminated at once within a single thought-moment.
It is called "not uniform" because from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downward, one practices the myriad practices sequentially.

[Commentary]: The reason why the Mahāyāna pāramitās are subsumed [under these stages] is that those from the eighth stage upward are designated as such because they clarify the "three desires," which are the mental states of aspiring to attain these three practices. It is permitted that these exist from the seventh stage downward;
however, these three practices are all employed within a single mind from the eighth stage upward, though they are established as distinct according to their specific meanings.

Because it is titled "The Ear," it says: "If one forgets the dharmas, then the three practices are entirely forgotten; once the three practices are forgotten, the desire for those three practices is also forgotten.
It should have included the "desire for the *pāramitās*," but this was omitted for brevity. When listing the practices, "reception" (*parigraha*) is placed first;
when listing the desires, the "Mahāyāna" is placed at the beginning. This is merely done for convenience and does not represent the primary intent.

[Commentary] Regarding "following the sequence" and so forth: it refers to following the sequence within the three practices, as one intends to list the *pāramitās* immediately after the third practice.
Since the sūtra has already omitted the three practices, it now forgets the three intentions (*chanda*).
[Commentary] From "Entering according to one's inclination" onwards, it clarifies that failing in practice leads to the arising of evil.
[Sub-commentary] If one cannot enter the Dharma-gates according to one's inclination and furthermore cannot transcend the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), is this not a great fault?
This section of text generally takes the three realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) from the seventh ground and below as its scope.
Regarding "Because of the precept of wholesome dharmas," the Commentary states: "It is permitted that they exist.
[Commentary] Third, the conclusion on non-forgetfulness:
I have seen such immeasurable great transgressions, and I also see the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who will, in the future, uphold the True Dharma.
Because of his immeasurable merit and benefit, the Bodhisattva accepts this great acceptance.
[Commentary] From "I see that... onwards is the third section, which concludes by stating that he does not forget. Forgetting leads to calamity, whereas not forgetting brings about blessings;
therefore, he accepts it without forgetting.
[Commentary] The *Wuming shu* (Commentary on the Nameless) comprehensively summarizes the latter two chapters as not exceeding the practices prior to the seventh stage;

this accords with the present intent. It states: "When retribution is superior, the Way is lofty; when practice is refined, the fruit can be realized within oneself. Advancing one's virtue is called 'practice' (*xing*);
benefiting others is called 'vow' (*yuan*). Thus, among the ten types of reception, maintaining the precepts without transgression is primary—this constitutes the three vows.
This is because making the consolation of sentient beings the foremost priority. Among the ten precepts, five clarify the cessation of evil and five explain the cultivation of goodness.
The cultivation of goodness takes the upholding of the True Dharma as its source, while the cessation of evil takes the observance of the precepts as its foundation.

Therefore, these two ends are established to unify all practices. Since the advancement of virtue through the cultivation of goodness takes compassion as its primary principle, the first two [precepts]...

The first two practices clarify loving-kindness (*maitrī*), while the latter two clarify compassion (*karuṇā*). Since the profundity and magnitude of gain and loss are about to be elucidated, they are explained through successive stages.
"Desire" (*chanda*) is the initial gateway for approaching the Path; "Pāramitās" are the sublime practices of the Mahāyāna;

and "Mahāyāna" is the ultimate designation for the pinnacle of principle. Furthermore, "encompassing the True Dharma" (*saṃgraha-saddharma*) is a compound name combining both person and dharma. Indeed.
"When the end is forgotten, the beginning is lost; such is the nature of numbers. The meaning of this chapter is thus elucidated below.
[Commentary] From "The Dharma-lord World-Honored One" onwards, this is the third section of the chapter, "Taking an Oath to Eliminate Doubts," which itself contains four parts.
The first is "Taking an Oath before the Buddha."

The World-Honored One, Lord of Dharma, is present as my witness; yet, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows this directly before him, sentient beings possess meager roots of goodness and give rise to nets of doubt regarding the precepts, for the ten major precepts are extremely difficult to fulfill.
Consequently, they may for a long night fail to obtain benefit, welfare, or peace and happiness. To bring them peace, I now speak these words of truthful vow before the Buddha.
If I receive these ten great vows and practice them as described, by virtue of this oath, may celestial flowers rain down and celestial wondrous sounds emerge amidst this great assembly.

[Commentary] Regarding the third section, "Establishing an Oath to Eliminate Doubts," the citation of the Buddha as a witness means that the "witness" (zhèngzhě) refers to one who provides verification (*sākṣin*).
One who receives [the teachings] must be able to practice them; if faith is thin, doubt arises. Once doubt arises, one enters the net.
Having entered the dense net of birth and death, how can one attain the peace and joy of Nirvana?
[Commentary: The second section, from "When these words were spoken" onwards, clarifies that the raining of celestial flowers and the emergence of sounds serve as proof.
When these words were spoken, various celestial flowers rained down from the void, and a wondrous voice issued forth, saying:
"So it is, so it is! What you have said is true and not otherwise."
[Commentary]: It is said that where there is sound, there must be speech; thus, sound is used to prove that speech is not non-existent. Where there are flowers, there must be fruit;

thus, the flowers are used to prove that practice will necessarily bear fruit. Thirdly, from the passage "He saw those exquisite flowers" onwards, it clarifies that the doubts of the assembly were severed and they subsequently made vows.
Upon seeing those exquisite flowers and hearing those sounds, all those in the assembly had their doubts entirely dispelled;
leaping for joy beyond measure, they made this vow: "May we always be together with Śrīmālā, sharing in her every practice."
[Commentary: Fourth, it is evident that the Buddha bestows predictions (vyākaraṇa).
The World-Honored One grants predictions to the entire great assembly according to their respective aspirations.
[Commentary: From the passage "At that time, Śrīmālā again before the Buddha" onwards, this is the third section within the stage of practicing one's own level.
In the Chapter on Great Vows, since taking refuge and receiving the precepts differ from those of the past, the vows are likewise further developed as superior vows.
These look forward to the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, which differs from the former vows regarding the body’s extinction and wisdom’s cessation. Within this, three sections are established:
first, clarifying the making of vows for the sake of vows; second, from "By means of these roots of goodness" onwards, the actual formulation of the three [vows].
The third vow is elucidated by the Buddha’s confirmation, beginning from the words "At that time, the World-Honored One...
At that time, Śrīmālā again made three great vows before the Buddha, speaking these words: "By means of these true vows, may I bring comfort to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings."
[Commentary: Regarding these "actual vows," it is said generally that they refer to my present three great vows.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s establishment of his resolve is not merely for himself, but must first be for the sake of others; thus it says, "to comfort sentient beings.
One interpretation states that "actual vows" refers to necessarily putting those practices into action.

[Commentary]: The third section, the Chapter on the Three Sets of Three Great Vows, concerns the vow to become a "vower" (the one who makes vows). It consists of making vows before the Buddha and resolving to practice these three vows.
Because the vow necessarily entails the practice of those deeds, ensuring that the vow is not in vain, they are called "true vows."
[Commentary]: Within the second section, the actual formulation of the three vows, there are three specific vows. The first vow is the aspiration to attain the wisdom of the True Dharma.
By means of these roots of goodness, one attains the wisdom of the True Dharma in every birth; this is called the first great vow.
[Commentary] "The wisdom of the True Dharma" refers to the wisdom of eternal abiding.
[Sub-commentary] "By means of these roots of goodness" points to the roots of goodness derived from the preceding refuge in the eternally abiding precepts and practices.
Because one takes refuge in the eternally abiding True Dharma endowed with the three virtues and gives rise to understanding based upon this, it is called "eternal abiding."
If one’s own practice of wisdom is perfected, one will necessarily transform others; the merit of transforming others must, in turn, strictly refine one’s own practice.
[Commentary] The second vow is the aspiration to preach for the sake of sentient beings.
"Having attained the knowledge of the True Dharma, I shall, with an insatiable mind, preach it for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the second great vow.
[Commentary] The third vow is the vow to protect the Dharma.
"My third great vow is to protect and uphold the True Dharma by relinquishing body, life, and wealth in order to embrace it.
[Commentary] The first and third vows primarily concern one's own practice while concurrently clarifying the transformation of others;
the middle vow clarifies the transformation of others through its causes and simultaneously reveals one's own practice, which is identical to the aforementioned ten great precepts.
[Commentary: Third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation that [the vows] are visible.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately prophesied that Śrīmālā’s three great vows are such that, just as all forms enter the realm of space, so too do the *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) number of bodhisattva vows all enter into these three great vows. As for these three vows:
"Truly vast. [Commentary:
These three vows are all vows made prior to abiding [in the stages], yet they are said to "encompass all vows";
this refers only to the various vows prior to abiding and does not include those from the eighth stage and above.

[Commentary]: The *Śāstra* takes up the various vows prior to the [Ten] Abodes; the *Yingluo Jing* (Jewel Garland Sutra), in its first fascicle, explains that there are ten levels of "faith-mind" (*śraddhā-citta*) preceding the Ten Abodes.

Because there are ten such faith-minds, one practices the "Dharma-gate of the Hundred Clarities" (*śata-dharma-prakāśa-mukha*), constantly generating immeasurable great vows—both those with formal practice and those beyond practice—to enter into the lineage of cultivation (*śikṣā-gotra*).
The sutra text extensively elaborates upon these ten faith-minds and the universal practice of all vows.
Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, precepts, dedication, protection of the Dharma, relinquishment, and vows—these are the seeds of the lineage.

What is called the "stage of ten faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā*) is the position of one worthy person (*eka-ārya*). As for the statement that all vows as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are entirely subsumed within these three great vows, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* says:
"My causes, fruits, and vows are all fully perfected; all vows and practices are contained therein."
Now, before all the Buddhas, he has received the great vows; these vows are now fulfilled, and he cultivates the remaining practices.
If any Bodhisattva enters this vow, there is none who does not gain entry into the ocean of *sarvajñā*.
He dwells in the superior meaning, having already completed the chapter on self-practice above the preliminary stages. Thus ends the third chapter.

[Commentary: From the passage "At that time, Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha" onwards, within the explanation of the essence of the vehicle (*yāna-tattva*), the second section presents two chapters to clarify the practice of others (*parapratipatti*).
These two chapters are further divided into two parts. The first, the chapter on "Upholding the True Dharma" (*saddharmaparigraha*), clarifies the meaning of the arising of all virtues;
it states that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, within a single moment of mind, one can give rise to the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*).
The "Chapter on Skillfully Entering the Second Vehicle" subsumes the meaning of "entering into one," stating that all wholesome practices capable of producing the stages up to the eighth ground,
as well as the various virtues produced by the five vehicles, are all included within the One Vehicle.

[Commentary] The fourth chapter, "Receiving and Upholding the True Dharma" (*Saddharmaparigraha*). Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the arising of the myriad virtues," this distinguishes between the similarities and differences of these two chapters.
In the chapter on "Receiving and Upholding," from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, all vows and practices are subsumed within a single moment of mind (*ekakṣaṇacitta*);
because this mind is able to give rise to the causes and fruits of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), it is termed "that which can produce."
The "Chapter on the One Vehicle" (Yi Cheng Zhang) comprehensively subsumes both the subject and the object, such that all enter the One Vehicle.
[Commentary] To explain this briefly: the mind that embraces the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is able to encompass the myriad practices;
because it embraces the goodness being cultivated, it is "correct" (*zheng*); because it serves as a model for sentient beings, it is "Dharma" (*fa*). Thus, it is explained in this way.
The various ways of embracing the True Dharma differ.
[Commentary] First, regarding the explanation of "embracing the True Dharma" (*saddharma-parigraha*), below is the explanation of its name, essence, and the breadth or narrowness of its scope.

First, from the phrase "firstly" (*yīwǎng*) up to "for the sake of embracing" (*wèi shèshòu*), the two characters "embracing" (*shèshòu*) explain the wholesome virtues that are cultivated; the character "Dharma" (*fǎ*) explains that which accords with principle.
Because it is not erroneous, the character for "correct" (zheng) is explained.

[The Commentary] states: Alternatively, it is said that because all that is good can encompass the various practices of sentient beings, everyone from ordinary worldlings to sages takes it as the "Correct Dharma" to be embraced and sustained.
[Commentary]: From the passage "gathering in living beings" (*saṃgraha-sattva*) onwards, the breadth and narrowness of the essence [of the bodhisattva path] is explained.
