Because it encompasses the various practices for gathering in living beings, the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the practice of upholding the True Dharma (*saddharma-parigraha*), which can encompass all practices; thus, all virtues from the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) are included.

[Commentary]: Some say that because the virtues of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) are all performed with a mind focused on signs (*nimitta*), they cannot be considered the "upholding of the true Dharma" (*saddharmaparigraha*);
rather, only those from the level of internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) upward may be so regarded.

[Commentary] Some say that, excluding the ten stages of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi), which belong to ordinary beings, all stages from the ten abodes (vihāra), which belong to inner-worldly practitioners, and above, are included.
[Sub-commentary] Others say that because inner-worldly practitioners have not yet attained true understanding, they are not yet sufficient to be included;

rather, it is precisely from the first stage (bhūmi) upward that one enters true contemplation, and thus from this point on they may be included. However, what is required here is from the eighth stage upward.

The mind that fully cultivates the myriad practices within a single thought-moment is "right" (*samyak*) because it encompasses the practices one has cultivated in accordance with principle and is not erroneous;

it is called "Dharma" (*dharma*) because it serves as a standard for sentient beings. Since the practices from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage are truly untainted (*anāsrava*), they should also be described as "right," as they likewise serve as a standard for sentient beings.
One may indeed call it "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena), yet within a single thought-moment one cannot fully cultivate the myriad practices nor simultaneously contemplate them all;

therefore, it still does not receive the name of "comprehensive inclusion. Furthermore, if one were to personally verify this according to the text, and if one were to take everything from the seventh stage downward as being included within the "Right Dharma," how could one say that the Bodhisattva possesses [merits] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
May all enter into one great vow, namely, the upholding of the True Dharma;
what is called "one's own part" and "the part of others" is distinguished by this. Within this, the first section is further divided into two:

first, from the beginning until [the passage on] "great merit and great benefit," which clarifies the inclusion of the vow; second, from when Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying, "I... [and so forth].
Now, by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, the chapter concludes with the clarification of how practice is encompassed.
[Commentary]: Alternatively, from the stage of the inner ordinary person (*ābhyantara-prthagjana*) up to the first bhūmi and above, all may take the three aforementioned teachers as their guides;

this is one path. Our own school, however, takes those from the eighth bhūmi upward who have made vows to provide such guidance. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states regarding the eighth bhūmi: [text continues].
Among the ten *pāramitās* of a bodhisattva, the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* (perfection of aspiration) is predominant.
[Commentary] My private interpretation differs slightly from this chapter, which takes the meaning of "giving birth" as its primary thesis.

However, because people hear of the aforementioned three aspirations and assume that aspiration culminates therein, I have first explained them from the beginning through to the great benefits they entail.
All the vows as numerous as the sands of the Ganges from the seventh stage and below are entirely contained within a single thought-moment of a vow from the eighth stage and above;
if one discusses their ultimate limit, it resides precisely here. Second, from "I shall uphold the Buddha's [teaching]" onwards, the meaning of "arising" is correctly elucidated.
First, within the section clarifying that vows encompass [all], there are also two parts; first, the actual exposition.

The second section, "Clarifying the Inclusion of Vows," consists of three parts: first, "Clarifying the Praise by the Tathāgata for Accomplishment"; first, within "Clarifying the Inclusion of Vows" itself, there are three [subsections], the first of which is "Clarifying Vaśitā’s Receiving the Mandate.

[Commentary] My private interpretation: The above is the master’s judgment regarding the general meaning of the commentary; it does not take this as the primary structural division (*zhengke*). This is because the wording appears in the text [of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*].
Regarding "taking birth as the primary principle," this single point clarifies that Bodhisattvas who embrace the True Dharma are able to give rise to the meaning of the five vehicles;
this constitutes the essential thesis within this chapter.
At that time, Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "I shall now, further relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, speak of the great vow of subduing."
"It is truly without difference.

[Commentary: Regarding "receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power" (*adhiṣṭhāna*): outward deportment that is upright and solemn is called "majesty" (*vīrya*), while the inner mind that is difficult to fathom is called "spiritual power" (*śakti*).
What is received here is simply the Tathāgata’s granting permission to speak, allowing one to expound according to one's own discernment; it does not refer to some extraordinary technique.
To add wood and stone so that they may speak—this was not sought in the first three chapters; it is only from this chapter onward that one requests the acceptance of majesty (*prabhāva*).
Thus, what is called "distinguishing between self and other" can also serve as proof of the mind of one whose great vow of subduing (*vinaya*) is ever-attached to principle.
One does not expect to possess no virtue for the sake of a great vow; the reality of being without distinction is precisely this.
This means that it is no different from the Buddha’s former vows; furthermore, it is said to be no different from what the Buddha has taught.

[The Commentary] states: When the Tathāgata permits someone to speak, the *Vajraśāstra* says that because the Buddha bestows the power of merit and wisdom upon the body of a bodhisattva, it is called "empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Regarding the statement that one may also verify this through both one's own part and the other's part:
From the seventh ground onward, one’s own division (*svabhāga*) is no longer dependent on the majesty [of others], yet the division of others (*parabhāga*) cannot be described by one’s own power;

it must rely on majestic spiritual power. This is a judgment made from the perspective of their manifest traces (*vyañjana*). As for "great vows," from the eighth ground upward, vows necessarily accord with principle;
therefore, it is said that "the mind constantly adheres to principle. The three virtues, the four meanings, and the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constitute [this adherence].

There is no virtue that is not encompassed; if expanded, the myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are fully subsumed, and if abbreviated, they are entirely contained within the three virtues and four meanings.
[Commentary] Second, it clarifies the Buddha’s permission for the teaching.
The Buddha told Śrīmālā, "I grant you leave to speak as you wish.
[Commentary on the *Sūtra*] "Granting leave" (*kṣānti*) may be understood as permitting.
[Commentary on the *Vyākhyā*] "Granting leave" (*kṣānti*) is read as *tì* (with the tone *dìng*, or alternatively *tíng*).
[Commentary]: Third, from the passage where Śrīmālā addresses the Buddha onwards, the text properly elucidates the inclusion of vows.

Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "All the vows of a bodhisattva, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are entirely contained within one great vow, namely, the vow to uphold the True Dharma (saddharma-parigraha). To uphold the True Dharma is truly the Great Vow."
[Commentary: Third, the explicit clarification that the vows encompassing the sands of the Ganges all enter into one great vow:

"one vow" refers to the single thought-moment of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and above; because the vows numbering as the sands of the Ganges from the seventh stage and below all enter into the single thought-moment vow of the eighth stage and above, it is said that they all enter into one great vow.
What is called "embracing the True Dharma" refers to the essence of a single vow and the True Dharma of myriad practices;
because this is the function of a single thought-moment from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, it is said that embracing the True Dharma is truly the Great Vow.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "function in a single thought-moment" from the eighth stage upward, both the function of one's own practice and the function of transforming others are fully present within that single thought-moment.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Among the ten pāramitās of this bodhisattva, the pāramitā of aspiration is predominant;
it is not that the other pāramitās are not practiced, but rather they are practiced according to his capacity and according to his lot."
[Commentary: From the passage beginning with the Buddha’s praise of Śrīmālā, the second section within the "Inclusion through Vows" clarifies the "Accomplishment through the Tathāgata’s Praise.
This section also contains five parts; first, he praises her manifest virtues.
The Buddha praised Śrīmālā, saying, "Excellent, excellent! Your wisdom and skillful means are profoundly deep and most subtle.

[Commentary] The commentary praises her manifestation of virtue, stating that what is nameless is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); because she uses wisdom to illuminate emptiness and skillful means to enter into existence, being able to realize emptiness while preaching existence, she may be said to possess that which is "profoundly deep and most subtle."
[Commentary]: The second section, from "You have, for a long night... onwards, praises his past causes. It states:
"You have planted various roots of goodness throughout a long night; only those sentient beings of the present world who have long cultivated roots of goodness can understand what you have spoken."
[Commentary] Regarding "the long night" and so forth: within the night of ignorance, one plants the roots of all virtues; wisdom is the root of all virtues.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Great wisdom is the fundamental practice."
[Commentary: Third, from the words "What you have said" onwards, he praises what has been taught as being identical to that of all Buddhas.
What you have taught regarding the upholding of the True Dharma is precisely what all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have already taught, are now teaching, and will teach.

[Commentary] Third, regarding the praise that [the Master’s realization] is identical to that of all Buddhas: the *Wuming* (The Nameless) states, "Although the Buddhas of the three periods differ, their Way is not two.
Since you are able to unify this non-dual Way, how could attaining it be far off? The Way has no dualistic school;
how could one who attains it be different? This is considered his own realization.
[Commentary]: The fourth section, from "Now that I have attained unsurpassed bodhi" onwards, praises and explains how [this teaching] is identical to that of Śākyamuni.
"Now that I have attained unsurpassed bodhi, I too constantly preach this Dharma for the upholding of the True Dharma."
[Commentary]: However, because Śākyamuni is none other than one of the Lords of Transformation among all Buddhas, he is mentioned separately.
Fifth, from "Thus have I spoken" onwards, there is praise for all the merits of upholding the True Dharma.
In this way, I say that all the merits of upholding the true Dharma are without limit, and the wisdom and eloquence of the Tathāgata are likewise without limit.
Why is this? Because upholding the true Dharma possesses great merit and great benefit.
[Commentary: "Unable to reach its limit" means that because the principle of upholding the True Dharma is profound and far-reaching, it cannot be fully expounded;
hence it is said that one cannot reach its limit. Regarding the statement that "the Tathāgata’s wisdom and eloquence are likewise without limit," this is intended to resolve a doubt:
if the merit of upholding [the Dharma] has no limit, then there should likewise be no one capable of understanding this principle.
Who would say that sentient beings are explained by means of this principle? Therefore, the commentary states:
Since the Buddha’s wisdom arises from the boundless principle, the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise without limit.

Now, for it to use this limitless wisdom to illuminate the limitless principle—what difficulty could there be in this being called "Buddhahood"? Why is it called "the Wisdom of All Aspects" (sarvākārajñatā)? For what reason?
The following continues the explanation of the boundless nature of the Buddha’s wisdom. Anticipating a doubt, it asks: "Why is the Tathāgata’s wisdom and knowledge also boundless?

The explanation states: Because this principle of upholding the True Dharma possesses great merit and benefit, the Buddha-wisdom produced thereby is likewise boundless. It also explains why all merits [are to be] upheld.

Regarding "virtue without limit": this refers to the supreme upholding of the True Dharma, which can, at its highest level, induce the attainment of omniscience and, at its lower level, transform sentient beings;
because such meritorious benefits cannot be fully described, they possess no boundary.

[Commentary] Regarding "wisdom, eloquence," and so forth: there are four kinds of eloquence—first, unimpeded eloquence regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); second, unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*);
third, unimpeded eloquence regarding language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and fourth, unimpeded eloquence regarding confidence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
These four are collectively termed "unimpeded eloquence" because the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding these four dharmas is swift, discerning, clear, thoroughly penetrating, and free from obstruction.
Therefore, it is collectively termed "unimpeded wisdom" (*pratisaṃvid*). First, regarding the unimpeded wisdom of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*):

it is so called because one knows the meanings of all phenomena (*dharma*) with perfect clarity and penetrates them without obstruction; furthermore, it is because one can know that all meanings enter into the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Second, regarding the unimpeded wisdom of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): "phenomena" refers to all meanings and their names; for the sake of knowing these meanings, one thoroughly penetrates all phenomena.

The analytical knowledge of names (*nāma-pratisaṃvid*) is unimpeded; furthermore, by means of this unobstructed knowledge of dharmas (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one can analyze the three vehicles without destroying the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and there is no impediment in the speech one utters.
The analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) uses language to explain the meanings of names, adorning speech with various ornaments according to what is appropriate.
Fourth, he is able to cause understanding of what are called the various and diverse languages of all sentient beings—
whether one word or two words, whether abbreviated terms such as those for male or female, or languages of the past, future, and present—
and he can cause each person to attain comprehension through his unimpeded eloquence, so that all who hear him understand his speech.
The unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is the ability to speak all syllables within a single syllable, all words within a single word,
and all dharmas within a single dharma; and that all these spoken dharmas are entirely true and provide benefit according to those who can be guided—
namely, the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand [teachings].
The Dharma-treasury accords with the faculties and natures of all sentient beings; it skillfully responds to their capacities so that speech is never obstructed and listeners never grow weary.
Even if one were to preach for immeasurable eons, what difficulty would there be in becoming a Buddha? By employing wisdom to illuminate the principle, one achieves Buddhahood.
Since there is no limit to such preaching, what difficulty could there be? There is no fault of failing to accord with the capacities [of beings]. The above is all...
This is the authentic text of the sutra and treatise. [Commentary:

From the passage "I shall now rely upon the Buddha’s spiritual power" onwards is the second section, clarifying the inclusion of practice (*caryā-saṃgraha*). [Private Note: This primarily clarifies the meaning of "production.
Furthermore, it is divided into two parts: first, the primary clarification of the inclusion of practice; second, from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One... [the following section].

From the section following what was spoken by Śrīmālā until the end of the chapter, it is further clarified that the praise of the Tathāgata’s accomplishment is primarily explained as the inclusion of practice (*caryā-saṃgraha*).
This is further divided into three parts: first, the presentation of the essence of the inclusion of practice, which is also the essence of its potential for arising;
second, from the passage beginning "For example, when the kalpa first begins to form," the explicit explanation of the meaning of its arising.
Third, from the passage "The World-Honored One upholds the True Dharma" down to "upholding those who uphold the True Dharma," the characteristics are clarified;
this serves to resolve the doubts regarding the first [section], which also contains three parts, the first being the reception of the mandate.
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "I shall, relying upon the Buddha's spiritual power, further expound the vast meaning of the upholding of the True Dharma.
[Commentary] The second section: granting permission to listen.
The Buddha said, "Speak then.
[Commentary] The third section, from the point where she addresses the Buddha downward, clearly shows the actual practice of the essence of the path.
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "The vast meaning of embracing the True Dharma is the attainment of the immeasurable all."
The Buddha-dharma comprises eighty-four thousand *dharmaparyāyas*.

[Commentary: The meaning of "vast and great" refers to the essence of practice. One interpretation states that the preceding phrase, "From this, it is immeasurable," and all that follows, explain "vast and great.
Regarding the eighty-four thousand *dharmaparyāyas*, there is a record in other commentaries which is not included here.
Commentary.

[The *Chao* states: Regarding the "eighty-four thousand dharma-gates," this concludes the essence of the three practices of the eighth stage, which do not exceed these eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
Although the explanations found in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras differ, we shall here preserve one interpretation from the *Bhadra-kalpa*.
The Sūtra states that from the Buddha’s initial generation of the mind until the distribution of the *śarīra*, there were three hundred and fifty *pāramitā* gates;
each of these possesses the six *pāramitās*, totaling two thousand one hundred. When further multiplied by four, they total eight thousand four hundred;
when transformed into ten, they total eighty-four thousand. The phrasing of this sūtra passage is somewhat obscure, yet it has been so utilized since ancient times.
Taking this as the standard, although the various sūtras that have been produced are numerous, they do not go beyond the Four Noble Truths.
The eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma are comprised within these: the gate of afflictions is the Truth of Suffering; the gate of antidotes is the Truth of Origination;
the gates of the three samādhis and the various dhāraṇīs—these three combined—are the Truth of the Path; and the gates of the various pāramitās are the Great Truth of Cessation.
Question: What is the distinction between samādhi and dhāraṇī? Answer: Dhāraṇī has the nature of wisdom (prajñā), while samādhi has the nature of concentration (samādhi).
Therefore, these two are combined as the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya); they function solely in the sense of being antidotes (pratipakṣa).
[Commentary: Regarding the second [section], which clarifies the meaning of "giving birth," there are four analogies divided into two parts.
First, the initial two analogies clarify that the Dharma can give birth; second, the latter two analogies clarify that persons can give birth.
The reason this is known is that while the former two analogies speak directly of embracing the True Dharma (*saddharma*), they do not mention virtuous sons or daughters; the latter two [do].

In the "Parable" section, all [passages] speak of "good sons and daughters"; regarding the first of the two parables that illustrate how the Dharma can be brought forth from within illumination, it is itself divided into two parts, the first being the Parable of the Rising Clouds.
Just as at the time of the formation of a kalpa, great clouds arise everywhere raining down various colored waters and diverse jewels,
so too does the rain of the True Dharma bring forth the rain of immeasurable rewards of merit and immeasurable roots of goodness.

[Commentary] To clarify the meaning of "sheltering and covering," it is said that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, those who embrace the True Dharma are able to shelter and cover sentient beings who are like impoverished people.
Furthermore, regarding the second great water analogy, it clarifies the function of "cleansing and washing away";
it is said that from the eighth stage upward, those who embrace the True Dharma are also able to cleanse and wash away the defilements and burdens of sentient beings. This refers first to the cloud.
The analogy consists of two parts—opening and closing—and within these two, there are four propositions. The first proposition is like the formation of the world at the beginning of a kalpa;

it serves as an analogy for the initial establishment of the true body (*dharmakāya*) from the eighth stage upward. The second proposition is the universal rising of great clouds; it serves as an analogy for the *nirmāṇakāya* preaching the Dharma.
These two propositions both serve as analogies for that which produces and sustains [the rain]. The third proposition is the raining down of various...

The rain of form (*rūpa-varṣa*) is a metaphor for that which can produce the causes of the five vehicles (the fourth phrase), and the various jewels are also a metaphor for that which can produce the fruits of the five vehicles;
these two phrases both serve as metaphors for the five vehicles that are produced. Second, the synthesis of the metaphors consists of three phrases:
the first phrase, "thus receiving and upholding the True Dharma," combines with the aforementioned capacity to produce [the clouds] during the intermediate eon (*antara-kalpa*).

The first phrase regarding the arising of the two metaphors means that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the True Body (*dharmakāya*) is initially established, and its manifestation as a provisional response (*nirmāṇakāya*) to transform sentient beings is analogous to the formation of a kalpa;
the second phrase regarding the raining of immeasurable merit and retribution corresponds to the aforementioned "producing" and the various jewels.
From the eighth stage upward, the capacity to receive and produce the fruits of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*) is analogous to the rain.
The third phrase, "various jewels," along with the rain of immeasurable roots of goodness, collectively refers to the aforementioned "rain of various colors" produced therein;
the statement that it can produce the causes for the five vehicles is synonymous with the rain of various colors.

[Commentary]: Regarding "sheltering sentient beings who are like the poor," it means that sentient beings lack the wealth of the Dharma of the five vehicles and are defiled by the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*).
As for "the True Body first establishing itself and the Responsive Body preaching the Dharma," the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Necklaces) states:
"From the First Ground to the Buddha-ground, there are two kinds of Dharmakāya: first, the Dharmakāya of the Ultimate Fruit; second, the Dharmakāya of Responsive Transformation."
Because the body arises from wisdom born of the true nature within the stream of the Dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), this true wisdom constitutes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
"Dharma" signifies its own essence, and "body" (*kāya*) signifies the sense of accumulation; thus, it is the Dharma-body.

Since the roots of goodness of all sentient beings evoke this Dharma-body of true wisdom, the Dharma-body is able to manifest as immeasurable response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), namely throughout all worlds.
The bodies of the buddha-lands, the bodies of all sentient beings, and the bodies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can all manifest;

inconceivable lands are likewise so. The characteristics of the transformation body preaching the Dharma are fully complete, no different from the half and full teachings expounded throughout a single transformation of Śākyamuni.
[Commentary]: Regarding the second section on the analogy of the great flood, it is divided into three parts. First, the analogy is established:

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, just as at the beginning of a kalpa when the world is formed, there is a great mass of water that gives rise to the storehouse of the trichiliocosm and the four hundred and ten million kinds of various continents."

[Commentary]: Within these analogies there are also four propositions. The first proposition—likewise as when a kalpa is formed—is an analogy for the initial establishment of the True Body (dharmakāya) from the eighth stage upward.
The second proposition—there being a great mass of water—is an analogy for the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya) preaching the Dharma.
These two propositions both serve as analogies for the act of generating and sustaining. The third proposition concerns the production of the three thousandfold world system.
The "Treasury of the Thousandfold World" (*sāhasracūḍika*) corresponds to the fourth phrase of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, which can produce [beings];
and the four hundred billion kinds of lands correspond to the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*) that can be produced. This is the second combined correspondence.
Thus, by upholding the True Dharma, there arises the immeasurable treasury of the Mahāyāna realm, the supernormal powers of all bodhisattvas,
the peace and happiness of all worlds, the sovereign mastery according to one's wishes in all worlds,
and supramundane bliss.

[Commentary] The second section, the combination of analogies, consists of five phrases. The first phrase, "thus receiving and upholding the True Dharma," also combines with the preceding analogy of generating the intermediate kalpa to form the great waters;

this refers to the statement that at the eighth stage, the true body first establishes the provisional response-body to preach the Dharma, which is identical in meaning to the formation of the kalpa and the emergence of a great mass of water. The second phrase is "producing the Great... [The text continues].

Riding upon the power of the supernatural faculties of all Bodhisattvas, which are the treasury of immeasurable realms—this corresponds to the third phrase of the "Arising of the Treasury of the Three Thousand Great Thousandfold World-Systems" within the aforementioned "Arising.

All that is secure and happy in all worlds—this refers to human vehicles, corresponding to the fourth phrase of the "One Hundred States" within the aforementioned "Four Hundred. All that is like [the nature of] all worlds...
The mastery of mind (*citta-vaśitā*) refers to the celestial vehicles (*deva-yāna*), which are combined with the two hundred states from the upper four hundred; this corresponds to the fifth phrase.

Furthermore, the supramundane peace and happiness refers to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), which are collectively combined with the three hundred and forty states from the upper four hundred, because both vehicles equally transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*). This third section concludes the opening and closing of the pairings.
"From the formation of the kalpa until that which has never before been obtained by devas and humans all emerges therein.

[Commentary]: Regarding "from the formation of the kalpa until that which has never before been obtained by devas and humans all emerges therein," the third pair concludes both the opening and the closing;
"the formation of the kalpa" takes the opening as its point of comparison, while "that which has never before been obtained by devas and humans" takes the closing as its point of comparison.

Regarding the end of this [passage], it says "up to" (*yāvat*) because the mundane and supramundane bliss—which has never before been obtained by devas and humans—is taken from its beginning and its end, while the middle is abbreviated.
As for the phrase "all emerge from within," this is a dual conclusion:
that both the treasury of the great trichiliocosm and the four hundred million types of continents all emerge from within the kalpa; these, too, have never before been obtained by devas and humans.
That which has not yet been attained all arises from grasping (*parigraha*). These two analogies can be distinguished by three points:

first, regarding the analogy of the original creation (*mūla-kṛta-upamā*), both analogies state that it was at the time of the formation of the kalpa; thus, the meaning of the texts is identical. Second, regarding the analogy of the manifested traces (*vyañjana-kṛta-upamā*):
in the former analogy, a great cloud arises universally, while in the latter analogy, there is a great mass of water; therefore, the textual intent is one and the same.

The first three [reasonings] establish the produced effect by inferring from the preceding and combining it with the person, whereas the latter inference establishes the person by combining them with the cause;
thus, the meaning of the texts differs. Nevertheless, there is no difference in their essential intent; rather, the Sage expounds the Dharma by citing these various perspectives to clarify the truth.

[Commentary] Regarding the three points to be distinguished: within the two analogies of "clouds arising" and "great waters," both contain the formation of a kalpa, which serves as a metaphor for the True Body (dharmakāya) of the eighth stage and above;
thus, the text is identical and the meaning is likewise identical. Within these two analogies, both also contain the traces of manifested response (nirmāṇakāya);
thus, while the text differs, the meaning is the same. As for the difference in text, it is as follows:
The first simile speaks only of the great clouds arising everywhere and the vast accumulation of water;

within this pair of similes, the former mentions that it rains various colored rains as the cause and various jewels as the fruit, yet it does not clarify that human beings are included within these causes and fruits.
The latter simile mentions only the bodhisattvas’ supernormal powers and their bringing of peace and security, yet it does not clarify the relationship between cause and fruit.
Because cause and effect are combined within the human realm, the meaning of the passages differs; they are cited alternately to clarify this.
It is said that in the original source, the fundamental essence of the true bodies (*dharmakāya*) of all bodhisattvas is identical, and thus the meaning of the passages is identical to manifest this.

Although all bodhisattvas are the same in descending from their origin to manifest traces, their manifested traces of transformation differ individually; therefore, while the intent is the same, the phrasing varies.

The distinction made by the third [section]—wherein the former inference refers only to the Dharma and the latter inference refers only to the person—is clarified through mutual illustration. Why is this?

Because when the True Body first establishes itself in the eighth stage and manifests responsive transformations to preach the Dharma, it does not merely present the causes and effects of the five vehicles.
Sometimes the Dharma is cited to reveal the person, as in the previous inference; sometimes the person is cited to reveal the Dharma, which is as follows:
As for the various teachings throughout the successive generations of the Dharma, these are extensively expounded in the sutras and śāstras.

They manifest the five vehicles to be transformed; sometimes they distinguish cause and effect to reveal differences among persons, and sometimes they distinguish persons to reveal differences in cause and effect.
Therefore, it is said that they are explained by being raised alternately. Nevertheless, they do not transcend the teaching of the five [vehicles] arising as a response from the True [Dharmakāya].
The Vehicle of Multiplication transforms those of the five vehicles by teaching causes and fruits, whether in separation or combination;
thus it encompasses all capacities for establishing the Dharma among those to be transformed, leaving no sound of the transformer or the transformed unaccounted for.
This is called "the inclusion of practices," because within a single moment of a bodhisattva’s effortless (anābhoga) activity, all various practices and dharmas are subsumed.
[Commentary]: From the passage "Furthermore, like the great earth" onwards, it clarifies the second point within the section on "Birth.
Within the clarification of how a person can bring about accomplishment, there are also two analogies, which are divided into two parts:

the first is the analogy of the heavy burden, clarifying the meaning of the Great Beings from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upwards who shoulder the burden of sentient beings; the second is the analogy of the treasure store, clarifying [the state] from the eighth stage upwards...
Regarding the meaning of the Great Beings as a treasury for sentient beings: first, in comparison to those who can bear the heavy burden, this is divided into two parts;

second, in comparison to those who open [the treasury], there are two parts. First, the initial two lines serve as a comparison for those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward who are able to bear the burden.

[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of "bearing the burden of sentient beings": because the Bodhisattva manifests forms within the nine realms of existence to gather them through shared activities, the Sūtra says:
"He is born into the five realms to manifest his body as a Great Physician King who skillfully cures all ailments.

Regarding the meaning of "containing and storing": because a single thought-moment contains the teachings of the five vehicles, the Sūtra says: "He gathers the jewel-treasures of the various dharmas."
Like a sea-captain, and like the great earth bearing four heavy burdens.
[Commentary] The second section, from "What are the four? onwards, provides analogies for the dharmas that are borne.
What are the four? First, the great ocean; second, the various mountains; third, grasses and trees; and fourth, sentient beings. [Commentary] There are four points:
first, comparing the great ocean to the Bodhisattva—speaking of his vastness in embracing sentient beings, he is like the great ocean which embraces and contains them without end;
therefore, it is used as a comparison. Second, comparing the various mountains to the Pratyekabuddhayāna—speaking of their true loftiness.

1. It is also likened to the height of various mountains; this serves as a metaphor for the Mahāyāna. 2. Grasses and trees are compared to the Śrāvaka-yāna because their number is as numerous as grasses and trees;
thus they are used as a point of comparison. 3. Sentient beings are collectively compared to the Human and Deva yānas (Manuṣya-deva-yāna);
since the Human and Deva yānas remain within the cycle of birth and death, just as sentient beings undergo rebirth in all places, they are used as an illustration.
[Commentary]: Since Pratyekabuddhas surpass Śrāvakas, they are compared to mountains; how could Bodhisattvas not be exalted?
Because Bodhisattvas manifest forms within the six realms of existence, blending with the world to benefit sentient beings, they are compared to the ocean for its vast embrace.
[Commentary] The second section, "Applying the Analogy" (*upanaya*), is divided into three parts: first, the actual application; second, the synthesis;

and third, the praise of the person capable of bearing the burden. Within the first part, the actual application, there are also two sub-sections: first, applying the analogy to the person capable of bearing the burden.

Thus, the sons and daughters of good family who embrace the True Dharma establish a "Great Earth" that is capable of bearing four kinds of heavy responsibilities, surpassing even that [ordinary] earth. [Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "surpassing that earth," the ordinary earth bears only physical forms, whereas the Great Being (Mahāsattva) concurrently bears both form and the spirit of the Teaching.
Because it causes one to reform evil and cultivate goodness, it is said to "surpass that great earth.
[Commentary] The "establishment of the great earth" in the sutra refers to the ground of the two bodies, the True and the Responsive, for they are able to give birth to the five vehicles.
"Surpassing" (yú)—with the pinyin *yáng zhū*—means to transcend or to cross over.
[Commentary] Second, the analogy of the burden one carries. What are the four?
They are: for sentient beings who lack virtuous friends, have not heard the Dharma, and follow what is not the Dharma, one brings them to maturity through the roots of goodness of humans and devas;
to those seeking the vehicle of the Śrāvaka, one grants the Śrāvaka-yāna; and to those seeking the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha, one grants the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.
"To those who seek the Mahāyāna, he bestows the Mahāyāna.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the synthesis of the dharmas to be borne: it is only through inversion that they are combined. First, the sentient beings are combined with the preceding grasses and trees;

this can be inferred. From the Śrāvakas downward, they are combined with the preceding mountains; this can likewise be inferred. From the Pratyekabuddhas downward, they are combined with the preceding [mountains]. From... [text ends].

The phrase "the Mahāyāna and below" is combined with the preceding "compared to the great ocean" to mean that Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are able to carry the sentient beings of the five vehicles;
thus, in meaning, they are like the great earth carrying these four kinds [of beings]. The second point, regarding the synthesis, can be seen [in the text].
This is called the way in which sons and daughters of good family who embrace the true Dharma establish the great earth and are capable of bearing the four kinds of heavy responsibilities.
[Commentary] From the passage beginning with "World-Honored One" onwards, the third section within the synthesis, which praises those capable of bearing the burden, may also be observed.
World-Honored One, those sons and daughters of good family who thus uphold the True Dharma establish the great earth,
becoming capable of bearing its fourfold heavy responsibilities; they act as uninvited friends for all sentient beings, comforting them with great compassion, having pity for them,
and serving as the mother of the world’s Dharma.

[Commentary: A friend is defined by the sense of mutual rescue; however, one who waits to be entreated before providing rescue is not a true friend. Therefore, it is said that [the Bodhisattva] acts as a "friend who does not wait to be asked.
Because the Bodhisattva transforms sentient beings with the knowledge that they are like a compassionate mother approaching her infant, it is said that he acts as the "mother of the world's dharmas."

[Commentary]: Regarding the "uninvited friend," the world regards those with shared aspirations as friends. Among the Bodhisattva’s four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), there is the integration through common purpose (*samānārthatā*).
By skillfully aligning with the faculties and conditions [of others], one causes them to cultivate the virtues of the five vehicles and thereby attain the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).

As a sutra says: "The two of us shall also act together with you. And as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If people are not at peace because they have no uninvited friend, then they are not yet at peace."
The Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) is precisely what establishes one in the Truth of the Path; this is entirely identical to the "Great Compassionate Consolation" in the present sutra.
Wuming says: "Great Compassion arises within, providing salvation without waiting for a request; its pitying consolation is like that of a compassionate mother.
By citing this at the conclusion of the section, he clarifies the profound virtue of the Grounds (bhūmi), which support all beings with great weight.

[Commentary] From the passage "Furthermore, just as the great earth has four kinds of treasure-troves" onwards, the second section uses the analogy of the treasure-trove to clarify the meaning of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) as a storehouse for the masses of sentient beings.
This is further divided into two parts; within the first part, which provides the direct analogy, there are also two sub-sections, the first of which is the formal analogy itself.
Furthermore, it is like the great earth, which contains four kinds of treasure troves. What are these four? First, those of priceless value;
second, those of superior value; third, those of middling value; and fourth, those of inferior value.
[Commentary] Within the formal analogy (*upamāna*), there are also two parts. First, the initial two phrases constitute the analogy for that which acts as the "repository" (*āśraya*);
second, there is the analogy for the "dharma to be stored" (*āśrita-dharma*), which consists of four points: the priceless analogy for the Bodhisattva vehicle (*bodhisattvayāna*);

the high-priced analogy for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle (*pratyekabuddhayāna*); the medium-priced analogy for the Śrāvaka vehicle (*śrāvakayāna*); and the low-priced analogy for the human and celestial vehicles (*manuṣya-devayāna*).
The second summary:
these are called the four kinds of great earth treasure-treasuries.
[Commentary] "These are called the four kinds of treasure-treasuries" is the second summary; it also serves as a synthesis of the second section.
There are three parts: first, the formal correspondence; second, the praise; and third, the clarification. Within the formal correspondence, there are also two parts:
first, the correspondence regarding the ability to store and preserve [the Dharma].
Thus, sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma establish the great earth and attain the four [qualities] of sentient beings.
The supreme great jewel of the seeds.

[Commentary: Regarding the attainment of the four kinds of greatest jewels of sentient beings, there are four interpretations. The first interpretation states that the goodness of the five vehicles belongs to sentient beings;
because the Great Beings of the eighth stage possess these fully within their minds, it is said they "attain" them among sentient beings.
The second section on "Producing Jewels" states that bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward obtain the jewel of teaching and transforming the four kinds of sentient beings;

thus it is said they "obtain the jewel of sentient beings. The third section states that they embrace the true Dharma because it is obtained through the teaching and transformation of the four kinds of sentient beings;
thus it says they "obtain the jewel of sentient beings. The fourth section explains the roots of goodness of these four kinds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, because it is attained by Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, it is called "attaining the treasure of sentient beings";
while the first and second interpretations differ in their treatment of the fundamental and the derivative, their general meaning appears to be the same.

[Commentary]: To say merely that there is a difference between the beginning and the end means that when one first prepares [the practice] within the mind, this constitutes the "beginning" (the root) as one's own cultivation;
subsequently, using this Dharma to transform sentient beings constitutes the "end" (the branch). Combining these two passages establishes, in general, the present school’s doctrine of "arising."

[Commentary] Regarding the third and fourth [explanations], although they both concern attainment, because the locations of the upper and lower [realms] differ, their verbal meanings are entirely distinct.
[Sub-commentary] As for the phrase "but their locations of attainment," etc.: the third [explanation] attains it in the lower [realm], while the fourth attains it in the upper [realm].
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the fourth interpretation, although it follows the text directly, it does not yet accord with what is being stored [in the underlying intent].
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, regarding the fourth interpretation, although it follows the text directly":

the text states, "In this way, sentient beings who obtain the great jewel all do so by virtue of being sustained by sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma; they thereby attain these extraordinary and rare merits. This refers to...
Praise for one who is able to store what is not fit to be stored.
[Commentary (Shu): However, it is also correct to take the concluding text as the basis for this inference. [Sub-commentary (Chao):
Regarding taking the concluding text as the basis for inference, it refers to the concluding exhortation at the end of this chapter, which says: "Therefore, it is superior..."
"Māla should receive, reveal to sentient beings, teach, and establish sentient beings in the True Dharma.
This passage is identical to the interpretations of the first two masters; therefore, it is now used as that which is capable of containing [the teachings].
[Commentary] The third interpretation is indeed excellent, yet its application is extremely remote.
[Sub-commentary] Its application is extremely remote because it requires the transformation of four types of sentient beings before one can achieve the inclusion and upholding of the True Dharma;
thus, its meaning is far-fetched.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first and second [jewels], they function as objects of recollection (*anusmṛti*). Among the four kinds of jewels, why is it that only the priceless one is called "supreme"?
It is because the superior includes the inferior, and thus they are collectively termed "supreme.
Furthermore, it is said that since the other three ultimately result in a supreme value from beginning to end, they are collectively termed "supreme."

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the remaining three [vehicles] ultimately converge to form the aforementioned price": because they meet at the beginning and return to the end, becoming one in the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), they are collectively termed "supreme.
[Sūtra] Second, the comparison of what is contained within.

What are these four? They are: bestowing upon sons and daughters of good family who uphold the true Dharma the roots of goodness of the merits of humans and devas for those sentient beings who have not heard the Dharma and follow what is not the Dharma; bestowing the Śrāvaka-yāna upon those who seek the Śrāvaka vehicle;
bestowing the Pratyekabuddha-yāna upon those who seek the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and bestowing the Mahāyāna upon those who seek the Mahāyāna.
[Commentary] From "Of what four kinds? onwards is the second section, which combines the dharmas contained within the treasury.
From "lacking learning" onwards, it combines those of lower and middle value. From "śrāvakas" onwards, it combines those of upper-middle value.
From "pratyekabuddhas" onwards, it combines those of the highest value. From "Mahāyāna" onwards, it combines those of priceless value. From "In this way" onwards...
This is the second eulogy within the section on conjunction.
Thus, sentient beings who have obtained this great treasure all derive it from good sons and good daughters who uphold the True Dharma,
thereby attaining these extraordinary and rare merits.
[Commentary]: From "The World-Honored One" onwards, the third section within the synthesis clarifies identity.
That which is called the Great Treasure Store of the World-Honored One is precisely the upholding of the True Dharma.
[Commentary]: Whereas the previous analogy of the heavy burden merely established a connection without clarifying identity, this current analogy of the treasure store clarifies that very identity.
Regarding the "unbound" [state], the preceding analogy of the heavy burden refers to taking the body itself as the burden;
since this is difficult to accomplish, yet the burden is not another's body, its meaning is credible. Therefore, although it is bound and not explicitly stated to be identical, it is so.

Regarding the analogy of the treasure storehouse, because it is said that there is a treasure within, its identity is difficult to clarify; however, since it is not a matter of the body being a burden, the task is easy to accomplish.

Therefore, just as the previous analogy of the heavy burden spoke of transcending that great earth, this current analogy of the treasure trove speaks directly of attaining the treasure of sentient beings; the meaning here is the same as that.

[Commentary] Regarding the third point, "the identity of the characteristics," the phrase "the World-Honored One’s Great Treasure Store" and so forth is a metaphor for the upholding of the True Dharma from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
As for the previous analogy of the heavy burden and below, it clarifies that within these two comparisons, there is mutual emergence and disappearance; why is this?
Because the preceding comparison establishes a metaphor that is naturally consistent with the meaning, making it easy to believe, and thus requires no further elaboration.
The reason for presenting [the second case] separately is that it is difficult to establish the identity of the words with the facts; therefore, it is concluded separately.
Later, when establishing the analogy, the meaning is not immediately clear, which is why it is presented separately.

As for the first case, the identity of the words with the facts is easy to demonstrate, so no conclusion is used. Although there is a conclusion in the former, they are not the same, and thus two analogies are provided.
Since both possess superior principles and there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority, it is said that "this also has the same meaning.

[Commentary] From the passage "The World-Honored One’s upholding of the True Dharma" onwards, the third section within the correct exposition of the practice of upholding (*dhāraṇī*) clarifies its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), thereby resolving the doubts of sentient beings; this follows the previous two sections which correctly explained the establishment of the manifestation.
The clarification of the Dharma can bring about the latter two types of inference; the clarification of the person can bring about the accomplishment of things.

This is because the person is not the Dharma and the Dharma is not the person, as their two natures are each distinct. Therefore, the resulting inferences are also not the same. Furthermore, based on this, various doubts extensively arise:
that the various practices of the True Dharma differ from the Dharma of Uplift; that the Dharma of Uplift differs from the Wave [of Practice]; and so forth.
Regarding the citation of these characteristics as an explanation for the sake of the *pāramitā*, this is divided into two parts:
first, from the beginning up to "receiving and upholding the True Dharma," which clarifies the identity of the dharma and its characteristics;
second, from "World-Honored One, I now rely on the Buddha’s majestic power to further explain the great meaning" onwards, which clarifies the identity of the person and the dharma.
However, the root of doubt lies solely in the person; this mental state is difficult to dispel all at once.

Therefore, first the mutual identity of phenomena (*dharmas*) is clarified to bring about a slight understanding, and subsequently the mutual identity of person and phenomena is clarified to dispel it.
Within the first section on the mutual identity of phenomena, it is divided into two parts: first, the correct Dharma of the myriad practices is that which encompasses and receives [all beings].
Mind. Blessed One, the upholding of the true Dharma and the one who upholds the true Dharma are not different; there is no difference between the true Dharma and the upholding of the true Dharma.
The true Dharma itself is the upholding of the true Dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding the clarification of non-duality in both [aspects], the first phrase is taken from above to establish non-duality for the subsequent phrases.
For instance, when first explaining the single phrase "non-dual True Dharma," one takes the two subsequent phrases from the double-reference section above;
thus it is said: "The mind that encompasses is non-dual with the myriad practices of the True Dharma that are encompassed. Next, the non-duality of "encompassing" is explained.
To receive even a single phrase of the True Dharma means to take up the supreme, non-differentiated phrases of the True Dharma;

therefore, it is said that the myriad practices are subsumed within the True Dharma, and there is no difference between the practices and the mind that subsumes them. This principle recurs frequently in the subsequent text, so it is explained here in detail.
[Commentary]: "The True Dharma" refers to those who uphold the True Dharma; this clarifies that the True Dharma of the myriad practices is precisely the mind that upholds it.
Next, one should state that "upholding the True Dharma" is itself the True Dharma, yet the scriptural text is deficient here.
Since from the eighth stage upward one is already the Dharmakāya, the True Dharma of the myriad practices is taken as the mind, and the mind is taken as the myriad [practices].

Because the practice of the True Dharma and the mind are of one essence and possess no further dual characteristics, it is said that the myriad practices of the True Dharma are themselves the mind, and the mind itself is the myriad practices of the True Dharma.

This is not possible for those at or below the seventh stage, as they have not yet attained the Dharma-body and are unable to cultivate all practices fully in a single thought-moment. Thus, it cannot be so for them.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that those from the seventh ground downward do not lack the Dharmakāya:

the *Ābharaṇa-sūtra* says, "O Son of the Buddha, at the first moment of thought on the first ground, the wisdom of the signless Dharmakāya is accomplished, achieving a million asaṃkhyeya merits. It simultaneously illuminates the two truths;
every thought is quiescent within the stream of Dharma, which cannot be measured by the consciousness of an ordinary person. Thus, there are two kinds [of realization].
This is true for the Dharma-body; how much more so for the second stage up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

[Commentary: The second section clarifies that the *pāramitās* are identical with the myriad practices (*sarva-caryā*), and is divided into three parts. First, it correctly clarifies their mutual identity.
The World-Honored One said: "There is no difference between the pāramitās and the embracing of the true Dharma; the embracing of the true Dharma is itself the pāramitā.
[Commentary] The second section, from "no difference between the pāramitās" onwards, clarifies that the pāramitās are identical to the myriad practices.
That there is no difference between the Dharma and the pāramitās means that the upholding of the true Dharma is not distinct from the pāramitās;
that the upholding of the true Dharma is itself the pāramitā clarifies that even if the text is incomplete or deficient, it is still so.
Second, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are cited to explain the True Dharma, that is, the *pāramitās*.
Why is this? A son or daughter of good family who upholds the True Dharma should accomplish it through generosity (*dāna*).

They should accomplish it by means of generosity, even to the point of sacrificing their own limbs and members to protect the minds of others, thereby bringing it to fulfillment. That which is thus accomplished—
To establish the True Dharma for sentient beings is called *dānapāramitā*.

For those who should be accomplished through ethical discipline (*śīla*), one accomplishes them by guarding the six sense faculties, purifying the actions of body, speech, and mind, and even by maintaining the four correct deportments to protect their minds;
to establish the True Dharma for those sentient beings thus accomplished is called *śīlapāramitā*.

Those who should be accomplished through patience: if those sentient beings revile, insult, slander, or terrify them, they accomplish them by maintaining a mind free from anger and a mind intent on benefiting others, through the power of supreme patience such that even their facial expression does not change, and by protecting the minds of those beings.
When those beings whom they have accomplished are established in the True Dharma, this is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Those who are to be accomplished through diligence do not give rise to a mind of indolence toward those sentient beings, but instead generate a great desire for awakening and supreme diligence;
even at the cost of hardship throughout the four modes of deportment, they protect the minds of those beings and bring them to accomplishment.

When those beings thus accomplished are established in the True Dharma, this is called the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Those who are to be accomplished through meditative concentration...
With an undistracted mind and a mind not turned outward, through supreme right mindfulness, he does not forget for a long time what was done or said long ago;
protecting the intentions of those beings, he brings them to fulfillment.
When he establishes the True Dharma for those beings thus brought to fulfillment, this is called the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā), which should be accomplished through wisdom.
Furthermore, when those sentient beings inquire about all matters, he expounds upon all treatises and all fields of knowledge regarding the ultimate perfection of arts and crafts,
even down to various manual tasks, protecting their inclinations and bringing them to fulfillment.
When he establishes the True Dharma for those sentient beings whom he has thus fulfilled, this is called Prajñāpāramitā.

Pāramitā. [Commentary] Second, from "For what reason" (*kasmāt*) onwards, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are cited as the Dharma to explain the meaning of the "True Dharma," which is *pāramitā*.
The doubt is raised: "How is it that the True Dharma is itself *pāramitā*? The formal explanation consists of eight points.
Because the Earth-Mahāsattva wishes to deliver sentient beings according to their capacities, he cultivates these six perfections within a single thought-moment.
Since these six perfections accord with principle and are not deviant, they are the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Because they serve as a standard for sentient beings, they are the Dharma.
Because they consist of the cultivation of signlessness (*animitta*), they are the *pāramitās*. Thus, it is said that they are "the True Dharma. This...
The six perfections in the middle [stages] are all explained according to this same principle. "That" refers to the eighth stage and above. [The *Commentary* states:
"The Great Being of the eighth stage desires to save sentient beings according to their capacities," and so forth;

this is from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s explanation of the eighth stage, wherein it says that this Bodhisattva, in accordance with the various differences in the bodies, minds, faiths, and understandings of all sentient beings, [dwells] in those Buddha-lands.
Within the midst of the assembly, he manifests his body; that is to say, among śramaṇas he displays the form of a śramaṇa,
and likewise displays the forms of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, householders, the four heavenly kings,
the thirty-three gods, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, as well as the forms of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas— all these he displays.
All lands are likewise so, emitting the light of great wisdom that universally extinguishes the dark ignorance of the afflictions of sentient beings,
for it is able skillfully to open and reveal the gates of wisdom.
[Commentary] The third section, from "Therefore, World-Honored One" onwards, concludes the meaning of the preceding points.
Therefore, O World-Honored One, there is no difference between the pāramitās and the upholding of the true Dharma; the upholding of the true Dharma is itself the pāramitā.
[Commentary] From the passage "World-Honored One, from now on... onwards, the second part within the section clarifying mutual identity explains the mutual identity of person and dharma.
Furthermore, it is divided into three parts. First, the primary clarification of the identity of person and dharma:
"World-Honored One, now, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall further expound the great meaning. The Buddha said, "Speak. Then Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha:
"The upholding of the True Dharma is not different from the one who upholds the True Dharma; the one who upholds the True Dharma is not different from the upholding of the True Dharma."
The Dharma is that which those sons and daughters of good family who embrace the True Dharma [possess]; this is precisely what it means to embrace the True Dharma.

[Commentary]: Regarding "embracing the True Dharma," the first instance of the phrase restates the preceding clause concerning the Dharma, while the second instance restates the subsequent clause concerning the person.

There is no difference between them; "those who embrace the True Dharma" refers to persons who are not different from the Dharma, and there is no difference between embracing [the Dharma] and being the Dharma itself.
"Phenomena" (dharma) refers to the fact that phenomena are no different from persons; these two phrases together clarify their non-difference.

Next, one should clarify their identity (*tādātmya*), yet the text is insufficient and lacks this portion. We know that this clarifies the mutual identity of person and phenomenon because it speaks of "sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma.
The second section, beginning with "For what reason," also provides an explanation.
The meaning of identity.
Why is this? If a son or daughter of good family who upholds the True Dharma, for the sake of upholding the True Dharma, relinquishes the three bases.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning of "identity" begins by raising a doubt: "How can the person be identical with the Dharma? The explanation states:
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the person is one who has undertaken the upholding of the True Dharma (*saddharma-parigraha*) and has abandoned the three types of divisions.
This mind of abandonment is itself the mind that upholds the True Dharma. Since this very mind constitutes such a practitioner, it is thus the upholding itself.
How could the mind that receives the True Dharma be different from the person who abandons these three types of divisions?

[Commentary] Regarding the second explanation of the meaning of identity: "Because this very mind has already become such a practitioner" means that by means of this mind that embraces the True Dharma, one is able to accomplish this abandonment of the three divisions; thus, one knows the [nature of] the True Dharma.
The mind is itself the renunciation of the three parts; humans have no other name than "the master capable of renouncing," while the principle of what is renounced by people is called "Dharma.
Therefore, the person is indeed the Dharma. One may be called a "person" because they renounce the three parts for the sake of upholding the True Dharma.
This second vow opens the beginning, and this chapter establishes its meaning.
[Commentary] The third section, beginning from "What are the three? and following, sets forth the meaning of the three aspects of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
This third exposition of the three aspects of relinquishment follows upon the preceding clarification of the "flaming light" (*jvālā-prabhā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because of the preceding radiant flame," since the characteristics of the three parts to be relinquished were not yet explained in the previous section, the meaning of these three parts is now clarified once again.
[Commentary] Furthermore, this is divided into four parts: first, the correct elucidation of the meaning of the three divisions;
second, from "Thus, World-Honored One... onwards, the praise of those who have abandoned the three divisions; third, from "Furthermore, World-Honored One, good sons...
onwards, the clarification of the timing for abandoning the three divisions; fourth, from "World-Honored One, I see that the True Dharma has been upheld... onwards.
Citing the Buddha as witness, within the first section which clearly elucidates the relinquishing of the three things, there are two parts.
First, the direct and general enumeration of the three things: what are these three? They are body, life, and wealth.
"What are these three? They are body, life, and wealth.
[Commentary] The second section, from "The son or daughter of good family who gives up the body" onwards, separately sets forth the substance of the three parts.
"The son or daughter of good family who gives up the body" means that after the limit of birth and death, they will be free from old age, sickness, and death, and attain...

One who abandons the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body—which is indestructible, eternally abiding, immutable, inconceivable, and endowed with merit—attains equality with the limits of birth and death, ultimately transcending old age, sickness, and death, and achieves boundless, eternally abiding, inconceivable merit.
One who penetrates all profound Buddha-dharmas attains equality with the limits of birth and death. One who relinquishes wealth attains [equality with the limits of birth and death].
Together with all sentient beings, they possess inexhaustible and undiminishing, ultimately ever-abiding, inconceivable, and fully perfected merit,
receiving the most excellent offerings from all sentient beings.

[Commentary]: From "giving up the body" (*śarīra-tyāga*) downward, the text specifically clarifies the relinquishing of the body; from "giving up life" (*jīvita-tyāga*) downward, it clarifies the relinquishing of life;

and from "giving up wealth" (*bhoga-tyāga*) downward, it clarifies the relinquishing of wealth. The ancient interpretation held that "giving up the body" meant voluntarily becoming a slave, while "giving up life" meant seeking death at the hands of others.
However, the present explanation states that both "giving up life" and "giving up the body" refer to death; they differ only in the resolution of the intention. If...

Just as throwing oneself before a starving tigress is fundamentally about the relinquishment of the body, if a man of principle sees a situation where his life must be given, his intent lies in the sacrifice of life.
To "relinquish wealth" refers to things external to the self. Regarding the phrase "the future limit" (*paścimā koṭi*): it means the future;

since the future has no end, it is clear that he intends to relinquish [himself] eternally. Furthermore, it is said that the "diamond-like mind" (*vajracitta*) constitutes the future limit, for it is free from old age, sickness, and death.

This refers to the fact that the *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death) is without transformation; "transformation" here refers to *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death).
Regarding the term "attainment," it means causing sentient beings to attain [it]. As for the "meritorious wealth of the Dharma," it is not like worldly wealth, which is shared by the five families.
"Attaining the supreme offerings of all sentient beings" is a slight error of phrasing; it should rather be stated as "attaining supreme offerings."
"Surpassing all sentient beings," or "following the literal text for a direct explanation," refers to obtaining the extraordinary offerings of humans and devas.

[The *Chao* states: If one were to act like the one who threw himself to a starving tiger, this refers to the account of Prince Sattva’s self-sacrifice in the fourth chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the "Chapter on the Sacrifice of the Body.
In that section, the Bodhi-tree deity questioned the Tathāgata regarding his past deeds.
During this time of ascetic practice, through the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, the great earth shook and a stupa made of the seven precious gems emerged from the ground.
After the Buddha had paid homage to the stupa, he commanded Ānanda to take the relics and show them to the great assembly. The Buddha said:
"These relics are that which have been perfumed and cultivated by morality, concentration, wisdom, and even the immeasurable pāramitās. At that time...
In order to sever the doubts of the assembly, the World-Honored One spoke of the past causes and conditions regarding the śarīra relics.
In a past age, there was a king named Mahāratha who had three sons:
the first was named Mahāpuruṣa, the second was named Mahādeva, and the youngest was named Mahāsattva. While these three sons were wandering through a garden grove, they saw one...
A tigress had recently given birth to seven cubs; their bodies were emaciated and their lives were on the verge of ending.
Prince Sattva, observing the impurity of his own body, conceived a profound sense of revulsion and renunciation, vowing to seek unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

For this reason, he threw himself from the peak of the King of High Mountains before the tigress. The tigress devoured him, leaving behind nothing but his bones. The Buddha told the tree deity: [the rest of the discourse follows].

At that time, the *Sattva* was my own body; the first prince was Maitreya, the second prince was Devadatta, the tigress was Gopī, and the seven cubs were the five bhikṣus of today—Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Regarding the one who gave his head as light, the fourth fascicle of the *Mahā-upāya-buddha-pratyupakāra-sūtra* states: "In the past..."
The king of Vārāṇasī was named Mahāprabha; his heart was compassionate toward all, and he never acted contrary to the wishes of others.
A small kingdom envied him and hired a brahmin to beg for the king’s head. The king reflected to himself:

"Since beginningless time, I have never yet sacrificed my life for the sake of the Dharma, though I have exhausted my spirit through the toil of birth and death. Now, with this very body, I desire to seek Bodhi."
"Excellent! If you do not oppose my original intention, when shall we attain unsurpassed bodhi? The king said, "Excellent!
He then tied his own hair to a tree in the rear garden and commanded the Brahmin to sever his head and take it away.
King Prabhāsa was none other than Śākyamuni. Regarding that which is shared by the five families: first, water.
[The five perils are: second, fire; third, enemies; fourth, oppressive creditors; fifth, the calamity of kings. [Commentary:
From "From the World-Honored One" onwards, the second section praises those who have abandoned the three parts, as can be seen.
World-Honored One, when sons and daughters of good family thus relinquish the three parts and uphold the True Dharma,
they are constantly prophesied by all Buddhas and are gazed upon with reverence by all sentient beings.
[Commentary]: From the passage beginning "Furthermore, O son of good family" onwards, the third section clarifies the timing for relinquishing the three parts.
It is said that the merit of protecting the Dharma lies in its resurgence when it is about to perish; thus, the merit of protection is made manifest through this revival.
Within this section, there are two parts: first, the formal clarification of the timing for relinquishing the three parts.
Furthermore, World-Honored One, when the True Dharma is about to perish, those sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma—
whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās— will, amidst factions, disputes, destruction, and dissension,
enter the ranks of the Dharma through their lack of flattery, lack of deception, and lack of artifice, out of their love for and upholding of the True Dharma.
[Commentary] It clarifies that the essential requirement is that when the Dharma is about to perish, one must act with a mind of the true path.
[Sub-commentary] "Must act with a mind of the true path" refers to all the passages in the sutra from "without flattery or crookedness" onwards.
[Commentary] Second, from the passage "entering the ranks of the Dharma-friends" onwards, it clarifies that when the Buddha grants them predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*),
those who have abandoned the three parts [of the self] can all see this.
Those who enter the ranks of the Dharma-friends will necessarily receive the prediction of enlightenment bestowed by all Buddhas.
[Commentary: From the passage beginning with "World-Honored One, my view... and following, the fourth of the threefold meanings is established:
citing the Buddha as testimony to prove that his words are not empty.
"World-Honored One, my view of upholding the True Dharma possesses such great power; the Buddha is the true eye and true wisdom for the sake of the Dharma."
The root is the penetration of phenomena; it is the reliance upon the True Dharma, and one fully knows and sees it.
[Commentary] Regarding the citation of the Buddha as proof: "The Nameless One" says that with the true eye one sees, and with true wisdom one knows.
As the root of phenomena, one illuminates their beginning; as the penetration of phenomena, one discerns their end; this is the person who relies upon the True Dharma.
May the Buddha, whom I revere and trust, having already known and seen [this], deign to grant his manifest certification.
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra-artha-sic-chao*, Fascicle Two;
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra-artha-sic-chao*, Fascicle Three.

[Commentary] From the section beginning "At that time, the World-Honored One [spoke to] Śrīmālā" onwards, within the second part, the "Accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s Praise," there are also two sections:
first, the praise and accomplishment; second, from "Therefore" onwards, the summary and exhortation.
Regarding the first, the praise and accomplishment, it is further divided into two: first, the direct exposition.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his approval for the great power of diligence in upholding the True Dharma as expounded by Śrīmālādevī.
[Commentary] Upholding the True Dharma refers to one of the myriad practices among those of the eighth stage and above. Second.
In this further exposition, there are three parts. First, the analogy of the strong man is presented to clarify the vehicle of superior humans and devas.
Thus, Śrīmālā, as you have said, the great power of diligence in upholding the True Dharma is like a strong man;
even a slight touch upon his body produces intense pain.
[Commentary] Regarding "such as a great strongman" and so forth: it is like a person of little strength who experiences great pain from even a slight touch upon their body by a great strongman.

[The Master] said: Although I have received your instructions and spoken thus, if I were not to receive the Tathāgata’s elegant exposition of these matters, sentient beings in future ages would have little faith or reverence.
Thus, Śrīmālā, I do not see any other single wholesome dharma that causes such affliction and distress to Māra as the slight upholding of the true Dharma.
[Commentary]: Second, the analogy of the bull-king is raised to clarify that [the Mahāyāna] surpasses the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Just as the form and color of a bull-king are incomparable and superior to all other oxen, so too this Mahāyāna—by virtue of its vastness—is superior to all the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the two vehicles, for it extensively embraces the true Dharma.
[Commentary] Third, the analogy of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is raised to clarify that the Mahāyāna surpasses all stages from the seventh downward.
Just as Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is majestic and uniquely distinguished, excelling all other mountains,

so too does this Mahāyāna— by relinquishing body, life, and wealth with a mind of gathering (*saṃgraha*)— surpass the initial stage of the Mahāyāna which does not relinquish body, life, and wealth, yet still upholds the True Dharma.
All roots of goodness, let alone those of the Two Vehicles, because they are vast.
[Commentary: Within these three, both the expansion and the contraction can be seen. "The mind of gathering" refers to the mind of the ten thousand practices;
although those from the seventh ground downward are also able to sacrifice body and life, this is manifested only at the single thought-moment of the eighth ground and above.

Because she has fully cultivated [these practices], it is said that she "does not abandon" them. Regarding the second section, the summary exhortation, there are also four parts. First is the extensive exhortation:
"Therefore, Śrīmālā, you should, for the sake of receiving and upholding the True Dharma, reveal it to sentient beings, instruct sentient beings, and establish sentient beings."
[Commentary: "Revealing and instructing sentient beings" refers to the vehicles of humans and devas, which corresponds to the preceding analogy of the strongman.

"Transforming and teaching sentient beings" refers to the two vehicles, which corresponds to the preceding analogy of the bull king. "Establishing sentient beings" refers to those from the seventh stage downward, which corresponds to the preceding analogy of Mount Sumeru. These are all extensive exhortations.
[Commentary] "Revealing and instructing sentient beings" refers to the vehicles of humans and devas and so forth;
