it is called "revealing and instructing" (*kaishō*) at the beginning, "transforming and educating" (*kyōka*) in the middle, and "establishing" (*konryū*) at the end. Having already expounded the meaning through three analogies, he further adds three exhortations to cause that Way to spread widely.
The intent of the present commentary is likewise the same as before: the three metaphors were first cited to describe the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
Because the upholding of the True Dharma surpasses those of the five vehicles, the present summary and exhortation are likewise directed toward the five vehicles as an exhortation.
"Revealing and instructing sentient beings" corresponds to the aforementioned Great Mallas; this refers to those in the vehicle of humans and devas who have not yet been opened to instruction.
"Establishing through self-deliverance" refers to those of the two vehicles; it is established in contrast to the superior Bodhisattvas who have not yet reached the eighth stage.
[The text says: "Because establishing the True [Body] is thus superior to the mere reception of the Right Dharma, one must necessarily reveal it to those of the five vehicles," and so forth.
[Commentary: Second, the extensive conclusion.
"In this way, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*’s upholding of the True Dharma possesses such great benefit, such great merit, and such great fruit.
[Commentary]: "Such great benefit" concludes the discussion of the vehicles of humans and devas; "such great merit" concludes that of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*);

and "such great fruit" concludes that of the Mahāyāna up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). These also correspond to the three metaphors as their respective conclusions; thus, this is called the "Extensive" [section].

[The section on] "Concluding" [states]: [The *Chao* (Commentary) says: In all instances within the "Extensive Concluding" section, the term "concluding" (*jie*) is used; "concluding" means to demonstrate and reveal. By revealing this to humans and devas, one immediately attains great benefit;
by teaching and transforming those of the Two Vehicles, one immediately attains great merit; and by establishing it upon the seventh stage, one immediately attains the great fruit. This is so.

Therefore, all [these teachings] arise from the "upholding of the True Dharma. Regarding the extensive and concise [explanations]: the extensive version enumerates the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*), while the concise version speaks of them as being immeasurable and boundless, etc.
[Commentary: Third, the brief exhortation.
"Śrīmālā, even if I were to speak for incalculable upon incalculable kalpas regarding the meaning and benefits of the merit of upholding the True Dharma,
I could not reach their limit.
[Commentary] Fourth, the brief conclusion.
Therefore, Śrīmālā’s upholding of the True Dharma possesses immeasurable and boundless merit.
[Commentary: From the passage "Śrīmālā, I... below, the brief exhortation is to be seen; from the passage "Therefore... below, the brief conclusion is to be seen.
[Commentary] ○ Fifth, the Chapter on the One Vehicle. Wuming says: "The profound purport of this sutra and its extraordinary names and meanings are all revealed in this chapter.
Its naming at the outset transcends ordinary rhythms, such that it cannot be sought through words;
its meaning surpasses all categories, such that it cannot be grasped by the intellect. One must necessarily broaden one's habitual attachments to things and abandon the self."

Only those who preserve the Way can then seek it within causes and conditions. Now, in explaining this chapter, I shall first provide a formal analysis of its meaning and then interpret the scriptural text.
This formal analysis is divided into nine sections. First: Explaining the intent of the chapter and providing a brief division of the text.
[Commentary]: From the passage "The Buddha told Śrīmālā, 'Now you should further explain...

onwards, the second chapter, the Chapter on the One Vehicle within the Section on the Practice of Others (*parapratipatti*), clarifies how the five vehicles—both the producers and those produced—are subsumed and gathered into the One Vehicle.
Within this, it is first divided into two parts: first, the formal exposition that all enter the One Vehicle; second, the clarification of their single essence. Third.
The "Precious Single Vehicle" is the cause of the "Single-Entity Triple Gem," and the "Single-Entity Triple Gem" is the fruit of the "Single Vehicle.

Because one wishes to use the fruit— the single entity— as an analogy for the cause being single, the second point cites the "Single-Entity Triple Gem" to clarify that since the fruit is one, the cause is likewise one.
[Commentary] Second, clarifying the present by contrasting it with the past.
[Sub-commentary] Now, as for the past, the distinctions between the three jewels as a ladder and the five vehicles were all provisional teachings and not ultimate teachings;
now, having integrated the five vehicles into the one vehicle, they are all equally eternal.
Because it is the cause for the single fruit, it also clarifies that the Three Jewels of the past—the ladder and the steps—were not the ultimate;
rather, only the eternally abiding, single essence of today is the supreme refuge.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the distinctions of the five vehicles are equally expedient means," this chapter clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage subsume the previously manifested five vehicles to return to the One Vehicle.
This manifestation is the provisional (śūnyatā-upāya), while this subsumption is the entry into the ultimate reality.

Thus, it is no different from Śākyamuni’s single transformation, which first employed the three vehicles and subsequently the one; therefore, the text of this chapter is used in its entirety [to explain that].

The ritual manifestations of transformation throughout a single lifetime are explained herein; thus, there is praise and censure, suppression and exaltation, yet the general intent is no different from that of the *Vimalakīrti* or the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.

If this is so, how does it differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? The answer is: what is called "attaining" or "awakening" in this present assembly refers to what will be attained and awakened [in the future].
The Chinese term "present awakening" and "present attainment" means that this sutra discusses the beginning and end [of the path] while manifesting them within the present assembly. ○
Third, the explanation of the meaning of the name. [Commentary]:
First, "One" (Eka) is a designation for non-duality; "Vehicle" (Yāna) has the meaning of transporting one forth. Regarding the interpretation of this single term, various schools differ.
One school says: "One" is originally non-existent; it is merely called "One" because one wishes to refute the notion of "Three."
The second [interpretation] states: "One" refers to the fruit (*phala*), while "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the cause (*hetu*).
Although the virtuous categories within the cause are manifold, they ultimately converge upon a single fruit; thus, because the meaning of the fruit is one, it is called "one" by way of the cause.
The third [interpretation] states: Both "one" and "vehicle" are names for the cause. Although the virtuous categories within the cause differ in their various forms, [they are unified].
Since the underlying principle of this interpretation is consistent, it is called "the first. While this first explanation is indeed excellent, one might raise the following doubt:

if the pure lands of the ten directions do not distinguish between the three vehicles, they likewise should not preach the path of the One Vehicle. Yet, in all the pure lands of the ten directions, the One Vehicle is preached.
If that were so, how could one say that the One Vehicle is taught solely for the purpose of subverting the three? This is merely a preliminary objection.
Both the second and third explanations may be employed; however, contemporary scholars mostly rely on the first cause for their interpretation.

[Commentary] Regarding the three explanations of the meaning of the name, the second master takes the end to signify the beginning. The third master holds that the single "sovereign cause" (īśvara-hetu) is like the waters of the four great rivers:
although they do not yet reach the ocean at their source, they flow toward it. The single word "flowing toward" (quèr qù) signifies the ten thousand things.
The meaning of the dharmas of the happy realms (*sugati*) is one and the same. ○ Fourth, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles.

[Commentary]: To further distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles: that which does not seek its own deliverance but prioritizes saving sentient beings, and whose natural outflow is the fruit of Buddhahood, is called the Mahāyāna.
That which regards the transformation of others as a burden and seeks only its own deliverance—being inferior to the former and lacking in reality—is termed the Hīnayāna.

[Commentary]: Because it shares the same destination as the substance [of the true city]—namely, the fruit of Buddhahood—it is called an "equal-flow" (*niṣyanda*) transformation-city. Its provisional establishment is designated as "excellent," yet it lacks reality.
5. Distinguishing the similarities and differences between the one [great vehicle].
[Commentary: Although the general intent of the Mahāyāna and the Ekayāna is the same, there is a slight difference.
"Mahāyāna" remains a specific designation within the context of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), whereas "Ekayāna" carries no such designation of three or two.

This is why, although the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* are called "Great Teachings," they are not termed "Ekayāna. Following this principle, when explaining "Mahā" (Great) as being identical to "Ekayāna," one should proceed accordingly.
Regarding the meaning of the "two fruits," one school says that "Great" refers to the fruit, namely the Buddha-fruit as the great cause.
Another school says it is also the cause, referring to the Bodhisattva who does not seek their own deliverance but flows equally with all beings;
because they thus transport their minds on a vast scale, it is called "Great."
[Commentary] Fifth, regarding the discernment of the similarities and differences between the One Vehicle and the others: first, the similarities and differences are established;

within the explanation, first the differences are explained, followed by examples below to explain the similarities. Regarding the Mahāyāna, first, within the explanation of the differences, it is because the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* both state that there are three vehicles through which one attains the Way.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, if one attains the vehicle of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Bodhisattva, it is all said that one "should [attain it]."
In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, while studying the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and the entire great assembly saw themselves seated upon precious lotus flowers.

When the Buddha manifested this land as adorned and pure, five hundred sons of elders attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and eighty-four thousand people resolved their minds on Bodhicitta. The Buddha then withdrew [the manifestation].

The divine power was thus restored to its former state in this world. Thirty-two thousand devas and humans who sought the vehicle of the śrāvakas realized that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely impermanent;
they became free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).

Eight thousand bhikṣus, no longer grasping at any phenomena, attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and liberation of mind. All such instances were cases where the three [vehicles] were combined.
This interpretation is largely incorrect. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "In the worlds of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle of the Dharma;

there is neither a second nor a third; there is only the One Buddha Vehicle. Furthermore, this sūtra’s teaching on the convergence of the five vehicles into the one vehicle means that it is simply "one" and not "great.
If one were to interpret "great" by analogy with "one," then this "great" would merely refer to the greatness of a single family.
As before, we shall provide two explanations: first, clarifying the greatness of the Result Vehicle (Phala-yāna), and second, clarifying the greatness of the Cause Vehicle (Hetu-yāna).
This may be seen as follows. 6. Discerning the Essence.

[Commentary] If one discusses the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*), there are two kinds of goodness: first, innate goodness (*vipāka-kuśala*); second, acquired goodness (*samudānīta-kuśala*). Although innate goodness exists...
The capacity to shed what is heavy and render it light can merely conceal the vajra;
because it does not lead to the fruit of Buddhahood, it is merely a causal condition and does not constitute the primary essence. Therefore, we now take the cultivation of goodness as the essence.
Furthermore, it is explained that "good understanding" is the root of the vehicle, while "goodness" is the branch of the vehicle. Here, we take the branch as the vehicle rather than the root.
By what means does the Path attain penetration or lack it? If one takes "understanding" (*jñāna*) as the vehicle (*yāna*), then the designation "vehicle" would not be comprehensive;

for even a single recitation of "Namo" is not non-virtuous, and thus the name "vehicle" would indeed be broad. Therefore, [the text] takes only the "conventional" (*mṛdu*) as the essence of the vehicle.
Furthermore, why is the virtue of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) directed toward the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) also not considered the essence of the vehicle? Why is this so?
Furthermore, riding upon this serves as the cause for birth in the state of permanence during the period of transcending birth and death.

[Commentary] In the analysis of the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*), the essence is first established. Regarding the phrase "the two types of goodness, retributive and cultivated," "retributive goodness" refers to the goodness of karmic fruition, such as being liberated from the heavy [suffering] of the four miserable destinies and obtaining the retribution of gods and humans; it liberates one from the six paths of existence.

They again obtain the retribution of liberation for the two vehicles; Bodhisattvas of the two vehicles [liberate themselves] up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi), liberating themselves from the retributions of the lower stages.

Upon reaching the Buddha-ground, there is no longer any exiting from retribution; therefore it is said that "the three levels of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood possess fruit-retribution, while only the One Person, the Buddha, dwells in the Land of Dharma-nature.
This is because his body is identical to Vairocana and thus possesses no retribution of change. As for the place he dwells in...
This is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) constitutes the land, as the essence of the subject and object are one; therefore, it is said that one does not "attain" the fruit of Buddhahood.
Rather, these are merely auxiliary conditions that lead one to the final stage, never serving as the primary essence itself.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the basis of this vehicle," among the various practices of cultivating goodness, there is the goodness that is cultivated, and there is first the mind capable of understanding and knowing that goodness.
Since one must first understand and know what is wholesome before one can practice it, understanding is the root while wholesomeness is the branch.
Now, regarding the selection of the branch—namely, that all that is wholesome may serve as the substance of the vehicle—it is because the substance is universal that understanding is not selected.
There are those who cultivate wholesome deeds yet do not necessarily understand them; therefore, understanding is not taken, for the mind of understanding is not universally applicable.
For example, even when children play by gathering sand to make stūpas for the Buddha, they may not necessarily know that this is a virtuous act;
yet, although they lack conscious awareness, the virtue is nonetheless present and is fully capable of serving as the essence [of the practice]. Such cases can all be understood by this analogy.
Therefore, the mention of a single instance in the text—namely, the invocation "Namo"—is intended precisely to convey this meaning.
[Commentary] The wholesome roots of ordinary beings directed toward the three realms of existence merely aspire to that which is within the triple world and do not point toward the eternally abiding;
therefore, they also do not constitute the essence of a vehicle.

[Sub-commentary] Next, regarding the phrase "the wholesome roots of ordinary beings directed toward the three realms of existence," it clarifies that the wholesome roots aspired to are no different from those mentioned previously, because of their object.
Because the period [of its application] is near, it likewise does not constitute the essence of a vehicle.

[Commentary: If one discusses the convergence and unification, it is said that while the three teachings are subsumed and the three vehicles are abolished, and the three attachments are shattered, "goodness" remains the same despite the differences between the present and the past;
as for the principle (*li*), there is nothing to be unified, but as for the teaching (*jiao*), names and meanings are each distinct.

Therefore, the reason for synthesizing [the teachings] into one is that, while the literal expression concerns the duration and disappearance of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), it is taught as the Mahāyāna;
thus, the three attachments are as previously explained.

[Commentary]: Third, regarding the inclusion and synthesis—when speaking of the "three virtues" in the lower synthesis, humans and devas constitute the first virtue, and the two [types of] goodness constitute the second.
The vehicles constitute one excellence; the Mahāyāna of the seven stages constitutes another excellence. The three teachings and the three attachments may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the explanation of the three attachments as before: this is as clarified in the previous "Chapter on Reception," where it is shown that the persons encompassed within the five vehicles do not transcend the three attachments;
according to their attachments, the teachings are bestowed upon them. ○ Chapter Seven: Extensive Classification.
[Commentary] Within the first section, which correctly elucidates the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), it is further divided into three parts:

first, from the beginning up to "supramundane wholesome dharmas," the five vehicles are collectively integrated; second, from "As the World-Honored One has said regarding the six bases" onwards, the causes of the two vehicles are specifically integrated;
third, from "World-Honored One, Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have fear... onwards...
The following section then brings together the fruits of the two vehicles.
[Commentary] The seven broad divisions of the chapters may be seen therein. ○ Eighth, explaining the intent of the separate assembly for the two vehicles.
[Sub-commentary] In the previous chapter on "Accepting the True Dharma," only the mind capable of generating it was taken as the acceptance of the true dharma.
If one does not grasp the practices of the five vehicles that arise [from the One Vehicle], then the meaning has not yet been fully exhausted;
however, in this present chapter, both the producer and the produced are fully grasped as they all enter the One Vehicle, and thus there is first a general synthesis.

Since humans and devas do not yet seek separately, nor are the names "Great" and "Small" yet fixed, the principle of the general synthesis is naturally sufficient for those from the seventh stage downward.
Originally, the Buddha sought to establish the Mahāyāna for himself, yet there was no need for a second assembly;

however, because those of the Two Vehicles were trusted by sentient beings, and none among them failed to believe that there were distinct causes and effects, he earnestly convened this second assembly.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement in the section clarifying the separate assembly for the two vehicles, "merely taking the mind that is able to produce [the teachings]," etc.:
why was it previously called "upholding the True Dharma"? Because from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) that encompasses all dharmas constitutes upholding;
this mind is able to produce the practices of the five vehicles and transform sentient beings, and is therefore termed "able to produce."
The meaning of the preceding chapter lies solely in the fact that the mind capable of producing [the teachings] possesses the function of giving birth to the five vehicles;

it has not yet integrated these five vehicles back into the One Vehicle. This present chapter, however, fully integrates both the three practices within the mind capable of producing and the five vehicles produced from it into the One Vehicle;
therefore, it differs from the preceding chapter. As for humans and devas, they do not yet seek anything distinct [from this].
Because it is the Mahāyāna, the names "Great" and "Small" are not yet fixed; a general assembly is sufficient. From the seven stages onward, one originally seeks the fruit of wondrous enlightenment;
however, as long as one is still practicing, even when the merit is fulfilled and one enters the stage of non-effort (*anābhoga*), one spontaneously attains the fruit of Buddhahood.

There is no need for a further assembly with those of the Two Vehicles. These are the monastic inner assembly who constantly follow the Buddha; though all people say they are distinct, [they are not].
Because the causes differ and the fruits vary between humans, devas, and bodhisattvas, it is necessary to meet again. ○ Nine:
Resolving Doubts and Revealing Sameness.

[Commentary]: However, the preceding "Chapter on Receiving and Upholding the True Dharma" clarified only the meaning of receiving and upholding [the Dharma] from the eighth stage (bhūmi) upward. Therefore—
As for what is called "the portion of others" (*parabhāga*), its principle can indeed be verified by oneself;

yet, in this chapter, all that which gives rise to and encompasses the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*)—which are the "arisen"—is taken as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). How, then, can what is called "the portion of others" serve as proof? The commentary explains:

Although the interpretation of the text is thus, there is a specific reason for what is termed "the portion of others. Why is this? It is because, when discussing the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), one must establish the definitive position (*niyata-sthiti*).
Since one has already gained faith in the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as described above, what need is there to mention the seventh stage (*bhūmi*)?
Nevertheless, speaking according to the teachings, from the first stage up to the seventh stage, the severing of fetters and the objects of contemplation are equal to those of the Two Vehicles;

therefore, regarding the meaning of the One Vehicle, they are not yet clearly understood. As for the matter of clear penetration, it occurs only from the eighth stage upward. For this reason, this chapter also...
This explains that [the preceding section] pertains to the practice of others.
[The *Chao* (Commentary) states: Regarding the phrase "Now, this chapter takes all... within the ninth section, "Dispelling Doubts," this constitutes a formal objection. The objection asks:
Among the five vehicles, from the seventh stage downward is the practice of oneself; why then are they all designated as the practice of others?
Regarding the phrase "Is it practice?", the commentary states: Although the literal text is thus, one must seek the intended meaning within the text.

Why? Because if we discuss this in terms of the actual capacity and the actual teaching, a Bodhisattva at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is called one who has attained the fixed position (*niyata-pada*);

at this time, they already believe that all phenomena arise from the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and ultimately all return to the principle of the One Vehicle—how much more so for those in the seventh stage!
If you do not believe this, it is simply because the Tathāgata has taught the provisional transformation of the path of instruction;

that is, because one practices the ten *pāramitās* and so forth within the sequential stages of mind up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). Thus, one is not yet clearly enlightened regarding the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*);

only when one practices within the single mind of effortlessness (*anābhoga*) does one become truly clear and penetrating. Therefore, this chapter also serves as the practice for those of other dispositions. Part One.
Regarding the dwelling in the doctrine of the One Vehicle as fully present in the *Avataṃsaka*, the text on the "Initial Resolve Dwelling" (*Prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*) states:
"The entire body of wisdom is not realized through another; it divides itself into hundreds of parts to accomplish the Buddha-way and transform sentient beings.

This is the teaching of the definitive (real) vehicle. As for the phrase "from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage," this refers to the *Ratnaketu-śikhara-sūtra* (or *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*).
The scroll states: "From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, one subdues and eliminates the karmic fruits of the three realms entirely;
from the eighth stage upward, the residual habits (*vāsanā*) of ignorance remain.
[Commentary] Within the first general summary, there are two parts. The first concerns the Buddha’s command to preach.
The Buddha told Śrīmālā: "Now you shall further expound upon the 'Upholding of the True Dharma' as taught by all Buddhas. [Commentary]:
In the previous chapter on "Upholding the True Dharma," whenever a statement was made, Śrīmālā first requested that it be taught.

In this current chapter, the Buddha himself first issues the command. This is because, in the preceding chapter, since those were the profound practices of others, she did not dare to proclaim them herself; therefore, [the Buddha] commanded her.
Furthermore, regarding what has been said above, there is nothing that does not accord with principle and nothing that is open to doubt;
therefore, without waiting for a request, I have first commanded you to speak further. You should now further explain that which all Buddhas have taught concerning the upholding of the True Dharma:
namely, that both that which is produced and that which produces must all enter into the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), just as the Buddhas have taught.

[Commentary] Next, regarding the statement in the sutra that "in each preceding chapter, before speaking, one first requests the speaker," the initial passage on receiving the mandate—which begins with the previous vow—is precisely this request for the teaching. At that time, Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall now, further, relying upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, proclaim the mantra of the great vow of subduing. Subsequently, the Tathāgata granted his permission.
The commentary states: The Buddha told Śrīmālā, "Speak freely. First, regarding the inclusion of the sequence of practice, it says:
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, "I shall, relying upon the Buddha’s spiritual power, further expound the vast meaning of the upholding of the True Dharma.

Next, the Buddha spoke, and she then proceeded to speak. Furthermore, because the characteristics of persons and dharmas are identical within this [teaching], it is said that "whenever she speaks," it is so.
[Commentary] Second, regarding "Śrīmālā receives the command and speaks": this consists of two parts. First, the primary assembly that gives rise [to the teaching];
second, from "From the World-Honored One, like Lake Anavatapta" onwards, the assembly that is produced [from that].
Within the first, the primary assembly that gives rise [to the teaching], there are also two parts: first, the actual assembly itself.
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. She then said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, that which upholds the True Dharma is precisely the Mahāyāna."
[Commentary] "That which is the Mahāyāna" clarifies that the mind capable of generating and embracing [the teaching] is one and the same as the Mahāyāna mind.
[Sub-commentary] First,
regarding the phrase "the mind capable of generating and embracing" within the section on "generating," it is explained that this is identical to the Mahāyāna mind.
In the preceding chapter, it was shown that the mind of reception can give rise to the five vehicles; now, the Mahāyāna is likewise able to give rise to the five vehicles.
Since the meaning of "ability to give rise" is identical in both instances, they are said to be "one."
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the assembly.
Why is this? Because the Mahāyāna gives birth to all the wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the mundane and supramundane realms.
[Commentary]: Second, the explanation clarifies that since that which is produced is one, how could that which produces it be different?
This appears to be a reconciliation of the "produced," yet by citing the "produced" to explain the "producer," it is not actually a reconciliation of the "produced."
[Commentary] Next, regarding the explanation of the statement within the assembly that "since that which is produced is one,

how could that which produces it be different," this clarifies that the five vehicles produced from the One Vehicle are no different from the five vehicles produced by the previous [stage of] reception.
Since that which is produced in both places is identical, it reveals that there is no difference between the two producers in those two places.
[Commentary: Within the second assembly, regarding that which is produced, there are also two parts. First, citing two analogies to correctly illustrate the assembly:

Just as the World-Honored One [is like] Lake Anavatapta from which eight great rivers flow, so too does the Mahāyāna give birth to all the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those of the mundane and supramundane realms.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first point, the analogy of the eight rivers involves both expansion and contraction. "Anavatapta" means "Without Heat. Because a dragon dwells in this lake, it takes its name from him.
The lake is situated on the summit of Mount Kunlun; its waters flow out in four directions as the eight rivers.
These waters of the eight rivers are none other than the water of the lake itself; they do not originate from elsewhere. Internally, they are unified within [the lake].
The four vehicles produced from the Mahāyāna are themselves the Mahāyāna; there is no other vehicle distinct from it. This comparison clarifies the meaning of its initial arising;
the second point, concerning their convergence, may be seen [in the text]. [Commentary]:

Regarding "the Lake Anavatapta" and so forth, the third chapter of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "First, the Gaṅgā; second, the Jāhnavī. (Note: *Jāhnavī* is a variant for *Yamunā* or a specific river name in this context).
The three Sarā, the four Ariravati, the five Mahā, the six Sindhu, the seven Vakṣu, and the eight Sītā rivers emerge from the lake.
These eight rivers correspond to the eight stages [of the bodhisattva path] and above; they signify the initial emergence of the mind that embraces [sentient beings].
Because they represent the meaning of the causes and effects of the five vehicles, it is said that they "correspond" (*bi*) to the sense of their initial arising.
World-Honored One, just as all seeds depend upon the earth to grow and flourish,
so too do all the wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— both mundane and supramundane— depend upon the Mahāyāna to increase and develop.
[Commentary]: Second, by analogy with seeds, it is clarified that seeds arise depending upon the earth; thus, the seed is itself the earth-element.
Internally, the four vehicles depend upon the Mahāyāna for their growth; therefore, they are also the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, it is explained that seeds arise depending upon the earth, and the seed is not separate from the earth. Likewise, the five vehicles emerge from the Mahāyāna, and the five vehicles are not separate from the Mahāyāna.
If it is as you say, that these two things are merely inseparable, how can they be understood as one? The commentary states: "In the end, it returns to being earth.
This analogy clarifies that ultimately it becomes the second [element]; this is what should be seen in the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). "Worldly" refers to humans and devas;
"supramundane" refers to the Mahāyāna up to and including the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). However, the reason for focusing specifically on the seven stages is...

Regarding the "re-combination" (還為合): from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downward, because Mahāyāna practitioners of former times entered into the three [realms], they are still considered to be in a state of re-combination. [Commentary]:
In comparison with seeds, the earth element possesses the four subtle particles (*paramāṇu*); these are not different from the four subtle particles of the seed itself.
Returning to the ground means that after a long period, all Buddha-dharmas must ultimately teach the truth and finally converge upon the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the "four subtle elements," these are form, odor, taste, and touch.
[Commentary] The second section concludes with the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, World-Honored One, to abide in the Great Vehicle and embrace the Great Vehicle is to abide in the two vehicles and embrace the two vehicles,
as well as all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas.
[Commentary] From "For this reason" onwards, the second section concludes the discussion on that which is produced;
herein, "Mahāyāna" refers to the Mahāyāna from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downwards.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the second conclusion, the phrase "abiding in the Mahāyāna," etc., indicates that since the five vehicles produced are themselves...
The Mahāyāna of the eighth stage is subsumed within abiding in the Mahāyāna of the seventh stage;
the Mahāyāna of the seventh stage is subsumed within abiding in the Two Vehicles (Dvayayāna) and subsumes the Two Vehicles. Why is this? Because that which is produced is itself the producer.
Furthermore, all worldly phenomena and so forth should be understood according to this principle.
[Commentary: From "As the World-Honored One [said]... onwards is the second section, which separately addresses the causes for the convergence of the Two Vehicles.

This is further divided into five parts. First, the six bases are raised to provide a general overview; because those who studied the Lesser Vehicle in the past possessed these six bases, they are brought together to enter into the One.

These six bases consist of: (1) the teaching has its rise and decline; (2) the precepts have their attainment and abandonment; (3) persons have their beginning and end; (4) the combination [of these factors]; and so forth.
This constitutes the sixth [section]. Second, from "For what reason? onwards, there is a separate reconciliation regarding the arising and decline of the teaching.
Third, from "The Prātimokṣa" onwards, there is a separate reconciliation regarding the attainment and abandonment of the precepts.
Fourth, from "This renunciant" onwards, there is a separate reconciliation regarding the beginning and end of persons. Fifth, from "Arhat" onwards, the fruits are presented.
How much more so regarding the causes.
As the World-Honored One said concerning the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*):
[Commentary] "As the World-Honored One said concerning the six sense bases" refers to the general proclamation of the six sense bases; these six constitute the knowledge of the exhaustion of birth.
The place where knowledge arises.

[Commentary]: Regarding these six as the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, the Abhidharma states: "Knowledge of exhaustion" means "I have known suffering," up to "I have cultivated the path.
"Knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*) means "I have known suffering and shall no longer know it again," and so forth.

It is said that once one has attained the cultivation of the Path, one no longer cultivates it further; furthermore, the statement "my outflows are exhausted" is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), while the statement "they will not arise again" is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
It is also said that the severance of defilements through worldly wisdom is the knowledge of exhaustion, whereas the severance through untainted wisdom is the knowledge of non-arising.
What are the six? They are: the endurance of the True Dharma, the extinction of the True Dharma, the Prātimokṣa Vinaya, renunciation, and full ordination.

[Commentary] Next, the six points are listed: "the endurance of the True Dharma" and "the extinction of the True Dharma. These two clarify that the teaching has its periods of flourishing and decline.

The conditions for the two vehicles to attain the fruit—the abiding of the True Dharma—refers to the period of five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when the remaining influence has not yet been destroyed;
this phrase clarifies the flourishing of the True Dharma. "The extinction [of the Dharma]" refers to the period of the Semblance Dharma (śaddharmapratirūpaka) after those five hundred years;
this phrase clarifies its decline. "Prātimokṣa" and "Vinaya"—these two phrases clarify that there is attainment regarding the precepts.
Apart from this, there is the *prātimokṣa*, which is the cause for the two vehicles to attain their fruits;
"this term means 'preserving liberation'" clarifies the attainment of the *vinaya*, and "this phrase means 'extinguishing evil'" clarifies the precepts that transcend verbal expression.
These have the function of attaining the good and extinguishing evil. "Leaving home and receiving full ordination"—these two phrases clarify the beginning and end of the person.

These are people who receive the teachings and practice virtue; they have a beginning and an end. Leaving home, parting from kin, and departing from the secular world to receive the Three Refuges clarifies the beginning.
Receiving full ordination—meaning the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) and being fully equipped with the *vinaya* precepts—clarifies the end.
These six phrases enumerate six locations.
[Commentary]: Regarding the flourishing and decline of the True Dharma, those known as śrāvakas receive transformation by inheriting the Sage’s edification and thereby attain self-communication;
there is no separate principle for their flourishing or decline. Therefore, the abiding and extinction of the Dharma depend solely upon the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the conditions for attaining the fruit, the Sūtra states: "The lineage of the Buddha arises from conditions; therefore, it is called the One Vehicle. This leads to the great realization.
Even the Lesser Vehicle takes the teaching as its condition and the *vinaya* (discipline) as its fruit. As for the causes:
the thirty-two marks have observance of the precepts as their general cause, while each individual mark has its own specific cause; thus, there is the fruit of Arhatship.
Precepts serve as the cause; it can be seen that the immediate conditions are proximate while the remote conditions are distant.
These six bases are taught for the sake of the Mahāyāna.
[Commentary]: "These six bases are taught for the sake of the Mahāyāna" is the correct general summary.
[Commentary]: These six bases are taught for the sake of the Mahāyāna because such mental phenomena are the source from which the One Vehicle arises;
therefore, since they are now brought back to accord with the One Vehicle, it is said that they "correctly accord with and enter" [it].
[Commentary]: From "Why is this? onwards is the second section, which specifically reconciles the teachings regarding the arising and decline [of the Dharma].
Why is this? That which is called the abiding of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is for the sake of the Mahāyāna; thus, when it is said that the Mahāyāna abides, it means the True Dharma abides.
That which is called the extinction of the True Dharma is for the sake of the Mahāyāna; thus, when it is said that the Mahāyāna is extinguished, it means the True Dharma is extinguished.
[Commentary: First, the duration [of the teaching] is reconciled, and subsequently, its cessation is reconciled. Why is this? It serves as a general heading for what follows. [Sub-commentary:

Regarding the phrase in the Sūtra, "the duration of the True Dharma," which refers to the Mahāyāna: while the teachings of the five vehicles and so forth are collectively termed "True Dharma," the present intent is merely to reconcile the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha).
Nevertheless, it must be explained universally: how is it that the True Dharma originally emerges from the One Vehicle?
The source of birth is the One Vehicle; it is for the sake of bestowing this Dharma that it is taught.
If there are people who constantly preach the true Dharma of the One Vehicle, it will abide; if no one preaches the true Dharma of the One Vehicle, it will perish.
Because the One Vehicle is the root of the true Dharma, its abiding and its perishing both depend upon the true Dharma of the One Vehicle. Since it arises from the One Vehicle, yet...

Thus, that which is produced is precisely the Mahāyāna. As for the previous analogies regarding the seeds of the eight rivers, all must be understood as superior to the general meaning previously stated;
only when one has not yet entered into the specific details can this commentary on the text fully exhaust its intended meaning.
The two subsequent pairs may be understood by analogy with this.
[Commentary] From the *Prātimokṣa* onwards, the third section concerns the distinct assemblies of the precepts (*śīla*) and their attainment and separation;
within this, there are four parts, the first of which clarifies that the *Prātimokṣa* and the *Vinaya* are of one essence.
*Prātimokṣa-vinaya*: these two dharmas are identical in meaning though different in name.
[Commentary] The second section, "Correctly Harmonizing with the Vinaya," refers to this phrase concerning the study of the Mahāyāna.
The Vinaya is precisely the Mahāyāna study.
[Commentary: The third section, from "Why is this? onwards, explains the reconciliation. Why is this?
Because one has left the household life and received full ordination by relying on the Buddha.
[Commentary: Since the Buddha is great, how could those who leave the household life and receive the precepts under him not also be great?
The fourth section, beginning with "Therefore," and so forth, can be understood accordingly.
Therefore, it is said that the majestic discipline (*vinaya*) of the Mahāyāna is the *vinaya*.
[Commentary: From "From this he left the household life" onwards, the fourth section separately assembles those who have attained the beginning and the end; it also has three parts.
First, it clarifies that this is the Great [Vehicle].
"This is going forth; this is receiving full ordination.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this is going forth; this is receiving full ordination," because the preceding text states that one goes forth and receives full ordination by relying on the Buddha, it is known that this refers to the Mahāyāna.
[Commentary] The second section, from "Therefore" onwards, clarifies that [the Arhat] is not a Lesser Vehicle practitioner.
Thus, there is no separate act of going forth and receiving full ordination for an Arhat.
[Sub-commentary] To say "not a Lesser Vehicle practitioner" means that it is not the case that the Lesser Vehicle has [its own distinct] going forth and receiving of full ordination.
[Commentary] Third, from "Why is this? onwards, it explains that [the recipient] is great and not small.
Why? Because an arhat has left the household life and received full ordination in reliance upon the Tathāgata.

[Commentary]: It is said that since the Buddha is the Great Refuge, how could those who have left home under him be "small"? Furthermore, why is it that only the *vinaya* of the *prātimokṣa* is said to be mutually identical?

This is because the periods of the flourishing and decline of the True Dharma differ in their temporal sequence; the beginning and end of leaving home and receiving the precepts are not uniform. Therefore, they do not mutually identify.
The *vinaya* of the *prātimokṣa*, however, is of the same essence and occurs at one and the same time.
It is precisely so.
[Commentary] The statement that "this is great and not small" is self-evident from the text of the *Śāstra*.
[Śāstra] From the Arhat downward, the fifth section cites the fruition as an illustration; herein there are also two parts.
First, two topical headings are established:
"The Arhat takes refuge in the Buddha" and "The Arhat has fear. [Commentary:
Regarding "the Arhat takes refuge in the Buddha," this clarifies that the wholesome dharmas of the Arhat are not yet complete; thus, the Arhat has fear.
"Fearful" clarifies that evil has not yet been eliminated. Second, from "Why is this so? onwards, there is an explanation of the two topical headings (*dvāra*).
Within this second explanation, there are also two parts; first, there is the explanation of the topical heading "evil has not yet been eliminated."
Why is this? Because an Arhat dwells with a sense of fear toward all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*), just as if a person were approaching with a drawn sword to kill him;
therefore, the Arhat does not possess ultimate bliss.
[Commentary: "Regarding all non-practitioners" refers to those who lack the practice of the remedial path outside the three realms.
"Abiding in the perception of fear" means that because they have not yet escaped the death and rebirth of *pariṇāmi-ja* (transformative birth), they abide in the perception of fear.
To explain this by way of analogy: it is like a person who, holding a sword, intends to come and harm oneself; the expression "fear" is likewise used. Therefore, Ānanda... [text continues].

Regarding the statement that Arhats do not possess ultimate bliss: this is a summary statement meaning that because the transformation and change (*pariṇāma*) have not yet been exhausted, it is not ultimate bliss.

[The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "There is no practice of the path of cultivation beyond the three realms" means there is no unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), for this path is able to counteract the unconditioned Suffering and Origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). As for the statement "there is no practice," since they have already emerged from the three realms, why is this so?
It is the great cause for all dharmas that have not yet entered the realm of the Buddha. As for those who dwell in the perception of fear, they are called "nameless" (anāmakāḥ).
Indeed, although an Arhat has exhausted the great terrors of the triple world, he has not yet escaped the subtle fears of that stage;

Next, in the fourth fascicle, explaining three specific names, the first chapter on Impermanence states: "The mind-born body is of three kinds:

first, the body produced by the bliss of entering samādhi, also called 'right reception' (*samāpatti*), because in the third, fourth, and fifth stages the mind is tranquil and unmoving; second, the [body born of] awakening..."

The *dharmasvabhāva-manomayakāya* (body made of mind whose nature is the Dharma) refers to entering Buddha-fields simultaneously within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), and thus takes the Dharma as its intrinsic nature.
The three types of *sahaja-anabhisamskāra-manomayakāya* (spontaneously born body made of mind without volitional effort) refer to the realization of the Dharma realized by the Buddhas;

these are both "attainment" and "birth," and are collectively explained from the perspective of the fruit. This *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is used exclusively for the exposition of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages in the present text.

The cases of those of the single vehicle and the two vehicles who have not yet severed ignorance can be understood by analogy with this. It is also called "the three meanings based on shifting," meaning that because the cause shifts, the fruit changes.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that there are also noble ones (*ārya*) within the three realms: because those in the four stages of the three fruits (*phala*) and four stages of the candidates (*pratipannaka*) have not yet transcended the realms, the retributions (*vipāka*) of the three realms are compared as being coarse or subtle;
the lifespans of these persons differ, being unequal in length or brevity. As for the retribution of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it lacks the physical forms of the three realms;

Having extinguished all outflows (*āsrava*) and relinquished the retribution body (*vipākakāya*), one relies on various wondrous practices to perfect this [body]. Since its substance is accomplished through practice, how could it not have an end?

Yet, as it departs into the profound darkness and returns from it, its limits cannot be measured; because it undergoes successive transformations like the mind, it is called the "mind-born body" (*manomayakāya*).
Depending on whether its duration is long or short, it is not that there is no end to what is not unwholesome; thus it is so named.
This is the death of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*). That one dies yet is not extinguished—how can this be conceived?

[Commentary] Third, the fruit induced by taking impure superior goodness as the cause and the residual habits of the three realms as the condition still possesses form and color, and its lifespan is limited;

Fourth, regarding the transformation and change known as the birth and death between two lands: when first flowing [into existence], one is outside the three realms;

The meaning of this is that because physical form and substance are distinct, lifespans have fixed limits, and nations have fixed boundaries, all [beings below the eighth stage] undergo birth-and-death by segments (*paricchinna-utpāda-maraṇa*).
Although those from the eighth stage upward have a limit in terms of kalpas, this is explained in relation to others;

because each preceding thought-moment serves as the cause and each succeeding thought-moment serves as the fruit, changing and renewing itself moment by moment, they all undergo birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-utpāda-maraṇa*). This refers to the Bodhisattvas.
Although it possesses form and color, because it is not produced by direct karmic fruition (*vipāka*), it is not called "segmented" (*paricchinna*);

yet, although it arises and ceases moment by moment, because it still possesses form and color, it is not called "transformational" (*pariṇāmika*). Because it hovers between these two poles, it is termed "intermediate" (*antara-bhava*).
As for the birth-and-death of those who have first flowed into this stream, it cannot be equated with transformational death, because they lack untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) at that time.

Because those who have not yet entered the triple world grasp at signs, their segmentation is not correct; they merely continue through the stream of dark consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), falling downward moment by moment.

Therefore, this is established separately as one type of birth-and-death. Now, regarding the twelve truths (*dvādaśa-satya*) that exist within the three types of birth-and-death—segmented, transformative, and intermediate—the first two, flowing and coming, consist only of the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and origination (*samudaya-satya*). Generally, there are fourteen truths; some say that when first flowing [into this world], one may encounter a Buddha, cultivate the path, and attain Buddhahood, and thus there are also the two truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), making sixteen truths in total. when first flowing [into this world], one enters the triple realm (*tridhātu*) and only then gives rise to the grasping of marks (*nimitta-grāha*), subsequently distinguishing between suffering and pleasure and seeking to cultivate cessation.
The Path is precisely the Path of Non-Cessation; thus, the Two Truths are clarified. Regarding the intermediate state between the two lands, it is not the primary causal agent.
When first flowing forth, if one has not yet clearly severed the fetters, it is insufficient to realize the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.

"Although he has attained liberation, in reality he has not yet attained all liberations.

[The *Śrīmālā-sūtra*] says: "The Sun was seized by Śrīmālā.

Because it severs all afflictions and the like.

second, a comparative analysis of the functional efficacy and relative superiority or inferiority of these two types of afflictions against all higher afflictions based on the power of these four *āśrayas*;
third, [the section] beginning from "Furthermore, like taking [something] as a condition" (*tadyathā upādānapratyaya*); and so forth.

Section Four: Clarifying that the moistening karmas are not identical. From the passage beginning with "Thus, O World-Honored One, there is the ground of craving" (*tathā hi bhagavan tṛṣṇā-vāsabhūmi*), the meaning of their eradication is clarified.
Within the first part, which correctly sets forth the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are further two sections;
the first explains the afflictions of the four grounds of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*).
There are two kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*). What are the two? They are the afflictions of the abiding ground (*ālaya-kleśa*) and the arising afflictions (*utthāna-kleśa*).

There are four kinds of abiding grounds. What are the four? They are the abiding ground of views (*dṛṣṭi-ekadeśa*), the abiding ground of desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), the abiding ground of form-attachment (*rūparāga*), and the abiding ground of existence-attachment (*bhavarāga*).
From these four kinds of abiding grounds, all arising afflictions are produced. "Arising" refers to the momentary [afflictions].
"The mind is associated with moments.
[Commentary] "Moments of mind" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*); "associated" refers to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth.
The second section, from "From the mind of the World-Honored One, it is dissociated... onwards, explains the affliction of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
The World-Honored One’s mind-dissociated *anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsabhūmi* (the ground of beginningless ignorance abiding in the mind).
[Commentary]: "Mind-dissociated" means that it fundamentally lacks association with the four types of mind. "Beginningless" means it has no beginning.
Regarding oneself:
[The *Chao* states] "Fundamentally, there is no association with the four minds" means that ignorance (*avidyā*) does not associate with the four minds, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the term "non-associated with mind" (*citta-viprayukta*), there are two meanings: first, it clarifies that the characteristic of the mind is fundamentally pure...

That which is defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*) is not associated with the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Second, it is clarified that the layered accumulation of the three realms arises from mind-consciousness;

therefore, they are associated with the mind. However, because the subtle fetters of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) obstruct the pure wisdom of the two vehicles, they are not associated with the mind.
Thus, the four grounds of abiding are termed "mind" and "outflows" (*āsrava*); the [ground of] ignorance is not.
That which is called the "ground of illumination" (*vidyā-sthiti*) is named wisdom (*jñāna*) and is untainted (*anāsrava*). Therefore, the *Ābharaṇa-sūtra*, upper fascicle, states:
"Ignorance (*avidyā*) is named the failure to comprehend all phenomena; it is the delusion regarding the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that gives rise to the karmic fruits of the three realms.
For this reason, I say that from the treasury of ignorance arise the thirteen afflictions, namely: false view, the view of self, eternalism, and nihilism."

The view of clinging to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the view of clinging to fruits (*phalaparāmarśa*), the view of doubt (*vicikitsā*), and the seven views—because one seeks [the truth] through all these views—they are called "views.
Furthermore, from these views arise six types of attachment: greed, hatred, delusion, desire, pride, and [wrong] views.
Within the *dharmadhātu*, at all times, all afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; with these thirteen as their basis, ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the root of these thirteen.
This is because within the Dharma-realm, they are separately manifested as the retributions of the three realms. How may this be verified?

When the spiritual faculties first stir, they necessarily proceed from non-being into being, and from the subtle to the coarse; yet when momentum reaches its limit, it must revert, and when one is exhausted, one seeks penetration.
Thus, they return from the coarse to the subtle and from existence back to non-being. Those sentient beings set their course from non-being.
Those who clearly abide in the stages [of existence] ultimately sink into the Avīci hell; yet those who emerge from the stainless state soar aloft to re-enter the wondrous realm of Nirvāṇa.
Since the beginning of ignorance is unfathomable and the end of Nirvāṇa is unknowable, is this not the process of entering existence from non-existence and returning to non-existence from existence?
For this reason, this sutra regards the Formless Realm as being characterized by craving for existence.
Regarding the remaining scriptures on the dwelling stages (*bhūmi*), they take the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception as the "Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*);

this marks the end of the formless realms. The *Wuming* (Five Names) explains the five dwellings as follows: "To abide securely in one's respective portion is called 'dwelling' (*zhu*'); to be capable of producing [phenomena] is called 'stage' (*di*');

that which arises from them is termed 'arising' (*qi*'). Although these views pervade the three realms, they constitute afflictions arising from delusion regarding principle and delusion regarding phenomena.

Thus, the four quarters shift their positions; upon awakening, all is vast and empty, leaving nothing behind. Therefore, although various views are numerous, they collectively constitute a single ground.
As for the affliction of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), its roots are deep and difficult to uproot. Why is this? Since the three realms are distinct, their karmic actions and retributions are likewise different;

yet the water of craving secretly moistens them, its taints sinking deep and becoming firmly established. According to the ground from which it arises, it clings with firm attachment and is not relinquished.
Therefore, the attachments of the three realms each constitute a distinct ground.
[Commentary] From this point downward, within the second section of "Defining the Essential Nature and Characteristics" which evaluates their functional efficacy, there are five further divisions.
First, it clarifies the inferiority of the four grounds of abiding.

“World-Honored One, the power of these four stages of abiding (catasraḥ sthitayaḥ) cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy compared to the stage of abiding in ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi), which is the basis and seed for all higher afflictions.
[Commentary: "All higher afflictions" refers to the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which arise from the stage of abiding in ignorance.
Furthermore, because they obstruct the superior conduct of sentient beings, they are called "superior afflictions. Regarding the seeds that serve as the basis for these superior afflictions:

while the specific-characteristic (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa) afflictions depend upon the universal-characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), it is said that the universal-characteristic afflictions are able to produce the specific-characteristic ones;

thus, they are designated as "seeds. These take the five abodes (pañca-vāsabhūmi) as their basis to give rise to the seeds of affliction, specifically taking the four abodes (catur-vāsabhūmi) as their fundamental basis.
Next, taking up the characteristics [of the afflictions], it clarifies that the *avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi* (the ground of ignorance) is inferior.

[The *Chao* states: "Regarding 'depending on the seeds,' the 'Ganges-sand' [afflictions] are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), while the four *nivāsabhūmi* (abiding grounds) are the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). As for their pervasiveness:

the general [grounds] universally obstruct all, while the specific [afflictions] specifically obstruct practice and the specific knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). This depends on the category of the five *nivāsabhūmi*."

The "arising of afflictions" refers to the *āsravas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Because these exist both within and outside the realms (*dhātu*), they arise from the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) and simultaneously obstruct all internal and external formations (*saṃskāra*) as well as knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). Therefore, this [passage] takes up the basis of support. Regarding the phrase "taking the four abodes and so forth":

the four abodes are the root of the sands-of-the-Ganges [afflictions]; this [passage] takes up that which gives rise to them, namely, the grasping at signs (*nimitta-grāha*). This is the fourth [point].
This is another name for "abiding" (*sthiti*).

[Commentary] Second, from the passage beginning with "World-Honored One, such is the ground of abiding in ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) below, it clarifies the supremacy of the ground of abiding in ignorance.

"World-Honored One, thus the power of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is the greatest among the four grounds of abiding, including the ground of craving for existence (*bhavarāga-vāsabhūmi*).
[Commentary] From "World-Honored One" onwards, the second section clarifies the superiority of the ground of abiding ignorance, which serves as a reversal of the preceding discussion.
Second, regarding the four abodes categorized under craving for existence (*bhavarāga*): "craving for existence" refers to the afflictions of the formless realm;

furthermore, by counting those of the form realm in reverse, one takes the craving for the lower realms and the craving for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), together with views (*dṛṣṭi*), as the four abodes.

[Commentary]: Regarding the repetition with the preceding section to form a pair: previously, the inferior was presented first and the superior explained afterward; here, the superior is explained first and the inferior presented afterward.
[Sub-commentary]: The third section, beginning from "For example, like an evil Māra," cites a comparison to clarify the superiority.
For example, just as Māra Pāpīyān possesses such sovereign excellence in power, lifespan, retinue, and all requisites among the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven,
so too does the power of the ground of ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi) prevail most supremely over the four grounds of abiding in existence and craving (bhavarāga-vāsabhūmi).
[Commentary] Third, citing analogies to clarify superiority; herein, the opening and closing [of the argument] may be observed.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding "citing analogies to clarify superiority": that which is nameless is called Pāpīyān (Māra), who, as the lord of all demons, dwells at the highest level while presiding over those below.
Ignorance is the root of worldly afflictions, and thus it occupies the fundamental position to govern all that follows.
[Commentary: The fourth section, from "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" downwards, explains the superiority of the Dwelling Place of Ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).
It shows that the afflictions which serve as the basis for those [afflictions] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges also cause the four kinds of afflictions to persist long-term;
these cannot be severed by the wisdom of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, but can only be severed by the Bodhi-wisdom of the Tathāgata.

[Commentary: From the passage "equal in number to the sands of the Ganges" onwards, the fourth section explains that [the Buddha-nature] is superior and abides for a long time, acting as the remote foundation.
This first clarifies superiority in terms of arising; it shows that the two vehicles cannot sever [afflictions], whereas only the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom can sever them.

This next section clarifies superiority in terms of severance, which refers to the wisdom of emptiness. Although this has not yet explicitly explained severance, it relies on the power of what is clarified by severance.

One interpretation states that because the Vajra-mind has severed all delusions to their end, it is called "learning from the Buddha"; thus it is said to be the Tathāgata’s wisdom of bodhi and severance.

[The *Chao*] explains that within the commentary on "superiority," since the substance of the delusions is fundamentally empty, it is called "empty liberation" and "nameless," and is referred to as being "above the three realms."
The afflictions may indeed be numbered as many as the sands of the Ganges; their heavy obscurity and profound darkness cannot be illuminated by fireflies or candles.
Were it not for the Buddha to sever them, they could be called "great.
[Commentary] The fifth section, from "Thus, World-Honored One" onwards, concludes the excellence [of the teaching].
"In this way, the World-Honored One, the ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is the most powerful.
[Commentary] From "In this way" onwards, the fifth section concludes the demonstration of its superiority.

From "Furthermore, conditioned by grasping" onwards, it presents the third aspect within the essential characteristics of the afflictions, clarifying how their moistening of karma differs; this is further divided into...

Fourth, the first clarification: the afflictions of the four stages of dwelling (catasraḥ pṛthagjanabhūmayaḥ) moisten contaminated karma (sāsrava-karma) to produce the three realms of existence (trayaḥ bhavāḥ).
World-Honored One, it is also like how contaminated karma, with grasping as its condition, arises from causes to produce the three realms of existence.

[Commentary: "Conditions" refers to the afflictions of the four stages of abiding (*catur-vāsa-bhūmi*). This means that these afflictions can assist karma in grasping a fruit, acting as the conditions for that fruit.
"The causes of tainted karma" refers generally to all karmas, both wholesome and unwholesome.

[Commentary]: The "three realms of existence" (*traya-bhava*) refer to the existence of desire (*kāma-bhava*), the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*), and the existence of formlessness (*ārūpya-bhava*). The *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 4, states:

"Existence of desire refers to the karma bound to the desire realm which, through the conditions of grasping (*upādāna*), is capable of producing future births; it is also the retribution of that karma. Existence of form and existence of formlessness are likewise."

[Commentary] Second, from "In this way" onwards, it clarifies how the delusion of the ground of ignorance (avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi) moistens untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) to bring about transformational birth (*nairmāṇika-jāti*).
In this way, with the ground of ignorance as the condition and untainted karma as the cause, [the states of] Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, and Great Power [Bodhisattvas] arise.
The Bodhisattva’s three kinds of mind-made bodies.
[Commentary] Third, from this third stage downward, it is explained that the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) universally moistens all karmic actions for the sake of taking birth.

The arising of those three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) in these three stages, as well as their arising from outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*), has ignorance as its dwelling-place (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) as its condition;
it is not without a condition.
[Commentary]: "These three stages" refers to the stages of the three realms (*dhātu*). "Those three kinds" refers to the mind-made bodies of those belonging to the three vehicles (*yāna*).
"Transformational birth" refers to the birth of the *parināmika-kāya* (transformation body), while "segmented birth" refers to the birth of the *aupapaduka-kāya* (birth by transformation).

Furthermore, "birth from untainted karma" (*anāsrava-karma*) refers precisely to what is called "karmic birth. Another interpretation states that the previous term "mind-made birth" (*manomaya-kāya*) spoke directly of the arising of the fruit of transformation;

therefore, this present term specifies that it arises with untainted karma as its cause. Moreover, although the three stages were mentioned above, it was not clarified whether they possess form (*rūpa*) or are formless (*arūpya*); thus, [the text] further...

This is reiterated by citing the two types of birth to clarify the point. Regarding "depending on the ground of abiding ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), this explains that the ground of abiding ignorance universally moistens all karmic entities;
that is to say, while the ground of abiding ignorance serves as a condition only for the *pariṇāmi-cyuti* (transformation-death), it does not condition the *prādeśika-cyuti* (segmented-death).
Therefore, it is said that there is a condition, and not that there is no condition. From "Because of this... onwards, the fourth section concludes [the discussion of] non-existence.
The *avidyā-āvāsabhūmi* (ground of ignorance) moistens untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), resulting in the attainment of transformation-birth (*pariṇāmi-jāti*).
Therefore, the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) and untainted karma take the *avidyā-āvāsabhūmi* as their condition.

[Commentary] From the passage beginning with "From the World-Honored One thus... onwards, the fourth section of the explanation of the essence and characteristics of afflictions is presented, clarifying their abandonment.
The meaning of this exclusion is further divided into three parts. First, it can be seen that the two types of abiding grounds (*āśraya*) differ in their functions.
World-Honored One, such is the case: the four abiding grounds associated with craving do not share the same function as the abiding ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*);
the abiding ground of ignorance is distinct from and separate from the four abiding grounds.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Sūtra distinguishes [them] as having departed from the four abodes": it means that while the Two Vehicles have already departed from the four abodes, ignorance still remains; this is what constitutes their distinction.
[Commentary] Second, the actual clarification of abandonment:
that which is abandoned at the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) is abandoned by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment (*buddhabodhi-jñāna*).

Regarding "that which is abandoned at the stage of Buddhahood," this is a general statement concerning all the merits of the stage of Buddhahood; [it is abandoned] by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment.
"Severance" (prahāṇa) refers specifically to the liberation through the emptiness that severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
[The *Chao* states: "All merits of the Buddha-ground": in the *Yíngluò jīng*, it is explained that the term "ground" (*bhūmi*) used generally for the lower stages has two meanings:
the sense of being able to produce and the sense of sustaining. Here, taking the sense of sustaining, it is called "all merits."
[Commentary] Third, the explanation of the raised doubt. Why is this?
[Commentary] Why is it said that only the Buddha-ground can sever [the afflictions], whereas the two vehicles cannot? The explanation states:
The Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have severed the four kinds of abiding grounds (*sthiti-bhūmi*), yet their outflows (*āsrava*) are not exhausted and they do not attain sovereign power;
furthermore, they do not realize that which is called "the non-exhaustion of outflows," which is precisely the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
[Commentary: The two vehicles eliminate only the four abodes of existence (*catur-āśraya-bhūmi*), yet their outflows (*āsrava*) are not exhausted.
"Outflows are not exhausted" means that they have not yet fully realized the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*).

"They do not attain sovereign power" means that because they have not yet fully realized the state of being without outflows, they do not attain sovereign power. This clarifies that since they have neither realized nor attained sovereignty, they cannot sever ignorance (*avidyā*).
The "dwelling-place of ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is that which neither realizes nor exhausts the outflows (*anāsrava*).

This means that because the dwelling-place of ignorance has not yet been severed, one fails to realize what ought to be realized. That which "ought to be realized" is that which is to be realized through its severance.
One interpretation states: "the non-exhaustion of the outflows" refers to the fact that those outflows which ought not to exist have not been exhausted; they ought not to exist.

Regarding the statement "those with outflows," this refers to the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*). Thus, the subsequent passage stating that "outflows are not yet exhausted" refers precisely to this ground of the abiding of ignorance.
The explanation provided here—identifying it as the doubt to be resolved—is that the Buddha alone can sever it;
the explanation that the two vehicles do not sever it is intended to provide a comprehensive interpretation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the untainted [outflows] are not exhausted," this means that because they have not yet severed the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), they remain bound by ignorance;
how, then, could they attain sovereignty? What serves as proof that ignorance is not yet exhausted?
[Commentary]: From "The World-Honored One, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas," and so forth, this is a separate section concerning the fifth stage among the fruits of the Two Vehicles.
The preceding four sections merely followed the sequence of the above matters, providing explanations without fully clarifying their specific characteristics;
therefore, this section further distinguishes and summarizes them. This is divided into four parts, the first of which begins from the outset.
The conclusion [of the section] titled "Tending Toward the Realm of Nirvāṇa" summarizes the first segment, which refutes the four types of knowledge and the [incomplete] attainment of nirvāṇa.
The second [segment], beginning from "If one knows all suffering," summarizes the second segment, clarifying that ultimate realization resides solely in the Buddha and not in the two vehicles.
The third [segment], beginning from "World-Honored One, regarding this, afflictions arise," [summarizes the following].

To conclude the fourth [section], two kinds of afflictions are cited to explain the third [section] concerning the two types of death, while the fourth—concerning the wisdom that does not receive further existence within the world—is excluded. Regarding this, there are two kinds [of wisdom]. Thus concludes the third segment;
citing the two types of birth-and-death, it explains the second [section] on the ultimate and non-ultimate meanings. As the original text says: "From..."
Below this, the preceding second section—concerning how only the Tathāgata is ultimate while the two vehicles are not—is concluded. This section is divided into four parts:
first, the conclusion that the two vehicles are not ultimate; second, from "If one knows all suffering... onwards, the conclusion that the Tathāgata is ultimate;
third, from "World-Honored One, if the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is not severed... onwards...
The following section, from "From the World-Honored One’s arising of afflictions here" onwards, explains the resolution of the second point:
that the two vehicles are not ultimate, while the Tathāgata is ultimate. If this were the case, one would only resolve the first and second [points] but not the third and fourth;
and if one were to resolve what has already been resolved, the process of resolving would be endless. Therefore, this [approach] is somewhat inappropriate.

It is not necessary [to state this separately]. Previously, at the first conclusion, it was stated that the four knowledges (*jñāna*) and nirvāṇa were incomplete; there, it was simply said they were incomplete.
Now, however, because it concludes that the seven virtues are incomplete, [the former] is set aside.

[Commentary] Fifth, regarding the sequential conclusion of the preceding four points, it says: "As for 'merely receiving the aforementioned matter' and 'immediately explaining,' etc."—above, as we were about to reconcile the fruits of the Two Vehicles, we first refuted the four wisdoms and the fruit of nirvāṇa as being not ultimate.

Receiving this text of refutation, one then explains the intent behind both granting and refuting. Why are they granted and refuted? It is because the two types of death are cited to provide the explanation.
Furthermore, because there are two kinds of afflictions, there are two different types of death. Although this is so, it has not yet been extensively analyzed;
therefore, the present text first cites the seven virtues as incomplete to conclude that the four wisdoms and nirvana are likewise incomplete.
Second, it extensively cites the seven virtues as fulfilled to contrast them with the two vehicles’ seven virtues, which are incomplete.
The third section concerns the meaning of "giving and taking" from above; it cites two kinds of afflictions to conclude the fourth point above.

The fourth section cites the two types of death to conclude the third point above. Each of these is more extensive than the preceding text, and their specific characteristics will become clear in the commentary below.
[Commentary: Regarding the seven virtues that are incomplete, first is the incompleteness of wisdom.

Because the World-Honored One, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas in their final birth are obscured and hindered by the Dwelling Place of Ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), they do not know or awaken to various dharmas.
