[Commentary]: Among the seven virtues, "one whose wisdom is incomplete" refers to those without a specific name; generally speaking, this refers to those who have not yet exhausted their karmic allotment of birth.
As for "Great Power Bodhisattvas," they encompass those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward through the three stages [of the tenth stage].

Because they are currently at the limit of being shrouded by the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), the term specifically refers to those in their final body (*paścima-deha*). Their final body—

Upon this first transformation, one becomes a Buddha; yet because subtle obstructions have not been exhausted, and these subtle obstructions are difficult to dispel, one does not yet attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) regarding each and every phenomenon.
One knows through this the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) by means of awakening.
[Commentary]: Second, the insufficiency of abandonment due to lack of knowledge and vision, as indicated by the passage beginning "because of not knowing and not seeing.
Because of this lack of knowledge and vision, that which ought to be abandoned is neither abandoned nor brought to completion.
[Commentary]: "Seeing" is synonymous with "awakening. To awaken is to sever [delusion]; to sever is to reach the ultimate. To say that one does not sever refers to the severing of the head.
[Sub-commentary]: From "the three liberations are not yet fulfilled" down to "because they do not sever" and so forth.
Because they are not severed, they are called "liberation with remaining faults," rather than liberation through the severance of all faults.
[Commentary] Regarding those whose three liberations are not yet fulfilled, from this point onward,
further statements concerning what remains are raised to clarify the Tathāgata’s true four wisdoms as being of inexhaustible merit, and the four truths as having a remainder within the four wisdoms.
Because cause and effect are not yet exhausted, that which remains is designated as "partial" (śeṣa) with respect to the "remainderless" (anupadhiśeṣa).
[Commentary]: The passage beginning with "The four purities are not yet perfected; hence they are called 'purified with remainder'" follows from this.
It is called "purified with remainder" and not "completely purified.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "the five virtues are not yet fulfilled" down to "accomplishment by name":
it is called accomplishment by name because one has accomplished certain virtues, but has not accomplished all virtues.
[Commentary]: "The six knowledges do not encompass all objects" refers to the passage beginning with "Because one has achieved a partial liberation, a partial purity, and partial merit.

This means that because one has achieved only partial liberation, partial purity, and partial merit, it is known that there remains a portion of suffering to be abandoned, a portion of its origin to be realized, a portion of cessation to be attained, and a portion of the path to be cultivated.
[Commentary]: The preceding six fetters supplant the four wisdoms. From the phrase "the seventh, nirvana, is not yet ultimate" onwards:
this is called "attaining a small portion of nirvana. One who attains a small portion of nirvana is said to be "heading toward the realm of nirvana."
[Commentary]: This concludes the sixth matter by seizing the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. As for why the sixth matter cites the third, fourth, and fifth matters:
the second [matter] already cited the first, and the third already cited the second;
however, the fourth did not cite the third, and the fifth did not cite the fourth. Therefore, within these six, they are cited collectively.
[Commentary]: Regarding the reference to the third, fourth, and fifth points mentioned previously: the second statement, "because of not knowing and not seeing," refers back to the first;

the third statement, "because of not severing [the afflictions]," refers back to the second. The fourth merely states that the name is "pure with remainder," and thus does not refer back to the third;
the fifth merely states that the name is "accomplished with remaining effort," and thus does not refer back to the fourth.
Because [the third] has already been mentioned due to its virtue, the fourth is not restated; therefore, within the sixth [section], the third, fourth, and fifth are restated collectively.
[Commentary: From "If one knows all suffering" onwards, the second point—clarifying that ultimate [realization] resides in the Buddha—is concluded.
Within the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*), this is further divided into two parts: first, the conclusion that the Buddha’s state is ultimate;
second, from the passage "World-Honored One, if there were no ground of ignorance" (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) onwards, the conclusion that the two vehicles are not ultimate.

Since it was stated directly above that ultimacy exists only in the Buddha, the present section concludes that he is "ultimate" because his seven virtues are fully perfected, thereby contrasting him with the two vehicles.

The seven virtues not being fulfilled in their full measure are divided into eight sections: first, because the initial four [virtues] are all treated as distinct and separate, the "fulfillment of the objects of wisdom" is established in contrast to the sixth section, where the objects of wisdom are not yet comprehensive.
"If one knows all suffering, abandons all origins, realizes all cessations, and cultivates all paths. [Commentary]:
First, regarding "the four 'all' [knowledges] take the noble truths as their objects": this means that taking the Four Noble Truths as their objects constitutes knowledge.
"All" refers to the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), while "with remainder" refers to the conditioned (*sābhisaṃskṛta*).
[Commentary]: Second, by means of the two types of impermanence, he clarifies the fulfillment of nirvāṇa in contrast to the aforementioned seventh nirvāṇa which is not fully realized.
Within the world of impermanent destruction and the world of the disease of impermanence, one attains the realm of eternal nirvāṇa.

[Commentary]: "Impermanence as destruction" refers to the death of the physical body within the *paricchinna-śarīra-janma* (segmented birth-and-death). "Impermanence as illness" refers to the *pariṇāmi-śarīra-janma* (transformative birth-and-death);
although there is no destruction of the body, there is still the sense of moment-to-moment transition, which constitutes its own inherent illness.

Third, because he is fully endowed with the virtue of being a light, a refuge, and a resort for those who are unprotected and without support, he acts as their protector and support for those in this unprotected and unsupported world without interruption. [Commentary]:
"Without protection" (*anāvaraṇa*) means that he is not overshadowed by anything superior; "without shelter" (*anāśraya*) means that he lacks no power to bestow [aid] upon others.
"Those without refuge" refers to those sentient beings subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*) who lack a refuge; they are also slighted because they lack protection.
[The *Commentary* states: Regarding the virtue of providing a refuge and protection, it means that the Tathāgata’s virtue of providing a refuge and protection is already perfected.
Sentient beings within the realm have not yet attained the supramundane wholesome dharmas for protection, and the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* subject to transformation require them even more.
One takes refuge in the Tathāgata because he has extinguished [suffering] through the path of non-action; thus, he is called "the one to be relied upon.
To deliver people by means of the Path is called "protection" (hu), and to bring peace to beings through extinction is called "reliance" (yi).
[Commentary: Fourth, the dharmakāya and so forth are cited to explain the fulfillment of nirvāṇa. First, the dharmakāya is cited.
Why? Because phenomena have no superiority or inferiority, one attains nirvāṇa.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, this does not refer to what was stated above. Why? Because it applies universally to the three virtues below as a general heading.
Regarding the statement that "the dharmakāya of all Buddhas has no superiority or inferiority," this is the fundamental meaning. The same applies to the purity of *prajñā* and *vimukti*.
The current explanation, however, is directed toward the three faults of the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvaka vehicle from days of yore.
The two types of nirvana—with remainder and without remainder—commonly possess three faults: first, they are not simultaneous; second, they are incomplete; and third, they are unequal.
They are unequal because of the disparity in the excellence of their three virtues.
[Commentary]: Regarding the first fault, that of superiority and inferiority, the various masters of the Lesser Vehicle claim that beneath the Bodhi tree, the Buddha—
At the time of his initial attainment of the Way, although the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) was already perfected, the bonds of the fruit still remained;

liberation was not yet complete, his body still consumed impure food, and it still bore the mark of impermanence. This constitutes one superior and two inferior aspects, comparable to a fire spreading across a river. The commentary states:

through thirty-four moments of mind—eight patiences (*kṣānti*), eight knowledges (*jñāna*), nine non-obstructions (*ānantarya*), and nine liberations (*vimukti*)—one severs the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).
At that time, although the Prajñā known as "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvajñatā) was already perfected, his physical body born of parents had not yet entered parinirvāṇa;
thus, while the "bondage of the fruit" still remained, even though the pervasive afflictions (vighna-kleśas) were severed, he did not yet possess the Dharma-body.

His body was impermanent and still relied upon material food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra); because such food is manifold, it is called "mixed food. This is because the teacher of the Hīnayāna shares the same retribution as ordinary beings.

First, "superior" refers to the perfection of the *prajñā* of the seed of omniscience; second, "inferior" refers to liberation not yet being fully realized and the body still subsisting on coarse food.
Although these two are inferior, they already possess a small portion of fulfillment. In terms of their great significance, they are comparable at one time to a crosswise stream and a blazing fire:
when both are extinguished, one is long and the other is short. Although the three virtues are one, [they differ in this way].
This is said because at that time, there is an inequality between superior and inferior.
[Commentary] Because the three virtues are not shared, they do not coexist.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the two not coexisting: the former takes up the meaning and fully encompasses it, while the latter returns to the former; thus, speaking of "at one time" refers to the present manifestation.
Because it is attained distinctly before and after, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).
[Commentary] Because the three virtues (*triguṇa*) have not yet reached their ultimate consummation, they are incomplete.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "the three virtues have not yet reached their ultimate consummation": the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) consists merely of the fivefold Dharma-body, and Prajñā is merely...
The liberation through untainted wisdom merely eliminates the four abodes;
how could it be the same as the Great Vehicle’s equal Dharma-body, the wondrous essence of Vairocana, and the omniscient wisdom that completely eliminates all five abodes?

[Commentary] The reason it is called "partial" [nirvāṇa] is that today’s nirvāṇa is free from these three faults; because it is entirely equal [to the ultimate], it is called the eternally abiding realm of nirvāṇa.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding the statement that today’s nirvāṇa is free from these three faults: the meaning of these three virtues is derived from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The ultimate meaning of that sutra is that when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he establishes sentient beings within the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*), and that "I too shall not long remain apart from it.
This secret treasury is none other than *nirvāṇa*, and *nirvāṇa* is the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Although this sutra is brief, its intent is the same; therefore, one must cite the extensive text of that sutra for application.
To provide a brief exposition of this present sutra, I shall first cite the scriptural text and subsequently explain its meaning. Thus, the "Chapter on the Difficulty of Compassion" states:

"I shall now cause all sentient beings, as well as my own sons—the fourfold assembly—to all dwell securely within the Secret Treasury; I, too, shall dwell therein and enter into nirvana. Why is this so?
These are called the secret treasury, just like the three dots of the letter *i*: if they are aligned horizontally, they do not form the *i*;
if they are vertical, they likewise do not form it. Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara does one obtain the *i*.
If the three dots are separate, they also cannot form it. I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa, nor is it as if it were not.
The body that has come forth is not *nirvāṇa*, and *mahāprajñā* is also not *nirvāṇa*; these three dharmas being distinct from one another are also not *nirvāṇa*.
Because I now abide in these three dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, it is called "entering *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "like the worldly letter *i*": in foreign lands, there are two traditions, the new and the old.

The "new" *ī* and the "old" *ī* differ in that they are severed vertically and horizontally and remain distinct. Borrowing this to illustrate the other: the horizontal stroke is like a blazing fire, while the vertical stroke is like water being dropped.
[In the new form,] they do not connect with one another; it is neither horizontal like a blazing fire nor vertical like falling water. This should be understood as follows:
in this land, when writing characters beneath the grass radical, the fine strokes are connected; this is the characteristic of the new *ī*. The old *ī* may be compared to this.
In the former teachings, it was held that the Dharma-body of the three virtues is inherently existent, while Prajñā is accomplished through cultivation;
only upon entering the nirvana without remainder does one attain liberation, at which point body and wisdom no longer exist.

This is like a vertical drop of water where the drops fall apart and remain separate, or like a horizontal row of blazing fires where each flame is unrelated to the others. Such is the meaning of "vertical" and "horizontal" within the Mahayana of the former teachings.
The commentary (*shu*) initially explains [the deficiency] by contrasting it with the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), yet one should know that it universally refutes both the Great and Small Vehicles.

The new "I" character (*i-ji*) may serve as a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) in this present teaching: it is simultaneously illumination and simultaneously sovereignty;

thus it is called the "three threes. Since they have no separate substance, they are not horizontal; because they are neither before nor after, they are not vertical. Thus, one is precisely three, and so forth.
The three great dots are one, just as in the case of the fine strokes; yet, because one cannot be thought of as three and three cannot be thought of as one, they are called "inconceivable.
That which is inconceivable is neither three nor one, and is thus named the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*).
It is like the letter *i* of the world. This phrase is the root of that sutra, established extensively in order to manifest this meaning.
The questions and answers extend through twenty-five chapters, vast and inexhaustible. If one loses this meaning, they will become confused regarding the fundamental source;
what then could serve as a point of guidance? By deeply comprehending this principle, one can explain and resolve the present sutra with such subtlety that nothing remains unexhausted.

As for the mention of "three eyes" in that other sutra: Maheśvara dwells at the summit of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu), ruling over a great trichiliocosm, and each of his three faces possesses three eyes.
The three eyes and one face cannot be described as either one or three, whether arranged vertically or horizontally, in union or in separation.

They can adorn the celestial countenance and act as the Lord of the World; they illuminate the three thousandfold world-system. Whether not vertical nor horizontal, adorning the Lord and illuminating the world, all things are accomplished through the Three Virtues (triguṇa).

It is likewise with the vertical, horizontal, united, and separate: the secret treasury (guhyakośa) is not accomplished [through these modes]. That which is neither vertical nor horizontal is the secret [treasury].
If hidden, it is accomplished.
[Commentary] Next, Prajñāpāramitā is cited to contrast with the aforementioned first wisdom that is incomplete;
because their wisdoms are equal, one attains nirvāṇa.
[Commentary] Next, liberation (*vimukti*) is cited to correspond to the aforementioned third [perfection], the non-completion of liberation.
Because liberation is equal, one attains *nirvāṇa*.
[Commentary] Next, purity (*viśuddhi*) is cited to correspond to the aforementioned fourth [perfection], the non-completion of purity.
Because it is pure and so forth, one attains nirvāṇa.
[Commentary] Next, three points are raised to conclude that the seven virtues are fulfilled.
Therefore, nirvāṇa is of a single flavor and an equal flavor, which refers to the flavor of liberation.
[Commentary: Therefore, "Nirvana has one taste and equal tastes" means that the taste of liberation is the one taste, while the taste of *prajñā* (wisdom) and so forth are the equal tastes;

this refers to the Dharma-body. To say that this Nirvana is the general name for the three virtues clarifies that the meaning of Nirvana—as understood by those who maintain it is untranslatable—encompasses all these meanings.
Alternatively, it may be that in the past, Nirvana was not identified as being identical to the three virtues.
The eternal abiding in nirvana today is precisely because the three virtues (triguṇa) eternally abide; therefore, it is said to be "of one flavor" and so forth.
The previous conclusion regarding the two vehicles' lack of fulfillment did not clarify their refuge in the Dharmakāya;
this conclusion clarifies that the Tathāgata’s ultimate lack of ignorance is his severance [of defilements] and his meritorious qualities. These are cited alternately for the sake of clarification.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that *nirvāṇa* has no equivalent translation, it means that because the single term *nirvāṇa* encompasses multiple meanings, it cannot be translated [into a single Chinese character].
It is like the term *sindhuva*, which refers to four different substances. Although this is so, the meaning of "quiescence" (*śama*) serves as the primary standard;

therefore, from ancient times, various masters have sometimes said there is an equivalent translation and sometimes said there is none. Whether there is a translation or not—though this may be the case...
Although these differ, they do not depart from the meaning of *śānti* (quiescence). Thus, Zhuangyan Dabi translated it as "Quiescence" (*jimiè*).
Quoting a passage, he said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence is bliss.
Zhu Daosheng translated it as "Cessation-Samadhi" (*mièdìng*), Lin Rou translated it as "Liberation from Entanglements" (*wúlè jiětuō*), and the Liang Emperor translated it as [the following].
Sengzhao says that "non-arising" is "the unconditioned," while Kaishan, Zang, Guangzhai, and Yun all use "extinction" (nirvāṇa);
although the explanations of these various masters differ, for the most part they do not go beyond the meaning of quiescence.
[Commentary: From "The World-Honored One" onwards is the second section, which concludes that the Two Vehicles are not ultimate. This is further divided into four parts;
the first correctly explains that because the Two Vehicles have not yet severed the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), they do not attain samādhi, and thus are not ultimate.

“World-Honored One, if the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is not severed and not brought to ultimate end, one cannot attain the single flavor, the equal flavor—namely, the flavor of the liberation of clear understanding.
[Commentary] The first part is easily understood. The second part, from “Why is this? onwards, explains the non-severance of ignorance.

Regarding the fact that the Dwelling Grounds (*bhūmi*) do not attain a single flavor, within the second explanation there are two points. First, it clarifies what should be abandoned but is not abandoned. Why?

Because if the Dwelling Ground of Ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is neither abandoned nor fully realized, then those things that ought to be abandoned—which exceed the sands of the Ganges in number—[remain unextinguished].
The dharmas are neither severed nor perfected.
[Commentary: That which "should be severed" refers to the ignorance regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Second, it clarifies that which "should be attained" but is not attained:
because the dharmas that should be severed—those exceeding the sands of the Ganges—are not severed, the dharmas that should be attained, likewise exceeding the sands of the Ganges, are not attained.
"One should realize but does not realize.

[Commentary]: "That which should be attained" refers to the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the specific characteristics of cognition and vision; "that which should be realized" refers to the cessation of ignorance.

[Commentary]: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the wisdom that cognizes their specific characteristics" refers to the myriad practices as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and the wisdom that illuminates the diverse aspects of the conventional world.

[Sub-commentary]: The third section, from "Therefore, there is no named ground of dwelling" (*tasmād anāmaka-āśraya-bhūmi*) onwards, further clarifies that the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is [the basis].
It is the root of all delusions;

therefore, the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) accumulates and gives rise to all afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), as well as the higher afflictions arising from them:

the higher afflictions of the mind, the higher afflictions of cessation (*śamatha*), the higher afflictions of insight (*vipaśyanā*), the higher afflictions of dhyāna, and the higher afflictions of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

The afflictions regarding skillful means, the afflictions regarding superior wisdom, the afflictions regarding the fruit of superior wisdom, the afflictions regarding attainment, the afflictions regarding power, and the afflictions regarding fearlessness. [Commentary]:
From the phrase "Therefore, for this reason" onwards, it clarifies that the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) is the root of all delusions, briefly enumerating ten aspects.

Second, to clarify its characteristics: the statement that "the accumulation [of ignorance] gives rise to all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation" clarifies that those afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation all arise from the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*). This single sentence provides a general clarification;
the following eleven sentences clarify how the various afflictions that obscure and hinder objects of perception all arise from the ground of abiding ignorance.
"That ground of abiding ignorance is able to produce the 'higher-order afflictions' (ūrdhvabhāgīya-kleśa) of the mind. Regarding "that": it refers to that very mind.
[The *Chao* states: "In the sutra, 'therefore, the ground of abiding ignorance,' etc., 'the producer' refers to ignorance, and 'the produced' refers to the higher-order afflictions of the mind;
'mind' here is a general term for the minds of the three realms. The four grounds of abiding constitute the fetters and hindrances."
Regarding the obstruction of pure wisdom by the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) within the mind-consciousness, there are two types:
first, that which obstructs the two vehicles; second, that which obstructs the bodhisattvas. Now, it is explained that the ground of ignorance gives rise to all these various fetters.

Prior to practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one first trains in calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). This specifically analyzes the afflictions of the desire realm; the higher [stages] refer to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) within dhyāna.

Regarding "samādhi" (正受): it refers to the cessation of the mind at the highest level of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding "expedient means" (方便): it refers to the untainted expedient means (*anāsrava-upāya*). Regarding "knowledge" (智):

it refers to what is known through hearing and wisdom. Regarding "fruit" (果): it refers to the fact that conditioned states (*saṃskṛta*) have not yet been exhausted and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has not yet reached its ultimate limit;
this constitutes the cognitive obstacle for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Regarding "powers" (力) and "fearlessnesses" (無畏): these belong to the Bodhisattva.
This is the hindrance of knowledge.
[Commentary] The fourth section, from "Thus, more than sands of the Ganges" onwards, concludes that the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is the root of all afflictions.
In this way, all the higher afflictions, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, which are severed by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom,

are all established upon the ground of the dwelling of ignorance; the arising of all higher afflictions is caused by the ground of the dwelling of ignorance and conditioned by the ground of the dwelling of ignorance.

[Commentary]: From the passage "Thus, [afflictions] exceeding the sands of the Ganges... onwards is the fourth section, which concludes that the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is the root of all delusions.
It states that "all are caused by the ground of ignorance" because although the sands of the Ganges are originally non-existent, they arise by depending upon the ground of ignorance;

hence it is said "all are caused by [the sands]. Furthermore, there is the sense that these sands can also be produced, as the ground of ignorance assists in their manifestation; thus it is so stated.
"All are conditions.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "all are due to the ground of ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), it says that because its nature is simply non-knowing, it is called the "cause";
yet, because even wisdom remains deluded by it, it is termed a "condition."
[Commentary]: From the passage "The World-Honored One [arose] from this, and afflictions were produced" onwards, the third section concludes the fourth by explaining two kinds of afflictions.
This serves as a summary placed at the third location because it both excludes and does not exclude [certain factors].

The reason for this summary is that the previous section concluded that the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) are not ultimate, citing their failure to sever the *avidyāvāsabhūmi* (the ground of ignorance) as the basis for that conclusion.
"It concludes according to the context.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "it concludes according to the context": the preceding section on the division of the text is fourfold. First, the scripture states:

"World-Honored One, if there were no ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*)... and so forth, up to: "...ignorance is the root of all delusions. It says, "conditioned by the ground of the dwelling of ignorance."
Taking advantage of this continuity, the text now brings forward the passage on the fourth affliction from the second section to conclude it;
only then does it clarify the conclusion of the preceding third section, wherein the two types of death are to be observed.
[Commentary: The fourth section above cited two kinds of afflictions to explain the two types of death, while also addressing what is eliminated and what is not among the four original points.
First, it set forth the essence and characteristics of the afflictions; second, it clarified their relative strength and function; third, it clarified the differences in how they moisten karma;
and fourth, it clarified their abandonment and elimination. Now, we shall briefly discuss [the third point], the differences in how they moisten karma, without concluding it here.
The remaining three are all fetters; from the beginning up to the end, the first is the fetter of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-ālaya-bhūmi*).
World-Honored One, regarding this, the arising of afflictions is associated with the moments of mind (*citta-kṣaṇa*), whereas the World-Honored One’s [state] is dissociated from the moments of mind.
The ground of beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
[Commentary: Regarding this, the four grounds of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) are cited as being associated with the moments of mind that give rise to afflictions;
the ground of beginningless ignorance is cited as being dissociated from the mind of the World-Honored One. From the World-Honored One...
Furthermore, to summarize the second point regarding the power of measurement by exceeding what has been stated above:
"World-Honored One, if there were dharmas to be abandoned by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom that exceeded the sands of the Ganges River,
all of them would be sustained and established by the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), just as all seeds depend upon the earth to grow."
If the earth were to perish, those [phenomena] would likewise perish along with it;

in the same way, all the dharmas to be abandoned by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom—which exceed the sands of the Ganges—in their establishment and growth, all depend upon the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
If the ground of the dwelling of ignorance is severed, then all the dharmas to be abandoned by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom—which exceed the sands of the Ganges—[are likewise severed].
All of these are also severed accordingly.

[Commentary: Regarding the second section above, "Examining the Power of the Grounds," there were originally two parts: first, the inferiority of the four abodes (catur-vihāra-bhūmi), and second, the superiority of the ground of ignorance (avidyā-vāsabhūmi).
Now, by merely concluding that the ground of ignorance is superior, the inferiority of the four abodes is understood to depart of its own accord.

In the preceding middle section, there were both explanations of the doctrine and metaphors; now, in this concluding section, there are likewise explanations of the doctrine and metaphors that can be seen.

Above, it was stated directly that the power of the *avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi* (the ground of ignorance) is supreme; here, it is clarified that the formation and destruction of all afflictions are rooted in the *avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi*, and thus they are concluded.
[Commentary] Regarding that which is maintained and established by the Sūtra: "Nameless" refers to the initial arising; this constitutes "maintenance. "Final accomplishment" refers to establishment.
Since birth and death arise from that [namelessness], how could their cessation possibly be different?
[Commentary: "All such as these" and below concludes the fourth section on eradication.
All such afflictions and secondary afflictions are severed; that which transcends the sands of the Ganges, all dharmas attained by the Tathāgatas, are thoroughly penetrated without obstruction.
Through all-knowing vision, one is free from all faults and evils and attains all merits.
The Dharma King and Lord of Dharma, who has attained mastery and realized the stage of sovereignty over all dharmas—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—utters the true lion’s roar:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, by means of the lion’s roar, provides a definitive declaration based on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
[Commentary: From "In this way, all such" onwards concludes the fourth section, "Eliminating the Above.

It states that what is eliminated at the stage of Buddhahood is eliminated by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment (*buddhabodhi-jñāna*). This clarifies that because the Tathāgata’s causes and effects are already perfected, he is able to eliminate [all obscurations].
Within this, there are three parts: first, it clarifies that he is able to eliminate them because the causes are perfected; second, from "From the Dharma... [it continues].

The King is the Lord of Dharma; from "below" [this point], the fulfillment of the fruit is clarified, whereby he is able to sever the third [category]. From "therefore" onwards, the conclusion can be seen as follows:

all afflictions (*kleśa*) are categorized such that the "root" and "universal" afflictions are termed "superior afflictions," while the "branches" and "specific" afflictions are termed "subsidiary afflictions.
However, for the sake of establishing the stages of the path, it is said: "What was to be done has been accomplished; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established."
Originally abiding in the diamond-like [samādhi] and now illuminating the Buddha-fruit Dharma-body, one has performed what was to be done through the wisdom of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
This is explained for clarity according to the general gate. [Commentary]:
From the passage "all-knowing and all-seeing" in the sutra, it is specifically termed "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is fully present here amidst these various evils.
Having eternally exhausted all conditioned phenomena and universally transcended the assembly of the sages, he is called the Lord who possesses mastery over all dharmas;
entering the realm of nirvana and attaining ultimate bliss, he is named one who has realized the stage of self-mastery.
Only such a person as this may correspond to the virtue of the ten titles and utter words of fearlessness. His speech does not conceal the principle, which is to say:

That which is taught in the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) without remainder is the categorical explanation (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*). As for the placement [of the term] "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the discussion, this is a case of using the great to represent the small;

that is, while the four knowledges (*jñāna*) being complete in the Hīnayāna is called "Nirvāṇa with Remainder," by analogy, in the Mahāyāna, this [state] should correspond to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).

This is the meaning explained according to the specific gate (*paryāya*); as for the meaning explained according to the general gate, the meaning is as follows: *Note: The final sentence appears to be a fragment or a scribal error regarding the transition to the general gate. The provided text ends abruptly.*

Because it is the stage of the fruition of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*), it is called "Nameless. As for the phrase "all such as these," it means that all dharmas that ought to be abandoned have been entirely abandoned.
"Exceeding the sands of the Ganges" refers to having attained what is to be attained and having realized what is to be realized.
[Commentary: From the passage "The World-Honored One does not receive further existence" onwards is the fourth section, which concludes the third.

Having previously raised two types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to explain the second point regarding ultimate and non-ultimate [attainment], it was stated directly that the Tathāgata eliminates both types of death, whereas the Two Vehicles eliminate only one.
Therefore, this section now specifically summarizes and concludes: since the Tathāgata has already subdued the four Māras, for this reason...
It is said that both types of death are eliminated, whereas the two vehicles cannot subdue the four māras; therefore, they eliminate only one.
The primary meaning states that from this point onward, the section concludes by incorporating [the teachings] into one. Within this, there are two parts:
first, the conclusion regarding the Tathāgata’s simultaneous elimination of both types of death; second, from "World-Honored One, Arhat" onwards, the conclusion regarding the two vehicles.
Setting aside one for now, first regarding the initial binding of the Tathāgata, there are two aspects to the simultaneous removal of the two deaths (*mṛtyu*).
First, as for the actual binding: since the Tathāgata has already subdued the four Māras, he therefore simultaneously removes the two deaths.
The Tathāgata’s knowledge that he will not undergo further existence is of two kinds:
namely, that by means of his unsurpassed mastery, he has subdued the four māras, emerged from all worlds, and is gazed upon by all sentient beings.

[Commentary]: Regarding the two kinds of knowledge of "no further existence" (*anupapatti-jñāna*), because one intends to conclude by combining the two types of death—whether they are eliminated or not—one first takes this knowledge of no further existence as the primary heading.

As for the "two kinds," the first is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of no further existence, and the second is the knowledge of no further existence of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As for "subduing the four Māras," the celestial Māra (*deva-māra*) is...
The affliction-māra is the evil cause; the aggregate-māra and death-māra are the evil effects.
Since the Tathāgata has already subdued these four māras, both forms of death are simultaneously eliminated.

"Transcending all worlds" refers to surpassing the two worlds of *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative). "Being gazed upon by all sentient beings" clarifies that, having subdued the four [māras], he is thus honored.
Because Māradhvaja transcends the two worlds, he is venerated by all sentient beings; thus, it is clear that the two types of death are both eliminated.
Second, from "attaining the inconceivable" onwards, [the text] cites ten thousand virtues to prove that the two types of death are both eliminated.
Having attained the inconceivable Dharma-body, one attains mastery over unimpeded dharmas throughout all stages of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

Beyond this, there is nothing further to be done and no further ground to be attained. With the ten powers (*daśabala*) and heroic vigor, one ascends to the foremost, unsurpassed stage of fearlessness.
Through the observation of unimpeded wisdom regarding all aspects of omniscience, one does not rely on others; this is the knowledge of a teacher who shall not undergo further existence.
The Lion’s Roar.
[Commentary]: From "Attaining the inconceivable" onwards is the second section, which cites various virtues on the level of fruition to prove that both forms of death are eliminated.
Since he already possesses such venerable virtues, how could he possibly still be subject to the two deaths?

[Commentary]: Regarding the "Ten Powers of the Valiant One," they are: (1) the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*); (2) the power of karma; (3) the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*); (4) the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*);

(5) the power of aspirations (*adhimukti-bala*); (6) the power of dispositions (*dhātu-bala*); (7) the power of the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-bala*); (8) the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-bala*); (9) the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-bala*);

and (10) the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*). These ten are collectively termed "powers" because they are the wisdom of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) attained by all Buddhas.
Because it penetrates all things with complete clarity and distinctness such that nothing can equal or surpass it, it is called a "power" (*bala*).

Regarding the first power, the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*): the Buddha knows the fixed nature of the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of all phenomena;
he knows that from such causes and conditions this kind of retribution arises, and that from such causes and conditions this kind of retribution does not arise.

It is impossible for one to receive a wholesome retribution for unwholesome karma; since unwholesome karma cannot even bring about worldly happiness, how much less could it bring about supramundane bliss?
The same applies to unwholesome conduct. It is impossible for one whose mind is shrouded by the five hindrances and distracted to attain nirvana despite practicing the seven factors of enlightenment;
if one’s mind is shrouded by the five hindrances, one will not attain it even while practicing the seven factors of enlightenment.
If even the path of the śrāvaka, when free from obscurations, can lead to the attainment of the Buddha-way, how much more so for the śrāvaka path itself?
In this way, the Buddha universally knows all such instances of what is possible and what is impossible; it cannot be destroyed and it cannot be surpassed—this is the first power.
Second, regarding the power of karma: the Buddha knows all the past, future, and present karmas of all sentient beings.

Regarding the power of karma: having fully and universally known all feelings, the places where karma is created, the causes and conditions, and the retributions, it is exactly as described in the passage on the first power below.

Third, regarding the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): the Buddha knows all dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and the distinctions between the defiled and pure aspects of concentration as they truly are, knowing them universally. Fourth, regarding the power of the faculties (*indriya*): the Buddha...
1. The power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings. 2. The power of the five desires: the Buddha knows the various desires of sentient beings.
3. The power of the six dispositions: the Buddha knows the various lack of spiritual dispositions in the world.
4. The power of the path leading to all destinations: the Buddha knows the destination reached by every path. 5. The power of recollecting past lives: the Buddha knows one... [past life].
All various common characteristics and common causes and conditions— through one lifetime, two lifetimes, and even up to hundreds of thousands of lifetimes and kalpas from the beginning of time—
I was among those sentient beings with such-and-such a name, eating such-and-such food, experiencing such-and-such suffering and pleasure,
having such-and-such a lifespan, long or short; dying there, being born here, dying here, and being born again in that place, with such-and-such a name in this interval.
Regarding the extent of their length: as for the divine power of sight of the Tathāgata, his divine eye is pure and surpasses that of all devas and humans;

he sees sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—whether they are handsome or ugly, great or small, whether they fall into evil destinies or good destinies—and how these sentient beings, having performed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, receive retribution according to such karmic causes and conditions.

Because he does not slander the sages and has accomplished right view and right action through these causes and conditions, at the time of death—when the body perishes—he enters a good destination and is reborn in the heavens, and so forth.

Regarding the tenth power, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-bala*): because the Buddha’s outflows are exhausted, he possesses the liberation of mind through the absence of outflows (*anāsrava-ceto-vimukti*) and the liberation of wisdom through the absence of outflows (*anāsrava-prajñā-vimukti*); within the present phenomena, he personally cognizes and knows for himself: "My outflows are exhausted."
"Birth has been exhausted, the precepts have been established, and the non-occurrence of future existence is known as it truly is.
[Commentary] From the passage "The World-Honored One, the Arhat," onwards, the second section concludes the discussion of the Two Vehicles by excluding only one of the two aspects;

this section is further divided into two parts. The first clarifies that the Two Vehicles have only eliminated the cause of *pariccheda-bhava* (segmented existence), meaning they have already departed from birth.
Death. The World-Honored One, the Arhats, and the Pratyekabuddhas, having crossed over the fear of birth and death, sequentially attain the bliss of liberation and form this thought:
"I am free from the terror of birth and death; I shall no longer undergo the suffering of birth and death."
[Commentary]: "Crossing over the fear of birth and death" means fearing the crossing over of the *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death).

"Successively attaining the bliss of liberation" clarifies that by severing the delusions of the three realms in successive order, the principle of being free from delusion naturally becomes a source of joy;
thus, it is called the "bliss of liberation. "Forming this thought" clarifies that because of this, one has already departed from the terror of birth and death and will no longer undergo rebirth.
The suffering of death; this is one of the two kinds of "knowledge that does not receive further existence" (anupādāya-jñāna), and it is also one kind of knowledge.
The commentary states: "Therefore, the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) eliminate only one of these.

Regarding the phrase "gradually severing the afflictions of the three realms," etc.: first, one severs the afflictions of the three realms through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and attains the first fruit (srotāpanna); next, one severs...
By abandoning six grades of afflictions in the desire realm through volition, one attains the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin; next, by further abandoning nine grades, one attains the fruit of Anāgāmin;
and finally, from the first grade of the first dhyāna up to the ninth grade of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the exhaustion of these is termed the fruit of Arhatship.

If one were to subdivide these categories in detail to clarify those such as the *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family) or the *ekavīcika* (one-seeded), they could not be fully exhausted here.
The *Abhidharma* explains this extensively.
[Commentary: The second section, from "World-Honored One" onwards, also clarifies that it is only the *ānantarya-karma* that eliminates the *pariccheda* (segmented existence);
because they falsely claimed to have already attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), only that one [type of karma] was eliminated.
When the World-Honored One, the Arhat, and the Pratyekabuddha observe, they attain the vision of no further existence and the ground of Nirvana,
the supreme place of rest.
[Commentary] From "The World-Honored One" onwards, the second section clarifies that this is also because they have already attained the vision of the foremost state.

"Examining the timing" means illuminating the time of the Four Truths; one interpretation says it means that at the time of illuminating the Four Truths, one is naturally able to infer and look upward toward the supreme state to be attained.

From the passage "From the stage previously attained by the World-Honored One," and below, this separately reconciles the sixth section on the fruits of the Two Vehicles within the primary meaning of the One Vehicle. It states: "The preceding [section] was a preliminary analysis of the Buddha."
The departure is not from a single vehicle; rather, the three vehicles are subsumed to form one vehicle. Within this, there are four points:
first, it clarifies that when those of the two vehicles are on the causal stage, they know for themselves that they have not yet reached the ultimate.
"Blessed One, regarding that stage previously attained, he is not deluded about the Dharma and does not rely on others;
he also knows for himself that there are further stages remaining, and that he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

[Commentary: "Those" refers to those followers of the Two Vehicles who, having previously attained the five expedient means and the three fruits or four stages of the path, were not deluded regarding the Dharma—that is, they did not lose sight of the principle of eternal abiding—and were not dependent on others—that is, they did not rely on the instruction of another.

[Commentary] Regarding the "five expedients," these consist of the four foundations of mindfulness—both in their general and specific aspects—along with the four roots of goodness, making five in total.
[Sub-commentary] Second, from the passage beginning "Why is this? onwards, he explains "self-knowledge."
Why is this? Because the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas all enter the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is itself the Buddha-vehicle.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of how one knows for oneself. The commentary states: if we discuss this according to ultimate reality, there is logically no such thing as three [vehicles].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because, when discussing from the perspective of ultimate reality, there are not three [vehicles]," this means that while the principle of the Two Vehicles was provisionally established as a "City of Transformation," when discussed from the perspective of ultimate reality, that principle does not actually exist. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "There is only the One Buddha Vehicle;
[the other two] were taught because they are places of rest. Now, for your sake, I shall explain the reality: what you have attained is not extinction.
[Commentary] Third, from "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards, the text formally concludes by entering into the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Therefore, the Three Vehicles are precisely the One Vehicle.
[Commentary] This is the formal conclusion that the Three Vehicles enter into the One. Fourth, from "Attaining" (*prāpti*)...

Regarding the fourth section, which clarifies the meaning of the fruit attained through the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), since the first part—explaining the causal basis for this fruit—is now complete, it is appropriate to clarify the characteristics of the fruit that has been attained; therefore, this is explained here. Within this, there are two parts:
first, a direct explanation of the fruit of *bodhi* that is attained.
Those who attain the One Vehicle attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary] The second section cites the three virtues of *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *dharmakāya* to clarify the meaning of their mutual identity (*xiāngjí*).
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself the realm of nirvāṇa; the realm of nirvāṇa is itself the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
One who attains the ultimate Dharma-body then reaches the ultimate One Vehicle, which is no different from the Tathāgata, and no different from the Dharma-body.
The Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; one who attains the ultimate Dharma-body then reaches the ultimate One.
That which "rides upon the ultimate" is precisely the boundless and uninterrupted.

[Commentary: The reason for clarifying this identity of characteristics is that when beings hear of attaining *bodhi*, they might think that the One Vehicle only attains *bodhi* and does not attain other virtues;
therefore, this identity of characteristics is necessary. When one attains the ultimate *dharmakāya*, then...
The ultimate One Vehicle is realized through the ultimate cause; thus, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the Dharma, while the Tathāgata is the practitioner.
Although their meanings appear distinct, they are further cited to clarify their identity. The cause is cited again according to the fruit, and the identity is likewise clarified once more:
the Dharma-body is the true essence of all virtues, and the One Vehicle is the true nature of the Dharma-body.
The reason for specifically citing the *dharmakāya* is to clarify that the cause reaches its ultimate fulfillment.
[Commentary] "To clarify that it is obtained through the ultimate cause" means to clarify that this fruit of the *dharmakāya* is obtained by means of the aforementioned One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) cause.
Following this passage which clarifies the fruit, to further cite its cause is the One Vehicle cause.
This is because the meaning also becomes increasingly clear.

[Commentary] From the passage beginning "The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, dwells for a time that has no limit," the second section raises the Three Jewels as a single essence to establish the cause.
Since the fruit manifested by a single word is of a single essence, then the cause—
Regarding the first [section] on what can be realized, it is initially divided into two parts. First, from the beginning up to this point, there is the reliance upon the finite;
since one intends to clarify that the single essence (*ekatva*) of today is the ultimate, one first clarifies that the distinct essences (*pṛthaktva*) are not the final goal.
Second, from "If there are sentient beings... onwards, the single essence of today as the ultimate is correctly elucidated. Regarding the first [of these two], first...

Within the clarification of the distinct essence (*bhedatattva*), it is further divided into two parts. First, from the beginning up to the phrase "making an inexhaustible refuge," he first praises the single Jewel of the Buddha within the distinct essence.

Why is this? Although the distinct essence is not as ultimate as the identical essence (*ekatva*), the single Jewel of the Buddha is itself a singular principle that cannot be diminished; therefore, he first praises the single Jewel of the Buddha within the distinct essence.

The first, the Jewel of the Buddha, is the foundation of refuge. From the second point, "taking refuge in that which is eternally abiding," onwards, it correctly clarifies that the distinct entities of the Dharmakāya and Saṃgha Jewels are not ultimate.

While their former distinct entities were merely provisional means, their present distinct entities are the true teaching. Yet, whether they are considered real or unreal, neither is equal to today’s single essence (ekakāya).
Because it is the ultimate, it is said to be "not final. Regarding the first section, the initial praise, there are five points;

the first clarifies that this is eternally abiding. [Commentary]: This refers to the principle of the Buddha-jewel; the eternal abiding of the Buddha-jewel is also the principle within the single essence.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the distinct entities of the past were equal [to the present], the distinct entities of the past could indeed be seen;

however, today this One Vehicle teaching of the sutra constitutes the Dharma Jewel, its true sons who possess the threefold patience constitute the Sangha Jewel, and the discussed Dharmakāya constitutes the Buddha Jewel.
In none of these cases does the Dharmakāya—as elucidated by this sutra—possess the principle of the Three Jewels inherent within itself.
This is the ultimate limit.
World-Honored One, the Tathāgata abides for no limited duration; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, abides equally until the end of time (*paścimakoṭi*).

[Commentary: "The end of time" refers to when all sentient beings have become Buddhas. Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, the Buddha remains as long as there are those to be saved. Thus, the Tathāgata abides until the end of time.
It is clear that [the Tathāgata] is eternally abiding. Second, his clarity is great compassion.
The Tathāgata’s limitlessness is equal to the limitlessness of great compassion; he brings comfort to the world through limitless great compassion and limitless comfort for the world.
[Commentary]: Third, exhorting the exposition of great compassion.
One who speaks in this manner is called one who skillfully expounds the Tathāgata.
[Commentary]: Fourth, exhorting the exposition of permanence.
Furthermore, if it is said that the Tathāgata is the inexhaustible Dharma, the eternally abiding Dharma, and the refuge of all the world, this too is called a well-spoken teaching.
[Commentary] Five: Conclusion.
Therefore, for the sake of the world that has not yet been delivered and the world that is without refuge, one acts as an inexhaustible refuge, equal to the future limit.
[Commentary: All of this is visible. Regarding the second section, which correctly clarifies that the two jewels of Dharma and Sangha are not ultimate, there are four parts;
first, the preliminary enumeration.
The eternally abiding refuge refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; the Dharma is that which explains the path of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna);
and the Saṅgha consists of the assemblies of the Three Vehicles.
[Commentary] The original meaning states that from the beginning until the end, it refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, clarifying that today’s [refuge] is one...

The essence [of the Dharma] is the foundation of refuge, yet at present there is no need for a ladder; the Three Jewels are precisely what is taught in the scriptures, with no distinction between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as all constitute the Jewel of the Dharma.
Those who study these teachings likewise make no distinction between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as all constitute the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Now, by citing the superior while including the inferior, it refers specifically to those of the One Vehicle who follow the teachings of the Three Vehicles. And...
Although the Mahāyāna was taught in the past, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) was not yet clarified; it is only this present sutra that takes the One Vehicle as the Dharma Jewel.
Second, from the passage "Taking refuge in these two" onwards, it correctly clarifies that these two refuges are not ultimate.
"These two refuges are not ultimate refuges; they are called partial refuges.
[Commentary] The third section, from "Why is this? onwards, explains why these two refuges are not ultimate.
Why is it said that the Dharma of the Single Vehicle Path can attain the ultimate Dharmakāya, and that above this there is no further teaching of the Single Vehicle Dharma?
[Commentary]: By teaching the path of the Single Vehicle, one attains the Dharmakāya; above the Dharmakāya, there is no further matter of teaching the Single Vehicle Dharma.
Thus, the ultimate pinnacle of the Dharma-jewel resides solely in the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is said that the teaching of the One Vehicle is not the ultimate Dharma-jewel.
As for those of the Three Vehicles, they possess fear and take refuge in the Tathāgata, seeking liberation and practicing with the aim of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Samyak-saṃbodhi]. [Commentary]:
The explanation of "monk" (bhikṣu) shows that it is not ultimately visible. Fourth, from "Therefore" onwards, the conclusion is reached that it is not ultimate.
Therefore, these two bases are not ultimate bases; they are limited bases. [Commentary:

The fourth section, the conclusion, may also be seen. From the passage "If there are sentient beings... onwards is the second part, which correctly elucidates that today the Three Jewels are of one essence.
Within this, there are five points: first, clarifying the reliance on the Dharma and Sangha of today’s single essence.
This is precisely taking refuge in the Tathāgata.

If there are sentient beings whom the Tathāgata has disciplined, and who, having taken refuge in the Tathāgata, receive the moisture of the Dharma and give rise to a mind of faith and joy, they take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
These two refuges are not [independent] refuges; rather, it is by taking refuge in the Tathāgata that one takes refuge [in them].
The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is taking refuge in the Tathāgata; this twofold refuge is the ultimate refuge, for the Tathāgata is the ultimate refuge.
[Commentary: These two refuges refer to the Dharma and the Saṃgha as being of one essence with the Tathāgata; they do not refer to these two as independent bases of refuge.

Regarding the two bases of reliance as distinct entities, these cannot be used for inference. This is because those who take refuge in the Tathāgata today take refuge in the Dharma and Saṃgha as being one with the Tathāgata himself.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that when one generates the aspiration for enlightenment and takes refuge in the Dharma and Saṃgha due to being tamed, this refers to relying on the Dharma and Saṃgha as distinct entities; thus, these two refuges are not [the ultimate ones], meaning they are distinct entities.

Because the [refuges] based upon what is not supreme, what is no longer distinct, and the Dharma and Sangha that are not ultimate have already been discussed, this is raised again in order to clarify that "not" [is actually] "is.
These two refuges—meaning today’s single essence and dual bases—are the taking of refuge in the Tathāgata;
since this also clarifies the single essence, we know from here downward that the single-essence Dharma is being elucidated.

Regarding the Sangha, it is because its distinct substance (*pṛthag-vastu*) has already been established above. As for taking refuge in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this refers to taking refuge in the Tathāgata.

"Ultimate truth" refers to the three virtues and four meanings. The original commentary states: "These two phrases specifically clarify that the Buddha-Jewel as a single substance (*eka-vastu*) is most supreme.
Now, if a distinct substance is also permissible, how is it that the single substance is uniquely supreme? This is what [the text] addresses.

The second point, "Taking Refuge in the Ultimate Truth," clarifies that taking refuge in the Tathāgata is ultimate by relying on the single essence of the Dharma and Saṃgha, as well as the three virtues and four meanings;
this is precisely what constitutes taking refuge in the Tathāgata in the ultimate sense. The *Benyi* (Original Meaning) states:
"From this section on the two refuges downward, it concludes that the single-essence triple refuge is likewise ultimate."

[Commentary]: Regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore, the ancients' interpretation of the following phrase is slightly different," their explanation of the meaning differs from that of our own school;
we preserve it here without refuting it because the intended meaning of the scripture is difficult to determine definitively.

From the passage "As for taking refuge in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)" onwards, our own school provides its own explanation of the fourth phrase: the three virtues (triguṇa) are as previously stated, and the four meanings refer to the four pāramitās.

The nectar of *nirvāṇa*—constancy, bliss, self, and purity—is also called the "four virtues," as seen in the following scriptural passage. Now, regarding the statement that "the essence (*tattva*) may also be equal":

if they possess distinct essences, it would be permissible for the Buddha-jewel to be superior and the other two jewels inferior; however, if they possess a single essence, there can be no distinction of superiority or inferiority among the three.

Therefore, if an ancient master were to say that within a single essence the Buddha-jewel is superior, how would that differ from [the case of] distinct essences? For this reason, he asks: "Why is this so?"
All are most supreme.
[Commentary] Second, from "Why is this so? onwards, it explains why one takes refuge in the Dharma and the Sangha by taking refuge in the Tathāgata.
Why is this so? Because there is no difference between the Tathāgata and the two refuges; the Tathāgata is itself the three refuges.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of why taking refuge in the Dharma and the Sangha is equivalent to taking refuge in the Tathāgata:
it is because the three refuges are of one essence (*ekakāya*). What is the original meaning? It is because they are equally ultimate and thus of one essence.
Third, from "Why is this so? onwards, there is also an explanation of why they are of one essence.
Why is it said that there is the path of the One Vehicle?
[Commentary: Third, the explanation of why this is of one essence: because one attains it by means of the One Vehicle, it is of one essence.
[Commentary]: "That which is attained by means of the One Vehicle" refers to attaining the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) through the path of the One Vehicle;
the very essence of the Dharma-body inherently possesses the Three Jewels.
[Sub-commentary]: The fourth section cites the Buddha as proof.
The Tathāgata, having accomplished the four fearlessnesses, delivers the lion’s roar.
[Commentary: Fourth, as for who it is that speaks thus, the Buddha is cited as the witness.

However, since the Three Jewels of distinct substance have names and essences that differ from one another, their principles may naturally be distinct; yet, how can there be a distinction within the single essence? The explanation says: "Constantly."
Abiding in the Dharma-body constitutes the Buddha Jewel; this Dharma-body can serve as a standard for all things and is itself the Dharma Jewel.
Furthermore, because this Dharma-body is able to be in harmony with ultimate principle, it also constitutes the Sangha Jewel.

If one distinguishes the objects of refuge for the purpose of cultivation, understanding, and the severing of delusions, then their distinct natures may be primary; however, if one does not lose sight of the essential goal of refuge, then their identity as a single essence is what is required.
Now, Śrīmālā wishes only to take the ultimate refuge as the foundation; it is not like the former "ladder," which seeks only the single essence of today.
[The Commentary] states that "their names and essences are each distinct" because the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha differ from the Dharma-body and the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
The bodies of those of the three vehicles are non-different; within this single essence, the eternally abiding Dharma-body, the nature of spiritual awakening and wisdom, constitutes the Buddha Jewel;
that which gives rise to the understanding of sentient beings constitutes the Dharma Jewel; and the harmonious union of principle and wisdom constitutes the Sangha Jewel.

Regarding the analysis of taking refuge and so forth: if one relies on those of the three vehicles, who cultivate practice based on the teachings to give rise to understanding and sever delusions, they may first [take refuge].

If they were of distinct entities, one would surely be confused regarding the underlying intent of the teaching; therefore, it is essential that they be of one entity. Regarding the "attainment of the four fearlessnesses" and so forth:
first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of obstacles to the path;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the path leading to the exhaustion of suffering. These four are collectively termed "fearlessnesses" because—
Having extensively explained within the assembly that his own and others' knowledge and abandonment are both certain and free from error, there is not even the slightest sign of fear.
Regarding the fearlessness of omniscience, the Buddha makes this solemn declaration: "I am an omniscient person.
If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or anyone else who, according to reality..."
"I declare that regarding these dharmas, I do not know them, nor do I perceive even the slightest sign of fear;

for this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I abide in the station of the Noble Lord, like a bull-king among the great assembly, roaring the lion’s roar and turning the Brahma-wheel.
Whether they be śramaṇas or brahmins, gods, Māras, or Brahmas..."

The remaining assembly is unable to truly overturn [his claim] regarding the first fearlessness. Second, regarding the fearlessness of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*): the Buddha makes this solemn declaration, "I have destroyed all outflows. If there were any [outflows] remaining, and so forth, it would be as stated previously; he speaks these words according to reality, stating that these outflows are not exhausted, down to the point where there is not even the slightest sign of fear. The subsequent text is the same as before. Third, regarding the fearlessness of declaring the obstacles to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*): [the Buddha declares], "These are the dharmas that constitute obstacles to the path. If one were to practice them and yet not fall into the miserable destinies, or if one were to practice them and yet attain supreme enlightenment, then I would be subject to censure by the wise. Since such a thing is impossible, I am without even the slightest sign of fear. The subsequent text is the same as before. Regarding the fearlessness of declaring the path leading to the cessation of suffering (*nairyāṇika-pratipad-vaiśāradya*): the Buddha makes this solemn declaration, "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. If one were to practice it and yet not attain nirvāṇa, then I would be subject to censure by the wise. Since such a thing is impossible, I am without even the slightest sign of fear. The subsequent text is the same as before. These are called the four fearlessnesses. Furthermore, the Buddha’s three knowledges (*trividyā*) are: first, the knowledge of past lives; second, the knowledge of death and rebirth; and third, the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows. These three knowledges are each divided into two types: mundane and supramundane. Among these, the mundane knowledge of past lives consists of recollecting various births from one lifetime up to a hundred thousand kalpas, or even further. The supramundane knowledge of past lives consists of recollecting the continuity of births through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, and even beyond, until reaching the limit of the beginningless cycle of birth and death. It is because he has attained such knowledge that he is called the Tathāgata. The mundane knowledge of death and rebirth consists of seeing sentient beings die in one place and being reborn in another, whether in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the world of humans, or the heavens of the gods. The supramundane knowledge of death and rebirth consists of seeing sentient beings die in one place and be reborn in another, whether in the form realm or the formless realm, or even in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. It is because he has attained such knowledge that he is called the Tathāgata. The mundane knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows consists of knowing that one has abandoned the outflows of the desire realm, the outflows of the form realm, and the outflows of the formless realm. The supramundane knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows consists of knowing that one has abandoned the outflows of the desire realm, the outflows of the form realm, and the outflows of the formless realm. It is because he has attained such knowledge that he is called the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*) are: first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; second, the power of knowing the maturation of karma; third, the power of knowing the various inclinations of sentient beings; fourth, the power of knowing the various dispositions of sentient beings; fifth, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings; sixth, the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere; seventh, the power of knowing the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and equanimities; eighth, the power of knowing the recollection of past lives; ninth, the power of knowing death and rebirth; and tenth, the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows. These are called the ten powers. Furthermore, the Buddha’s eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are: first, no bodily error; second, no verbal error; third, no mental error; fourth, no loss of mindfulness; fifth, no non-equanimity of mind; sixth, no loss of aspiration for the benefit of sentient beings; seventh, no loss of diligence; eighth, no loss of wisdom; ninth, no loss of liberation; tenth, no loss of the knowledge and vision of liberation; eleventh, all bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and accompanied by knowledge; twelfth, all verbal actions are preceded by knowledge and accompanied by knowledge; thirteenth, all mental actions are preceded by knowledge and accompanied by knowledge; fourteenth, his wisdom regarding the past is unimpeded; fifteenth, his wisdom regarding the future is unimpeded; sixteenth, his wisdom regarding the present is unimpeded; seventeenth, his body is invulnerable to harm; eighteenth, his speech is invulnerable to harm. These are called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, the Buddha’s thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) are: first, the mark of having feet with level tread; second, the mark of having wheels on the soles of the feet; third, the mark of having long fingers and toes; fourth, the mark of having broad heels; fifth, the mark of having high-arched insteps; sixth, the mark of having soft and tender hands and feet; seventh, the mark of having webbed hands and feet; eighth, the mark of having ankles hidden within the flesh; ninth, the mark of having legs like those of an antelope; tenth, the mark of having the male organ enclosed in a sheath; eleventh, the mark of having a body that is perfectly proportioned like a banyan tree; twelfth, the mark of having a tall and straight body; thirteenth, the mark of having the upper part of the body like that of a lion; fourteenth, the mark of having rounded shoulders; fifteenth, the mark of having no hollow between the shoulders; sixteenth, the mark of having a well-filled chest; seventeenth, the mark of having a sense of taste that is most excellent; eighteenth, the mark of having a broad jaw like that of a lion; nineteenth, the mark of having forty teeth; twentieth, the mark of having teeth that are even; twenty-first, the mark of having teeth that are without gaps; twenty-second, the mark of having teeth that are white; twenty-third, the mark of having a tongue that is long and wide; twenty-fourth, the mark of having a voice like that of Brahmā; twenty-fifth, the mark of having eyes that are blue like a lotus; twenty-sixth, the mark of having eyelashes like those of a cow; twenty-seventh, the mark of having a tuft of hair between the eyebrows; twenty-eighth, the mark of having a crown protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*); twenty-ninth, the mark of having a halo extending one arm’s length; thirtieth, the mark of having a skin that is golden in color; thirty-first, the mark of having hair that grows singly from each pore; thirty-second, the mark of having the hair of the head curling upward to the right. These are called the thirty-two marks of a great man. The Buddha makes this solemn declaration: "I have explained the obstructing dharmas," and so forth, as previously stated.
"These are obstructing dharmas and not dharmas that do not obstruct the Path," and so forth, as previously stated. Regarding the fourth fearlessness, the exhaustion of suffering:

the Buddha makes this solemn declaration: "The Noble Path I have taught is able to transcend the world; by practicing in accordance with it, one can exhaust suffering," and so on, up to "even for other beings."
"In truth, it cannot be turned.
[Commentary] The fifth section, from "If the Tathāgata... onwards, clarifies the intention behind not teaching the One Vehicle in the past.
If the Tathāgata had taught expediently according to their desires, that would have been the Great Vehicle itself, with no distinction between two vehicles.
"Those who ride [the vehicle] enter the One Vehicle; the One Vehicle is precisely the Vehicle of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-yāna). [Commentary:
Fifth, this clarifies the reason why the One Vehicle was not explained in the past. Since the principle is as stated above, for what reason did the past teachings still clarify the Three Vehicles?
Therefore, it says: 'This is that which the Tathāgata taught as a skillful means (upāya) according to the capacities of sentient beings.'"
The *Shiweilun* (Treatise on the Reality) states that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is without a second vehicle; its fundamental meaning explains that from the passage "If the Tathāgata...
onwards, it clarifies the Three Jewels as a single essence and concludes by entering into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the One Vehicle.

As the Sūtra says: "To speak of the One Vehicle is to speak of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); to speak of the Three Vehicles is to speak of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This is the meaning.
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra-vyākhyā-ṭippaṇī*, Fascicle Four;
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra-vyākhyā-ṭippaṇī*, Fascicle Five.
[Commentary] From "From the World-Honored One’s śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" onwards is the second section of the main exposition, which sets forth eight chapters.
To clarify the realm of the Vehicle (yāna), we say that goodness does not arise of itself but must originate from its objective conditions (viṣaya).
Therefore, both the conditioned and unconditioned Noble Truths are the realms of the One Vehicle.

Although this is the general principle, if one carefully examines the external texts that follow, they do not differ from what was explained above regarding the ultimate and the non-ultimate; thus, my personal reflections may also be set forth here.
Regarding the realization of the ultimate regarding the objective realm, it is said that both types of noble truths are conditions for cultivating goodness;
yet, while the followers of the Two Vehicles contemplate only one type of noble truth, the Tathāgata has fully realized both.

Since this is the case regarding the contemplated object, it is clear that what is realized by the former is not ultimate. Within this, it is divided into two parts: first, the first four chapters generally clarify the objective realm.

Regarding the second [section], the four subsequent chapters specifically clarify the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Because they collectively take both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) two kinds of noble truths (*āryasatya*) as their object without any exclusion—since all are the realm of the One Vehicle—they are termed "collective.
