Because they exclude the three truths and take only the unconditioned cessation (*nirodha*) as the ultimate, they are termed "specific. Within the first [of these], the collective clarification of the objective realm, there are four chapters, the first of which is as follows:
Chapter Two on the Boundless Noble Truths; Chapter Two on the Tathāgatagarbha; Chapter Four on the Dharmakāya; Chapter on the Hidden Meaning of Emptiness.

Regarding the first, the Chapter on the Boundless Noble Truths, it is divided into five sections. The first restates what has been attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles, namely, the four noble truths with effort (*saṃskṛta*).
[Commentary]: Second, the presentation of the eight chapters clarifying the "vehicle-object" (*yāna-viṣaya*) refers to the objects of contemplation within the preceding five chapters.

Regarding the phrase "Virtue does not arise of itself," etc., it means that while the preceding five chapters take the myriad virtues as the substance of the vehicle, this principle does not arise in isolation;
rather, it must arise in dependence upon an object. Therefore, the two noble truths constitute the vehicle-object. Why is this so?
The essence of the minds of sentient beings is fundamentally quiescent; this is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) which is non-constructive.
However, the two types of suffering and the two types of origination (*samudaya*) serve as the obscuring factors, while the two paths and the single cessation serve as that which is revealed.

To reveal this cessation, one must cultivate myriad virtues, beginning from the initial resolve and culminating in wondrous enlightenment—all of which ride upon these myriad virtues to reveal the single cessation. This is the purport of the subsequent seven chapters.
This merely serves to clarify once more that while the names given to the single cessation differ and its manifestations vary in prominence, the vehicle and its object have never been separated.
The true son is precisely the person who rides the vehicle; although divided into three sections, they are in fact a single dharma.
Since the person is the dharma, these words may be relied upon. As the text is already manifest, how could the principle remain hidden?
World-Honored One, when the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas first contemplate the Noble Truths, they sever all the stages of abiding with a single wisdom;
with that same single wisdom, they realize the merit of the four types of knowledge of abandonment, and they also skillfully understand the meaning of these four dharmas.
[Commentary]: "First, the initial contemplation of the Noble Truths" refers to the initial contemplation of the four noble truths as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

"By means of one wisdom" means by means of the wisdom regarding the conditioned truth. "Severing the various stages of abiding" (*bhūmi*) refers to severing the delusions of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa-kleśa*).

Regarding the "four knowledges of severance," this refers to the knowledge that severs the cause; because it attains the severance of delusion, it is called "knowledge of severance. Alternatively, it may also be understood through the four [knowledges].

To summarize the knots severed through the realization of the truths as the merit of the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*) and their realization means that one also realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merit.
Furthermore, to "well know the meaning of these four dharmas" refers to the meaning of the Four Truths; this clarifies that one has attained a small portion of insight (*vipaśyanā*).

[Commentary] First, the explanation of the Chapter on the Boundless Noble Truths. Regarding the contemplation of the Noble Truths, there is an extensive exposition of the Four Truths within the "Noble Practice of Great Wisdom" in the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. The sūtra states: "Furthermore, there is the noble practice, namely the Four Noble Truths:

suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), its cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). 'Suffering' is characterized by oppression; 'origin' is characterized by the capacity to produce and grow [it]; 'cessation'..."
That which is the mark of quiescence is the path; that which is the Great Vehicle is the mark. Furthermore, suffering has three marks:

the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned existence, and the suffering of change. Origination consists of the twenty-five states of existence. Cessation is the extinction of those twenty-five states of existence.

The path is the cultivation of morality, concentration, and wisdom. The scriptural passages on this are very extensive. Furthermore, son of good family, out-flowing phenomena have two kinds of marks. There are...

Regarding "causes with fruits" and "outflow-free dharmas," there are also two types: those that have both causes and fruits which are with-outflows, and those that have both causes and fruits which are outflow-free.

Causes with-outflows refer to the cause of origination (*samudaya*) and the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha*); causes that are outflow-free refer to the cause of the path (*mārga*) and the fruit of cessation (*nirodha*).

Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the Four Noble Truths, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Fetters refer to the nine fetters: attachment (*anunaya*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), grasping (*parāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), as well as stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*)."
[Commentary: Second, from "There is no supramundane... onwards, it clarifies that the supreme stage is not the domain of the two vehicles.
The World-Honored One’s supramundane, supreme wisdom consists of the four wisdoms gradually attained and the four conditions gradually attained;
the dharma of non-gradual attainment is the supramundane, supreme wisdom.

[Commentary] From the passage beginning with "The World-Honored One" onwards, the second section clarifies that [the two vehicles] do not possess the capacity for the supreme-of-the-supreme, as they lack supramundane supreme wisdom.

Previously, it was explained that the Vajra-mind of the Arhat represents the ultimate limit among those in training (*śaikṣa*), and thus the mind of the Arhat fruit was termed "supreme-of-the-supreme" within the mundane realm. Now, it is clarified that the two vehicles have not yet reached fulfillment.
Therefore, it is also not the "supreme of the supreme. Regarding the phrase "the four wisdoms gradually arrive," this explains "not the supreme of the supreme" by means of wisdom (*jñāna*):

because the essence of clear wisdom is not yet fulfilled, there is still something further to be reached. Furthermore, regarding "the four conditions gradually arrive," this explains "not the supreme of the supreme" by means of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*):

since there are still the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) Four Truths that ought to be reached, and one says that both wisdom and its objects are not yet complete, how could it be the "supreme of the supreme"? There is none.

Regarding the phrase "gradually reaching the Dharma": this refers to the supreme, unsurpassed wisdom of those who transcend the world, which cites the Buddha’s true, supreme, and unsurpassed state as proof that the wisdom of the Two Vehicles is not supreme.
Because the Buddha’s wisdom is perfectly consummate and has nowhere further to reach, it is said that there is no "gradual reaching."
[Commentary]: "The diamond-like mind of an Arhat" refers to the mind that has severed the afflictions (*kleśa*). "The four wisdoms" refers to the wisdom regarding the four truths;
"the objects" refers to the objects of the four truths.
[Sub-commentary]: The third section, from "From the World-Honored One’s diamond-like [samādhi]" onwards, clarifies that the wisdom of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-jñāna*) is likewise not [the case].
The Section on the Two Vehicles.
The World-Honored One’s diamond-like [samādhi] is the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*); the World-Honored One is not a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.

The wisdom regarding the first noble truth that has not yet severed the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is the wisdom of the ultimate truth; the World-Honored One, by means of the non-dual noble truth...
The wisdom that severs all stages of dwelling, O Bhagavān, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is not within the domain of any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha;
it is the inconceivable wisdom of emptiness that severs the treasury of all afflictions.

O Bhagavān, if the ultimate wisdom were to destroy the treasury of all afflictions, that would be called the wisdom of the primary truth, the wisdom of the first noble truth, and not the ultimate wisdom. It is directed toward [the ultimate].
The wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary] From the passage beginning with "From the World-Honored One" onwards, the third section clarifies that the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*) is not within their scope.

Within this, there are six phrases organized into three pairs. The first pair restates the distinction between what is and is not [the case] to clarify that the wisdom of the ultimate truth belongs to the Buddha.

The second section, from "Not [the path] of the two vehicles" down to "By means of the World-Honored One’s wisdom of the non-dual noble truths," provides a dual explanation of what is not and what is;
first explaining what is not, and subsequently explaining what is. The third section, from "If one destroys all... down to the end, provides a dual conclusion regarding what is not and what is;

first concluding what is not, and subsequently concluding what is. That "all can be seen" is illustrated by the analogy of the diamond (*vajra*); it refers to the Buddha’s severing of all [afflictions].
The "stages of abiding" (zhùdì) refers to the four stages of abiding. [Commentary]:

That which possesses the wisdom of the two non-dual Noble Truths is simply the aforementioned prior wisdom. When one passes through the wisdom of inconceivable emptiness, it is called "enlightened" (zhèngjué) because it is nameless;
it is "void and quiescent" (xūjì). Yet, being able to illumine emptiness—illumining emptiness means it is not empty, and being quiescent means... [it is not merely void].
"Neither existent nor empty; 'neither existent' refers to the inconceivable wisdom of emptiness.
[Commentary] The fourth section, from "From the Holy Meaning of the World-Honored One" onwards, clarifies that this holy meaning is also not within the domain of the Two Vehicles.
The Noble Meaning, O World-Honored One, does not refer to all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
rather, they are called "Noble" because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have accomplished limited merit and Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have accomplished only a small portion of merit.
[Commentary]: From the passage "The holy meaning of the World-Honored One" onwards, it clarifies that the holy meaning is not within their scope; this consists of two parts:
first, directly clarifying that it is not within their scope; second, citing the finite and the limited as an explanation, which can be seen [in the text].
[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of "sage" (*ārya*) in the sutra, it does not apply to all śrāvakas and the like;

indeed, one who is called a sage is subtle, profound, and far-reaching, such that they cannot be measured or exhausted. Since the wisdom of those of the two vehicles does not fathom the minute and their virtues do not reach the pinnacle of subtlety, how could they fulfill the meaning of a Great Sage?
[Commentary: The fifth section, from "derived from the Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*) onwards, clarifies that these truths are not the domain of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
As for the "Noble Truths," they are neither the truths of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, nor are they the merit of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
World-Honored One, these truths were first realized by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he subsequently [taught them] to the world, which is like a storehouse of ignorance.
Because it reveals, manifests, and expounds [the truth], it is called the "Noble Truth" (*āryasatya*).

[Commentary: From the phrase "from the Noble Truths" onwards, the fifth section clarifies that [the truths] are not their own portion; this consists of two parts: first, directly clarifying that they are not their own portion;
second, clarifying that while these are the Tathāgata’s truths, they are not [inherently] truths—namely, that suffering and its origin are not their own portion.

That even the truths (*satya*) are not [exclusive] virtues means that cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are not [exclusively] their truths. Second, it clarifies that these are the Tathāgata’s truths;
since "truth" (*satya*) has the meaning of being verified and real, it is said that these belong to the Buddha and are not the portion of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Furthermore, this applies equally to the truth of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-satya*). If so, why would the truth of action (*abhisaṃskāra-satya*) not also be their portion? Even though it is a truth of action, it is...
Because the Tathāgata has profoundly penetrated this, it is said that this is not their domain. Why?

That which is called the Two Vehicles observing the conditioned Four Noble Truths to sever the delusions of the three realms is merely a provisional means; when discussed according to ultimate reality, the actual observation of the conditioned Four Noble Truths to sever the delusions of the three realms occurs precisely from the seventh stage upward.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "suffering and its origin are not their truths" and so forth: because the two vehicles cannot discern and realize the two kinds of suffering and origin as they truly are, these are not their truths;

the same applies to the path and cessation. Although the two vehicles do attain the conditioned truths (*saṃskṛta-satya*), they do not penetrate them as deeply as the Tathāgata does, for the two kinds of suffering and origin are precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*. As the subsequent passage states: "Inversion is itself the truth."

This is indeed so. When the Sūtra speaks of the "egg-store of ignorance" (*avidyā-aṇḍakośa*) and so forth, it refers to what is called the "world" (*loka*), namely the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
The "egg-store of ignorance" is the nesting place and dwelling of the mind. Those sentient beings, having taken ignorance as the abode of their minds, dwell in darkness without understanding;
they sleep forever in the long night, flowing against the current and failing to reach the ford.
Were it not for the Great Sage’s manifestation of spiritual power, how could one awaken oneself?
How else could he guide the masses of deluded commoners, open up divine merit as a level path, and illuminate with the radiance of wisdom like a bright torch? Who else could have brought this about?

*Kǎo* (the first character is pronounced *kǔ jiǎo*; the second is *kǔ hóu*): "egg. When a bird is inside its egg, it must wait for its mother’s warmth; this is called an *lǎn*. (*Jiàn* is pronounced *xīn jiā*).
Regarding the *Yùnshuō* (Discourse on Rhymes), according to this principle, the character [穀-禾+卵] (*luǎn*) should be used to signify that it encompasses both emotion and consciousness. [Commentary]:
From the section "Following the Noble Truths" onwards is the second chapter, the Chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha. This serves as a praise for the profound depth of the Eight Noble Truths.

While it has already been directly clarified above that the two kinds of Noble Truths are exclusively the Tathāgata and do not reside within the Two Vehicles, this point has not yet been explicitly explained.
This is precisely why its profundity is such; therefore, the *tathāgatagarbha* is cited here to praise the two kinds of noble truths.
Today, these eight truths are taught as being within the *tathāgatagarbha*. Since the *garbha* itself is profound, how could the eight noble truths not be profound?
Thus it is said that the two kinds of noble truths exist only in the *Tathāgata* and not in the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Within this context:
The opening is divided into five sections: first, directly citing the Tathāgatagarbha to praise the profound depth of the Eight Noble Truths;
second, from "If [one considers] the immeasurable... onwards, citing the Tathāgatagarbha as identical to the Dharmakāya to exhort faith in the Eight Noble Truths;
third, from "Thus difficult to know and difficult to understand... onwards, extensively clarifying the names, essence, and characteristics of the Eight Noble Truths.
Fourth, from "Thus, regarding these unconditioned Four Noble Truths" onwards, it concludes that the unconditioned Noble Truths exist only in the Buddha.
Fifth, from "World-Honored One, because it is not a dharma that can be destroyed, it is called the cessation of suffering" onwards, it analyzes the two truths of cessation.
Regarding the first [section], citing the *tathāgatagarbha* to praise the profound depth of the Eight Noble Truths also has three parts.
First, it directly extols the profoundness [of the Noble Truths]:

the Noble Truths are said to have a profound meaning that is subtle and difficult to know; they are not the domain of discursive thought but are known by the wise, and cannot be believed by anyone in the entire world.
[Commentary] The second chapter, "The Tathāgatagarbha. Regarding the phrase "subtle and difficult to know" and so forth:

it is called "subtle" (*miao*) because it is nameless; it is called "void yet not non-existent. It is called "fine" (*xi*) because it is real yet not existent. It is called "profound" (*shen*) because its depths cannot be measured.
Only those who have attained the wisdom of *bodhi* can know it; it is that which is known by the wise.
[Commentary] Second, from "Why is this? onwards, there is the explanation of the praise.
Why is this? This teaching of the profound Tathāgatagarbha—the Tathāgatagarbha being the realm of the Tathāgata—is not something known by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
[Commentary: This statement regarding the "profound Tathāgatagarbha" refers to the teaching of the Tathāgatagarbha within the context of the Eight Truths (aṣṭasatya).
From the third section, beginning with "From the locus of the Tathāgatagarbha," onwards, it serves as a concluding eulogy.
In the context of the *tathāgatagarbha*, the meaning of the Noble Truths is taught; because the *tathāgatagarbha* is profound,
the Noble Truths are also said to be profound, subtle, difficult to know, beyond the sphere of discursive thought, known only by the wise,
and something that the entire world cannot believe.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the meaning of the Noble Truths, it clarifies that these eight truths are taught based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Because the locus of the *tathāgatagarbha* is profoundly deep, it is said that the Noble Truths are likewise profound. The truth of cessation without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-nirodhasatya*) is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*, and thus it is profoundly deep.
The two truths of suffering and the two truths of origination can obscure this *garbha*, whereas the two paths and the one truth of cessation can reveal it.
This treasury is thus difficult to clarify in its hidden and manifest aspects; for this reason, it is also profoundly deep. [Commentary:
From the passage "If, regarding the immeasurable... onwards is the second section, which cites the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *dharmakāya* to exhort faith.
Those who hear that the Noble Truths are profoundly deep and constitute the exclusive domain of the Buddha might then say: "If that is so, then [it must be that] they are not [the truth]..."
Since there is nothing that comes forth to which one could respond, for whom then should this Truth be taught? Therefore, by citing this Tathāgatagarbha and Dharmakāya, he exhorts faith, saying:
"The unconditioned Truth of Cessation is the Tathāgatagarbha; when this Garbha is manifested, it is the Dharmakāya.
If one can have faith in this Tathāgatagarbha and Dharmakāya, then one can have faith in these Eight Truths.
This is for the purpose of encouraging faith. Furthermore, it is heard that the Tathāgatagarbha is profoundly deep and not to be measured by consciousness;

thus, one might conclude that this Tathāgatagarbha has already transcended the burdens of affliction and is inherently pure by itself. Therefore, it is known that it is not the domain of consciousness.
For this reason, it is also clarified that this Tathāgatagarbha is hidden within the afflictions and does not emerge from them.
If one can be free from doubt regarding the hidden meaning, one will likewise be free from doubt regarding the manifest Dharma-body.

If one can believe in this principle of the hidden and the manifest, one will then be able to believe in the Eight Truths. Previously, the principle was not understood because one was within delusion;
furthermore, among the two types of Noble Truths, only one kind of Noble Truth was clarified, all of which were merely expedient teachings. Within these...
There are also two [aspects of] supreme clear faith: first, faith in the treasury [of the Dharma-body].

If one has no doubt regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, which is enveloped by immeasurable stores of afflictions, then one will likewise have no doubt regarding the Dharmakāya that emerges from those immeasurable stores of afflictions.

[Commentary] Second, from the passage "Regarding the teaching of the Tathāgatagarbha" onwards, the text correctly clarifies that those who can believe in the Tathāgatagarbha and the Dharmakāya should likewise believe in the Eight Truths.
This concerns the teaching of the Tathāgatagarbha, the inconceivable Buddha-realm of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, and the provisional teaching of the mind.
Those who have attained certainty thus explain the meaning of the two noble truths through faith and understanding.

[Commentary: Since the "Treasury" (*pitaka*) is by nature concealed, it is appropriate to raise questions regarding it; therefore, it is transmitted to encourage one toward the Dharma-body at the time of manifestation.
[Commentary]: The Sūtra states that for those "enveloped by immeasurable stores of afflictions," there is no such name [as "sentient being"].

This is because although people harbor superior aspirations, their minds are dull and thus they do not understand; yet, even if they have not yet understood, one can examine that it is not non-existent.
Since it has not been non-existent from the beginning, it must certainly exist at the end. Therefore, it says: "If one is enveloped by immeasurable afflictions, there is no doubt."
Such a person will likewise have no doubt regarding the Dharma-body from which the immeasurable storehouse of afflictions has emerged;

this is the explanation of faith as the Noble Truth of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-āryasatya*), while the explanation of the conditioned Noble Truth (*saṃskṛta-āryasatya*) is taught as the skillful means (*upāya*).
[Commentary] From the section "Thus difficult to know" onwards is the third part, which sets forth the names, entities, and characteristics of the eight truths.
Previously, although the two kinds of noble truths were directly mentioned, their names, entities, and characteristics had not yet been revealed; therefore, they are explained here in detail.
This section is further divided into eight parts, the first of which is the general proclamation of the two kinds of noble truths.
"That which is thus difficult to know and difficult to understand" refers to the teaching on the meaning of the two noble truths.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage in the sutra, "that which is thus difficult to know and difficult to understand," the *Wuming* (無名) states that this collectively summarizes both the beginning and the end.
Initially, the teaching of the "truths as being produced" (*zuo-di*) is called the ultimate; subsequently, the teaching of non-existence...

The act [of cultivation] is also called "ultimate" (niṣṭhā); the names are the same, yet the realities are different. Who can know this? The meaning is distant while the words are near; who can understand it?
One who is able to know and understand must infer the distant from the near and seek the cause by observing the fruit.
Therefore, it was said above: "If one can thoroughly understand that which is entangled as being Buddha-nature, then that is the Dharmakāya already emerged."
[Commentary]:
Second, from the passage "What are the two noble truths? onwards, the names of the two noble truths are listed.
As for the meaning of what is called the two noble truths, it refers to the meaning of the conditioned noble truth and the meaning of the unconditioned noble truth.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the listing of the names of the Noble Truths: the phrase "How can that which is nameless... and so forth intends to clarify the names in order to distinguish the reality.
[Sub-commentary] Third, the explanation of the assembly as being conditioned and finite.
"To speak of the meaning of the noble truths as being 'made' is to speak of the four noble truths as having a limited measure.
[Commentary] These two phrases refer to speaking of the meaning of the noble truths as being "made," which implies that the four noble truths have a limited measure.
The fourth section, from "Why is this so? onwards, explains the reason why [the Buddha] is called "one who acts" and "one who has limits.
Why is this? Because he does not know all suffering, abandon all origins, realize all cessations, and cultivate all paths through the power of another.

[Commentary: Regarding the first three levels, they can be understood; however, regarding the fourth, there is a doubt concerning its definition, asking: "Why is it called 'with effort' (*sābhisamskāra*) and 'limited' (*pramāṇa*)?
The explanation states: "Not by means of another" refers to those who cannot know all suffering through another—that is, the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) and those on the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
It means that these others are unable to know all the suffering, origin, cessation, and path within and without the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Therefore, that person is said to have activity and limitation; likewise, the truths they illuminate are also said to have activity and limitation.

[Commentary]: "Not because of another can one know all suffering and so forth" means that those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) up to the seventh stage must necessarily rely on the teachings of others.

Those who rely on the teachings of others know only that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and limited (*pramita*); they do not know that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and immeasurable (*apramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that "this cannot be known by those who rely on others. "All" in the phrase "all suffering and so forth" refers precisely to the unconditioned and the immeasurable.
Consequently, the person who relies on others to know this is called one who possesses the conditioned and the limited. Since the person...

That which is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to the person; when one designates the Dharma by means of the person, the Truths (*satya*) illuminated thereby are also termed "conditioned," and so forth.

[Commentary: The fifth section, from "Therefore, the World-Honored One" onwards, cites two types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and two types of nirvāṇa to explain that there are two types of Noble Truths (*āryasatya*).
Therefore, the World-Honored One has conditioned birth-and-death and unconditioned birth-and-death; likewise, there are nirvana with remainder and nirvana without remainder.
[Commentary] The fifth section cites two types of birth-and-death and nirvana as an explanation for the phrase "therefore the World-Honored One has conditioned birth-and-death."
Since the objects of "death as non-conditioned birth-and-death" (amṛta-saṃsāra) necessarily follow from persons, there must be a distinction between conditioned and unconditioned action;
therefore, birth-and-death also follows from persons, resulting in both conditioned and unconditioned birth-and-death.

It is said that for those of the Two Vehicles and the seven stages, it is called "birth-and-death of persons" (*pudgala-saṃsāra*), which is conditioned birth-and-death known to ordinary persons; from the eighth stage upward...

That which is called "unconditioned" refers to the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) of unconditioned persons, because it is what unconditioned persons illuminate; thus it is called conditioned birth-and-death and unconditioned birth-and-death.
Conditioned birth-and-death is precisely the finite suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), while unconditioned birth-and-death is precisely the infinite suffering and its origin.
Those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are also able to illuminate segmentary birth-and-death (*prābandhika-jāti-maraṇa*). However...
Because the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) has not yet illuminated the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmanī-bhava*), it is distinguished as a cause.

Nirvāṇa is likewise categorized as *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder); since both its object and the cycle of birth and death are named after the person, Nirvāṇa is also named after the person who realizes it, resulting in these two types:
with remainder and without remainder. The seventh stage of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is termed "with remainder."
The nirvana realized by other persons is called "nirvana with remainder," while that realized by the Tathāgata— the person who has no remainder—
is called "nirvana without remainder. Nirvana with remainder comprises both the conditioned cessation and the path,
whereas nirvana without remainder comprises both the unconditioned cessation and the path.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "from the eighth stage upward, one can also illumine the birth-and-death of limited segments (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) and so forth," this is because those below the seventh stage cannot yet illumine the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa*), and are thus termed "those with outflows" (*sāsrava-pudgala*);
whereas from the eighth stage upward, one can illumine the birth-and-death of transformation and is thus termed "those without outflows" (*anāsrava-pudgala*).
This distinction is made for the sake of clarity. In reality, however, from the eighth stage onward, one illumines both types of death simultaneously.
[Commentary] Sixth, from the passage "explaining the meaning of the noble truth of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-āryasatya*) onwards, the immeasurable nature of the unconditioned is explained.
"Explaining the meaning of the noble truth of the unconditioned" means explaining the meaning of the four noble truths as being immeasurable.
[Commentary]: The section explaining the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Noble Truths is the sixth, which reconciles the unconditioned with the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) Noble Truths.
The seventh section, beginning from "For what reason," explains the grounds for naming them the unconditioned and the immeasurable.

Why is this? Because, by means of one’s own power, one is able to know all suffering that arises from sensation (*vedanā*), to sever all accumulation of sensation, to realize the cessation of all sensation, and to cultivate the path to the cessation of all sensation.
[Commentary: From "Why is this? onwards, the reason for naming it "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is explained. A doubt may arise as to why it is so named.

Is it called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and "immeasurable"? It is because those who are able to know all things through their own power—referring to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward who have entered the stream of the Dharma and self-know in every thought-moment—are also so named based on others; hence it is called "unconditioned" and "immeasurable.
However, as for attaining self-knowledge regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), this is termed "reverent faith" (*adhimukti*) and does not refer to direct, manifest knowledge.
[Commentary]: To be able to know all sensations and so forth by means of one’s own power is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*);
because it arises from within to exhaustively investigate conditions and illuminate them to their limit, it is termed "self-power. When self-power gives rise to wisdom, one attains the immeasurable;
therefore, when the Tathāgata illuminates that unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) with immeasurable wondrous wisdom, there is no truth that is not [fully realized].
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is all-pervasive; "feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the stream of the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Generally, whatever cognition encounters pain or itching is termed "feeling.
[Commentary] The eighth section, from "In this way" (*evam*) onwards, summarizes the two kinds of noble truths.
"Thus, regarding these eight noble truths, the Tathāgata has taught four noble truths.
[Commentary] From "Thus" onwards is the eighth section, which provides a summary. Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata taught four truths among these eight truths:
in the past, for the sake of those of the two vehicles at the seventh stage, the Tathāgata spoke only of the four truths involving conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*).
The *Dì* (諦) further states: "Although there are eight truths within and without the three realms, the Tathāgata has combined them into four truths.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata has combined them into four truths": Wuming says that because they are distinguished as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are eight;
yet when one examines the names to determine the reality, there are only four—namely, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

[Commentary]: Now, these two kinds of Noble Truths together comprise ten names: those within the three realms are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), limited (*parimita*), finite (*saparyanta*), conditioned, and with remainder;
those outside the three realms are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), infinite (*ananta*), unconditioned, and without remainder.
[Commentary]: Regarding the fact that these two types of Noble Truths together comprise ten names, all of these are present within the text of this sutra and can be seen through careful examination.
[Sub-commentary]: Generally, these ten names may be designated according to their essential nature; however, in this specific context, they are applied solely from the perspective of the person.

Regarding the designations "five existences" (*pañca-bhava*) and "five non-existences" (*pañca-abhava*): the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) apply the term "five existences" up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), while from the eighth stage upward, all are termed "five non-existences.

As for why the two vehicles apply the term "five existences" up to the seventh stage, it is because they have not yet completed their external activities within the triple world (*tridhātu*) and still have further tasks to perform.
As for why those from the eighth stage upward are termed "five non-existences," it is because their cultivation has reached its ultimate limit.

There is nothing newly created; this can be inferred from the terminology used. From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, all [stages] likewise illumine matters within the triple world (*tridhātu*), yet they are distinguished by the fact that the seventh stage does not illumine matters outside the triple world. Regarding the designation based on their essential nature:

the two truths of accumulation (*saṃudaya*) and the path (*mārga*) within the triple world act as the causes that evoke the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and cessation (*nirodha*). These two truths of suffering and cessation—[are the result].
It is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) because it arises from a productive cause (*kāraka-hetu*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the two truths of origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*) acting as causes for themselves: the truth of origin is the cause that produces the fruit of suffering, while the truth of the path is the cause that produces the fruit of cessation (*nirodha*).

As for "origin," it refers to the arising of craving and views through the mutual encounter of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*); as for "suffering," it refers to birth from the conditions of ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, parents, and so forth.
Because they exist within consciousness and so forth, one knows that both truths arise from causes of production.
[Commentary] Furthermore, these Four Truths have not yet exhausted their source; therefore, they are called "with remainder," "limited," and "measurable.
The three truths of Suffering, Accumulation, and the Path are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) because they arise and perish by their own nature. The single Truth of Cessation arises from the conditioned.

Because they are attained through causes, they are also designated as "causes. Although the two truths of the origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*) outside the three realms possess the sense of "activity" (*abhisamskāra*), their functional operation is subtle and does not manifest as it does within the realms; therefore, they receive the name "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Why is this?

Because the preceding moment serves as the cause and the succeeding moment as the fruit, and since each moment is newly renewed, the characteristic of activity is difficult to perceive. This applies to the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Furthermore, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) because it is attained through the cause of non-action. Regarding the original meaning of "unconditioned":

the two truths of suffering and cessation cannot themselves act as causes to produce an effect; therefore, they are termed "unconditioned. If that were so, then the two truths of suffering and cessation within the triple world would also have to be unconditioned;

however, this is not necessary. Since the principle of the Four Truths is exhaustive and their origin has been thoroughly investigated, they are said to be "non-existent" [in the sense of being unconditioned].

The measure is without remainder, boundless, and singular; because the essence of the one Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is neither arising nor ceasing, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
The other three truths all derive their names from the Truth of Cessation.
[Commentary] From the section beginning with "Thus, the four noble truths of non-action" onwards, this is the fourth chapter, which concludes the eight noble truths.
Since the names and essences of the eight truths have been fully explained, it is now appropriate to clarify those who exhaustively realize this principle;

therefore, the text further concludes by showing that the Tathāgata alone has reached the ultimate realization of this principle. Within this, there are four sections, the first of which clarifies that only the Buddha has reached the ultimate realization.

"In this way, the meaning of the four noble truths as being 'without volitional effort' (anabhisaṃskāra) is realized only by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has reached the ultimate consummation.
[Commentary] The second section, from "not an arhat" onwards, clarifies that [this realization] is not the ultimate goal of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
"It is not the case that for Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, their task is ultimately accomplished.
[Commentary] Third, from "Why is this? onwards, the text explains why the two vehicles are not ultimate. Why is this?
Because Nirvana is not attained through inferior, middling, or superior dharmas.
[Commentary: "Neither inferior, middling, nor superior" means that the inferior refers to the Śrāvakas, the middling to the Pratyekabuddhas, and the superior to those of the seven stages;

this clarifies that these three types of persons do not attain ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, it is said that "superior" refers to the Buddha, meaning that none of the three types of persons attain it, but only the Buddha alone does.
The fourth section, from "For what reason? onwards, explains [the reason] why [only the Buddha attains it].
The Buddha has reached the ultimate.
Why? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has reached the ultimate regarding the meaning and matter of the four noble truths of non-action;
for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know all future suffering and have severed all afflictions.

[He] realizes the cessation of all that is comprised by afflictions, the cessation of all accumulations, and the realization of the extinction of suffering regarding all mind-born bodies and aggregates.
[Commentary: The fourth section explains the doubt concerning the Buddha’s ultimate perfection, asking: "Why is it that only the Buddha is ultimately perfected? Because he knows all."

Regarding future suffering, although the Buddha has already transcended it, this statement is made from the perspective of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), who do not yet know future suffering;

therefore, it is said that their realization of suchness is not ultimate. Furthermore, one may understand that while all sentient beings sever future suffering and all afflictions (*kleśa*), these refer to the root afflictions as the fundamental basis and the derivative afflictions as the branches, with karma and afflictions constituting their essence.

Therefore, it is said: "That which is grasped—the cessation of all mind-born aggregates (*manomaya-skandha*) and the realization of the extinction of all suffering"—this refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), because it pervades both the internal and external realms of the three worlds; hence it is called "all. However, this does not manifest the Path (*mārga*). Furthermore, it is said:
"That which is grasped" clarifies that untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is itself grasped by afflictions (*kleśa*); "all accumulations" (*sarva-samudaya*) is the general [term].

The gathering of prior karma and afflictions as the cause (*samudaya*) refers to the cessation of all mind-born aggregates (*manomaya-skandha*). This is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is the realization of the extinction of all suffering.

The path that brings about this realization is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). According to one interpretation, that which is "appropriated" refers to the four stages of dwelling (*catur-vāsabhūmi*).
[Commentary]: It is said that those of the Two Vehicles who do not yet know future suffering and so forth lack the name "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*).
For the Two Vehicles, this [ignorance] constitutes future suffering; if they were able to know this suffering, there would be no suffering. Yet they do not know it.

If they were to extinguish the aggregates (*skandhas*) of the mind-made body, there would be no suffering; yet they do not extinguish them. One who can realize this extinction is one for whom the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) manifests.
This is what is called the *dharmakāya*.
[Commentary: From the passage beginning with "World-Honored One" onwards, this is the fifth section analyzing the two types of cessation (*nirodha*).

Although the remaining six truths (*satya*) differ in their depth and shallowness, they are all existent phenomena (*dharma*), and their principles can naturally be distinguished; however, it is difficult to distinguish between these two truths of cessation.

The reason for this analytical discrimination is stated as follows: "The cessation of the past is non-existence; the cessation of the present is wondrous existence. Although the names of these cessations are the same, that which they refer to differs.
Within this, there are two points, the first of which clarifies that the cessation of the past is not ultimate truth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the remaining six truths have differences of depth and shallowness," etc.: suffering differs between the *paricchinna-vipariṇāma* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma-vaśitā* (transformative);

accumulation differs between the four abodes (*catur-vāsana*) and ignorance (*avidyā*); and the path is divided into the conditioned (*kṛta*) and the unconditioned (*akṛta*). Thus, it is said there is a distinction of depth and shallowness.
These six are all phenomena (*dharma*), whereas the two truths of cessation differ in what they eliminate; yet they share the common name "cessation" (*nirodha*). Therefore...
One should know its characteristics: suffering ceases, existence returns to non-existence, and now the essence of cessation contains ten thousand virtues;
therefore, it is said that what they refer to differs. Because the World-Honored One does not destroy phenomena, it is called the cessation of suffering.
[Commentary]: "Not a destroyer of dharmas" means that one severs the afflictions (*kleśa*), clarifying that true cessation does not consist in the extinction of the afflictions themselves.
The second section, from the words "the cessation of suffering" (*duḥkhanirodha*) onwards, clarifies that this present cessation is existent.

That which is called the extinction of suffering is named beginningless, uncreated, unarisen, inexhaustible, free from exhaustion, eternally abiding, naturally pure, and free from the storehouse of all afflictions.
[Commentary] "Named beginningless, uncreated, and unarisen" clarifies that it is without birth and without exhaustion; "free from exhaustion, eternally abiding" [clarifies its permanence].
This clarity is unceasing; this clarity is not a phenomenon belonging to the three periods of time. Its self-nature is pure and free from the storehouse of all afflictions (*kleśa-kośa*).
Although it is not something destroyed, it is naturally free from afflictions. Regarding this beginninglessness of clarity, there are two interpretations:

first, it is said to be beginningless because this Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is primordially existent; second, it is said that from the perspective of the fruit, the fruit itself is not [newly produced].
Because it pertains to the dharmas of the three periods of time, it is said to be "without beginning.

[The Sub-commentary] states: Regarding "without beginning" and "without creation," the *Wuming* (Treatise on Non-Name) says: "Birth must have a beginning; a beginning implies creation; because of creation, there is arising.
Now, since these three are absent, one should know that there is no birth. Furthermore, that which has an end is an end because it was not created.

The extinction of these three phrases clarifies that there is no extinction. Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus, that which is without arising or ceasing is called true quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).
Taking this as extinction, what phenomenon could there be to destroy? This clarifies that one who understands the extinction of phenomena has already attained the ability to empty them;
therefore, it is called extinction. Furthermore, because one accomplishes the purity of mind, it is extinction. As for the defilements of the mind, they arise from...
This is because they have lost the principle and reversed their course; it is by relying on the realization of the fundamental source that one can discern the nature of dharmas.
If one considers the spontaneous cessation of the nature of dharmas to be the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), then the intrinsically pure mind will be liberated from afflictions.
That which is liberated from afflictions is also called "cessation," yet it is not the cessation of dharmas as such. The Dharma-body is not encompassed by the three periods of time. Just as...
"Just as empty space is not of the three periods of time," this meaning is explained at length in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
[Commentary] From the section beginning with "The World-Honored One surpasses the sands of the Ganges" onwards, this is the third chapter, titled "The Dharma-body Chapter.
Regarding the purpose for the introduction of this chapter: having heard the preceding second chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha, which exhorted faith in the Eight Noble Truths, sentient beings...
If one can have faith in the Tathāgatagarbha, one is thereby able to have faith in the Dharmakāya; by having faith in these two, one is also able to have faith in the Eight Noble Truths.
Furthermore, because it is said that this Tathāgatagarbha and the Dharmakāya must be distinct entities, it is stated that "having faith in the Garbha enables one to have faith in the Dharmakāya.
If they were of one essence, why would they be mentioned separately? Therefore, what is clarified here is their state of being hidden.
The Tathāgatagarbha manifests as the Dharmakāya; though their modes of manifestation and concealment differ, they are of one and the same essence, with no distinct entities.
Within this, there is further a threefold division. First, it clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha and the Dharmakāya are of one and the same essence.
“World-Honored One, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which is accomplished through the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas that exceed the sands of the Ganges—
dharmas that are inseparable, non-detached, and non-different— is called the ‘Tathāgata-garbha’ when it is not separated from the storehouse of afflictions.”

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is accomplished through the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, which exceed the sands of the Ganges and are neither separate from nor detached from [the afflictions], and are not different [from them]:
this refers to the *tathāgatagarbha* as the Dharmakāya itself. "Exceeding the sands of the Ganges" clarifies that the afflictions exceed the sands of the Ganges;
thus, the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, when not separated from the afflictions, is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This refers to the Dharmakāya, which is the Tathāgatagarbha.
[Commentary] Chapter Three: The Dharmakāya. First, clarifying that the Tathāgatagarbha and the Dharmakāya are of one essence:
when it is nameless, it is called the Dharmakāya; when not separated from the store of afflictions (*kleśakośa*), it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; and when perfected, it is called...
Because it is the Dharma-body, one knows the single principle of ultimate reality; yet, from beginning to end, there are two conventional designations, for "afflictions" (kleśa) serve as its name.
[Commentary] Second, citing wisdom to demonstrate the single essence.
The World-Honored One’s Tathāgatagarbha-wisdom is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of emptiness.
[Commentary] "The Tathāgata’s Tathāgatagarbha-wisdom is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of emptiness" is the second instance of citing wisdom to prove that the two bodies are one essence.
Since wisdom is precisely one object, how could there be two? Because they have not yet abandoned afflictions, the *garbha* (womb/store) is considered non-empty; once [afflictions] are abandoned...
Because the Dharma-body is empty due to afflictions, the treasury is called the Tathāgata-garbha. When wisdom illuminates the Dharma-body, it is the emptiness-wisdom of the Tathāgata;
when wisdom illuminates the treasury, it is the illumination of the Dharma-body. This wisdom that illuminates is ultimately a single essence of wisdom;
this wisdom is itself the single object of illumination. How could they be of different essences?
[Commentary]: Second, regarding the presentation of wisdom as the realization of the single essence:
"Tathāgatagarbha-wisdom" refers to the beginning, while "Tathāgata-emptiness-wisdom" refers to the end. Although the beginning and end differ, the nature of wisdom is non-dual.
[Commentary: The third section clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is not the domain of the two vehicles.
The World-Honored One states: "The Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally unseen and fundamentally unattained by all Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and even Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattvas."
[Commentary] Third, it clarifies that the *tathāgatagarbha* is not the domain of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

This explains that the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* is profound, mysterious, and subtle, such that it is not cognized by those of the two vehicles; furthermore, because it was not taught to them in the past, they have never seen its fundamental nature nor attained its fundamental meaning.
The "Chapter on the *Tathāgatagarbha*" and the "Chapter on the *Dharmakāya*" contain no separate texts [regarding this], but are merely appended here for clarification.
Having already demonstrated that no separate exposition is required, it is further stated: "From 'transcending the sands of the Ganges' onwards, the meaning of the ninth emptiness is concealed.
This refers to the reality of the objective realm (*ālambana-viṣaya*), which was previously obscured by the meaning of emptiness and thus not revealed.
From "World-Honored One, there are two kinds of Tathāgata-garbha-emptiness-wisdom" onwards, this section provides a general explanation.
The fourth section within the "Objects of Cognition" (viṣaya) is titled "The Chapter on the Obscuration of the Meaning of Emptiness. Regarding the intent behind this chapter:

when sentient beings heard the preceding third chapter on the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which states that [the Tathāgatagarbha] is hidden as the Tathāgata-garbha and manifest as the Dharma-body—thereby being of one essence—and further that wisdom realizes this single essence, they immediately gave rise to doubt: "Since the principle is thus, for what reason was it not explained in the past? Or...

Is it because this wisdom was not comparable [to its present state] in the past that it is only now attained? Therefore, the commentary explains: the wisdom that illuminates reality has always existed from the beginning;
however, because the past was not the proper time for it, it was not taught. It remained obscured by suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so forth, and thus was not manifest.
Within this, there are two points: first, the wisdom of correct enlightenment is eternally present from the beginning.

There is a second [point]; from this point downward, it is explained that because it is not the proper time [for the first], one does not rely on the first, but directly explains that the clear wisdom has three aspects.
First, regarding the clear wisdom itself, there are three. First, there is the clear wisdom itself.
The World-Honored One possesses two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha-śūnyatā-jñāna*.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that there are two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha-śūnyatā-jñāna*, this refers to the wisdom of the *tathāgatagarbha* and the wisdom of the *dharmakāya*.
It would suffice simply to say "two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha-jñāna*"; why then is it called "wisdom of emptiness"? It is because the object (*ālambana*) is empty.
Since non-empty wisdom (*aśūnyajñāna*) is identical to the single wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyajñāna*), the term "wisdom of emptiness" is used to indicate the presence [of that which is not empty].
[The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "In the fourth chapter on the 'Concealment of the Meaning of Emptiness,' it says directly that the two kinds of Tathāgata-garbha wisdom are also sufficient," etc.
This refers to what is called "the wisdom of the ultimate truth" (*paramārthajñāna*), which severs all afflictions and stores; when one speaks of "emptiness," it corresponds to this.

The wisdom of the *tathāgatagarbha* should properly be called "non-empty," yet it is called "empty" to clarify that although it exists within the midst of afflictions (*kleśa*), its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is pure and is not defiled by them; for this reason, it is also called "empty.
What was previously referred to as the "wisdom of the *tathāgatagarbha*" is precisely this "emptiness-wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is what is meant by the name "*tathāgatagarbha*" arising.

The designation "emptiness-wisdom" (śūnyatā-jñāna) first emerged from the perspective of the ultimate; now, by speaking of the two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha, we verify the ultimate through the beginning.

These two kinds of emptiness-wisdom verify the beginning through the ultimate. Since the garbha is revealed by means of the ultimate, and the cause is manifested by means of the beginning, is this not a case of reaching a comprehensive realization?
When "emptiness-wisdom" is mentioned, it refers to the two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha emptiness-wisdom.
Wuming says: "Now it is said that there are two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha*.
Thus, the *dharmakāya* is also called *tathāgatagarbha*, because it clarifies for the first time that the wondrous cause emerges from the true fruit; hence it is called a 'garbha.

Finally, it clarifies that the true fruit gives rise to the *nirmāṇakāya*, which is also called a 'garbha. Therefore, the *Siddhārthasūtra* states: 'The body of the Tathāgata is also the *dharmakāya*...'"
"Treasury" (*garbha*) refers to the Treasury of Immeasurable Light; if it is this Treasury of Light, it is also the treasury of the Dharmakāya.
Although the name "treasury" is the same, that which is contained within each differs, and thus there are two kinds. Since there are two kinds of treasuries, wisdom is likewise so;
therefore, the treasury is explained in order to clarify wisdom. One who possesses the full text should say as follows:
There are two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha and two kinds of wisdom regarding emptiness; now, by means of one, those two are distinguished.
"One" clarifies that their essence is identical.

[Commentary: Second, citing the three [aspects]: if one considers the wisdom that exists with respect to the object of emptiness, the World-Honored One stated that the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is separate from, liberated from, or distinct from all stores of afflictions.
[Commentary] Third, by citing the fourfold non-emptiness, it is shown that wisdom exists with respect to the object of non-emptiness:

"The World-Honored One’s non-empty Tathāgatagarbha contains inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, which are inseparable, non-detached, and non-different [from it]."
[Commentary: From this point on, following the wisdom of these two emptinesses, the second section clarifies that [the path] is not used because it is untimely.
Within this, there are three parts: first, a hypothetical presentation that cites the deluded to suppress the Two Vehicles.
"World-Honored One, these two wisdoms of emptiness can be believed in by the great śrāvakas through the Tathāgata.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "these two wisdoms of emptiness can be believed in by the great śrāvakas through the Tathāgata," this is a hypothetical illustration used to humble the Two Vehicles;
these two wisdoms are not within the scope of what they have heard. One interpretation states that "the great śrāvakas" refers to those at the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
[This refers to] the bodhisattvas among them.
[The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "To provisionally cite the ignorant and so forth" means to provisionally cite the great śrāvakas who are deluded regarding the two types of wisdom;
if even the śrāvakas merely believe [in this], how much more so would arhats and pratyekabuddhas not be deluded?
[Commentary: Second, it is correctly explained that [this wisdom] is not employed because it pertains to an improper time.

Since the wisdom of emptiness of all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas operates within the four non-perverted realms, it is something that all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have fundamentally never seen and fundamentally never attained.

[Commentary: Regarding the four non-perversions, they are as explained in the usual manner. Therefore, the concluding statement below says that because there is this underlying reason, it was not spoken;
for this reason, the followers of the Two Vehicles did not previously see or hear it.

[Commentary]: Because those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) form four misconceptions—such as impermanence—regarding the Tathāgata’s realm of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it is said that they do not err regarding these four [attributes].
[Commentary] Third, from "the extinction of all suffering" onwards, it clarifies that only the Buddha attains realization.
Only the Buddha attains the realization of the extinction of all suffering, having destroyed the storehouse of all afflictions and cultivated the path that extinguishes all suffering.
[Commentary]: From "the cessation of all suffering" onwards, the third section clarifies that only the Buddha attains realization.

The underlying intent of this passage is difficult to discern; it likely means that the Tathāgata, being free from the four inversions, has practiced the path that extinguishes all suffering—this refers to what has already been cultivated, not what is being cultivated now.

[Commentary] From the passage "From the World-Honored One’s [teaching on] these Four Noble Truths" onwards, the second section within the context of the vehicle's object (*ālambana*) is presented, specifically elucidating the four chapters concerning the objective realm.
Although each of these four preceding chapters clarifies the object, they merely describe it directly and do not yet clarify its ultimate nature as that which can be relied upon by the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, from this point onward, among the eight truths, those [aspects] to be excluded are distinguished.

Regarding the seven truths, among the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), only the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is the ultimate basis; therefore, it is said that the "object" (*viṣaya*) is explained separately.
As for the four chapters: first, the Chapter on the Single Truth; second, the Chapter on the Single Basis; third, the Chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha;

and fourth, the Chapter on Natural Purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*). Regarding the first, the Chapter on the Single Truth: because it is intended to clarify what constitutes the ultimate basis, it is distinguished [from the others].

Excluding the three truths within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one takes only the single truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as the ultimate. Within this, the first section is further divided into three:
first, a preliminary analysis of the eight truths showing that only the single truth of cessation is the ultimate;

second, from "Beyond this truth of cessation" down to "all sentient beings," a praise of the profound depth of the single truth of cessation; third, from "Or there may be some sentient beings... [down to the end].
To encourage faith in what follows, we shall first provide a preliminary analysis of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Within this initial analysis, there are two parts.
First, two topical headings are established:
"O World-Honored One, among these Four Noble Truths, three are impermanent and one is permanent."

[Commentary]: "Three are impermanent, one is permanent. The three that are impermanent refer to the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the two truths of origination (*samudaya-satya*), along with the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).

The one that is permanent refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Since the cessation attained through effort (*saṃskṛta-nirodha*) is already unconditioned and has nothing further to be eliminated, it is the cessation of what was to be severed;
there is nothing therein that can be grasped as an object of acquisition. Therefore, it is not employed [as an object of grasping].
This is indeed so. Above, two kinds of *nirvāṇa* were cited as an explanation for "with effort" (*sābhisamskāra*) and "without effort" (*anabhisamskāra*).

Since it was stated that the stages of the Two Vehicles up to the seventh ground are called "those with remainder," and what is realized by those with remainder is called "nirvāṇa with remainder," nirvāṇa with remainder thus encompasses both the limited cessation and the path. That which is realized by the Tathāgata, who is "one without remainder," is called [nirvāṇa without remainder].
Regarding "Nirvana without remainder," this term encompasses both cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
Now, in this context, we take only one aspect of cessation, yet it also excludes the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*). Why is this so? The explanation states: There are two kinds of paths:
first, the causal path; second, the resultant path. Since the discussion here proceeds from the perspective of the resultant path, Nirvana without remainder thus encompasses [both].

Regarding the phrase "the immeasurable cessation and path," this is explained with reference to the path as a cause; therefore, it specifically excludes the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) and takes only the single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as the ultimate.
[Commentary] Chapter Five: The Single Truth. Regarding the statement that "one is eternal," this refers to the teaching of the Single Truth. (8)
The four [stages] arise from skillful means; they originate from the definitive meaning (nītārtha) and exhaust names until reaching namelessness, and exhaust meanings until reaching meaninglessness.
That which forcibly establishes names and meanings where there is neither name nor meaning—is this not the One Truth? Therefore, next, the three are removed to preserve the one.
Regarding "the Path has two kinds," etc.: the former refers to the path of the fruit, while the latter refers to the paths of the stages (bhūmi).
How could it be that the cause is not eternal? From the state of being lost in delusion up to the attainment of Equal Enlightenment, all are impermanent.
[Commentary] Second, from "For what reason? onwards, the two topical headings are explained. First, the heading on impermanence is explained;
within this explanation of impermanence, there are also two parts: first, the formal explanation.
Why is this? Because the three truths enter into the characteristics of the conditioned; that which enters into the characteristics of the conditioned is impermanent;
that which is impermanent is a false and deceptive dharma; and that which is a false and deceptive dharma is not a truth, not permanent, and not a refuge.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "entering the characteristics of the conditioned through the three truths" and so forth: that which is nameless is called "name," and its meaning is established according to numerical categories;
because it changes on account of names, one enters the characteristics of the conditioned. Since it shifts and moves in relation to others, how could it not be false?
[Commentary] Second, the conclusion:
Therefore, the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of Origination, and the Truth of the Path are not the Ultimate Truth; they are neither permanent nor a refuge.
[Commentary] This concludes the subsequent explanation of the section on permanence.
The Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is free from conditioned characteristics; that which is free from conditioned characteristics is permanent;

that which is permanent is not a deceptive phenomenon; that which is not a deceptive phenomenon is the truth, the permanent, and the refuge. Therefore, the Truth of Cessation is the ultimate reality and is inconceivable.
[Commentary] Regarding the section explaining the chapter on "Permanence," the concluding remarks from "Therefore" (*is-gu*) onwards can all be seen therein.
[Sub-commentary] As for the scriptural passage "This is permanent, this is the refuge," etc., the *Wuming lun* (*Treatise on Non-Name*) states that what is not false is the Truth (*satya*).

This clarifies that because it is permanent, it is the Truth, and therefore it is a refuge. The concluding remarks "Therefore... and so forth clarify that this refers to the Single Truth (*eka-satya*). This pertains to the One Truth.
Within this section, it is further revealed that there is but one refuge, which is eternally abiding and secure.

[Commentary] From the passage beginning with "This is the Truth of Cessation" onwards, the second part praises the profound depth of the single Truth of Cessation. This is further divided into three sections:
first, it directly clarifies that neither ordinary beings nor those of the Two Vehicles can be regarded as such a refuge.
This Truth of Cessation transcends all that is an object of the mental consciousness of sentient beings, and it is not within the sphere of wisdom of any Arhat or Pratyekabuddha.

For example, just as one born blind does not see various forms, or a seven-day-old infant does not see the orb of the sun, so too is the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering: it is not an object of the mental consciousness of any ordinary person, nor is it...
It is not the realm of the wisdom of the two vehicles.
[Commentary: Because those born blind do not see any forms or images at all, they serve as a metaphor for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Because a seven-day-old infant can see other things but cannot see the solar disk, it serves as a metaphor for the two vehicles. This is explained from the perspective of the consciousness of ordinary beings.
Below, I shall briefly distinguish between two types of people who, though both are "not seeing," do not see in the same way.
For ordinary beings with consciousness, these two views are inverted; for all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas with wisdom, they are pure.

[Commentary] Second, the differences may be seen. Third, from the section on extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) onwards, there is an extensive explanation of the two types of views held by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the characteristics of the purity of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Within this third section of extensive explanation, there are two parts: first, an explanation of the consciousness (*vijñāna*) of ordinary beings;
second, an explanation of the wisdom (*jñāna*) of the Two Vehicles. Within the explanation of the consciousness of ordinary beings, there are also two parts; first, [the initial explanation].
Second, the subsequent explanation of the two views and the explanation of perversions. Within the explanation of the two views, there are also five parts: first, directly presenting the two views.

Regarding the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*): ordinary beings, through the deluded attachment of the view of self (*ātman*) toward the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), give rise to the two views; this is called the view of extremes.

[Commentary] Regarding the deluded discrimination of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi-vikalpa*): by falsely conceptualizing [the self] as either identical to or separate from the two types of self, one gives rise to the notion of annihilation because of identity, and one gives rise to the notion of permanence because of separation.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding "giving rise to annihilation because of identity" and so forth: because one holds that there is a self identical to the aggregates (*skandha*), and that this self is [identical to them], annihilation is established; because one holds that there is a self separate from the aggregates... [and so forth].
"Because my body perishes while I persist, I am therefore eternal.
[Commentary] Second, the enumeration of the names of the two views: namely, the view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism.
That is to say, the view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism.
[Commentary]: Listing the two names, if they were nameless, then "permanence" would mean arising without ceasing, and "annihilation" would mean ceasing without arising.
[Sub-commentary]: The third section, from "seeing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" onwards, cites birth-and-death and nirvana to explain these two views.

To see that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent is the view of annihilationism and not the right view; to see that nirvāṇa is permanent is the view of eternalism and not the right view.
Such views arise from the conceptualization of false imagination (*vikalpa*).

[Commentary: Regarding the two views: the first calculates that the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*) of birth and death is utterly annihilated; the second calculates that within birth and death there exists *nirvāṇa*.
From the fourth [section], beginning with "from the body and its various faculties," he cites the two dharmas of form and mind to explain these two views.
Because they conceptually analyze and contemplate the various faculties of the body, they perceive the destruction of the present life and,
failing to see the continuity of existence, give rise to the deluded view of nihilism; because they are ignorant and dark regarding the continuity of the mind,
not understanding or knowing that the objects of mental consciousness arise within a single moment, they give rise to the deluded view of eternalism.
[Commentary] Second, seeing the destruction of form (*rūpa*), one gives rise to the calculation of annihilation (*uccheda*);

seeing that the mind (*citta*) is not annihilated, one gives rise to the calculation of permanence (*śāśvata*). [Sub-commentary] Regarding the explanation of the two views and so forth in terms of the two dharmas of form and mind:

the *Wuming lun* (Treatise on the Nameless) states that this clarifies that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to views. It clarifies that they merely see its ruinous annihilation and do not perceive its continuous, hidden continuity.
Since one does not perceive the continuity of the bonds of darkness, how could one fail to give rise to the nihilistic view of conceptualization?
Since the objects of perception are non-dual and the characteristics of the mind are likewise so, how could one possibly avoid giving rise to the eternalist view?
Within name-and-form, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, if one fails to understand clearly whether they are identical or distinct, one will falsely reckon them as having a self.
Because it is the reality of "what belongs to me," it is called "self.
[Commentary] Fifth, from this point on, beginning with "this false conceptualization and view," it clarifies how two views lose the Middle Way.
This false conceptualization and view, regarding that object, either exceeds or falls short of it, forming diverse conceptual discriminations, whether as annihilation or...
"Permanence.
[Commentary] The meaning of that [term] refers to the meaning of the Middle Way; both extremes—excess and deficiency—are encompassed by the two views.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "excess or deficiency" in the Sūtra, it is called "nameless" because calculating annihilation is considered excess, while calculating permanence is considered deficiency.
[Commentary] From the passage "sentient beings who are inverted" onwards, the visible aspect of inversion is explained.

Sentient beings who are inverted harbor the notion of permanence regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) which are impermanent; they harbor the notion of pleasure regarding what is suffering; they harbor the notion of self regarding what is non-self;
and they harbor the notion of purity regarding what is impure.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning "sentient beings who are inverted with respect to the five aggregates of clinging" and so forth:

their minds falsely perceive what is actually impermanent as permanent; they perceive what is actually suffering as pleasure; they perceive what is actually non-self in volition and cognition as self;
and they perceive what is actually impure in the body as pure.
[Commentary: From the passage "all arhats" downwards, the wisdom of the two vehicles may also be understood.
The pure wisdom of all arhats and pratyekabuddhas has never before seen the realm of omniscience or the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.

[Commentary] From the passage beginning "There may be sentient beings... onwards, this is the third section of the chapter, which encourages faith in the single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Within this, there are three parts;
the first clarifies that [the teaching] is the correct view because it originates from the Buddha's word.
There may be sentient beings who, because they trust the Buddha’s words, give rise to the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of self, and the perception of purity;
these are not inverted views, and are thus called right view.
[Commentary] The second section, beginning with "For what reason," explains why giving rise to these four perceptions constitutes right view.
Yes. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is the perfection of permanence, the perfection of bliss, the perfection of self, and the perfection of purity.
[Commentary: Regarding the causes and effects of the pāramitās, there are two types; what is clarified here is entirely the fruition, the "other shore.
From the third section, beginning with "From the Buddha’s dharma-body," onwards, the conclusion provides an exhortation.
One who perceives the Buddha’s Dharma-body in this way is said to possess right view. Such a person of right view is a true child of the Buddha;
born from the Buddha’s mouth, born from the True Dharma, and born through transformation by the Dharma, they have obtained the remaining wealth of the Dharma.
[Commentary]: "Born of speech" means arising from the teachings; "born of the True Dharma" means arising by relying on principle;

and "born of the transformation of the Dharma" means arising by relying on both teaching and principle. Regarding the "remaining riches," these refer to the seven riches which the Buddha had already attained previously;
since they are now attained subsequently, they are called "remaining riches."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "arising from the teachings," etc.: since the teachings are spoken by the Buddha, one relies on the teachings to understand the principle;
because one relies on the principle to give rise to right view, the deluded views of ordinary beings are transformed into the right view of a sage.

The *Ratnavali* (Yingluo) states that the seven noble riches consist of faith, generosity, precepts, learning, reflection, shame, and dread of blame. Because these are utilized by the sages to achieve Buddhahood, they are called "riches."
[Commentary: From the passage "The World-Honored One, the Knower of Purity" onwards, the second chapter within the section specifically clarifying the object is titled "The Single Reliance.
This correctly elucidates that this single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the ultimate reliance for the multitude. Within this, four sections are opened;

first, because it is intended to clarify today’s single Truth of Cessation as the ultimate reliance, it first clarifies that the wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is not such [an ultimate reliance].
