Regarding the sphere of objects: O Bhagavān, for this wisdom of pure knowledge, which is the perfection of the wisdom of all arhats and pratyekabuddhas—
though it is called "pure knowledge"— even the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is not its sphere of objects, let alone the wisdom of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*).
[Commentary]: Furthermore, "the wisdom of the four reliances" refers to the wisdom arising from the Four Noble Truths among the five expedient means.
One interpretation states that it is called the "wisdom of the four reliances" because the Buddha taught the path of the four reliances for those practicing the five expedient means.
[Commentary] The sixth chapter, "The Single Reliance. Regarding the path of the four reliances, wisdom arises by relying upon the Four Noble Truths.
[Sub-commentary] Second, the explanation that this is not their domain.
Why is this? Because those who have newly entered the practice of the Three Vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma;
they shall realize and attain its meaning. [Commentary] The second explanation addresses the raised doubt: "Why is it said that this is not their domain? The response states:

Those who have newly entered the practice of the Three Vehicles shall merely realize and attain that meaning; it is not something they realize or attain in the present moment. One interpretation says: [This is] a doubt.

Why is this contradictory? It contradicts what was stated in the preceding "Chapter on the One Vehicle," which says that those who have first engaged in the practice of the three vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma.
The explanation for this is as stated above: "not being deluded regarding the Dharma" refers to that which is to be awakened to and to be attained;

it does not refer to that which has already been attained or already awakened to. Third, from the passage beginning with "For their sake," below, it clarifies the reliance [on the Buddha] in the past.
No. It is for their sake that the World-Honored One taught the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*). The World-Honored One stated that these four reliances are worldly dharmas.
[Commentary] The third section clarifies that the former reliances were incorrect; "for their sake that the World-Honored One taught the four reliances" clarifies the former...

The passage from "The Sun itself, for the sake of the two vehicles... explains that these four truths with their conditioned aspects (*saṃskṛta*) and these four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) are worldly dharmas, thereby clarifying that they are not the ultimate reliance.
From the fourth section, beginning with "From the World-Honored One’s single reliance...", it correctly elucidates that the single reliance of today is the ultimate reliance.
The World-Honored One’s sole reliance is the supreme reliance above all reliances, the transcendent and most excellent ultimate reliance, namely, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
[Commentary] The fourth section correctly clarifies that the single reliance of today is the pinnacle of all reliances; "the reliance above all reliances" applies generally.
Regarding the statement that among the eight noble truths of the three realms and beyond, this single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is supreme:
as for "supreme among the supramundane," it refers exclusively to the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), wherein this single Truth of Cessation alone is the ultimate.

As for what is called the "basis of the primary meaning" (*paramārtha-āśraya*), namely the Truth of Cessation, its essence is further revealed as follows: first, it is said that all things are based upon it. This refers solely to—
Regarding the fact that the Four Noble Truths with effort (*sābhisamskāra*) are supreme.
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra-artha-shi-chō*, Scroll Five;
*Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra-artha-shi-chō*, Scroll Six.
[Commentary: From "From the birth and death of the World-Honored One" onwards is the third section, titled "The Reality of Perversion," which specifically clarifies the objects [of cognition].
Regarding the purpose of this chapter's introduction: the preceding chapter on "Relying on the One" clarified that today there is nothing to be created;
based on the single cessation of all reliance, it emerged as the supreme object of the world-transcending, superlative reliance. Upon hearing this, some immediately claimed it was so and departed.
It is only after being free from delusion that one becomes the support for phenomena; it is not said that one is the support while still within delusion.

Therefore, the present explanation states that when the single cessation of non-action occurs, it is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha; the consciousness of birth-and-death depends upon the Tathāgatagarbha and continues without ceasing.

It is not only upon emerging from delusion that one becomes the support for phenomena; rather, even while remaining within delusion, one already serves as the support. Within this, there is further differentiation.
It consists of eight parts. The first directly clarifies that birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The World-Honored One said: "Birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*; because of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is said that their prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is unknowable."
[Commentary: Now, regarding the first point, the birth and death of the World-Honored One being based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*:
birth and death are themselves delusion (*viparyāsa*), whereas the *tathāgatagarbha* is the reality (*bhūtatā*). Here it is clarified that all sentient beings possess this true nature;

if this nature did not exist, the process of transformation through teaching would have come to an end, and they would be no different from grasses and trees. It is because this nature exists [that the teaching continues].
Therefore, because the continuity is uninterrupted, one ultimately attains great illumination; thus it is said that birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
In this context, if the principle (*li*) is taken as the direct cause, then the principle itself is the *tathāgatagarbha*;
if spiritual intelligence (*shenming*) is taken as the direct cause, then the actualized fruit (*dangguo shi*) is the *tathāgatagarbha*. That its primordial limit (*benji*) is unknowable—

Now, birth and death are not without beginning and end; however, because they are discussed in terms of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), their original limit (pūrvakoṭi) cannot be known. Why is this?

This storehouse consciousness is not a dharma belonging to the three periods of time. Since it serves as the basis for birth and death—which themselves do not belong to the three periods of time—it is impossible to know from what point in time they began.
Furthermore, it is said that birth and death are not without beginning and end, yet their beginning and end are difficult to fathom.
"Fundamental limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*) refers to the origin of sentient beings.

[Commentary]: This is the seventh chapter, "The Reality of Inversion. Regarding the statement that "the continuity is uninterrupted until one finally attains great illumination," both delusion and awakening depend upon the *ālayavijñāna*.
Furthermore, it says: "Birth and death are not without beginning or end," and so forth, up to "difficult to fathom."
The Forty-second Chapter of the *Yingluo* (Garland) Commentary: The Ground of the Mind of Quiescent Extinction and Sublime Enlightenment (*Jimie Xin Miaojue Di*).

It is eternally abiding in the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*), the foremost and supreme, as profound and still as empty space. The All-Knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) illuminates and penetrates non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding the beginning and end of all that is taught, only the Buddha exhaustively understands the root of sentient beings, which has both a beginning and an end. Furthermore, it is called the Ground of Abiding in Ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*).
Vajrabodhi knew that this initial arising of a single characteristic has an end, yet he did not know its beginning; only a Buddha knows both the beginning and the end.
[Commentary] Second, it is explained that relying on principle to speak is called "skillful exposition."
Because the World-Honored One possesses the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is called an "excellent teaching" to say that birth and death exist.
[Commentary: It can be seen that the second point is called an "excellent teaching" because it relies on principle. From the third point, "From birth and death...
onwards, it clarifies how the two dharmas of birth and death are able to conceal the *tathāgatagarbha*; within this section, there is also...
Second, first, the meaning of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is explained.

World-Honored One, as for "birth-and-death," the successive subsiding of the faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*) and the arising of the faculties of sensation that are not [yet] received— this is called birth-and-death.
[Commentary]: From the passage "From birth-and-death to birth-and-death" onwards, this is the third section, clarifying how birth-and-death can conceal the *tathāgatagarbha*.

The term "birth-and-death" is repeated because the author intends to explain two meanings of birth-and-death; the first instance serves as the introduction (*upanyāsa*), while the second serves as the explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
Furthermore, some say that the first clause reiterates the preceding statement, while the subsequent portion provides the explanation for the phrase "the various faculties of sensation perish."
All faculties possess a common characteristic of apprehending objects, which is termed "subsidence" (*mūḍha*). Regarding the arising of faculties in succession without being received:
this refers to the faculties that arise in succession without the common characteristic of apprehending objects.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "all the sense-faculties possess the common characteristic of perceiving objects," this means that all six faculties have the function of receiving (*ling-nang*) external objects, which is termed "perceiving objects" (*ling-yuan*).
The mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitta*) flowing into these external objects is termed "sinking" (*mo*). This explains the phrase "arising.
As for the statement that "the sense-faculties are unable to receive external objects and arise gradually," this is termed "arising" (*qi*), and this explains "death" (*si*).
[Commentary:
Second, the explicit explanation that the two dharmas of birth and death are able to conceal the Tathāgatagarbha.
"O World-Honored One, these two dharmas—death and birth—are the Tathāgatagarbha."
[Commentary]: Second, the correct elucidation of that which is capable of concealing:

it is stated that the principle of this *tathāgatagarbha* does not intend to conceal itself, but rather takes the two phenomena of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as its concealment. Fourth, from the phrase "following worldly discourse," the text analyzes the distinction between birth-and-death and the *tathāgatagarbha*.
According to worldly convention, there is death and there are those who undergo birth and death; that is, when the sense faculties perish, new sense faculties arise.

However, the *tathāgatagarbha* has neither birth nor death. The *tathāgatagarbha* is free from conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*); the *tathāgatagarbha* is eternally abiding and unchanging.
[Commentary] From the phrase "Because of worldly conventional discourse" onwards, the fourth section clarifies the difference between birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the storehouse (*ālaya*).
If the storehouse were identical with birth-and-death, it would be indistinguishably one with birth-and-death; therefore, it is clarified that birth-and-death and the storehouse are distinct.
First, birth-and-death is explained, and subsequently, the meaning of the storehouse is explained.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "the sense faculties of one who has died are destroyed," etc., there are two types: those pertaining to a single lifetime (*ekakāla*) and those pertaining to every moment (*kṣaṇa*).

In the case of a single lifetime, when this [present] aggregate (*skandha*) perishes and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises, it is called "new. In the case of every moment, however, the old sense faculties perish and new sense faculties arise;

this is because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subject to transformation by the four characteristics (*caturlakṣaṇa*). Regarding the passage "the sense faculties arise," etc. [it refers to the latter].

The previous explanation of birth and death was based on the mutual correspondence between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*); now, however, it is explained solely in terms of the five aggregates of maturation (*vipāka-skandha*).
This means that "death" refers to the gradual dissolution and destruction of the six old faculties, while "birth" refers to the gradual growth and emergence of the six new faculties.
[Commentary]: Fifth, from "Therefore" onwards, the text concludes that saṃsāra relies upon the tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, the tathāgatagarbha is the support, the sustainer, and the foundation.
[Commentary] The sixth section, from "The World-Honored One does not depart from nor is detached from" onwards, clarifies that sentient beings obtain their establishment by relying on the *ālaya*.

If the principle of the *ālaya* did not exist, there would be no basis for the weariness with suffering or the seeking of happiness. Within this, there are three parts; the first directly clarifies how they obtain their establishment by relying on the *ālaya*.
The Tathāgatagarbha is that which is the support, foundation, and establishment for the Buddha-dharmas— which are inseparable, uninterrupted, non-detached, and non-different from the inconceivable—
and for the external conditioned dharmas which are severed, detached, and different.

[Commentary] The fourth [point] does not clarify that one has not yet emerged from delusion; it further states that the essence of the *pitaka* is true reality (*tattva*), which cannot be separated from, severed, or abandoned, and is non-different from the principle (*li*).
[Sub-commentary] In the first section of the Commentary, "Directly Clarifying the Establishment Based on the *pitaka*" extends from the beginning up to "the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas."

Regarding the statement that "the *ālayavijñāna* is severed and detached from this dharmakāya, and both [it] and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are established by means of the *ālaya*," as well as the further remark that "the essence of the *ālaya* is reality (*tattva*)," etc.:
the former explanation directly clarifies that one attains establishment by relying on the *ālaya*;
the current explanation, however, clarifies that the essence of the *ālaya* cannot be severed or detached from.
[Commentary: Second, from "If there were no... onwards, it clarifies that without the *tathāgatagarbha*, liberation cannot be established.
World-Honored One, if there were no *tathāgatagarbha*, one would not be able to weary of suffering or joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*.
[Commentary]: If the sutras did not speak of the *tathāgatagarbha* and so forth, they would have no name.
What was explained previously—that one enters into birth-and-death by depending on the *tathāgatagarbha*—is now clarified as that one ascends to nirvāṇa by depending on the *tathāgatagarbha*.

This means that those who went in the past were at variance with the fundamental principle by even a hair’s breadth, whereas those who come now seek the source to accord with the Truth. Thus, one knows the nature of their departure.
Furthermore, both ascending and descending rely entirely upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
[Commentary: Third, from "Why is this? (*kasmāt*) onwards, it explains why [the seeds] cannot be established.
Why? Because within these seven dharmas—the six consciousnesses along with the mental factors and wisdom—they do not abide for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), nor do they plant [seeds].
One cannot grow weary of manifold sufferings nor seek nirvana through the pursuit of pleasure.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "these seven dharmas" in the sutra: if these seven dharmas lacked the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), they would not abide for even a single moment;
and if they lacked the storehouse consciousness, they could neither plant the seeds of manifold sufferings nor bring about weariness with suffering and so forth.
[Commentary] The seventh section, from "The Tathāgata-garbha of the World-Honored One" onwards, clarifies that the Tathāgata-garbha is not a phenomenon belonging to the three periods of time.

The Tathāgata-garbha of the World-Honored One is a dharma without a prior limit; it neither arises nor ceases, yet it is the seed from which all sufferings sprout, leading one to develop weariness toward suffering.
They joyfully seek nirvana.

[Commentary] From the passage "From the Tathāgata-garbha of the World-Honored One" onwards, the seventh section clarifies that the *garbha* is not a dharma of the three periods of time and has no prior limit:
"not arising in the future," "not ceasing in the present," and "not existing in the past."

[Commentary]: Regarding "having no prior limit" and so forth: although the Tathāgatagarbha is not established as a storehouse for the three periods of time, birth-and-death, or nirvāṇa, the Sūtra states it is "neither arising nor ceasing.
Because it is nameless, one cannot know its place of origin; thus, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because it does not arise, it can give rise to birth-and-death; because it does not cease, it extinguishes birth-and-death. This is the seed of the Dharma.
"All sufferings" refers to birth and death; "disgust with suffering and so forth" refers to nirvana.
[Commentary: The section beginning with "The eighth also from the tathāgatagarbha" clarifies that the tathāgatagarbha is distinct from arbitrary conceptualizations.
World-Honored One, the Tathāgatagarbha is not the self, not a sentient being, not a life-principle, and not a person.
The Tathāgatagarbha is not within the sphere of those sentient beings who have fallen into the view of a body, those who are inverted, or those whose minds are distracted by emptiness.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "It is not that our treasury of clarity differs from those who recklessly speculate on 'non-self' and 'non-sentient beings.

That which is called 'non-self' refers to the fact that within the mind, many falsely conceptualize these four; since the Tathāgata-garbha is the mind yet is not the [deluded] mind, it is not these four.
As for 'self,' if one is ignorant and lacks clear understanding regarding name-and-form, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases..."

Those sentient beings who, whether through identity or difference, falsely conceptualize a real self and what belongs to a self, falsely conceptualize a "self that arises" within name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth;
because they falsely conceptualize a "vitality" (jīva) as being identical to the life-span (āyus) within name-and-form and so forth;
and because they falsely conceptualize a "person" (pudgala) as the accomplishment and continuous maintenance of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) within name-and-form and so forth...

Those with deluded selves who are different from non-practitioners possess the inversion of the view of a self in the body; sentient beings with distracted minds reckon that there is existence, while those with disordered thoughts reckon that there is non-existence.
To reckon that there is existence gives rise to the view of eternalism, and to reckon that there is non-existence gives rise to the view of annihilationism.
Those who hold to the views of annihilationism and eternalism do not yet attain the Middle Way of dependent origination; how much less could they take the Tathāgatagarbha as their objective sphere?
As stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "The Dharma has no sentient beings, because it is free from the defilement of sentient beings; the Dharma has no self, because it is free from 'mine-ness';
the Dharma has no life-span, because it is free from birth and death; the Dharma has no person, because its anterior and posterior limits are severed;
the Dharma is eternally quiescent, because all marks have been extinguished."

[Commentary] From the passage "From the World-Honored One’s Tathāgatagarbha, this is the Dharmadhātugarbha" onwards, the fourth chapter within the section on the object is specifically elucidated as the "Chapter on Innate Purity.

Regarding the purpose of this chapter's introduction: when sentient beings heard the preceding third chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha, which states that this Tathāgatagarbha exists within afflictions and serves as the support for all things, they [realized] it is not merely something that emerges [from them].
If delusion were the basis for phenomena, doubt would immediately arise: "In that case, this Tathāgatagarbha must be defiled by birth and death; how can it be the honored basis?
If one says it is not defiled, then since they are distinct and separate, how can they be mutually dependent?
Therefore, the present explanation is as follows: the self-nature of this Tathāgatagarbha is intrinsically pure; although it exists amidst delusions, it is not affected by birth and death.
Defilement (*saṃkleśa*) merely consists in concealment; within this, the first section is divided into two:
first, the self-exposition by Śrīmālā herself, and second, the Tathāgata’s account of its accomplishment. Within the first, the self-exposition by Śrīmālā, it is further divided into four:

first, as she is about to clarify defilement and non-defilement, she first correlates the five kinds of *garbha*; second, from this point onward, [she explains] based on the intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).

The third section, beginning with "For what reason," clarifies the difficulty of definitively establishing defilement and non-defilement by citing mundane, proximate matters as analogies for distant principles;
the fourth section, beginning with "Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One," deduces and elucidates [the nature] of the Buddha.
First, we shall now harmonize these five types of *piṭaka*.

The World-Honored One, the Tathāgatagarbha, is the treasury of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-garbha*), the treasury of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-garbha*), the supreme supramundane treasury, and the treasury of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-garbha*).
[Commentary: First, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*) because the Tathāgata is contained within the afflictions; furthermore, it is called a "treasury" because it contains the future fruit.
1. The *dharmadhātu-garbha* refers to the Buddha-fruit containing the illumination of the *dharmadhātu*; it is also called the eternally abiding *dharmatā*. 2.
The *dharmakāya-garbha* refers to the *dharmakāya* containing all myriad virtues; therefore, it is called a "garbha. 3. The *lokottara-agrottama-garbha*. 4. The *prakṛti-viśuddhi-garbha*.
The first and the last [of these four] are designated according to their state of concealment, while the middle three are designated according to their manifestation.
At that time, although their manifestations as manifest or hidden differ, they are in essence one and the same.

[Commentary] Chapter Eight: Innate Purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). Wuming states: It is called "innately pure" because, while it is proximate within the afflictions, it is remote in its identity with *nirvāṇa*.
[Commentary: From this point on, starting with "this intrinsically pure nature," the second section clarifies the difficulty of definitively determining whether there is defilement or non-defilement.
This intrinsically pure *tathāgatagarbha* is defiled by adventitious afflictions (*kleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
it is the inconceivable realm of the *Tathāgata*.
[Commentary: "Adventitious afflictions" refers to the four abodes of affliction; "superior afflictions" refers to the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is difficult to determine definitively whether this Tathāgatagarbha is defiled by these afflictions or remains undefiled.
Why is this? Since it is intrinsically pure, how can one say it is defiled? Yet, while still within the midst of delusion, how could it not be undefiled? Therefore—
It is called the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata. [Commentary:
Regarding "adventitious afflictions" (*āgantuka-kleśa*): although they initially appear identical [to the mind] in form, their nature is contrary;

because they must ultimately be distanced from it as it remains solitary and absolute, they are termed "adventitious. Regarding "the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata": there is no... [text continues].
The name "Cloud-Nature" (Yunxing) signifies that although it does not sink, it is not untainted; how could this be conceivable?

[Commentary] From the section beginning with "For what reason? onwards is the third part, which raises mundane, proximate matters as difficult-to-determine analogies to illustrate the distant principle.
Within this, there are two sections: first, clarifying that within the path of real dharmas (*dharmatā*), there is no defilement.
Why is this? A momentary wholesome mind is not defiled by afflictions, nor is a momentary unwholesome mind defiled by afflictions.
Afflictions do not touch the mind, and the mind does not touch afflictions. How can a mind be defiled by phenomena that do not touch it?

[Commentary] One might doubt this, asking: "How can it be difficult to know? If a wholesome mind in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) is not defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), then within the reality of the Path (*mārga-dharma*), the wholesome mind ceases first and the affliction arises later; since they do not coincide, how could there be defilement?
Likewise, if a single moment of unwholesome mind is also not defiled by afflictions, then the very arising of the unwholesome mind would itself be the affliction."

What further affliction could come to defile this vexation? If the affliction does not touch the mind and the mind does not touch the affliction—where "touch" means reaching—then the affliction ceases of its own accord without reaching the subsequent moments of mind, and the mind likewise does not touch the affliction.
Since they do not reach one another, how can there be any defilement at all?
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "afflictions do not touch the mind," the mind is so named because its capacity is discernment and cognition;
afflictions function by obscuring illumination. It is like light and darkness occupying the same space while their natures are inherently separated by heaven;
therefore, they are said to be "mutually untouched. Since they do not touch one another, there is no meaning of defilement. This explains "non-defilement."

The five stages of the stained one (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) are clearly manifest; it is not that afflictions (*kleśa*) do not exist. The three vehicles are equally obscured by darkness, yet this is not a case of the mind being unstained.

Regarding the phrase "within the path of real dharmas": because the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are substantially existent dharmas, they are called "real dharmas.
Since sentient beings are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*), [the sixth stage] is the immediate [uninterrupted path].
Because the preceding thought ceases and the succeeding thought arises as consciousness is extinguished, they do not reach one another.
[Commentary] Second, it is explained that within the continuum of the path there is existence.
World-Honored One, there are afflictions, and there is a mind defiled by afflictions.
[Commentary: Second, it clarifies that within the continuum of the path, there is defilement; that is, the state where the mind is defiled by afflictions.

Regarding the statement that "within the continuum there is defilement by way of designation," this means that while the preceding wholesome mind has not yet ceased, it transforms into the subsequent evil [mind], which possesses defilement.
This refers to the principle that the preceding [state] is defiled. Such difficulties regarding worldly matters—namely, whether they are defiled or undefiled—are thus explained.
How much more so for the profound principle of Buddha-nature—how could it be definitively fixed?
[Commentary]: Within the continuum of the path, it is conventionally designated as such because the preceding thought-moment transforms into the succeeding one;
since the latter arises from the former, it appears as if there were defilement.
[Commentary: From the section on "innate purity" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) onwards, the fourth [section] investigates and clarifies that the Buddha is visible.
It is difficult to comprehend how the innately pure mind can be subject to defilement; only the World-Honored One, the Buddha, possesses the true eye and true wisdom.
He is the root of the Dharma, the one who has attained thorough penetration of the Dharma, and the refuge of the True Dharma, knowing and seeing it exactly as it is.
[Commentary: From the section beginning with Lady Śrīmālā onwards, within the second part concerning the Tathāgata’s exposition of accomplishment, there are two sections.
First, he directly restates what she has said above, namely that it is indeed difficult to definitively establish.
When Queen Śrīmālā spoke of this difficult-to-understand Dharma and questioned the Buddha about it, the Buddha immediately expressed his approval, saying:
"So it is, so it is! The intrinsically pure mind, while being subject to defilement, is difficult to comprehend. There are two things that are difficult to comprehend:
namely, the intrinsically pure mind is difficult to comprehend, and that this very mind is defiled by afflictions."
It is difficult to comprehend.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "it is difficult to comprehend how the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*) can be defiled," this means it is difficult to comprehend how the *ālayavijñāna* is defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the "two dharmas that are difficult to comprehend," these two dharmas refer to...
The principle of the *tathāgatagarbha* is also said to be difficult to comprehend because the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*) is difficult to understand;

this means that within the principle of the *garbha*, it is difficult to discern whether it is defiled or undefiled. Furthermore, the statement that "it is difficult to understand how that mind is defiled by afflictions" means that in worldly affairs, it is difficult to discern whether something is defiled or undefiled.
However, since the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* itself establishes its own definitive teaching, it [the commentary] infers [this meaning].
There are two intentions behind the fact that although [the interlocutor] is clear regarding the Buddha, the Buddha merely repeats his words:
first, that engaging in discourse within the realm of phenomena (*dharma*) appears to be defiled; second, that engaging in discussion within the realm of principle (*li*) is not defiled.
This is why he merely repeats those words.
[Commentary]: Regarding the two dharmas that are difficult to comprehend: "there being no name, one does not know why there is existence" refers to the first difficulty of comprehension;
"there being no consciousness, one is stained" refers to the second difficulty of comprehension.

When discussing this within the context of phenomena (*dharma*), it is similar to "staining" and so forth because one is deluded regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, taking the entirety of principle (*li*) to be phenomena (*shi*), just as water becomes ice. Therefore, it is said to be "similar."

Regarding defilement, one awakens to the *tathāgatagarbha*; it is eternally pure in its essence and has never undergone change. Because the entire phenomenal event (*dharma*) is identical to the principle (*dharmatā*), like the nature of moisture in ice, it is not defiled.
[Commentary] Second, from "these two dharmas" onwards, the text identifies those who are capable of believing in this difficult-to-establish principle.
Since Śrīmālā has already stated that it is difficult to determine [the meaning], and the Tathāgata likewise states it is difficult to determine, there would be no basis for faith;

therefore, he cites the person capable of faith to encourage belief and discourage doubt. Within this, there are three parts. First, it generally clarifies that those with profound understanding are able to believe in what ordinary people find difficult to believe.
"These two dharmas can be heard and received only by you and those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have accomplished the Great Dharma;
all other Śrāvakas can only believe in the words of the Buddha.
[Commentary] The Sūtra refers to "Bodhisattvas of the Great Dharma. Wuming (無名) states that "Great Dharma" is like the class of "Great Power" (Mahāsthāmaprāpta).
It is said that "hearing" refers to entering into the spirit [of the teaching], which is called "listening and receiving.
[Commentary] Second, from the passage "If my disciples... onwards, the text correctly identifies those capable of faith, namely the Bodhisattvas of the two types of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
Within this second section on the correct identification, there are two parts: first, the direct presentation of the two types of patient acceptance; second...
Chapter Heading.
If my disciples, following faith and with faith as their predominant factor, rely upon clear confidence and subsequently accord with the knowledge of the Dharma,
they shall attain the ultimate goal.

[Commentary: "If my disciples follow faith and have faith as their predominant factor" means that those who have faith and patience as their gateway and take faith as predominant are those whose faith has ascended to the stages (bhūmi).
This is the highest form of faith within faith. Having relied upon clear faith, they accord with the wisdom of the Dharma and attain the ultimate;
this refers to the gateway of "conformity-patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti). As for doubt, it is merely a matter of following the gateway of conformity-patience.
The phrase "faith is the sovereign of faith" merely cites that which accords with the fundamental [teaching].

[The *Chao*] states that the headings for the two types of patience are as follows: because faith is the initial gateway to entering the Path and wisdom is the profound art of ultimate realization, once one relies upon clear faith, one accords with the wisdom of the Dharma;
having accorded with the wisdom of the Dharma, one brings afflictions to their ultimate end.
Ultimately, afflictions are identical to a single truth and eternally abide in a single reliance.
[Commentary] The second section, from "following the knowledge of conforming dharmas" onwards, explains compliant patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
One who possesses knowledge in accordance with the Dharma observes the designation of the faculties, the mental inclinations, and the spheres of objects; observes karmic retribution;
observes the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of arhats; observes the bliss of mastery over the mind and the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
and observes the noble supernormal powers of arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of great power.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of "only" refers exclusively to the contemplation of compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*). The first contemplation observes the provisional designation of the faculties (*indriya*):
this refers to the five faculties as provisional designations; "mental resolve" (*adhimokṣa*) refers to the six consciousnesses; and "objects" (*viṣaya*) refers to the six sense-fields.

This constitutes the contemplation of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The second contemplation observes karma and its retribution (*vipāka*): this refers to the two contemplations of cause and effect. The third contemplation observes the *ā*... [text fragment].
The "sleeping arhat" refers to one who observes the delusions of the ground where ignorance resides through four types of observation.

The "bliss of meditative concentration" and the "bliss of mental mastery" refer to the two observations of wisdom and meditative concentration, wherein one dwells in bliss as wisdom illuminates the objects of perception.
The "fifth observation" refers to observing the supernormal powers of the three vehicles.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the Chapter on Accordant Patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), Wuming says: "In this way, defilement and purity, misfortune and fortune, take the mind alone as their master.
To know how to enter from darkness into light takes faith alone as the precursor.

Therefore, if one can tread upon faith to accord with wisdom, afflictions will extinguish themselves even without being severed, and the pure mind will clarify itself even without being polished. One observes these five matters..."
Regarding "taking mental comprehension as the beginning": the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are the foundation of all virtues.
Faith is the starting point of practice; it begins with mental comprehension. Once mental comprehension is established, one can subsequently ascend to the fruit of realization.

That one practices evil conduct to bring about bitter fruits and cultivates wholesome karma to summon joyful retributions is likewise due to the accumulation of powerful merit. First, one must rely upon...
Furthermore, because it is real, the retribution of karma is explained next. There are two kinds of cultivation: first, the accumulation of merit; second, the exhaustion of defilements.
Contemplating the retribution of karma clarifies the accumulation of merit; contemplating the sleep of an Arhat clarifies the exhaustion of defilements.
"Sleep" refers to the obscuration of body and mind; it is not the true, fundamental state of peaceful rest. Since one is already able to...
From the provisional to the real, one accumulates merit until all defilements are exhausted;
since the stage where defilements are exhausted must rely upon the various dhyānas, one relies upon them according to what one finds pleasing, thereby attaining the bliss one aspires to.
Because penetration is the fruit of dhyāna, penetration is clarified by means of dhyāna; because the provisional is the foundation of the real, it culminates in the sovereign mastery of the Sage.
[Commentary: Third, from this point on, beginning with the "five kinds of skillful means," the section concludes by identifying those capable of faith.

These five kinds of skillful means, when accomplished through contemplation, enable my disciples in future ages after my parinirvāṇa to follow faith, increase their faith, rely upon superior clarity, accord with the wisdom of the Dharma, and [realize] the self-nature purity of the mind; such individuals are [the ones so described].

Though defiled by afflictions, one attains the ultimate; for those who enter the Mahāyāna path through faith in the Tathāgata, there is such great benefit that they do not slander the profound meaning.
[Commentary] From these five types below, the third section concludes by clarifying that there are those capable of entering the Mahāyāna path with faith;

it explains that the Mahāyāna path serves as the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Furthermore, it states that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward is the Mahāyāna path, while faith and compliance with the two kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) are the causes of the Mahāyāna.
Those who place their faith in the Tathāgata receive such great benefits and do not engage in slander.
Regarding the profound meaning: it is said that because this person was previously able to have faith in the Buddha’s words, they obtained the benefits of these five kinds of contemplation;
therefore, by the power of these five contemplations, they are now also able to believe in this principle which is difficult to ascertain.

[Commentary]: From "At that time, Śrīmālā... onwards, the third section within the "Correct Body" (zhengtī) concludes the exposition on the person who rides the vehicle and the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*).
Therefore, this section on the "True Son" (*zhēnzǐ*) clarifies how Bodhisattvas of the Three Patiences (*sānti*) receive this vehicle and practice it.
The original text states: "From 'If I am a disciple... and so forth.

In the "Chapter on Entering the True Child," there are two parts. First, because the Tathāgata mentions only the two patiences of faith and compliance, it is called the "brief explanation of the true child.
From here below, as Śrīmālā fully enumerates all three patiences, it is called the "extensive explanation of the true child.
However, because the Tathāgata wishes to attribute the merit of this sutra to Śrīmālā, he provides only a brief explanation.
The two types of patient acceptance (kṣānti) in accord with faith are combined to form the "Chapter on the True Child of Śrīmālā. This may be applied according to one's inclination.
Within this, the first section is further divided into three parts: first, Śrīmālā’s request for the teaching.

[Commentary] The third is the "Chapter on the True Child," which extends from the passage beginning with "From the fundamental meaning" down to the end of the "Chapter on the True Child"; these are all by ancient masters.

[The Buddha said: "Excellent. At that time, Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: 'There is yet another great benefit; I shall now, relying on the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, further explain this meaning.'"

[Commentary]: Regarding the further great benefits: although the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*) and its objects have already been clarified above, the practice of the vehicle and the person who practices it have not yet been explained;

hence it is said that there are further great benefits. Alternatively, since the Tathāgata previously cited the benefits for those capable of faith—both those subject to defilement and those free from it—it is still said that there are further general benefits for those who practice this sutra.
Second, the Tathāgata commands him to speak;
the Buddha speaks, and he speaks accordingly.
[Commentary] Third, from the words "He addressed the Buddha" onwards is the actual exposition. Within this third section of the actual exposition, it is divided into five parts.
First, the three types of persons are proclaimed in general.

Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying: "There are three types of sons and daughters of good family who, regarding this profound meaning, avoid self-injury, generate great merit, and enter the path of the Mahāyāna."

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "free from self-destruction and injury" (*ātma-vidveṣaṇādi-vivarjita*) in the Sūtra: it is called "free from destruction and injury" because one does not slander as mentioned above;

it is a great merit of benefit because it is a supreme ultimate advantage as mentioned above; it is "entering the Mahāyāna" because it is what is referred to above as "following through faith" (*śraddhānusārin*).
[Commentary] Second, from "What are the three? onwards, the three types of persons are listed individually. As for what these three are:
they are those sons of good family or daughters of good family who have themselves accomplished the profound knowledge of the Dharma. If...
Noble sons and noble daughters who have accomplished the knowledge that accords with the Dharma— when these noble sons and noble daughters do not understand profound dharmas for themselves,
but look up to and defer to the World-Honored One, saying, "This is not within our sphere; it is known only by the Buddha"—
this is called noble sons and noble daughters deferring to the Tathāgata.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the Sūtra accomplishes the profound wisdom of the Dharma" and so forth: Wuming (Wu-ming) says that "profound wisdom of the Dharma" refers to the Great Bodhisattva.
Because the World-Honored One provides instruction by way of the secondary (the derivative), he identifies [the Bodhisattva] but does not name her "Śrīmālā.
However, because he wishes to expand upon its meaning, he places her above the "True Sons" (Bodhisattvas). Regarding the phrase "this name" and so forth in the Sūtra: Wuming says...
The title "True Sons" originally derives from their following by faith; thus, the text cites this secondary characteristic to conclude the eulogy.
[Commentary] Third, from the passage "Furthermore, these good sons... onwards, it clarifies the subduing of evil persons.
Apart from these good sons and good daughters, all other sentient beings who are stubbornly attached to false teachings regarding the profound dharmas,
who oppose the true Dharma, and who practice the rotten seeds of the non-Buddhist paths,
shall be subdued by the power of kings and the power of devas, nāgas, and spirits.
[Commentary] It is said that Śrīmālā herself was able to subdue them by means of the power of a king and the power of devas and nāgas.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "rotten seeds" and so forth in the Sūtra: Wuming (無名) states that to take what is false for what is correct, claiming it can lead to liberation, is a rotten seed.
By borrowing the power of humans and spirits, one subdues sentient beings and causes them...
Those who enter into faith are likewise the true children of the Buddha.
[Commentary] Fourth, from "At that time, Śrīmālā" onwards, it clarifies the conclusion of the discourse and the paying of homage.
At that time, Śrīmālā, together with her retinue, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.

[Commentary]: Regarding "prostrating at the Buddha's feet" in the sutra, the *Wuming* (Unnaming) states that since the exposition of the meaning has concluded, this is a respectful salutation to receive his instructions.
[Sub-commentary]: The fifth section clarifies the Buddha’s praise, which consists of two parts; the first praises his subduing of evil persons.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! Śrīmālā, you have skillfully guarded and subdued that which is contrary to the Dharma within this profound teaching;
you have attained what is most appropriate.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "attained what is most appropriate" in the sutra, Wuming states: "It does not rely on the power of human or divine spirits to reach the Ultimate Way."
There was no way for [Śrīmālā] to have previously excelled [the Buddha]; she began by stating that she spoke only after receiving his instructions. Now, the Buddha praises her, saying "Excellent!
which may be called a "divine meeting" (shenhui).
[Commentary: The second section, from "You have already drawn near" onwards, praises how her teaching is not merely for the present occasion.
"You have already personally approached hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas and are thus able to expound this meaning.
[Commentary] This "meaning" refers generally to all aspects, including the essence and the object, as well as the practices, vehicles, and persons.

From the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a supreme light" onwards, the third section of the sutra concerns the propagation of the teaching (*saṃprakāśana*). Furthermore, this is divided into three parts.
First, it clarifies that the Tathāgata, desiring to circulate this sutra, returns to the kingdom of Śrāvastī;
second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Jeta Grove" onwards, it correctly clarifies the circulation [of the sutra];
third, from "Then Śakra, Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha" onwards, it enumerates the sixteen names to conclude the title. Regarding the first point, the return to Śrāvastī:
In Śrāvastī there were also two foremost disciples who returned directly by chanting.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a supreme radiance that universally illuminated the bodies of the great assembly;
he ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and, treading through the void, returned to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
[Commentary] Third, the section on the dissemination of the teaching (*pariṇāmanā*). Regarding "emitting supreme radiance" and so forth:

it is said that [the Buddha] comes by responding to the conditions of beings to cleanse the minds of the assembly; thus, it is called "emitting. Because his response is completed and he departs once the ferrying toward awakening has become profound, it is termed "supreme.

Since the Dharma-body is formless and manifests form through its responsive activity, and this manifestation is revealed through the objects [of perception], what dharma is there that is not [thus manifested]?

Is this not a transformation? Therefore, every lifting and placing of the feet is an act of Buddha-work. This is to clarify that the Dharma is fundamentally empty by nature, existing only through causes and conditions;
thus, it first comes from within emptiness. Since it has already come into being, it returns again to non-existence;
therefore, it ascends from the earth back into emptiness. Because one who rides upon emptiness is no different from existence, it is said that he "walks with his feet."
Since he is able to abide in the state where existence and non-existence coexist, and wherein emptiness and non-emptiness are unified, he can transform and guide the two nations,
providing infinite salvation. [Commentary] The second section, from the passage concerning Śrīmālā onwards, clarifies the ritual of offering and escorting.
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā, together with her retinue, joined their palms toward the Buddha; they gazed at him without weariness, never for a moment averting their eyes from his presence.
Once he had passed beyond the range of their vision, they leaped for joy and, each praising the Tathāgata’s complete endowment of merits, they called the Buddha to mind as they returned to the city.
There, they praised the Mahāyāna before King Mitrasamudgata, and the women of the city who were seven years of age or older likewise did so.
The sovereign transformed others through the Mahāyāna; King Yu also transformed all the men through the Mahāyāna.
Those male citizens aged seven and above, as well as all the people of the nation, were led toward the Mahāyāna.
[Commentary: One may also physically leave the city to escort [the Buddha], or one may simply escort him with the mind alone; returning to the city is likewise so.
[Sub-commentary:
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, "The eyes never tire of gazing, not for a moment abandoning [him]," the *Wuming* (無名) states that this refers to leading the conditions while walking.
The profound essence reaches the limits of the mind’s eye as it sees [the Buddha] off; though the form is separated, the spirit remains united.
How is it that this passage of transition is fully endowed with mindfulness? One who possesses complete mindfulness is majestically moved by resonance until they reach the Buddha;

yet the Buddha has no coming in response, and when the journey is finished, one goes to the Buddha without departing. This is called being fully endowed with mindfulness. The sutra praises the King toward his friends, extolling him.

Those of the Mahāyāna maintain that since conditions differ, what is realized must likewise differ; thus, at the assembly of the Śrīmālādevī Sūtra, the companions were said to be near yet not included.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section, which correctly clarifies the propagation of the teaching, it is further divided into four parts. First, clarifying the intent to entrust the teaching.
First, he gathered the assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Jeta Grove and addressed the Elder Ānanda, instructing him to call upon Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Immediately, Śakra, together with his retinue, suddenly arrived and stood before the Buddha.
[Commentary: The second section, from the passage "Then to Śakra, Lord of the Devas" onwards, is the extensive re-exposition of this sutra for the assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded this sutra to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Elder Ānanda.
[Commentary] Third, from "Having finished speaking, he addressed Śakra" onwards, the text is attached to Śakra for its circulation in the heavens.
Having finished speaking, he addressed Śakra, saying: "You should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra.

Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to cultivate the practices for bodhi and practice the six pāramitās for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, and furthermore, if a son of good family..."
"Good son, good woman, listen: the merit of one who hears, receives, reads, recites, and even upholds this sutra scroll is greater than that;

how much more so for one who extensively explains it for others! Therefore, Kausika, you should read and recite this sutra and explain it in detail for the sake of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
[Commentary: Fourth, from "Again he addressed Ānanda" onwards, the text is appended to Ānanda for the purpose of circulating [the teaching] among humanity.
Again he addressed Ānanda: "You, too, shall receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it extensively for the sake of the fourfold assembly."
[Commentary]: Śakra is the Buddha’s donor (*dānapati*) and the constant host for requesting the Dharma; Ānanda is the Buddha’s personal attendant and is also preeminent in his great learning.
For these reasons, the two were entrusted with this matter.
[Commentary]: Regarding the fact that the Sūtra addresses Śakra, it is because Ānanda personally received the Sage’s instructions on every occasion and proclaimed what had not yet been heard;
therefore, he was informed first. Furthermore, Śakra is able to cause the Way to be bestowed upon devas and humans so that it circulates without limit; thus, he was commanded next.
Although his intention was to extend [the teaching] even more widely, he was nonetheless placed at the head as the foremost assistant. Moreover, the principle is profound and difficult to receive.
It is appropriate to limit [the assembly] to the fourfold community as those who shall constantly serve as the primary petitioners for the Dharma; as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"At that time, the various Brahma-kings, the various Śakras, Lords of the Devas, and so forth, requested me to turn the wheel of the Dharma."
[Commentary] Regarding the third section, listing the sixteen names to form the title of the work, there are seven parts.
First, it clarifies the request by Śakra for the name of the sutra. [Sub-commentary] As for requesting the name of the sutra, it is because one wishes to preserve the reality through the name.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named? How should it be upheld?
[Commentary] The second section, from "The Buddha told Śakra" onwards, consists of the Tathāgata’s praise of the merits of the sutra.

[Commentary] Regarding the praise of the merits of this sutra in the scripture: although it is said that "names are used to proclaim virtue," because names are fundamentally based upon reality, the text first speaks of that reality.
The Buddha told Śakra: "This sutra accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merits; all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas [cannot fathom them]."
One cannot thoroughly observe, know, or see it.
[Commentary] The third section, from "Kauśika" onwards, grants permission for the teaching and listening.
Kauśika, you should know that this sutra is profound, subtle, and a great mass of merit; I shall now briefly explain it for you.
"I shall now speak its name; listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
[Commentary] The Sūtra is profound, subtle, and vast; this clarifies that its principles are deep and its virtues are great, such that they are difficult to describe by name.
Although it is categorized into fifteen sections according to their respective meanings, this is still merely a summary. One should contemplate its meaning and harmonize it with its text.
[Commentary:
Fourth, from the time the Lord Śakra, King of Devas, and others received the instruction.
At that time, the Lord Śakra, King of Devas, and the Elder Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your teaching."
[Commentary: Fifth, from the Buddha’s words beginning with "This sutra... and following, the sixteen titles are formally listed to conclude the headings.
The Buddha said: "This sutra praises the Tathāgata’s true, primary-meaning merits; it is thus to be upheld as the inconceivable Great Acceptance (mahāparigraha);
it is thus to be upheld as the Great Vow that encompasses all vows; it is thus to be upheld as the Inconceivable Teaching..."
It is taught that upholding the gathering of the True Dharma is thus upheld; it is taught that entering the One Vehicle is thus upheld;
it is taught that the boundless Noble Truths are thus upheld; it is taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is thus upheld; it is taught that the Dharmakāya is thus upheld;
it is taught that the meaning of emptiness as the concealment of the Real is thus upheld; it is taught that the Single Truth is thus upheld.
It is to be upheld as eternally abiding, secure, and the sole refuge; it is to be upheld as the teaching on the subversion of reality;
it is to be upheld as the teaching on the obscuration of the intrinsically pure mind; it is to be upheld as the teaching on the true sons of the Tathāgata;
it is to be upheld as the Lion’s Roar of Queen Śrīmālā. Furthermore, Kauśika, regarding this sutra...
It is said that this [sūtra] severs all doubts, establishes the definitive meaning, and leads one into the path of the One Vehicle.
[Commentary: Now, since this sūtra takes the preceding fourteen chapters as its main body, its names should likewise number fourteen;
yet in the present listing, they are doubled to make sixteen. The first name is *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda*.

Thus one should uphold these two names. Furthermore, Kauśika, this sūtra expounds the severance of all doubts, the definitive meaning, and entry into the path of the Single Vehicle; yet these two names possess no separate essence.
The former name merely uses a person's name as a general designation for the single teaching it expounds, while the latter name likewise takes its [meaning] collectively.

The principle explained herein refers to this sutra; however, these fourteen chapters each have distinct names and essences, and thus it is not appropriate to take [a single chapter title] as the heading for the entire volume.

Therefore, these two names are raised to serve as the primary title. The sutra title says "Śrīmālā’s Lion’s Roar," which cites the fifteenth name, while "The Great Vaipulya of the One Vehicle’s Great Expedient Means" is cited [as the second].
The sixteenth title.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "indicating the one teaching and so forth that he expounded": the first [of the two preceding titles] cites the person, while the latter two cite the Dharma;
these person and Dharma together constitute the title. Here, the person is the speaker and the Dharma is that which is spoken; this thus encompasses all fourteen [titles].

This chapter summarizes and encompasses the specific principles without exception; as for the remaining fourteen chapters, each has a different name and a different substance (body) beneath that name.
Since both names and substances are fully present, it is not appropriate to select only a single name as the title.
[Commentary]: The sixth section, from "Kauśika, by means of this teaching" onwards, is a further exhortation for the circulation [of the text].
It says: "Kauśika, by means of this teaching, I entrust the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* to you, so that it may endure until the end of the Dharma;
you should uphold, recite, and explain it in detail."
[Commentary]: Regarding "one who upholds the sūtra," it means respectfully receiving [the teaching] as what has been received and maintaining it without falsehood.

As for the phrase "the sūtra, up to the abiding of the Dharma, being upheld," if one speaks in terms of names, Ānanda remains constantly by the Buddha's side; if one explains it in terms of lifespan, his life is exceedingly long.
Therefore, both cases take the abiding of the Dharma as their limit.
[Commentary: The seventh section, from "Śakra addressed the Buddha" onwards, concerns receiving and practicing the instructions.

When Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Excellent, World-Honored One! I receive the Honored One’s teaching upon my head," at that time, the Elder Śakra, the Deva King, along with Ānanda and the great assembly of devas, asuras, gandharvas, and others, rejoiced upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken.
"Carry out. [Commentary]:
Regarding "seven times receiving the imperial decree," the *Wuming* (無名) states: "Ānanda secretly received the holy decree, while Śakra openly accepted the venerable instruction."
Private Commentary on the Meaning of the Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra, Volume Six (End).
Respectfully sent: one volume of the *Śrīmālā-śāstra-ṭīkā*.
This aforementioned commentary was composed by a High Monk of the Great Tang and is a secret manual for the eyes of the Japanese realm. Recorded in the [Year] of the Zhenyuan era.
Observing the course of the thirteen years, although I requested [a copy] from our own court, it was regrettable that I could only find it at an abandoned tomb.
It is lamentable that the noble aspirations of the former sages have been forgotten, and pitiable that we have lost the mirror for the discernment of future generations.

Relying on this, I have transcribed one volume by the window, hoping forever that it may be transmitted and spread. I humbly pray that the sacred spirit of the Upper Palace Prince (Jōgū-ō) will look upon this from the East.
He was the ancestral patriarch of the corner of the Buddha-Dharma; Hōryū-ji, this monastery of learning, was the profound imperial vow of the Crown Prince.
Who among those who can discern cause and effect would forget the great grace of the Imperial Prince?
Those who aspire to repay his kindness must revere the people of Hōryū-ji. I, Gishō, have humbly preserved these commentaries for posterity at this temple.
My family’s prosperity has flourished once more; through diligent study during both summer and winter, I have had this commentary transcribed to be enshrined in that temple.

Furthermore, I have commissioned another copy to be written out and sent there permanently, solely to express my boundless gratitude for the holy spirit’s infinite grace and to serve as a resource for study and contemplation within the temple. Such is the intent of my sincere heart.
On the eighteenth day of the third month of the eighth year of Kenchō, the head monk of the Saṃgha at Saidai-ji, Eison, records this:
This commentary was obtained when the Great Master Jikaku, the presiding abbot of Enryaku-ji, was sent as an envoy to Tang China in the fifth year of Jōwa.
Having fortunately reached Yangzhou, he was able to inquire for and obtain this exegesis and commentary due to the karmic conditions planted in previous lives; it was then transcribed and sent back.
The draft was returned to Enryaku-ji and stored there; its author was the Great Master of Nangaku, the latter incarnation of Prince Shōtoku.
Furthermore, the abridgment was made by Zōyū, a disciple of the Sixth Patriarch of Tiantai, Miaole. This union of the Way between teacher and grandson is of supreme glory.
That our Master obtained it and transmitted it to this land may be called the firm establishment of the Dharma; he provisionally revealed the sequence of transmission to save through the teaching.
Those who study these teachings must have profound faith and reverence for them.
Recorded respectfully by the śramaṇa Enchin, who entered Tang China, on the eighteenth day of the twelfth month in the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
